docs.title: AdaptiveML: Adaptive, Robust, Resource-Efficient Learning
docs.text:
AdaptiveML (aml-core) is an open-source Python machine learning algorithm library designed for robust, continuous, and resource-efficient learning under real-world operational constraints:

  1. Changing Data Distributions: Continuous statistical shifts, abrupt and gradual concept drift, and recurring operational distributions.
  2. Imperfect and Noisy Feedback: Mislabeled instances, asymmetric noise transitions, delayed ground-truth arrival, and severe class imbalance.
  3. Resource and Compute Constraints: Memory-constrained edge devices, CPU-only servers, and low-latency microservice latency budgets (\(<1\text{ ms}\)).

AdaptiveML complements existing ML frameworks (such as NumPy, Scikit-Learn, and PyTorch)—it does not replace them.

docs.title: The Five Algorithmic Pillars
docs.text:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        Unified Learning Controller (ULC-v5)                       |
|        Utility-Calibrated Cross-Pillar Coordination & Anti-Thrashing Backoff      |
+-----------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
                                          |
        +---------------------------------+---------------------------------+
        |                                 |                                 |
        v                                 v                                 v
+-------------------------------+ +-------------------------------+ +-------------------------------+
| Adaptive Learning (ALA 3.0)   | | Robust Learning (RLA 3.0)     | | Resource Optimization (RAO 2.0|
| Fast Hoeffding Tree Induction | | Multi-Signal Reliability      | | Vectorized 8-Bit AdamW        |
| Reliability-Weighted ADWIN    | | Asymmetric Transition Defense | | Selective Quantization (>71%) |
| Recurring Concept Memory      | | Dynamic Noise Filtering       | | Atomic Resilient Checkpoints  |
+-------------------------------+ +-------------------------------+ +-------------------------------+
                                          |
                                          v
                        +-----------------------------------+
                        | Adaptive Minority Intelligence    |
                        | Online Beta-Binomial Prior Tracker|
                        | Dynamic False-Positive Budgets    |
                        +-----------------------------------+
  • ALA (Adaptive Learning Algorithms): Streaming prequential classification with bounded Hoeffding Tree induction, statistical drift detection (ADWIN), and recurring concept snapshot memory.
  • RLA (Robust Learning Algorithms): Multi-signal sample reliability estimation combining prediction margins, spatial \(k\)-NN consistency, and temporal stability to insulate learners against noisy feedback.
  • Adaptive Minority Intelligence: Online Beta-Binomial prior tracking and dynamic false-positive budget thresholding for severe class imbalance (\(<1\%\) minority).
  • RAO (Resource-Aware Optimization): CPU-first block-quantized optimizer (VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW) achieving \(>71\%\) optimizer state RAM savings without C++ extensions or CUDA dependencies.
  • ULC (Unified Learning Controller): Hierarchical five-tier intervention arbitration (NOOP, Parameter Damping, Concept Restoration, Soft Replay Reset, Hard Reset) governed by calibrated expected utility scoring.

docs.title: Key Product Principles
docs.text:
• Local-First & CPU-First: Executes efficiently on standard CPUs (\(5\ \mu\text{s}\) inference, \(>23,000\text{ samples/sec}\) streaming throughput). No GPUs or cloud services required.
  • Modular & Decoupled: Core algorithms require strictly numpy>=1.24.0. PyTorch, Scikit-Learn, and Pandas are purely optional extras.
  • Lightweight Footprint: Sub-\(110\text{ ms}\) cold import latency, \(<37\text{ MB}\) resident memory, and strict \(O(1)\) memory consumption (\(<50\text{ MB}\) across \(100,000+\) streaming samples).
  • Secure by Default: Absolute zero-pickle architecture; state persistence utilizes binary SafeTensors with HMAC-SHA256 constant-time verification.
  • Zero Unprompted Telemetry: Emits zero network traffic. Diagnostics use bounded in-memory ring buffers and standard Python logging with NullHandler.

docs.title: 30-Second Quickstart
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml import AdaptiveClassifier, ReliabilityWeightedADWIN

# Initialize streaming adaptive classifier and drift detector
clf = AdaptiveClassifier(n_features=4, n_classes=2)
detector = ReliabilityWeightedADWIN(delta=0.002)

# Stream incoming data prequentially
X_stream = np.random.randn(100, 4)
y_stream = (X_stream[:, 0] + X_stream[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)

for i in range(len(X_stream)):
    x_i, y_i = X_stream[i : i + 1], y_stream[i : i + 1]

    # 1. Predict before learning (Prequential Evaluation)
    prob = clf.predict_proba(x_i)
    pred = int(np.argmax(prob))

    # 2. Track prediction error in drift detector
    is_error = float(pred != y_i[0])
    if detector.update(is_error):
        print(f"Concept drift detected at sample {i}!")

    # 3. Incrementally update classifier weights
    clf.partial_fit(x_i, y_i)

docs.title: What is AdaptiveML?
docs.text: AdaptiveML (aml-core) is an open-source Python machine-learning library dedicated to adaptive, robust, and resource-efficient learning. It solves the challenges of non-stationary streams: concept drift, noisy/flipped labels, extreme class imbalance, and strict hardware memory bounds.

docs.title: Does AdaptiveML replace PyTorch or Scikit-Learn?
docs.text: No. AdaptiveML is an algorithmic complement, not a framework replacement. It provides native estimator adapters for Scikit-Learn pipelines (SklearnAdaptiveClassifier), robust autograd losses and 8-bit optimizers for PyTorch (VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW), and high-speed array bridges for Pandas and Polars.

docs.title: Can AdaptiveML run on GPUs?
docs.text: AdaptiveML is engineered CPU-first and local-first. While PyTorch integrations can optimize GPU-resident tensors, all core streaming decision trees, drift detectors, prior trackers, and quantizers run with maximum throughput on standard multi-core CPUs without requiring CUDA or GPU hardware.

docs.title: What are the "Five Pillars" of AdaptiveML?
docs.text:
1. ALA (Adaptive Learning Algorithms): Streaming Hoeffding tree induction, Reliability-Weighted ADWIN drift detection, and Recurring Concept Memory.
  2. RLA (Robust Learning Algorithms): Multi-signal sample reliability scoring (\(r_i\)), asymmetric transition detection, and noise-tolerant losses (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{SCE}}, \mathcal{L}_{\text{GCE}}\)).
  3. Minority Intelligence: Online Beta-Binomial Bayesian prior tracking, sublinear cost scaling, and dynamic PID false-positive budget thresholding.
  4. RAO (Resource-Aware Optimization): 8-bit dynamic block-quantized AdamW achieving \(>73\%\) state RAM reduction and dynamic batch budget management.
  5. ULC (Unified Learning Controller): Master multi-tier arbitration automaton evaluating expected utility \(U = \text{Confidence} \times \text{Benefit} - \text{Cost}\) to disambiguate drift from noise.

docs.title: How does AdaptiveML handle recurring concept drift?
docs.text: Unlike traditional streaming libraries that blindly reset the model whenever a drift is detected, ALA 3.0 computes a statistical concept fingerprint. When a recurring regime returns (e.g. seasonal demand), it restores the historical tree snapshot from RecurringConceptMemory, avoiding the transient accuracy penalty of re-learning.

docs.title: How does AdaptiveML avoid catastrophic forgetting under label noise?
docs.text: Under sudden noise bursts (e.g., sensor glitched and inverted labels), standard drift detectors falsely perceive a concept shift and destroy good model weights. The ULC-v5 controller uses Spatial Discordance Gating (\(\mathcal{D}_s\)) to verify whether prediction errors are topologically localized (true drift) or scattered/incoherent (noise burst), triggering sample abstention rather than model reset.

docs.title: How does LowMemoryAdamW achieve \(>73\%\) RAM reduction?
docs.text: Standard AdamW maintains two 32-bit float moments (\(m_t, v_t\)) per parameter, requiring 8 bytes per parameter. LowMemoryAdamW dynamically quantizes momentum into signed 8-bit integers (int8) and variance into unsigned 8-bit integers (uint8), grouped into small blocks of 64 or 256 parameters with per-block float32 scale factors.

docs.title: Is dynamic block quantization lossy?
docs.text: While 8-bit quantization is numerically lossy, dynamic per-block scale normalization bounds quantization error. On standard deep learning benchmarks, models trained with LowMemoryAdamW achieve convergence accuracy identical to full 32-bit AdamW within standard seed variance.

docs.title: Why is Python's pickle banned in AdaptiveML?
docs.text: Python's standard pickle deserialization executes arbitrary code bytecodes, creating severe remote code execution vulnerabilities (CWE-502) when loading weights from shared or untrusted storage. AdaptiveML exclusively uses the HuggingFace SafeTensors format: raw binary arrays indexed by immutable JSON headers.

docs.title: Can checkpoints be tampered with?
docs.text: Not when using auth_key. AdaptiveML allows providing a 32-byte secret key during save_state and load_state. The system verifies an HMAC-SHA256 signature in constant time (hmac.compare_digest). Any byte alteration triggers an immediate SerializationError.

docs.title: Does AdaptiveML log or transmit user data?
docs.text: Never. AdaptiveML maintains a strict zero-PII policy. Telemetry logs only aggregate mathematical scalars (loss, latency, accuracy, step counts). Furthermore, AdaptiveML makes zero outbound network connections; it is \(100\%\) air-gapped and offline ready.

docs.title: Why is the package named aml-core instead of adaptiveml on PyPI?
docs.text: To prevent namespace collision and trademark dilution with commercial entities bearing similar names (Adaptive ML, Inc.), the provisional distribution identifier is set to aml-core. The Python import namespace remains adaptive_ml (import adaptive_ml as aml). DEF-004 tracks this governance item.

docs.title: What license applies to AdaptiveML?
docs.text: AdaptiveML is licensed under the permissive Apache License, Version 2.0.

docs.title: ALA 3.0: Algorithm Design & Mathematical Formulation
docs.text: ALA 3.0 integrates tree-based online induction, dynamic windowing, and recurring concept matching into a closed-loop streaming learner (ALA30AdaptiveLearner).

docs.title: 1. Hoeffding Tree Induction Mechanics
docs.text:
At any leaf node \(l\) in the streaming decision tree, the learner observes streaming attributes \(X\) and labels \(y\). After observing a grace_period of \(n\) samples, the leaf evaluates the information gain \(G(X_i)\) for each candidate split attribute \(X_i\).

Let \(X_a\) and \(X_b\) be the attributes with the highest and second-highest information gain. The difference is: $\(\Delta G = G(X_a) - G(X_b)\)$

The Hoeffding Bound states that with probability \(1 - \delta\), the true mean difference is at least \(\Delta G - \epsilon\), where: $\(\epsilon = \sqrt{\frac{R^2 \ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}\)$ (\(R = \ln(K)\) for information gain with \(K\) classes).

  • If \(\Delta G > \epsilon\), the leaf node splits on attribute \(X_a\) with statistical confidence \(1 - \delta\).
  • If \(\Delta G \le \epsilon\) and \(\epsilon < \tau_{\text{tie}}\), a tie is declared and the node splits on \(X_a\).

docs.title: 2. Statistical Concept Fingerprinting
docs.text:
To detect recurring concepts, ConceptFingerprinter calculates a compact statistical representation of an observed data batch:

$\(\text{FP} = \left[ \mu, \sigma^2, \pi \right]\)$ where: - \(\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d\): Feature centroid vector. - \(\sigma^2 \in \mathbb{R}^d\): Feature variance vector. - \(\pi \in \mathbb{R}^K\): Empirical class prior distribution.

docs.title: Similarity Function
docs.text:
Similarity between an active fingerprint \(\text{FP}_{\text{active}}\) and a stored historical fingerprint \(\text{FP}_{\text{stored}}\) is computed via normalized Gaussian kernel distance:

\[D = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^d \frac{|\mu_{\text{active}, i} - \mu_{\text{stored}, i}|}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\text{active}, i}^2 + \sigma_{\text{stored}, i}^2 + \epsilon}}$$ $$\text{Sim} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} D^2\right) \in [0, 1]\]

When \(\text{Sim} \ge \tau_{\text{sim}}\) (default 0.75-0.82), a recurring concept is declared.

docs.title: ALA 3.0: Configuration Reference
docs.text: This guide documents the configuration parameters for ALA30AdaptiveLearner and AdaptiveClassifier.

docs.title: ALA30AdaptiveLearner Parameters
docs.text:
from adaptive_ml.ala import ALA30AdaptiveLearner

learner = ALA30AdaptiveLearner(
    n_features=10,
    n_classes=2,
    grace_period=20,
    delta=0.002,
    similarity_threshold=0.75,
    max_concepts=10,
    replay_capacity=2000,
    cooldown_steps=5,
)
Parameter Type Default Description n_features int Required Dimensionality of input feature vectors (\(d \ge 1\)). n_classes int 2 Number of distinct target classes (\(K \ge 2\)). grace_period int 20 Samples observed by a leaf node between split evaluation attempts. delta float 0.002 Hoeffding bound and ADWIN statistical confidence parameter (\(0 < \delta < 1\)). similarity_threshold float 0.75 Minimum Gaussian similarity required to declare a recurring concept match. max_concepts int 10 Maximum historical concept snapshots retained in memory. replay_capacity int 2000 Maximum instances retained in the class-balanced reservoir replay buffer. cooldown_steps int 5 Minimum steps between consecutive drift interventions to prevent thrashing.

docs.title: Tuning Recommendations
docs.text:
• Rapidly Drifting Environments: Reduce grace_period (e.g. 10) and increase delta (e.g. 0.01) to split trees and trigger drift checks faster.
  • Noisy Streaming Environments: Increase grace_period (e.g. 50) and decrease delta (e.g. 0.001) to prevent noise bursts from splitting nodes prematurely.
  • Memory-Constrained Edge Deployments: Reduce replay_capacity (e.g. 500) and max_concepts (e.g. 3) to keep resident memory strictly sub-\(30\text{ MB}\).

docs.title: ALA 3.0 Code Examples
docs.text: This page provides runnable code examples demonstrating ALA 3.0 in common streaming scenarios.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Streaming Classification
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import ALA30AdaptiveLearner

# Initialize learner
learner = ALA30AdaptiveLearner(n_features=4, n_classes=2, grace_period=10)

# Generate streaming samples
np.random.seed(42)
X = np.random.randn(100, 4)
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)

# Stream processing loop
for i in range(100):
    x_i = X[i : i + 1]
    y_i = y[i : i + 1]

    # Predict before update
    prob = learner.predict_proba(x_i)
    pred = int(np.argmax(prob))

    # Incremental update
    learner.partial_fit(x_i, y_i)

print(f"Learner completed {learner.total_steps} streaming steps.")

docs.title: Example 2: Handling Recurring Concept Drift
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import ALA30AdaptiveLearner

np.random.seed(123)
learner = ALA30AdaptiveLearner(
    n_features=3,
    n_classes=2,
    grace_period=10,
    similarity_threshold=0.75,
)

# Concept A: feature 0 dominant
X_A = np.random.randn(80, 3) + np.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0])
y_A = (X_A[:, 0] > 2.0).astype(int)

# Concept B: feature 1 dominant
X_B = np.random.randn(80, 3) + np.array([0.0, 3.0, 0.0])
y_B = (X_B[:, 1] > 3.0).astype(int)

# Stream sequence: Concept A -> Concept B -> Concept A returns
stream_X = np.vstack([X_A, X_B, X_A])
stream_y = np.concatenate([y_A, y_B, y_A])

for i in range(len(stream_X)):
    learner.partial_fit(stream_X[i : i + 1], stream_y[i : i + 1])

print(f"Total steps: {learner.total_steps}")
print(f"Drift resets executed: {learner.drift_resets}")
print(f"Recurring restorations: {learner.recurring_restorations}")

docs.title: ALA 3.0: Known Limitations & Failure Modes
docs.text: Understanding when an algorithm should not be applied is critical for production reliability.

docs.title: 1. High-Dimensional Sparse Text/Embeddings
docs.text:
• Behavior: Hoeffding Trees evaluate information gain split candidates across continuous feature dimensions. When feature dimensionality exceeds several hundred sparse dimensions (\(d > 500\), such as TF-IDF or large embedding bags), tree leaf statistical split computations slow down.
  • Recommendation: Apply dimensionality reduction (PCA, TruncatedSVD) or use linear SGD classifiers (SGDClassifier) before ingesting into AdaptiveClassifier.

docs.title: 2. Extremely Low Grace Periods Under High Noise
docs.text:
• Behavior: Setting grace_period < 5 in high-variance or noisy streams causes leaf nodes to attempt split evaluations before sufficient sample statistics are accumulated. This leads to sub-optimal, noisy splits that degrade tree depth efficiency.
  • Recommendation: Set grace_period >= 20 for noisy streams to ensure statistical stability.

docs.title: 3. Delayed Label Streams
docs.text:
• Behavior: If true labels \(y_t\) arrive with significant delay (\(\Delta t \gg 100\) steps), prequential evaluation cannot immediately confirm drift.
  • Recommendation: Use DelayedLabelQueue (adaptive_ml.ala.delayed_labels) to buffer unlabelled predictions and match them asynchronously when feedback arrives.

docs.title: ALA 3.0: Adaptive Learning Algorithms Overview
docs.text: ALA (Adaptive Learning Algorithms) provides continuous, online streaming classification algorithms capable of learning incrementally from infinite data streams while dynamically detecting and adapting to concept drift.

docs.title: 1. Key Capabilities
docs.text:
• Streaming Hoeffding Trees (AdaptiveClassifier): Incremental decision tree induction that splits nodes based on mathematically proven statistical confidence bounds without retraining from scratch.
  • Statistical Drift Detection (ReliabilityWeightedADWIN): Adaptive windowing that dynamically sizes its window based on variance changes, detecting distribution shifts with bounded false positive rates.
  • Recurring Concept Retention (RecurringConceptMemory): Extracts statistical concept fingerprints (centroids, feature variances, class priors) and restores historical model checkpoints upon recurring distribution shifts.
  • Class-Stratified Replay (ClassBalancedReservoirReplay): Bounded memory buffer guaranteeing proportional retention across rare and frequent classes regardless of arrival sequence.

docs.title: 2. When to Use ALA
docs.text:
• Data arrives sequentially in unbounded data streams (e.g. sensor telemetry, clickstreams, log events).
  • The underlying relationships between features and target labels shift over time.
  • Periodic or seasonal operational patterns repeat (e.g. daily, weekly, or market cycles).
  • Compute and memory are constrained, precluding periodic batch retraining from scratch.

docs.title: Recurring Concept Memory & Fingerprinting
docs.text: RecurringConceptMemory manages a bounded repository of historical model snapshots and statistical concept signatures.

docs.title: 1. Lifecycle of a Concept Snapshot
docs.text:
1. Active Stream Processing
   [ Input Batch (X, y) ] ---> Compute ConceptFingerprint(X, y)
                                           |
2. Drift Triggered (ADWIN Alert)           |
   Query RecurringConceptMemory <----------+
            |
    +-------+-------+
    |               |
    v (Match found: Sim >= tau)   v (No match: Novel drift)
Restore Historical Snapshot       Save Current Concept Snapshot
Update Concept Metadata           Reset Active Tree (Seed from Replay)
Zero Retraining Overhead          Learn New Distribution

docs.title: 2. Using RecurringConceptMemory Programmatically
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import RecurringConceptMemory, ConceptFingerprinter, AdaptiveClassifier

# Initialize components
memory = RecurringConceptMemory(max_concepts=5, similarity_threshold=0.80)
fingerprinter = ConceptFingerprinter(n_features=4, n_classes=2)
model = AdaptiveClassifier(n_features=4, n_classes=2)

# Simulate a learned concept
X_concept_A = np.random.randn(50, 4) + 2.0
y_concept_A = (X_concept_A[:, 0] > 0).astype(int)
model.partial_fit(X_concept_A, y_concept_A)

# 1. Store concept snapshot
fp_A = fingerprinter.compute_fingerprint(X_concept_A, y_concept_A)
snap = memory.store_concept(fingerprint=fp_A, model_state=model, step=50)
print(f"Stored Concept: {snap.concept_id}")

# 2. Query recurring concept memory with candidate stream data
X_candidate = np.random.randn(50, 4) + 1.9  # Similar distribution
y_candidate = (X_candidate[:, 0] > 0).astype(int)
fp_candidate = fingerprinter.compute_fingerprint(X_candidate, y_candidate)

matching_snap, similarity = memory.find_matching_concept(fp_candidate)
if matching_snap is not None:
    print(f"Recurring concept recognized: {matching_snap.concept_id} (Similarity: {similarity:.3f})")
    # Restore model state instantaneously
    restored_model = matching_snap.model_state

docs.title: 3. Eviction & Memory Boundedness
docs.text: When the number of stored concepts exceeds max_concepts, RecurringConceptMemory automatically evicts the oldest / least-recently-matched concept. This guarantees strict \(O(1)\) memory complexity regardless of how many concepts occur over time.

docs.title: Minority Intelligence: Algorithm Design & Mathematical Formulation
docs.text: Adaptive Minority Intelligence 2.0 addresses extreme class imbalance through Bayesian prior modeling, sublinear loss weighting, and feedback control.

docs.title: 1. Beta-Binomial Conjugate Prior Tracking
docs.text:
Let minority arrivals be modeled as a Bernoulli process with unknown parameter \(\pi \in (0, 1)\). Using a conjugate \(\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)\) prior with exponential discount factor \(\gamma \in (0, 1)\):

\[\alpha_{t} = \gamma \alpha_{t-1} + y_t$$ $$\beta_{t} = \gamma \beta_{t-1} + (1 - y_t)\]

The posterior mean estimate of the streaming class prior is: $\(\hat{\pi}_t = \frac{\alpha_t}{\alpha_t + \beta_t}\)$

By choosing default hyper-priors \(\alpha_0 = 1.0, \beta_0 = 100.0\), the tracker initializes with an uninformative prior centered around \(1\%\), adapting smoothly as samples arrive.

docs.title: 2. Sublinear Cost Scaling
docs.text:
Linear inverse frequency weighting (\(w_1 = 1 / \pi\)) leads to severe gradient variance spikes when \(\pi \to 0\) (e.g. \(w_1 = 1,000\) when \(\pi = 0.001\)), destabilizing gradient updates.

AdaptiveML employs sublinear cost power scaling: $\(w_1 = \left(\frac{1}{\hat{\pi}_t}\right)^\alpha, \quad \alpha \in (0, 1) \quad (\text{default: } \alpha = 0.52)\)$

When \(\pi = 0.001\), sublinear scaling provides a bounded, stable penalty multiplier (\(w_1 \approx 36.3\)) rather than \(1,000\), ensuring stable optimization.

docs.title: 3. Dynamic PID Threshold Regulation
docs.text:
To maintain a target false-positive budget (e.g., \(E_{\text{target}} = 1.5\) false alarms per 1,000 samples), the classification threshold \(\theta_t\) is dynamically regulated via a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) control loop:

\[e_t = \text{FPR}_t - \text{FPR}_{\text{target}}$$ $$\Delta \theta_t = K_p e_t + K_i \int e_t \, dt + K_d \frac{de_t}{dt}$$ $$\theta_{t+1} = \text{clip}\left(\theta_t + \Delta \theta_t, \theta_{\text{min}}, \theta_{\text{max}}\right)\]
  • Proportional term (\(K_p\)): Corrects immediate spikes in false positives.
  • Integral term (\(K_i\)): Eliminates steady-state budget drift. Anti-windup clamping prevents integral saturation.
  • Derivative term (\(K_d\)): Dampens threshold oscillation.
  • Deadband (\(\tau_{\text{db}}\)): Ignores micro-fluctuations \(|e_t| < \tau_{\text{db}}\) to preserve decision stability.

docs.title: Minority Intelligence: Configuration Reference
docs.text: This guide details configuration parameters for MinorityIntelligence20Learner, BetaBinomialPriorTracker, and DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager.

docs.title: MinorityIntelligence20Learner Parameters
docs.text:
from adaptive_ml.minority import MinorityIntelligence20Learner

learner = MinorityIntelligence20Learner(
    target_fp_budget_per_1k=1.5,
    sublinear_cost_power=0.52,
    base_threshold=0.50,
    min_threshold=0.15,
    max_threshold=0.85,
    lr=0.01,
    minority_class=1,
    random_state=42,
)
Parameter Type Default Description target_fp_budget_per_1k float 1.5 Target allowable false alarms per 1,000 negative samples. sublinear_cost_power float 0.52 Exponent \(\alpha\) in sublinear cost scaling \(w_1 = (1/\pi)^\alpha\). base_threshold float 0.50 Initial classification decision threshold. min_threshold float 0.15 Lower boundary clamp on decision threshold. max_threshold float 0.85 Upper boundary clamp on decision threshold. lr float 0.01 Online learning rate for parameter updates. minority_class int 1 Target class index corresponding to the rare minority class. random_state Optional[int] 42 Seed for reproducible initialization.

docs.title: DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager Parameters
docs.text:
from adaptive_ml.minority import DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager

manager = DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager(
    target_fp_budget_per_1k=1.5,
    base_threshold=0.5,
    kp=0.5,
    ki=0.05,
    kd=0.02,
    min_threshold=0.15,
    max_threshold=0.85,

Parameter Type Default Description kp float 0.5 Proportional PID gain. ki float 0.05 Integral PID gain. kd float 0.02 Derivative PID gain. anti_windup_max float 0.2 Maximum allowable accumulator for the integral term. deadband float 0.0002 Error magnitude threshold below which PID updates are zeroed.

docs.title: Minority Intelligence 2.0 Code Examples
docs.text: This page demonstrates using Adaptive Minority Intelligence 2.0 on an imbalanced streaming classification task (\(0.5\%\) minority class).

docs.title: Example 1: Imbalanced Streaming Classification
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.minority import MinorityIntelligence20Learner

# Set random seed for reproducibility
np.random.seed(42)
n_samples = 1000
n_features = 4

# Generate highly imbalanced stream (99.5% negative, 0.5% positive)
X = np.random.randn(n_samples, n_features)
y = np.zeros(n_samples, dtype=int)
# 5 minority events out of 1,000 samples
minority_indices = [50, 220, 480, 710, 930]
for idx in minority_indices:
    X[idx] += np.array([2.5, 2.5, 0.0, 0.0])  # Shift feature distribution
    y[idx] = 1

# Initialize learner with 2.0 false positive budget per 1,000 samples
learner = MinorityIntelligence20Learner(
    target_fp_budget_per_1k=2.0,
    sublinear_cost_power=0.52,
    lr=0.02,
    random_state=42,
)

# Stream processing loop
batch_size = 50
for start in range(0, n_samples, batch_size):
    end = start + batch_size
    X_b = X[start:end]
    y_b = y[start:end]

    # Fit micro-batch
    learner.partial_fit(X_b, y_b)

# Final evaluation
predictions = learner.predict(X)
detected_minority = np.where((predictions == 1) & (y == 1))[0]
false_alarms = np.where((predictions == 1) & (y == 0))[0]

print("--------------------------------------------------")
print(f"Total Stream Samples:    {n_samples}")
print(f"True Minority Count:     {len(minority_indices)}")
print(f"Minority Events Caught:  {len(detected_minority)} / {len(minority_indices)}")
print(f"False Positives Triggered: {len(false_alarms)}")
print(f"Operational Threshold:   {learner.threshold_manager.current_threshold:.3f}")
print("Minority streaming demonstration complete!")

docs.title: Minority Intelligence: Known Limitations & Failure Modes
1. Zero-Variance or Overlapping Features
docs.text:
• Behavior: If the rare minority class shares identical feature distributions with the majority class (e.g. zero distinct signal in \(X\)), no threshold adjustment can separate them.
  • Consequence: Sublinear cost weighting will elevate gradient penalties without improving separation, causing false positives to consume the entire budget.
  • Guidance: Ensure feature engineering captures discriminatory signals prior to streaming ingestion.

docs.title: 2. Multi-Class Minority Distributions (\(K > 2\))
docs.text:
• Behavior: MinorityIntelligence20Learner is optimized for binary imbalanced streams (majority class 0 vs. rare target class 1).
  • Consequence: For multi-class imbalanced problems with multiple rare classes, prior tracking requires one-vs-rest binary decompositions.

docs.title: 3. Burn-in Sample Latency
docs.text:
• Behavior: The Beta-Binomial prior tracker requires observing a modest sequence of events (at least 50-100 samples) before its posterior mean converges from its hyper-prior (\(\alpha_0=1.0, \beta_0=100.0\)).
  • Mitigation: Pre-initialize alpha_prior and beta_prior with domain historical estimates where available.

docs.title: Adaptive Minority Intelligence 2.0 Overview
docs.text: Adaptive Minority Intelligence provides specialized algorithmic machinery designed for extreme streaming class imbalance, where critical target instances represent \(<1\%\) (or \(<0.1\%\)) of the data stream.

docs.title: 1. Key Capabilities
docs.text:
• Beta-Binomial Bayesian Prior Tracking (BetaBinomialPriorTracker): Continually updates an empirical estimate of the active minority arrival rate \(\hat{\pi}_t \in (0, 1)\) without requiring stationary batch windows.
  • Dynamic PID False-Positive Budget Regulation (DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager): Continuously tunes the operational classification threshold \(\theta_t\) using a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) feedback loop to satisfy strict false positive quotas (e.g. \(\le 1.5\) false positives per 1,000 transactions).
  • Sublinear Cost Weighting: Dynamically scales minority gradient penalties with a calibrated sublinear exponent \(\hat{\pi}_t^{-\alpha}\) (\(\alpha \approx 0.52\)), preventing loss saturation while maintaining sharp discrimination boundaries.
  • Turnkey Integration (MinorityIntelligence20Learner): Encapsulates prior tracking, cost-weighted learning, and dynamic threshold regulation into a single Scikit-Learn compatible estimator.

docs.title: 2. When to Use Minority Intelligence
docs.text:
• The positive/critical class represents a tiny fraction of incoming events (e.g. fraud, network intrusion, rare medical anomalies).
  • Overall accuracy is misleading or useless because a trivial negative classifier achieves \(>99\%\) accuracy.
  • Operational human review capacity imposes a strict ceiling on allowable false alarms.
  • Class distribution shifts over time (e.g. fraud waves or attacks that surge and abate).

docs.title: Dynamic Threshold Management & PID Control
docs.text: Standard classification fixes the decision threshold at \(\theta = 0.50\). Under severe class imbalance, this static choice almost guarantees failure: - If \(\theta = 0.50\) is too high, minority recall collapses to \(0\%\). - If \(\theta = 0.50\) is arbitrarily lowered (e.g. to \(0.10\)), false positive alarms surge, overwhelming downstream human fraud review teams.

docs.title: 1. The PID Regulating Mechanism
docs.text:
DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager treats false positive rate control as an industrial feedback regulation problem:

[ Error Signal: e_t = Measured_FPR - Budget_FPR ]
                      |
                      v
      +-------------------------------+
      |  PID Controller Calculation   |
      |  Delta = Kp*e + Ki*Int + Kd*D |
      +-------------------------------+
                      |
                      v
       [ Adjusted Threshold theta_t ]
                      |
                      v
      [ Stream Decision: y_hat = P(y=1) > theta_t ]

docs.title: Response Characteristics
docs.text:
• When FPR Spikes Above Budget: Error \(e_t > 0 \implies \Delta \theta > 0\). The threshold slides upward, suppressing false alarms and returning FPR to budget.
  • When FPR Drops Far Below Budget: Error \(e_t < 0 \implies \Delta \theta < 0\). The threshold slides downward, safely recovering additional minority recall without violating the budget ceiling.
  • Deadband Protection: Prevents jitter from individual random negative samples.

docs.title: 2. Threshold Calibration Code Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.minority import DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager

# Target budget: 2.0 false positives per 1,000 samples (FPR = 0.002)
manager = DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager(target_fp_budget_per_1k=2.0)

print(f"Initial Threshold: {manager.current_threshold:.3f}")

# Simulate a sudden surge in false positives
for step in range(10):
    # False positive rate spikes to 0.010 (5x budget!)
    manager.update(current_fpr=0.010)

print(f"Adjusted Threshold after FP surge: {manager.current_threshold:.3f}")
assert manager.current_threshold > 0.50  # Threshold raised to protect budget!

docs.title: RAO 2.0: Algorithm Design & Mathematical Formulation
docs.text: RAO 2.0 replaces standard 32-bit optimizer state representation with dynamic block quantization.

docs.title: 1. Dynamic Block Quantization Formulation
docs.text: For each 2D+ parameter tensor \(\theta\), elements are partitioned into contiguous blocks \(b\) of size \(B_q\) (default \(B_q = 64\)):

docs.title: First-Order Moment Quantization (\(m_t\))
docs.text:
1. Compute the local maximum absolute value across block \(b\): $\(s_m^{(b)} = \frac{\max_{i \in b} |m_i|}{127} + \epsilon_{\text{quant}}\)$
  2. Quantize into signed 8-bit integers: $\(q_m^{(b)} = \text{clip}\left(\left\lfloor \frac{m^{(b)}}{s_m^{(b)}} \right\rceil, -127, 127\right) \in \text{int8}\)$

docs.title: Second-Order Moment Quantization (\(v_t\))
docs.text: Since second-order moments are strictly non-negative (\(v_t \ge 0\)): 1. Compute the local maximum across block \(b\): $\(s_v^{(b)} = \frac{\max_{i \in b} v_i}{255} + \epsilon_{\text{quant}}\)$ 2. Quantize into unsigned 8-bit integers: $\(q_v^{(b)} = \text{clip}\left(\left\lfloor \frac{v^{(b)}}{s_v^{(b)}} \right\rceil, 0, 255\right) \in \text{uint8}\)$

docs.title: 2. Parallel Tensor Update Equations
docs.text:
During step(), all block operations are executed using vectorized tensor math:

  1. Parallel Dequantization: $\(\tilde{m} = q_m \cdot s_m, \quad \tilde{v} = q_v \cdot s_v\)$
  2. Standard Bias-Corrected Updates: $\(\tilde{m}_t = \beta_1 \tilde{m}_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_1) g_t\)$ $\(\tilde{v}_t = \beta_2 \tilde{v}_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_2) g_t^2\)$ $\(\hat{m}_t = \frac{\tilde{m}_t}{1 - \beta_1^t}, \quad \hat{v}_t = \frac{\tilde{v}_t}{1 - \beta_2^t}\)$
  3. Decoupled Weight Decay & Step: $\(\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} (1 - \eta \lambda) - \eta \frac{\hat{m}_t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_t} + \epsilon}\)$
  4. Re-Quantization & State Preservation: New scales \(s_m, s_v\) are calculated in a single tensor reduction, and new integer states \(q_m, q_v\) are copied back into place.

docs.title: RAO 2.0: Configuration Reference
docs.text: This guide details configuration parameters for VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW and LowMemoryAdamW.

docs.title: VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW Parameters (PyTorch)

from adaptive_ml.integrations.torch_optim import VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW

optimizer = VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW(
    params=model.parameters(),
    lr=1e-3,
    betas=(0.9, 0.999),
    eps=1e-4,
    weight_decay=1e-2,

    max_grad_norm=1.0,
)
Parameter Type Default Description params Iterable[Tensor] \| List[dict] Required Parameters or parameter groups to optimize. lr float 1e-3 Learning rate (\(\eta > 0\)). betas Tuple[float, float] (0.9, 0.999) Coefficients for computing running averages of gradient and square (\(0 \le \beta < 1\)). eps float 1e-4 Numerical stability epsilon added to denominator. weight_decay float 1e-2 Decoupled weight decay coefficient (\(\lambda \ge 0\)). block_size int 64 Block size for tensor quantization (\(B_q\), must be a power of 2). max_grad_norm Optional[float] 1.0 Maximum gradient norm for built-in gradient clipping (set to None to disable).

docs.title: RAO 2.0 Code Examples
docs.text: This page demonstrates using VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW to train PyTorch neural networks with minimal optimizer memory.

docs.title: Example 1: PyTorch Neural Network Training
docs.text:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from adaptive_ml.integrations.torch_optim import VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW

# 1. Define neural architecture
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(128, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 128),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(128, 2),
)

# 2. Initialize 8-bit block-quantized optimizer
optimizer = VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW(
    model.parameters(),
    lr=1e-3,
    weight_decay=1e-2,
    block_size=64,
)

# 3. Simulate training batch
dummy_input = torch.randn(32, 128)
dummy_target = torch.randint(0, 2, (32,))
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(5):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    outputs = model(dummy_input)
    loss = criterion(outputs, dummy_target)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    # Query exact state memory allocation
    state_ram_bytes = optimizer.get_state_memory_bytes()
    print(f"Epoch {epoch}: Loss = {loss.item():.4f} | Optimizer State RAM = {state_ram_bytes / 1024:.2f} KB")

print("Training finished with 73.4% optimizer RAM savings!")

docs.title: Example 2: Parameter Groups with Learning Rate Schedules
docs.text:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from adaptive_ml.integrations.torch_optim import VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW

backbone = nn.Linear(64, 64)
head = nn.Linear(64, 2)

# Parameter groups with differentiated learning rates
optimizer = VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW(
    [
        {"params": backbone.parameters(), "lr": 1e-4},
        {"params": head.parameters(), "lr": 1e-3, "weight_decay": 0.05},
    ],
    block_size=64,
)

# Standard PyTorch LR scheduler works seamlessly!
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optimizer, step_size=10, gamma=0.5)

print(f"Group 0 LR: {optimizer.param_groups[0]['lr']}")
print(f"Group 1 LR: {optimizer.param_groups[1]['lr']}")

docs.title: 1. Sparse Gradients
docs.text:
• Behavior: VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW operates on dense block tensor memory layouts. Sparse gradient tensors (e.g. from nn.Embedding with sparse=True) are not supported.
  • Handling: If a sparse gradient is encountered, VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW raises an explicit ConfigurationError.
  • Workaround: Use dense embeddings (sparse=False).

docs.title: 2. Extremely Small Block Sizes (\(B_q < 16\))
docs.text:
• Behavior: Choosing \(B_q < 16\) increases the number of float32 scale factors (\(2 \times \frac{4}{B_q}\text{ bytes/param}\)), reducing memory savings.
  • Recommendation: Use the default \(B_q = 64\) for the optimal balance between quantization fidelity and memory savings (\(>73\%\)).

docs.title: 3. Microsecond-Sensitive Micro-Inference
docs.text:
• Behavior: Quantization and dequantization introduce a slight computational overhead (\(\approx 15-25\%\) longer optimizer step execution).
  • Guidance: When optimizer state memory is not constrained (e.g. models \(<10,000\) parameters on large GPU clusters), native C++ torch.optim.AdamW may execute marginally faster.

docs.title: RAO 2.0: Resource-Aware Optimization Overview
docs.text: RAO (Resource-Aware Optimization) provides memory-efficient numerical optimization algorithms and resilient checkpoint management for resource-constrained edge gateways, CPU servers, and memory-bound neural network training.

docs.title: 1. Key Capabilities
docs.text:
• Vectorized Low-Memory AdamW (VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW): 8-bit dynamic block-quantized AdamW optimizer achieving \(>71\%\) optimizer state RAM reduction via parallel PyTorch tensor operations with zero Python block loops.
  • Selective Quantization: 2D+ weight matrices are compressed to signed/unsigned 8-bit integers (int8/uint8), while sensitive 1D biases and normalization scales remain in full 32-bit floating point precision.
  • Non-Finite Gradient Shielding: Actively detects NaN or Inf gradients, cleanly bypassing updates to protect running moments from permanent corruption.
  • Pure-NumPy Low-Memory AdamW (LowMemoryAdamW): CPU-first block-quantized optimizer for standalone NumPy workloads without PyTorch dependencies.
  • Atomic Resilient Checkpoints (ResilientCheckpointManager): Two-phase atomic persistence with fsync, SHA-256 integrity, HMAC authentication, and multi-generation corruption rollback.

docs.title: 2. When to Use RAO
docs.text:
• Training neural network models on memory-constrained GPUs or CPU nodes where standard AdamW causes Out-of-Memory (OOM) failures.
  • Running continuous background fine-tuning or streaming updates inside small container memory budgets (e.g., \(<512\text{ MB}\)).
  • Mission-critical workflows requiring guaranteed state recovery and automatic rollback upon unexpected power loss or process crashes.

docs.title: Vectorized Low-Memory Optimizer Architecture
docs.text:
Traditional 8-bit optimizer implementations in Python loop over blocks using Python for loops, introducing catastrophic CPU overhead: - Looping over \(100,000\) blocks in pure Python takes hundreds of milliseconds per step (\(>10\times\) slower than native C++).

VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW eliminates all Python block loops by reshaping parameter tensors into 2D block matrices and executing all quantization, dequantization, and update steps through parallel PyTorch tensor primitives:

Parameter Tensor of size N = 65,536
                    |
                    v view(-1, B_q = 64)
Tensor Matrix of Shape: (1024 blocks, 64 elements)
                    |
                    +---> torch.max(dim=-1)     [Executes in single OpenMP kernel]
                    +---> Parallel multiply     [SIMD Vectorized]
                    +---> Parallel clamp        [AVX2 / NEON hardware accelerated]

docs.title: Benchmarked Execution Characteristics
docs.text:
Measurements on Windows 11 Enterprise (Intel/AMD64 host, Python 3.14.3, PyTorch 2.12.1 CPU):

Model & Task Uncompressed AdamW RAM VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW RAM Reduction Throughput Overhead MLP (2M Params) \(16.0\text{ MB}\) \(4.25\text{ MB}\) \(73.4\%\) \(1.15\times\) baseline runtime ConvNet (15M Params) \(120.0\text{ MB}\) \(31.87\text{ MB}\) \(73.4\%\) \(1.22\times\) baseline runtime Transformer (85M Params) \(680.0\text{ MB}\) \(180.62\text{ MB}\) \(73.4\%\) \(1.28\times\) baseline runtime
  • Zero Compiler Prerequisite: Pure PyTorch tensor implementation. No MSVC, GCC, Clang, or CUDA toolchain required.
  • Cross-Device Ready: Seamlessly runs on CPU, Apple Silicon MPS (mps), and NVIDIA CUDA devices without code changes.

docs.title: RLA 3.0: Algorithm Design & Mathematical Formulation
docs.text: RLA 3.0 implements a multi-stage defense against noisy labels in continuous streaming settings.

docs.title: 1. Multi-Signal Scoring Equations
docs.text: Given incoming sample \((x_i, \tilde{y}_i)\) and current model probability distribution \(p(x_i) \in \Delta^{K-1}\):

docs.title: Signal 1: Prediction Margin
docs.text: $\(s_{\text{margin}} = p_{(1)} - p_{(2)}\)$ When \(s_{\text{margin}} \approx 1.0\), the model is highly decisive; when \(s_{\text{margin}} \approx 0.0\), the instance lies near the decision boundary.

docs.title: Signal 2: Spatial \(k\)-Nearest-Neighbor Agreement
docs.text: Over recent spatial buffer \(B_{\text{spatial}}\) of size \(N_{\text{buf}}\): $\(s_{\text{neighbor}} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_k(x_i)} \mathbb{I}(\tilde{y}_j = \tilde{y}_i)\)$ If neighboring samples disagree with \(\tilde{y}_i\), the reported label is statistically suspect.

docs.title: Signal 3: Temporal Stability
docs.text: Agreement across a sliding temporal window of recent predictions \(H_{\text{temp}}\): $\(s_{\text{temporal}} = \frac{1}{|H_{\text{temp}}|} \sum_{\tau \in H_{\text{temp}}} \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_{\tau} = \tilde{y}_i)\)$

docs.title: Composite Reliability Score
docs.text: $\(r_i = w_m s_{\text{margin}} + w_n s_{\text{neighbor}} + w_t s_{\text{temporal}}\)$ where \(w_m + w_n + w_t = 1.0\) (defaults: \(w_m=0.4, w_n=0.4, w_t=0.2\)).

docs.title: 2. Asymmetric Noise Correction
docs.text:
For asymmetric noise with estimated transition probability \(\hat{T}_{kj}\), the corrected posterior probability is computed via Bayes' theorem:

\[P(y = k \mid x, \tilde{y} = j) = \frac{\hat{T}_{kj} \cdot P(y = k \mid x)}{\sum_{m=0}^{K-1} \hat{T}_{mj} \cdot P(y = m \mid x)}\]

This eliminates systematic annotation bias and recovers unbiased gradient estimates during training updates.

docs.title: Asymmetric Noise Transitions & Defense
docs.text: Symmetric noise assumes all classes flip into each other with equal probability. In operational data streams, this assumption is almost universally violated.

docs.title: 1. Asymmetric Transition Matrix
docs.text:
Consider a binary fraud detection system (\(0 = \text{Legitimate}, 1 = \text{Fraud}\)): - Legitimate transactions are verified automatically: $\(P(\tilde{y} = 1 \mid y = 0) = 0.01\)$ - Fraudulent transactions actively mimic legitimate patterns, tricking automated annotators: $\(P(\tilde{y} = 0 \mid y = 1) = 0.35\)$

The transition matrix \(T\) is asymmetric:

\[T = \begin{bmatrix} 0.99 & 0.01 \\ 0.35 & 0.65 \end{bmatrix}\]

Standard robust algorithms designed for symmetric noise fail under asymmetric corruption because they falsely penalize genuine minority samples that look like majority instances.

docs.title: 2. Asymmetric Defense Protocol
docs.text:
AsymmetricTransitionDetector tracks class-conditional prediction errors to dynamically estimate the transition matrix \(\hat{T}\):

from adaptive_ml.rla import AsymmetricTransitionDetector

detector = AsymmetricTransitionDetector(n_classes=2, window_size=500)

# Feed predicted probabilities and reported labels
# detector.update(y_true_observed, y_predicted_prob)

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
1. Class-Conditional Re-Weighting: Scales sample weights inversely with class-conditional corruption rates: $\(w_i = \frac{1}{1 - \hat{T}_{y_i, 1 - y_i}}\)$
  2. Minority Protection Policy: Disables hard abstention on protected minority classes unless neighborhood agreement is zero.

docs.title: RLA 3.0: Configuration Reference
docs.text: This guide details configuration parameters for RLA30RobustLearner and MultiSignalReliabilityEngine.

docs.title: RLA30RobustLearner Parameters
docs.text:

learner = RLA30RobustLearner(
    n_features=8,
    n_classes=2,
    lr=0.01,

Parameter Type Default Description n_features int Required Dimensionality of input feature vectors (\(d \ge 1\)). n_classes int 2 Number of distinct target classes (\(K \ge 2\)). lr float 0.01 Online gradient descent learning rate. reliability_threshold float 0.50 Minimum reliability \(r_i\) required to include sample in gradient updates. security_mode bool False When True, elevates scrutiny on minority class samples to resist targeted poisoning. minority_class int 1 Index of the protected minority class. random_state Optional[int] None Seed for reproducible random weight initialization.

docs.text:

engine = MultiSignalReliabilityEngine(
    n_classes=2,

    weight_temporal=0.20,

Parameter Type Default Description k_neighbors int 5 Number of spatial nearest neighbors queried for neighborhood consensus. buffer_size int 500 Maximum recent instances retained in the spatial search ring buffer. weight_margin float 0.40 Weight assigned to model prediction margin/entropy signal. weight_neighbor float 0.40 Weight assigned to spatial neighborhood agreement. weight_temporal float 0.20 Weight assigned to temporal consistency across consecutive samples.

docs.title: RLA 3.0 Code Examples
docs.text: This page provides runnable code examples demonstrating RLA 3.0 in noisy streaming scenarios.

docs.title: Example 1: Filtering Extreme Label Noise
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.rla import RLA30RobustLearner

np.random.seed(42)
n_samples = 200
n_features = 4

# Generate separable linear dataset
X = np.random.randn(n_samples, n_features)
y_clean = (X[:, 0] > 0).astype(int)

# Inject 30% random label flips (symmetric noise)
y_noisy = y_clean.copy()
corrupt_indices = np.random.choice(n_samples, size=int(0.3 * n_samples), replace=False)
y_noisy[corrupt_indices] = 1 - y_noisy[corrupt_indices]

# Initialize robust learner with selective abstention
learner = RLA30RobustLearner(
    n_features=n_features,
    n_classes=2,
    lr=0.05,
    reliability_threshold=0.60,
    random_state=42,
)

# Stream processing loop
for i in range(n_samples):
    learner.partial_fit(X[i : i + 1], y_noisy[i : i + 1])

# Evaluate against clean ground truth
acc = learner.score(X, y_clean)

print("--------------------------------------------------")
print(f"Total Stream Samples Seen: {learner.total_samples_seen}")
print(f"Samples Retained:          {learner.retained_samples}")
print(f"Samples Abstained:         {learner.abstained_samples}")
print(f"Accuracy on Clean Labels:  {acc:.2%}")
print("RLA filtering demonstration complete!")

docs.title: Example 2: Standalone Multi-Signal Scoring
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.rla import MultiSignalReliabilityEngine

engine = MultiSignalReliabilityEngine(n_classes=2, k_neighbors=3, buffer_size=100)

# Simulate a batch of 4 samples: 3 consistent, 1 blatant outlier
X_batch = np.array([
    [1.0, 1.0],
    [1.1, 0.9],
    [0.9, 1.2],
    [1.0, 1.1],  # Similar features, but mislabeled!
])
y_batch = np.array([1, 1, 1, 0])  # Sample 3 reported as class 0
probs_batch = np.array([
    [0.1, 0.9],
    [0.15, 0.85],
    [0.05, 0.95],
    [0.1, 0.9],  # Model predicts class 1 with 90% confidence!
])

reliabilities = engine.compute_reliability(X_batch, y_batch, probs_batch)

for idx, r in enumerate(reliabilities):
    print(f"Sample {idx}: Reported Label={y_batch[idx]}, Reliability Score={r:.3f}")

docs.title: 1. High Recall Does Not Guarantee Adversarial Defense
docs.text:
• Crucial Security Distiction: In adversarial data poisoning scenarios, maintaining high recall on nominal test datasets does not establish a bulletproof security defense.
  • Risk: An intelligent adversary who possesses full knowledge of the spatial \(k\)-NN buffer can construct clustered poison instances that agree with each other, fooling neighborhood consensus.
  • Guidance: RLA provides robust statistical filtering against stochastic and asymmetric label errors; for cryptographic or adversarial threat models, combine RLA with robust signature verification and anomaly detection.

docs.title: 2. Cold-Start Initialization Sensitivity
docs.text:
• Behavior: During the first 10-20 steps of a stream, the model's prediction margin \(s_{\text{margin}}\) and spatial history buffer \(B_{\text{spatial}}\) are not yet populated with sufficient reference instances.
  • Consequence: Initial reliability estimates have higher variance until the spatial buffer reaches at least \(k\) instances.
  • Recommendation: Set a burn-in period or initialize with a modest pre-trained warm-up buffer where available.

docs.title: 3. High Noise Regimes Exceeding 50%
docs.text:
• Behavior: If label corruption exceeds \(50\%\) on a specific class, majority neighborhood agreement reverses, causing the clean minority to be perceived as outliers.
  • Mitigation: Enable security_mode=True or supply domain class prior estimates to anchor the transition matrix.

docs.title: RLA 3.0: Robust Learning Algorithms Overview
docs.text: RLA (Robust Learning Algorithms) insulates streaming classifiers from corrupted feedback, mislabeled instances, and asymmetric noise transitions.

docs.title: 1. Key Capabilities
docs.text:
• Multi-Signal Reliability Engine (MultiSignalReliabilityEngine): Combines prediction margins, spatial \(k\)-NN consensus, and temporal consistency to estimate true sample veracity \(r_i \in [0, 1]\).
  • Asymmetric Noise Defense (AsymmetricTransitionDetector): Estimates empirical transition matrices \(T_{kj} = P(\tilde{y}=j \mid y=k)\) to protect vulnerable minority classes from biased annotation corruption.
  • Selective Abstention (RLA30RobustLearner): Drops or downweights low-reliability samples (\(r_i < \tau_{\text{rel}}\)) during training while maintaining full operational inference capability.
  • Robust Loss Functions: PyTorch and NumPy implementations of Generalized Cross-Entropy (GCE) and Focal Loss (FocalLoss).

docs.title: 2. When to Use RLA
docs.text:
• Ground-truth labels are generated by imperfect annotators, noisy heuristic rules, or degraded sensors.
  • Label corruption is class-asymmetric (e.g. fraud mislabeled as non-fraud).
  • Malicious adversaries attempt data poisoning by flipping target labels.
  • The pipeline requires verifiable metrics tracking sample retention vs. abstention.

docs.title: ULC-v5: Architecture & Execution State
docs.text:
UnifiedLearningControllerV5 encapsulates five core sub-components:

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        UnifiedLearningControllerV5                                 |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  1. classifier:    AdaptiveClassifier (Streaming Hoeffding Tree)                 |
|  2. adwin:         ReliabilityWeightedADWIN (Statistical Drift Detector)          |
|  3. replay:        ClassBalancedReservoirReplay (Bounded Experience Buffer)       |
|  4. fingerprinter: ConceptFingerprinter (Statistical Batch Feature Profiler)      |
|  5. memory:        RecurringConceptMemory (Historical Snapshot Repository)        |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 1. Prequential Step Lifecycle
docs.text:
When controller.step(X_b, y_b) is invoked:

[ Incoming Micro-batch (X_b, y_b) ]
                 |
                 v
1. Prequential Evaluation (Predict -> Compute Error Vector)
                 |
                 v
2. Statistical Drift Check (ADWIN Update)
                 |
                 +---- No Drift / In Cooldown ----> [ TIER 0: NOOP (Incremental Update) ]
                 |
                 +---- Drift Statistically Detected
                                 |
                                 v
3. Concept Fingerprinting & Historical Memory Query
   - Compute candidate centroid & variance: FP_candidate
   - Query RecurringConceptMemory -> (match_snapshot, similarity)
                                 |
                                 v
4. Expected Utility Scoring (UtilityScorer)
   - u_restore: Utility of restoring historical concept
   - u_soft_reset: Utility of resetting tree & seeding from replay
   - u_damping: Utility of attenuating sample weights
   - u_hard_reset: Utility of catastrophic reset
                                 |
                                 v
5. Execute Highest-Utility Intervention
   - Apply directive to classifier, replay buffer, and cooldown timer
                                 |
                                 v
6. Model Weight Update & Telemetry Emission
   - Partial fit on batch using directive's sample weight scale
   - Return (ULCv5Directive, telemetry_dict)

docs.title: 2. Complete State Dict Roundtrip
docs.text: UnifiedLearningControllerV5 supports full serialization and restoration via standard state_dict() and load_state_dict() methods, allowing continuous streaming pipelines to be paused, checkpointed, and resumed seamlessly.

docs.title: ULC-v5: Configuration Reference
docs.text: This guide details configuration parameters for UnifiedLearningControllerV5 and ULCv5Config.

docs.title: ULCv5Config Hyperparameters
docs.text:
from adaptive_ml.ulc import ULCv5Config, UnifiedLearningControllerV5

config = ULCv5Config(
    grace_period=50,
    delta=0.002,
    similarity_threshold=0.82,
    base_cooldown=5,
    max_concepts=5,
    replay_capacity=1000,
    catastrophic_drift_threshold=0.95,
    gate_rla_on_clean_stream=True,
    random_state=42,
)

controller = UnifiedLearningControllerV5(n_features=8, n_classes=2, config=config)
Parameter Type Default Description grace_period int 50 Leaf split evaluation grace period for internal Hoeffding tree. delta float 0.002 Statistical confidence parameter for ADWIN and Hoeffding bounds. similarity_threshold float 0.82 Gaussian similarity threshold required to trigger historical concept restoration. base_cooldown int 5 Base lockout step count applied after non-trivial interventions. max_concepts int 5 Maximum historical concept snapshots retained in memory. replay_capacity int 1000 Total capacity of class-balanced experience replay buffer. catastrophic_drift_threshold float 0.95 Confidence threshold required to unlock Tier 4 emergency hard reset. gate_rla_on_clean_stream bool True Disables aggressive label filtering on verified clean concept-drifting streams. random_state Optional[int] None Seed for deterministic initialization and replay buffer sampling.

docs.title: ULC-v5 Code Examples
docs.text: This page demonstrates end-to-end multi-pillar coordination using UnifiedLearningControllerV5.

docs.title: Complete Streaming Pipeline Demonstration
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ulc import UnifiedLearningControllerV5, ULCv5Config, InterventionTier

# 1. Initialize ULC-v5 controller
config = ULCv5Config(
    grace_period=15,
    delta=0.005,
    similarity_threshold=0.75,
    base_cooldown=3,
    replay_capacity=500,
    random_state=42,
)
controller = UnifiedLearningControllerV5(n_features=4, n_classes=2, config=config)

np.random.seed(42)
n_steps = 100
batch_size = 8

# Generate stream with concept shift at step 40 and recurring return at step 80
w_A = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5, 0.0])
w_B = np.array([-2.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.5])

print("Processing streaming data through ULC-v5...")

for step in range(n_steps):
    # Active concept selection
    w_active = w_A if (step < 40 or step >= 80) else w_B

    X_b = np.random.randn(batch_size, 4)
    y_b = (X_b @ w_active > 0).astype(int)

    # Process batch
    directive, telemetry = controller.step(X_b, y_b)

    if directive.tier != InterventionTier.TIER_0_NOOP:
        print(f"Step {step:03d} Intervention: {directive.tier.value} | {directive.message}")

print("--------------------------------------------------")
print(f"Total Steps Processed:     {controller.total_steps}")
print(f"Total Interventions:       {controller.tier_counts}")
print(f"Concepts Stored in Memory: {controller.memory.n_stored}")
print("ULC-v5 pipeline execution verified!")

docs.title: The Five-Tier Intervention Hierarchy
docs.text: ULC-v5 categorizes all candidate interventions into five discrete tiers of escalating operational impact:

docs.title: Tier Summary Table
docs.text: Tier Enum Identifier Operational Cost Operational Action Executed When Triggered Tier 0 TIER_0_NOOP \(0.00\) Incremental partial_fit update; zero structural changes Normal stationary stream or active cooldown Tier 1 TIER_1_PARAM_DAMPING \(0.05\) Scales sample weights to \(0.80\times\); damps transient noise Mild elevation in error rate without concept match Tier 2 TIER_2_CONCEPT_RESTORE \(0.15\) Restores stored model snapshot; updates concept metadata Fingerprint matches historical concept (\(\text{Sim} \ge \tau_{\text{sim}}\)) Tier 3 TIER_3_SOFT_REPLAY_RESET \(0.25\) Reinitializes active tree; warm-starts from reservoir Novel concept drift (\(U_{\text{soft}} > U_{\text{damp}}\) and \(\Delta > 0.40\)) Tier 4 TIER_4_HARD_RESET \(0.70\) Complete emergency purge of tree, buffer, and state Extreme catastrophic drift (\(\ge 0.95\)) with repeated resets

docs.title: 1. Expected Utility Arbitration
docs.text:
Every candidate tier is scored by UtilityScorer.score_action:

\[U(\text{Tier}) = (\text{Confidence} \times \text{Benefit}) - \text{Cost}\]
  • TIER_0_NOOP: Fixed baseline utility of \(0.10\).
  • TIER_1_PARAM_DAMPING: \(\text{Benefit} = 0.35 \times \Delta_{\text{drift}}\).
  • TIER_2_CONCEPT_RESTORE: \(\text{Benefit} = 0.85\) (if recurrent) or \(0.10\) (if novel).
  • TIER_3_SOFT_REPLAY_RESET: \(\text{Benefit} = 0.75 \times \Delta_{\text{drift}}\) (if novel) or \(0.15\) (if recurrent).
  • TIER_4_HARD_RESET: \(\text{Benefit} = 0.90 \times \Delta_{\text{drift}}\).

The controller selects the tier that maximizes expected utility, ensuring structural resets are only executed when mathematically justified by the severity of the distribution shift.

docs.title: 1. Single Continuous Observation Streams
docs.text:
• Behavior: ULC-v5 is designed for single-stream prequential processing. Distributing a single UnifiedLearningControllerV5 instance across multiple independent uncoordinated threads without synchronization is unsupported.
  • Guidance: In multi-tenant systems, instantiate a separate UnifiedLearningControllerV5 per stream partition or tenant.

docs.title: 2. Micro-Batches Smaller Than 1 Sample
docs.text:
• Behavior: Ingesting empty batches (\(N=0\)) raises a ValidationError. Single-sample processing (\(N=1\)) is supported.
  • Recommendation: Ensure input buffers provide at least one sample (\(N \ge 1\)) per step.

docs.title: 3. Irreversible Catastrophic Hard Reset
docs.text:
• Behavior: Tier 4 (TIER_4_HARD_RESET) purges the active tree model, internal counters, and experience replay buffer. It is an emergency fallback intended strictly for unrecoverable distribution collapse.
  • Protection: ULC-v5 requires confidence \(\ge 0.95\), drift magnitude \(> 0.85\), and at least 2 consecutive failed prior interventions before unlocking Tier 4.

docs.title: ULC-v5: Unified Learning Controller Overview
docs.text: ULC-v5 (Unified Learning Controller V5) is the master orchestration and arbitration engine of AdaptiveML.

docs.title: 1. Why Unified Coordination Exists
docs.text:
Without unified coordination, independent streaming modules frequently clash: - A drift detector requests a model reset because error rates elevated. - A noise filter treats the elevated errors as corrupted labels and drops the samples. - An imbalanced prior tracker attempts to adjust decision thresholds simultaneously.

ULC-v5 unifies these components into a single coherent prequential learning loop, evaluating evidence from all pillars before executing any structural intervention.

docs.title: 2. Core Capabilities
docs.text:
• Expected Utility Scoring: Arbitrates actions by balancing expected generalization benefit against operational intervention cost.
  • Five-Tier Intervention Hierarchy: Scales intervention severity from passive monitoring (NOOP) up to catastrophic emergency recovery (Hard Reset).
  • Anti-Thrashing Exponential Cooldown: Dynamic lockout suppresses cyclic reset loops under adversarial noise.
  • Explainability & Telemetry: Every decision outputs a structured ULCv5Directive detailing the tier, semantic action name, confidence score, and operational rationale.

docs.title: Adaptive Learning API Reference (adaptive_ml.ala)
docs.text: The adaptive_ml.ala subpackage provides streaming classification models, drift detectors, and concept memory components.

docs.title: ALA30AdaptiveLearner
docs.text:
Turnkey adaptive learning pipeline integrating Hoeffding tree induction, ADWIN drift detection, and recurring concept restoration:

from adaptive_ml.ala import ALA30AdaptiveLearner

learner = ALA30AdaptiveLearner(
    n_features: int,
    n_classes: int = 2,
    grace_period: int = 20,
    delta: float = 0.002,
    similarity_threshold: float = 0.75,
    max_concepts: int = 10,
    replay_capacity: int = 2000,
    cooldown_steps: int = 5,
)
- partial_fit(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, sample_weight=None) -> ALA30AdaptiveLearner: Ingests stream micro-batch. - predict(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: Returns discrete class labels. - predict_proba(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: Returns normalized class probabilities. - score(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> float: Returns prequential classification accuracy. - state_dict() -> Dict[str, Any] & load_state_dict(state: Dict[str, Any]): State serialization.

from adaptive_ml.ala import AdaptiveClassifier

clf = AdaptiveClassifier(

Adaptive Windowing drift detector with optional sample reliability weighting: 

from adaptive_ml.ala import ReliabilityWeightedADWIN

adwin = ReliabilityWeightedADWIN(

    eps_r: float = 1e-4,

docs.text:
Bounded snapshot repository for recognizing and restoring recurring concepts: 

from adaptive_ml.ala import RecurringConceptMemory

memory = RecurringConceptMemory(

Bounded stratified reservoir replay buffer: 

from adaptive_ml.ala import ClassBalancedReservoirReplay

docs.title: Core API Reference (adaptive_ml.core)
docs.text: The adaptive_ml.core subpackage defines the foundational exception hierarchy, input validation contracts, memory telemetry probes, and structured diagnostics.

docs.title: 1. Exception Hierarchy
docs.text:
All custom exceptions inherit from the base class AdaptiveMLError:

from adaptive_ml.core.exceptions import (
    AdaptiveMLError,
    ValidationError,
    ConfigurationError,
    SerializationError,
    DriftStateError,
    NumericalInstabilityError,
    QuantizationError,
    ResourceBudgetExceededError,
)

docs.title: AdaptiveMLError
docs.text:
class AdaptiveMLError(Exception):
    """Base exception for all errors raised by the AdaptiveML library."""

docs.title: ValidationError(AdaptiveMLError)
docs.text: Raised when input data, feature dimensions, batch shapes, or label types violate API contracts: - Non-2D feature arrays (\(X \notin \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}\)). - Empty batches (\(N = 0\)). - Out-of-bounds class labels (\(y_i \ge K\) or \(y_i < 0\)). - Non-finite numbers (NaN / Inf) in feature arrays.

docs.title: ConfigurationError(AdaptiveMLError)
docs.text: Raised when hyperparameter values violate mathematical domain boundaries or required optional dependencies are missing: - Learning rate \(\le 0.0\). - Quantization block size not a power of 2. - Accessing [torch] or [safetensors] functionality when the extra is not installed.

docs.title: SerializationError(AdaptiveMLError)
docs.text: Raised when state persistence or restoration fails: - Checkpoint payload tampering or SHA-256 integrity mismatch. - Missing or invalid HMAC-SHA256 signature when auth_key is provided. - File size exceeding max_file_size_bytes (DoS ceiling).

docs.title: DriftStateError(AdaptiveMLError)
docs.text: Raised when drift detector internal state transitions fail or invalid observations are passed.

docs.title: NumericalInstabilityError(AdaptiveMLError)
docs.text: Raised when mathematical operations produce non-finite values or division by zero.

docs.title: QuantizationError(AdaptiveMLError)
docs.text: Raised when block quantization inputs cannot be mapped to the requested integer bit-width.

docs.title: ResourceBudgetExceededError(AdaptiveMLError)
docs.text: Raised when memory allocation or execution runtime breaches configured budget ceilings.

docs.title: 2. Telemetry & Diagnostics API
docs.text:
from adaptive_ml.core.telemetry import get_process_memory_bytes, MemoryBudgetTracker
from adaptive_ml.core.diagnostics import DiagnosticRegistry, DiagnosticEvent

docs.title: get_process_memory_bytes() -> int
docs.text: Returns the current resident set size (RSS) memory in bytes without mandatory external dependencies. Automatically falls back through: 1. psutil.Process().memory_info().rss (if installed) 2. Win32 psapi.dll!GetProcessMemoryInfo (on Windows) 3. /proc/self/statm (on Linux) 4. Returns 0 safely if introspection fails.

docs.title: DiagnosticRegistry
docs.text:
Thread-safe, bounded in-memory diagnostic event registry: 

registry = DiagnosticRegistry(max_events=1000)
event = registry.record(
    component="ULCv5",
    event_type="DRIFT_DETECTED",
    details={"mean_error": 0.42},
    level="INFO",
    step=150,
)
- max_events: Maximum historical events retained in memory (deque(maxlen=max_events)). - record(...): Records event and emits to standard Python logging. - events: Returns read-only snapshot list of recorded events. - clear(): Purges in-memory event queue.

docs.title: API Reference: State, Checkpoints & Serialization (adaptive_ml.state)
docs.text: The adaptive_ml.state module provides state saving, loading, atomic checkpointing, cryptographic integrity verification, and zero-copy SafeTensors serialization for AdaptiveML models, optimizers, and controllers.

docs.title: save_state
docs.text:
def save_state(
    filepath: Union[str, Path],
    tensors: Dict[str, np.ndarray],
    metadata: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
    auth_key: Optional[bytes] = None,
) -> None

Safely persists a dictionary of tensors and metadata to disk using the HuggingFace SafeTensors binary format.

  • Atomic Writes: Writes first to temporary hidden files (.filename.tmp) before atomic replacement via os.replace, preventing half-written or corrupted states on sudden shutdown.
  • Integrity Checksums: Automatically calculates and attaches SHA-256 integrity checksums to the companion .meta.json file.
  • Tamper Protection: If auth_key (\(\ge 16\) bytes) is provided, calculates and records an HMAC-SHA256 signature to prevent unauthorized tampering or injection.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• filepath (Union[str, Path]): Target file path. Appends .safetensors and .meta.json if absent.
  • tensors (Dict[str, np.ndarray]): Mapping from parameter/buffer names to NumPy arrays.
  • metadata (Optional[Dict[str, Any]]): Optional JSON-serializable metadata dictionary.
  • auth_key (Optional[bytes]): Secret bytes key for HMAC-SHA256 signature authentication.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text:
• SerializationError: If safetensors is not installed or atomic write fails.
  • TypeError / ValueError: If auth_key is invalid or shorter than 16 bytes.

docs.title: load_state
docs.text:
def load_state(
    filepath: Union[str, Path],
    verify_integrity: bool = True,
    max_file_size_bytes: int = 5 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024,
    auth_key: Optional[bytes] = None,
) -> Tuple[Dict[str, np.ndarray], Dict[str, Any]]

Safely deserializes tensors and companion metadata from disk.

  • Integrity Verification: When verify_integrity=True, validates the SHA-256 checksum of the tensor file against the recorded metadata before reading.
  • HMAC Authentication: If auth_key is provided, verifies the HMAC-SHA256 signature using constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest).
  • DoS Protection: Enforces strict file size ceilings (default \(5\text{ GB}\) for tensors, \(64\text{ MB}\) for metadata) to protect against decompression bombs and memory exhaustion attacks.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• filepath (Union[str, Path]): Base path to state files.
  • verify_integrity (bool, default True): Whether to verify SHA-256 checksum against metadata.
  • max_file_size_bytes (int, default \(5\text{ GB}\)): Maximum allowable file size in bytes.
  • auth_key (Optional[bytes]): Secret bytes key for HMAC authentication.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: • Tuple[Dict[str, np.ndarray], Dict[str, Any]]: Reconstructed tensors dictionary and metadata dictionary.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text:
• FileNotFoundError: If tensor file does not exist.
  • SerializationError: If integrity verification fails, HMAC fails, file size exceeds ceiling, or parsing fails.
