docs.title: Security Architecture & Threat Model
docs.text: Document ID: docs/architecture/security-architecture.md Distribution Package: aml-core v0.1.0.dev0 Security Posture: Production Hardened, Zero-Pickle, Air-Gapped Compliant

docs.title: 1. Security Threat Model & Boundaries
docs.text:
AdaptiveML is designed to execute in untrusted or multi-tenant production environments, including cloud microservices, edge edge devices, and regulated on-premise infrastructure.

graph TD
    subgraph Untrusted Inputs
        RAW[Streaming Data Inputs]
        CKPT[Serialized Checkpoint Files]
        KEYS[Environment Configurations]
    end

    subgraph Security Boundaries
        VAL[Input Validation: NaN/Inf & Shape Check]
        HMAC[Cryptographic HMAC-SHA256 & Ceiling Check]
        CONF[Configuration Range & Type Verification]
    end

    subgraph Hardened Core
        CORE[Safe Execution Engine (Zero-Pickle, O(1) Memory)]
        PRIV[Zero-PII Aggregated Diagnostics Sink]
    end

    RAW --> VAL --> CORE
    CKPT --> HMAC --> CORE
    KEYS --> CONF --> CORE
    CORE --> PRIV

docs.title: Threat
docs.text: Python's standard pickle and torch.save(..., pickle_module=pickle) deserialize arbitrary Python bytecodes. An adversary with write access to model storage can construct a malicious payload that executes arbitrary operating system commands upon model loading (os.system, subprocess.Popen).

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Mandatory SafeTensors Serialization: AdaptiveML completely rejects pickle for model weights, using the HuggingFace SafeTensors binary tensor format.
  • Header Parsing Security: SafeTensors headers are constrained JSON metadata strings with explicit size offsets. Raw buffers are directly memory-mapped with zero bytecode execution pathways.
  • Repository-Wide Ban: Internal AST linters verify that pickle.load and pickle.loads are never invoked anywhere in adaptive_ml.

docs.title: Threat
docs.text: An adversary with file system access alters stored model weights or decision thresholds (e.g., lowering a fraud detection threshold to allow illicit transactions).

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Cryptographic Checksums: Every saved file automatically generates an unambiguous SHA-256 digest recorded in .meta.json.
  • HMAC Signatures: Production deployments can pass a secret byte string auth_key (\(\ge 16\) bytes). The signature is computed via: $\(\text{HMAC-SHA256}(K, \text{tensor\_bytes})\)$
  • Constant-Time Verification: When loading state with auth_key, the key is verified using constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest) to prevent timing side-channel attacks. Any tampering immediately halts execution with a typed SerializationError.

docs.title: Threat
docs.text: An attacker submits an oversized state file or decompression bomb, causing the application to allocate gigabytes of heap memory and triggering kernel Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminations.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Tensor File Ceiling: load_state inspects file sizes via OS metadata before reading contents, enforcing an immutable default ceiling of \(5\text{ GB}\) (configurable).
  • Metadata JSON Ceiling: Companion .meta.json files are constrained to a strict \(64\text{ MB}\) ceiling.
  • Bounded In-Memory Diagnostics: DiagnosticRegistry maintains an immutable FIFO ring-buffer (maxlen=1000 default) with thread-safe lock synchronization, ensuring logging never leaks memory.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• No Data Leakage: Diagnostic logs and telemetry dictionaries record only aggregated mathematical scalars (mean error rate, step latency in ms, norm of gradients, tier enum names).
  • No Raw Feature Buffers: Input feature rows and raw labels are never forwarded into diagnostic events or error tracebacks.
  • No Telemetry Sockets: AdaptiveML contains zero outbound network requests, phone-home telemetry, or external analytics pings. It is \(100\%\) air-gapped and offline-compliant.

docs.title: System Architecture & Technical Specifications
docs.text: Distribution Package: aml-core Import Namespace: adaptive_ml Architectural Baseline: Stage 14 Production Hardened Target Runtimes: Linux (AMD64, ARM64), macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows (AMD64)

docs.title: 1. High-Level Architecture Overview
docs.text:
AdaptiveML provides a unified, local-first streaming architecture engineered for non-stationary environments. The system is decomposed into five core algorithmic pillars, a central arbitration controller, an immutable data bridge, and a cryptographically authenticated state management engine.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Ingestion ["Ingestion & Interoperability Layer"]
        IN_NP["NumPy Array (ndarray)"]
        IN_PD["Pandas DataFrame / Series"]
        IN_PL["Polars DataFrame / Series"]
        IN_PT["PyTorch Tensor"]
        BRIDGE["Data Bridge: to_numpy() / inspect_dataset_contract()"]
        IN_NP --> BRIDGE
        IN_PD --> BRIDGE
        IN_PL --> BRIDGE
        IN_PT --> BRIDGE
    end

    subgraph Controller ["Master Coordination Layer"]
        ULC["UnifiedLearningControllerV5"]
        AUT["Arbitration Automaton"]
        UTIL["UtilityScorer (U = Conf * Benefit - Cost)"]
        DISC["Spatial Discordance Gating (k-NN)"]
        ULC --- AUT
        ULC --- UTIL
        ULC --- DISC
    end

    subgraph Pillars ["Five Algorithmic Pillars"]
        ALA["ALA 3.0: Hoeffding Tree + ADWIN + Recurring Concept Memory"]
        RLA["RLA 3.0: Multi-Signal Reliability Engine + Asymmetric Defense"]
        MIN["Minority Intelligence 2.0: Beta-Binomial Prior + Dynamic FP Budget"]
        RAO["RAO 2.0: 8-Bit Dynamic Block Quantizer + Budget Manager"]
    end

    subgraph Persistence ["Persistence & Security Layer"]
        SAFE["SafeTensors Serializer (Zero-Pickle)"]
        HMAC["HMAC-SHA256 Authenticated Verification"]
        CM["CheckpointManager (FIFO Rolling Retention)"]
    end

    BRIDGE --> ULC
    ULC --> ALA
    ULC --> RLA
    ULC --> MIN
    ULC --> RAO
    ULC --> Persistence

docs.title: 2. Ingestion & Data Contracts Layer
docs.text: The data layer standardizes inputs into C-contiguous NumPy float64/float32 buffers before reaching algorithm cores: 1. Zero-Copy Views: Memory is shared directly whenever source containers match target dtype and contiguity. 2. Strict Non-Finite Scans: All matrices are validated against NaN and Inf to prevent silent poison values. 3. Immutability Contract: Ingested buffers are never mutated in-place by downstream learners.

docs.title: Pillar 1: Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA 3.0)
docs.text:
• Hoeffding Tree Induction: Provable error bounds on streaming decision tree split choices via the Hoeffding inequality: $\(\epsilon = \sqrt{\frac{R^2 \ln(1 / \delta)}{2 n}}\)$
  • Reliability-Weighted ADWIN: Dynamically sizes a sliding window \(W\), cutting sub-windows when statistical mean differences exceed Hoeffding cut bounds.
  • Recurring Concept Memory: Fingerprints distribution statistics into high-dimensional concept vectors, enabling instantaneous \(O(1)\) memory restoration upon recurrence.

docs.title: Pillar 2: Robust Learning Algorithms (RLA 3.0)
docs.text:
• Multi-Signal Reliability Engine: Evaluates composite sample reliability \(r_i \in [0, 1]\) combining prediction margin, spatial \(k\)-NN neighborhood agreement, and temporal consistency.
  • Asymmetric Transition Defense: Detects adversarial label noise attacks using rolling contingency tracking.
  • Noise-Robust Losses: Symmetric Cross-Entropy (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{SCE}}\)) and Generalized Cross-Entropy (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{GCE}}\)) bound gradient influence on ambiguous points.

docs.title: Pillar 3: Adaptive Minority Intelligence 2.0
docs.text:
• Beta-Binomial Bayesian Prior: Maintains online posterior distributions over class frequencies under non-stationary drift.
  • Sublinear Cost Weighting: Scales minority gradient updates via \(W_c = (1 / \hat{\pi}_c)^{0.52}\) to prevent gradient destabilization.
  • PID False-Positive Regulation: Modulates decision threshold \(\tau(t)\) to strictly enforce operational alarm quotas.

docs.title: Pillar 4: Resource-Aware Optimization (RAO 2.0)
docs.text:
• 8-Bit Dynamic Block Quantization: Compresses optimizer momentum and second moments into int8 and uint8 with per-block float32 scales, achieving \(>73\%\) RAM reduction.
  • Dynamic Resource Budget Manager: Monitors per-step execution latency (ms) and resident memory (MB), dynamically throttling micro-batch sizes under resource contention.

docs.title: Pillar 5: Unified Learning Controller (ULC-v5)
docs.text:
• Arbitration Automaton: Disambiguates concept drift from label noise bursts via spatial discordance gating.
  • 5-Tier Intervention Hierarchy: Selects optimal interventions from TIER_0_NOOP through TIER_4_HARD_RESET based on expected utility scoring.
  • Anti-Thrashing Cooldown: Enforces non-zero cooldown intervals after adaptation events to prevent oscillatory thrashing.

docs.title: 4. State Persistence & Fault Recovery
docs.text:
• Zero-Pickle Specification: All weights are persisted via HuggingFace SafeTensors binary buffers.
  • Cryptographic Tamper-Proofing: Companion metadata stores SHA-256 digests and optional HMAC-SHA256 signatures.
  • Atomic Renames: Writes to .tmp files committed via atomic POSIX/Windows os.replace.

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

  • The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
  • Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
  • Public or private harassment
  • Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
  • Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

docs.title: Enforcement Responsibilities
docs.text:
Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces.

docs.title: Reporting Guidelines
docs.text: Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leadership at conduct@adaptiveml.internal. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

docs.title: Contributing to AdaptiveML (aml-core)
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in contributing to AdaptiveML!

AdaptiveML is an open-source Python machine-learning library dedicated to adaptive, robust, and resource-efficient learning. We welcome code contributions, documentation improvements, issue reports, and research discussions.

docs.title: 1. Code of Conduct
docs.text: All contributors and participants are expected to adhere to our Code of Conduct. Please treat all members of the community with respect, constructive feedback, and professionalism.

docs.title: 2. Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO 1.1)
docs.text:
To ensure that all code in AdaptiveML has verifiable legal provenance and complies with our Apache-2.0 licensing, we require the standard Linux Foundation Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO), Version 1.1.

Every commit must include a Signed-off-by line in its commit message:

git commit -s -m "feat(ala): add sliding window variance filter to ADWIN"

Which produces:

Signed-off-by: Jane Developer <jane.developer@example.com>

By adding this line, you certify that: 1. The contribution was created in whole or in part by you, and you have the right to submit it under the Apache-2.0 license; OR 2. The contribution is based on previous work covered under an appropriate permissive open-source license; OR 3. The contribution was provided directly to you by a person who certified points 1 or 2.

docs.title: 3. Clean-Room Implementation Rules
docs.text: AdaptiveML maintains strict clean-room implementation governance: - No Proprietary Code: Do not submit code derived from proprietary libraries, past employment under restrictive IP agreements, or decompiled binary sources. - Academic Grounding: Algorithms must be implemented from published academic papers, patents in the public domain, or original derivations. - Traceable Citations: Always document the mathematical reference (DOI / arXiv ID) in the module docstring.

docs.title: 4.1 Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14.
  • Git.
  • Virtual environment tool (venv, uv, or conda).

docs.title: 4.2 Local Installation
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/adaptiveml/adaptiveml.git
cd adaptiveml

# Create and activate a virtual environment
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate  # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate

# Install editable development build with all test and documentation tools
pip install -e ".[dev,docs,all]"

docs.title: 4.3 Running Test Suite
docs.text:
# Run complete test suite with coverage
pytest tests/ -v --cov=adaptive_ml

docs.title: 4.4 Documentation Preview

mkdocs serve

docs.title: Security Policy & Vulnerability Disclosure
docs.text:
Document ID: docs/community/security.md Distribution Package: aml-core v0.1.0.dev0 Import Namespace: adaptive_ml

AdaptiveML takes the security of its machine learning runtime and state serialization engine seriously. We appreciate responsible disclosure of security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 1. Supported Versions
docs.text:

Version Supported Status 0.1.0.dev0 (current development baseline) Yes Active Security Hardening < 0.1.0 No Experimental Prototypes

docs.title: 2. Reporting a Vulnerability
docs.text:
Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues.

If you believe you have discovered a security vulnerability in AdaptiveML, please report it privately via email:

  • Security Team Email: security@adaptiveml.internal
  • PGP Encryption: Available upon request.

Please include: 1. A detailed description of the vulnerability and its potential impact. 2. A minimal, self-contained Python reproduction script demonstrating the issue. 3. Relevant environment information (OS, Python version, installed extras).

docs.title: 3. Response Process & SLA
docs.text:
1. Initial Acknowledgment: Within 48 hours of receiving your disclosure.
  2. Triaging & Severity Assessment: Within 5 business days, evaluating CVSS score.
  3. Patch Development: A private patch will be prepared and tested across all supported Python versions (3.10–3.14).
  4. Coordinated Disclosure: We adhere to a 90-day coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy before public publication of advisory notes and CVE numbers.

docs.title: 4. Key Security Invariants
docs.text: When evaluating vulnerabilities, please note the following explicit security invariants enforced by AdaptiveML: - Zero-Pickle Rule: The use of Python's standard pickle for model weight deserialization is classified as an automatic high-severity defect. - Denial-of-Service Size Ceilings: State loading functions enforce a strict \(5\text{ GB}\) ceiling on tensor files and a \(64\text{ MB}\) ceiling on JSON metadata. - Cryptographic Signatures: Deserialization with an auth_key must strictly reject tampered files via constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest).

docs.title: Concept: Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA)
docs.text: The Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA) pillar addresses learning from continuous, non-stationary data streams where underlying probability distributions change over time (\(P_t(X, y) \neq P_{t+1}(X, y)\)).

docs.title: The Concept Drift Challenge
docs.text:
Standard machine learning models assume stationary data (Identically and Independently Distributed, IID). In production streams: - Abrupt Drift: Sudden macroeconomic shifts, sensor failures, or regulatory changes. - Gradual Drift: Seasonal behavioral variations or steady trend evolution. - Noise Bursts: Transient sensor spikes or corrupted labels that masquerade as concept drift.

Unweighted drift detectors frequently mistake noise bursts for structural distribution changes, triggering catastrophic model resets.

docs.title: 1. Reliability-Weighted ADWIN (ReliabilityWeightedADWIN)
docs.text: An extension of the classic ADWIN (Adaptive Windowing) algorithm that weights incoming prediction errors by an estimated sample reliability score \(r_i \in [0, 1]\): $\(\bar{\mu}_{W} = \frac{\sum_{i \in W} r_i x_i}{\sum_{i \in W} r_i}\)$ When transient label noise or high-entropy outliers occur, \(r_i \approx 0\), preventing false drift triggers while retaining statistical sensitivity to genuine concept shifts.

docs.title: 2. Vectorized Hoeffding Tree (VectorizedHoeffdingTree)
docs.text: An incremental decision tree that inspects streaming samples and splits nodes using the Hoeffding bound: $\(\epsilon = \sqrt{\frac{R^2 \ln(1 / \delta)}{2 n}}\)$ The split criterion (information gain) is computed using vectorized NumPy matrix operations, achieving high streaming throughput on CPU without storing raw historical samples.

docs.title: 3. Class-Balanced Reservoir Replay (ClassBalancedReservoirReplay)
docs.text: Maintains stratified reservoir buffers per class label. In extreme imbalance streams (\(100:1\)), minority instances are preserved perpetually using reservoir replacement invariants rather than being evicted by majority-class volume.

docs.title: Class Imbalance & Minority Intelligence
docs.text: Streaming class imbalance occurs when one or more target classes arrive with extremely low frequency (\(<1\%\) or \(<0.1\%\) of the stream).

docs.title: 1. The Imbalance Trap
docs.text: Under severe class imbalance (e.g. 999 legitimate events vs. 1 fraud event per 1,000 samples): - A trivial model predicting the majority class exclusively achieves \(99.9\%\) accuracy. - However, its minority recall is \(0.0\%\), rendering it useless for practical fraud detection or security defense. - Standard loss functions prioritize minimizing total error, effectively suppressing gradients from rare minority classes.

docs.title: 2. Online Beta-Binomial Prior Tracking
docs.text:
In non-stationary data streams, the true class prior \(\pi_t = P_t(Y=1)\) fluctuates over time. AdaptiveML tracks this prior continuously using a decaying Beta-Binomial Bayesian conjugate prior:

\[\alpha_{t} = \gamma \alpha_{t-1} + y_t$$ $$\beta_{t} = \gamma \beta_{t-1} + (1 - y_t)\]

where \(\gamma \in (0, 1)\) is an exponential discount factor. The expected posterior class prior at step \(t\) is:

\[\hat{\pi}_t = \mathbb{E}[\pi \mid \alpha_t, \beta_t] = \frac{\alpha_t}{\alpha_t + \beta_t}\]

This allows the model to immediately detect whether minority arrival frequency is increasing or diminishing without hardcoded historical thresholds.

docs.title: 3. Dynamic False-Positive Budget Management
docs.text:
In production operations, human review capacity or customer tolerance sets a strict upper bound on the allowable False Positive Rate (\(\text{FPR} \le \text{budget}_{\text{FP}}\), e.g. \(2\%\)).

Instead of using a static decision threshold (\(0.50\)): 1. The threshold manager dynamically slides threshold \(\theta_t \in (0, 1)\) to maximize minority recall subject to: $\(\text{FPR}(\theta_t) \le \text{budget}_{\text{FP}}\)$ 2. Threshold adjustments are smoothed with exponential moving averages to prevent oscillation across consecutive samples. 3. Sublinear cost weighting scales loss penalties inversely with prior \(\hat{\pi}_t\), ensuring the classifier maintains sharp discrimination boundaries for rare classes.

docs.title: Concept Drift Fundamentals
docs.text:
In streaming machine learning, concept drift refers to changes in the joint probability distribution of the data over time \(t\):

\[P_{t}(X, Y) \neq P_{t-1}(X, Y)\]

docs.title: 1. Types of Concept Drift
docs.text:
Feature Value / Time --->

Abrupt Drift:
[ Concept A: P(Y|X) ] --------> | Shock | --------> [ Concept B: P(Y|X) ]

Gradual Drift:
[ Concept A ] ====> [ Transitional Mixture A & B ] ====> [ Concept B ]

Recurring Drift:
[ Concept A ] -------> [ Concept B ] -------> [ Concept A Returns ]

docs.title: Abrupt Drift
docs.text:
• A sudden, discontinuous change in the data distribution.
  • Examples: A sudden macroeconomic policy change, COVID-19 lockdown announcement, or hardware sensor failure.
  • Challenge: The model must rapidly discard outdated statistical split criteria or reset without over-reacting to transient noise.

docs.title: Gradual Drift
docs.text:
• A smooth transition where instances from the old and new concepts coexist for a duration, with the proportion of new-concept samples increasing over time.
  • Examples: Changing fashion trends, creeping inflation, mechanical wear and tear.
  • Challenge: Balancing plasticity (learning the new distribution) with stability (not forgetting valid historical patterns too early).

docs.title: Recurring Concept Drift
docs.text:
• A previously active concept reappears after an absence.
  • Examples: Seasonal shopping spikes, weekday vs. weekend traffic, day vs. night fraud tactics.
  • Challenge: Storing historical concept representations in bounded memory and restoring them instantaneously without retraining from scratch.

docs.title: 2. Real vs. Virtual Drift
docs.text:
• Real Concept Drift: Changes in the posterior probability \(P(Y \mid X)\) with or without changes in \(P(X)\). The true decision boundary moves.
  • Virtual (Covariate) Shift: Changes in the input feature distribution \(P(X)\) while the relationship \(P(Y \mid X)\) remains unchanged.

docs.title: 3. Statistical Detection with ADWIN
docs.text:
Adaptive Windowing (ADWIN) maintains a variable-sized window \(W\) of recent real-valued observations (typically prediction errors \(e_i \in \{0, 1\}\)).

ADWIN mathematically checks whether two sub-windows \(W_0\) and \(W_1\) (where \(W = W_0 \cdot W_1\)) have statistically significant differences in their means:

\[|\hat{\mu}_{W_0} - \hat{\mu}_{W_1}| \ge \epsilon_{\text{cut}}\]

The cut threshold \(\epsilon_{\text{cut}}\) is derived from the Hoeffding/Bennett inequality with user confidence \(\delta\):

\[\epsilon_{\text{cut}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2m} \ln\left(\frac{4 |W|}{\delta}\right)}\]

where \(m\) is the harmonic mean of the sub-window lengths. When this condition is met, older samples from \(W_0\) are discarded, confirming drift with rigorous theoretical error bounds.

docs.title: Unified Controller Arbitration (ULC)
docs.text:
In multi-pillar streaming systems, individual components operating in isolation often trigger catastrophic operational conflicts:

[ ALA: Rapid Adaptation ] <---- CONFLICT ----> [ RLA: Noise Insulation ]
"Tree detects drift, attempts reset"            "Downweights samples as corrupt noise"

If RLA filters out genuine drift instances as "noise", ALA never adapts. Conversely, if ALA treats random noise bursts as "drift", the model resets repeatedly, destroying historical memory.

docs.title: 1. Expected Utility Optimization
docs.text:
The Unified Learning Controller V5 (ULC-v5) formalizes all adaptation interventions as a constrained expected utility optimization problem:

\[U(\text{Action}) = \left(\text{Confidence} \times \text{Expected Benefit}\right) - \text{Operational Cost}\]
  • Operational Cost: Resetting a model incurs high cost (temporary accuracy drop while learning from scratch). Incremental updates incur zero cost.
  • Expected Benefit: Measured as a function of statistical drift magnitude \(\Delta_{\text{drift}}\) and recurring concept similarity \(\text{sim}\).
  • Evidence Confidence: Derived from multi-pillar consensus (ADWIN variance ratio, neighborhood agreement, margin distribution).

docs.title: 2. Five-Tier Intervention Hierarchy
docs.text:
Instead of binary adaptation (do nothing vs. wipe model), ULC-v5 chooses the lowest-impact intervention justified by the utility score:

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Tier 0: NOOP (Incremental Update)                                       |
| Cost: 0.00 | Action: Continue standard prequential streaming learning.   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    v (Mild elevation in error variance)
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Tier 1: PARAM_DAMPING                                                   |
| Cost: 0.05 | Action: Attenuate learning rates / sample weights (0.80x).  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    v (Statistical match with historical concept)
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Tier 2: CONCEPT_RESTORE                                                 |
| Cost: 0.15 | Action: Restore stored snapshot from memory; 0 retraining. |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    v (Moderate novel concept drift)
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Tier 3: SOFT_REPLAY_RESET                                               |
| Cost: 0.25 | Action: Reset active tree; warm-start from reservoir.     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    v (Extreme unrecoverable divergence)
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Tier 4: HARD_RESET                                                      |
| Cost: 0.70 | Action: Emergency complete purge of tree, buffer, and state|
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 3. Anti-Thrashing via Exponential Cooldown Backoff
docs.text:
Under adversarial noise, controllers can enter an infinite reset loop ("thrashing"), causing catastrophic performance collapse.

ULC-v5 prevents this by enforcing dynamic lockout: $\(\text{Cooldown Lockout} = \text{base\_cooldown} \times \min(4, \text{consecutive\_interventions})\)$ - When an intervention occurs, subsequent structural resets are locked out for the cooldown period. - Repeated triggers increase the lockout window up to \(4\times\). - When the stream returns to steady state (Tier 0), consecutive intervention counters decay cleanly to zero.

docs.title: Label Noise & Sample Reliability
docs.text: In real-world data streams, ground truth labels \(y \in \{0, \dots, K-1\}\) are frequently corrupted, producing an observed noisy label \(\tilde{y}\).

docs.title: 1. Noise Taxonomy
docs.text:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Uniform Symmetric Noise                                                 |
| Any true class k is flipped to any other class with equal probability: |
| P(y_tilde = j | y = k) = eta / (K - 1)                                   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Asymmetric (Class-Conditional) Noise                                    |
| Corruption probability depends specifically on the source and target:    |
| P(y_tilde = j | y = k) = T_{kj} (Transition Matrix T)                    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Instance-Dependent Feature Noise                                        |
| Corruption probability is a function of both features x and class y:    |
| P(y_tilde = j | x, y = k)                                               |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

In high-stakes domains (fraud detection, cybersecurity, medical imaging), label noise is almost always asymmetric: - Fraudulent transactions are often mistakenly labeled as legitimate (false negative in annotation). - Legitimate transactions are rarely mislabeled as fraud.

docs.title: 2. Multi-Signal Reliability Estimation
docs.text: AdaptiveML estimates the true reliability score \(r_i \in [0, 1]\) of each incoming sample by synthesizing three orthogonal signals:

docs.title: 1. Prediction Margin & Entropy
docs.text: High model certainty indicates high sample reliability: $\(s_{\text{margin}} = p_{(1)} - p_{(2)}\)$ where \(p_{(1)}\) and \(p_{(2)}\) are the top two predicted class probabilities.

docs.title: 2. Spatial Neighborhood Consistency (\(k\)-NN)
docs.text: The fraction of the sample's \(k\) nearest neighbors in feature space that agree with the reported label \(\tilde{y}_i\): $\(s_{\text{neighbor}} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_k(x_i)} \mathbb{I}(\tilde{y}_j = \tilde{y}_i)\)$

docs.title: 3. Temporal Consistency
docs.text: Agreement across sequential predictions over a sliding temporal buffer \(H_t\): $\(s_{\text{temporal}} = \frac{1}{|H_t|} \sum_{\tau \in H_t} \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_{\tau} = \tilde{y}_i)\)$

docs.title: Composite Reliability Score
docs.text:
The final scalar reliability is a weighted linear combination: $\(r_i = w_m s_{\text{margin}} + w_n s_{\text{neighbor}} + w_t s_{\text{temporal}}\)$

Samples with \(r_i < \tau_{\text{noise}}\) are either downweighted in the loss function or filtered out before training, insulating the model from corrupt updates.

docs.title: Concept: Resource-Aware Optimization (RAO)
docs.text: The Resource-Aware Optimization (RAO) pillar addresses high optimizer memory consumption and computational bottlenecks on commodity CPU architectures.

docs.title: The Memory Footprint of Adaptive Optimizers
docs.text:
In standard deep learning and gradient-based learning, the AdamW optimizer maintains two full-precision running moment vectors per model parameter: - First-order momentum: \(m_t \in \mathbb{R}^P\) (FP32, 4 bytes/parameter) - Second-order momentum: \(v_t \in \mathbb{R}^P\) (FP32, 4 bytes/parameter) $\(\text{Total Optimizer State RAM} = 8.000\text{ bytes per parameter}\)$

For a model with \(100\text{M}\) parameters, the optimizer state alone demands \(800\text{ MB}\) of memory—often exceeding available L3 cache and memory bandwidth on edge and CPU devices.

docs.title: 1. LowMemoryAdamW (LowMemoryAdamW)
docs.text:
A pure-CPU block-quantized optimizer that achieves an exact \(73.44\%\) memory reduction (\(2.125\text{ B/param}\) vs. \(8.00\text{ B/param}\)): - First Moment \(m_t\): Quantized into signed 8-bit integers (int8, 1 byte/param) over 256-element blocks. - Second Moment \(v_t\): Quantized into unsigned 8-bit integers (uint8, 1 byte/param) over 256-element blocks. - Scale Factors: Stored as FP32 per block (\(4\text{ bytes} / 256\text{ params} = 0.0156\text{ bytes/param}\)).

Standard AdamW (FP32):
[    m_t (4 bytes)    ][    v_t (4 bytes)    ]  = 8.00 B/param

LowMemoryAdamW:
[ m (1B) ][ v (1B) ][ scale (0.03B) ][ overhead ] = 2.125 B/param  (-73.44%)

Zero mandatory C++ compiler or CUDA dependencies required. Operates across PyTorch tensors and NumPy ndarrays.

docs.title: 2. Adaptive Gradient Accumulator (AdaptiveGradientAccumulator)
docs.text: Dynamically adjusts micro-batch size based on available system RAM and step execution time, preventing memory exhaustion while ensuring exact mathematical gradient equivalence.

docs.title: Hardware Scope, Measured Performance & Architectural Boundaries
Supported CPU Behavior
docs.text:
• Architecture Independence: Executes natively on any standard 64-bit CPU architecture (x86_64, aarch64, ARM Neoverse) without requiring CUDA, ROCm, or custom C++ build tools.
  • Resource Footprint: Operates within constrained environments starting at \(512\text{ MB}\) total system RAM.
  • Dependency Invariant: Relies strictly on NumPy \(\ge 1.24.0\) for SIMD-accelerated array operations.

docs.title: Measured Empirical Performance & Limitations
docs.text: Empirical benchmarks on an x86_64 CPU (32 logical cores, OpenBLAS) demonstrated strict linear scaling up to \(1\text{M}\) parameters with a sustained quantization throughput of \(\approx 9.7 - 9.9\text{ MParams/s}\): - \(1\text{K}\) parameters: \(0.12\text{ ms}\) step latency (\(8.68\text{ MParams/s}\)) - \(10\text{K}\) parameters: \(1.04\text{ ms}\) step latency (\(9.86\text{ MParams/s}\)) - \(100\text{K}\) parameters: \(10.36\text{ ms}\) step latency (\(9.88\text{ MParams/s}\)) - \(1\text{M}\) parameters: \(107.74\text{ ms}\) step latency (\(9.73\text{ MParams/s}\))

docs.title: Large-Model Boundaries & When to Use PyTorch Accelerators
docs.text: For models with more than \(5\text{M}\) to \(10\text{M}\) parameters, pure-CPU NumPy quantization incurs \(>500\text{ ms}\) latency per step due to CPU memory bus saturation and Python chunk iteration overhead. In deep learning workflows where GPU accelerators are present, users should utilize GPU-native quantized optimizers (such as bitsandbytes CUDA kernels) via AdaptiveML's PyTorch adapter (adaptive_ml.integrations.torch_optim). LowMemoryAdamW remains explicitly tailored for local-first, streaming, embedded, and CPU-bound workloads.

docs.title: Resource-Aware Optimization (RAO)
docs.text: Resource-Aware Optimization (RAO) focuses on maximizing computational throughput and minimizing RAM/VRAM consumption in continuous streaming and deep learning environments.

docs.title: 1. The Optimizer State Bottleneck
docs.text:
When training neural networks with standard AdamW, the memory consumed by the optimizer often far exceeds the model parameters:

[ Model Parameters: float32 ] ---> 4 bytes / parameter
[ First Moment m_t: float32 ] ---> 4 bytes / parameter
[ Second Moment v_t: float32 ] --> 4 bytes / parameter
-------------------------------------------------------
Total Memory per Parameter    ---> 12 bytes / parameter
Optimizer Overhead            ---> 8 bytes / parameter (66.7% of total!)

For a 100-million parameter model: - Model weights: \(400\text{ MB}\) - Optimizer state: \(800\text{ MB}\) - Combined footprint: \(1.2\text{ GB}\)

On edge devices, microservice pods, or constrained CPU instances, this optimizer state overhead frequently causes fatal Out-Of-Memory (OOM) failures.

docs.title: 2. 8-Bit Dynamic Block Quantization
docs.text:
AdaptiveML's VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW compresses optimizer moments into signed 8-bit integers (int8) and unsigned 8-bit integers (uint8) across contiguous blocks of size \(B_q = 64\):

Continuous Parameter Tensor (2D+ Dense Weights)
[================================================================]
         |
         v Split into Blocks of size B_q = 64
[ Block 0 ] [ Block 1 ] [ Block 2 ] ... [ Block N ]
    |
    +---> Compute local max absolute value: s_m = max(|m|) / 127
    +---> Quantize: q_m = round(m / s_m) in [-127, 127] (int8)
    +---> Compute local max value: s_v = max(v) / 255
    +---> Quantize: q_v = round(v / s_v) in [0, 255] (uint8)

docs.title: Memory Footprint Comparison
docs.text: State Component Standard 32-bit AdamW VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW First Moment \(m\) \(4.00\text{ bytes}\) \(1.0625\text{ bytes}\) (int8 + scale) Second Moment \(v\) \(4.00\text{ bytes}\) \(1.0625\text{ bytes}\) (uint8 + scale) Total Optimizer RAM \(8.00\text{ bytes/param}\) \(2.125\text{ bytes/param}\) Savings Baseline \(>73.4\%\) Reduction

docs.title: 3. Selective Quantization
docs.text:
Not all parameters can tolerate 8-bit quantization without precision degradation: - 2D+ Matrices (Linear weights, Conv kernels): Block-quantized to 8-bit. They contain thousands of weights, which dominate total RAM (\(>99\%\)) and exhibit high spatial redundancy. - 1D Tensors (Biases, LayerNorm, BatchNorm): Maintained in full 32-bit floating point precision (float32). They represent \(<1\%\) of total parameters but are hypersensitive to numeric rounding errors.

This selective policy delivers \(>71\%\) total memory savings while preserving convergence curves matching uncompressed 32-bit AdamW.

docs.title: Concept: Robust Learning Algorithms (RLA)
docs.text: The Robust Learning Algorithms (RLA) pillar provides mathematically grounded defenses against corrupted labels, adversarial outliers, and extreme class imbalance.

docs.title: The Noisy Label & Imbalance Dilemma
docs.text:
Standard Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) under standard Cross-Entropy (CE) loss is vulnerable to corrupted labels: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(p, y) = -\ln(p_y)\)$ When a model encounters a mislabeled instance (\(p_y \approx 0\)), \(-\ln(p_y) \rightarrow \infty\), yielding unbounded gradient updates that corrupt model representations.

Furthermore, naive noise cleaning algorithms discard low-probability samples. In heavily imbalanced streams (\(100:1\)), rare minority instances are falsely diagnosed as mislabeled noise, resulting in total minority class elimination.

docs.title: 1. Density-Aware Margin Scorer (DensityAwareMarginScorer)
docs.text:
Couples prediction logit margins with local feature-space \(k\)-NN density: $\(r_i = \sigma\left(\alpha \cdot \text{Margin}(x_i) + \beta \cdot \text{LocalDensity}(x_i)\right)\)$ - Corrupted samples in dense regions have low margin and high surrounding support, yielding low reliability (\(r_i \approx 0\)). - Valid minority samples have low margin but reside in sparse clusters consistent with their class, yielding high reliability (\(r_i \approx 1\)).

Theorem 2 Guarantee: Density-aware margin scoring is proven to preserve minority recall under severe class imbalance and label noise (empirically confirmed: \(60.0\%\) minority recall vs. \(0.0\%\) for standard ERM).

docs.title: 2. Symmetric Cross-Entropy Loss (SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss)
docs.text: Combines standard Cross-Entropy with Reverse Cross-Entropy (RCE): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{SCE}}(p, q) = \alpha \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(p, q) + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\text{RCE}}(p, q) = -\alpha \sum_k q_k \ln p_k - \beta \sum_k p_k \ln q_k\)$ Reverse Cross-Entropy bounds the maximum gradient under corrupted labels, providing robust convergence under symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent label noise.

docs.title: Concept: Unified Learning Controller (ULC)
docs.text: The Unified Learning Controller (ULC) is an optional coordination layer that resolves conflicts between drift adaptation, noise filtering, and resource constraints.

docs.title: The Fundamental Conflict: Drift vs. Noise
docs.text:
When prediction error spikes in a streaming environment, two opposing hypotheses exist: 1. Hypothesis 1 (Concept Drift): The distribution changed. The model must adapt rapidly or discard old weights. 2. Hypothesis 2 (Noise Burst): A transient burst of corrupted labels occurred. The model must freeze updates or filter samples.

Executing drift adaptation during a noise burst causes catastrophic forgetting: the model learns incorrect labels and wipes valid historical knowledge. Conversely, executing noise filtering during genuine drift causes adaptation failure: the model stubbornly ignores new concepts.

docs.title: The ULC Dual-Evidence Arbitration Automaton
docs.text: The ArbitrationAutomaton evaluates a 4-dimensional normalized evidence vector \(E_t = [e_{\text{entropy}}, e_{\text{trend}}, e_{\text{density}}, e_{\text{mem}}]\): - Predictive Entropy (\(e_{\text{entropy}}\)): High entropy across inputs suggests genuine structural uncertainty (concept drift). - Loss Trend (\(e_{\text{trend}}\)): A sustained elevation indicates drift; an isolated spike indicates label noise.

docs.title: 5-State Operational Model
docs.text:
+-------------------+
            |    STATIONARY     |
            +---------+---------+
                      |
           Prediction Error Spike
                      v
            +-------------------+
            |     WARNING       | <---+  (Hysteresis deadband)
            +---------+---------+     |
                      |               |
          Evidence Arbitration        |
         /                     \      |
        v                       v     |
+---------------+       +---------------+
|     DRIFT     |       |  NOISE BURST  |
+---------------+       +---------------+
  1. STATIONARY: Standard incremental learning and gradient updates.
  2. WARNING: Elevated error rate; initiates evaluation window with hysteresis deadband \(\Delta_{\text{hyst}} = 0.15\).
  3. DRIFT: Genuine concept drift confirmed. Triggers adaptation directives (TRIGGER_DRIFT_ADAPTATION, adjust tree split parameters).
  4. NOISE_BURST: Corrupted burst detected. Directs RLA pipeline to filter samples (DISCARD_CORRUPTED_SAMPLE) and suppress ADWIN drift triggers.
  5. RECOVERY: Controlled cooldown period preventing oscillatory re-triggers.

docs.title: 3. Key Algorithmic Innovations Ratified
docs.text:
1. ALA: Vectorized Hoeffding Tree Splitting:
  2. Replaced single-instance Python dictionary traversals with contiguous 3D NumPy histogram arrays (\(\mathbf{S}_u \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times K \times C}\)), achieving \(8\times\) to \(25\times\) higher streaming batch ingestion throughput.
  3. ALA: Reliability-Weighted ADWIN (RW-ADWIN):
  4. Formulated sub-window cut bounds scaled by Kish's effective sample sizes \(N_{\text{eff}}\), provably suppressing noise-induced false drift alarms on dirty streams.
  5. RLA: Density-Aware Margin Reliability Scoring:
  6. Coupled normalized logit margins with local \(k\)-NN feature space density ratios (\(\rho_k\)), mathematically guaranteeing that legitimate rare-class instances are not misclassified as noise.
  7. RLA: Strictly Bounded Robust Losses (SCE & GCE):
  8. Derived closed-form analytical gradients whose \(L_2\) norm is bounded by \(2\alpha + \beta |\ln(\epsilon_{\text{clip}})| \sqrt{C}\), preventing gradient explosion under arbitrary label flips.
  9. RAO: CPU Block-Quantized AdamW (LowMemoryAdamW):
  10. Partitioned optimizer states into 256-element blocks, quantizing momentum into signed int8 and variance into unsigned uint8. Reduced state memory by 74.6% (\(2.031p\) bytes vs \(8.0p\) bytes) in pure vector NumPy/PyTorch with zero custom C++ compiler dependencies.
  11. ULC: Dual-Evidence In-Loop Arbitration Automaton:
  12. Formulated a 5-state finite automaton (\(\mathcal{S} \times [0, 1]^4 \to \mathcal{S}\)) with hysteresis deadbands, resolving the fundamental dilemma between concept drift adaptation and label noise suppression.

docs.title: 4. Key Architectural Decisions Ratified
docs.text:
1. Minimal Mandatory Dependencies: Strictly numpy >= 1.24.0 in core; PyTorch and scikit-learn are optional, lazily-loaded integration extras.
  2. Zero Mandatory C++ Compilation: Core speed is achieved through vectorized C-contiguous array layouts and SIMD loop unrolling, guaranteeing universal, compiler-free installation across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ARM.
  3. Safe Serialization Standard: Complete prohibition of Python pickle on untrusted data; all serialization uses safe Safetensors binary tensors paired with JSON schemas.
  4. Air-Gapped Zero-Telemetry: Prohibited all external network calls and telemetry; certified 100% air-gappable.
  5. Mandatory 5-Seed Scientific Reproducibility: All benchmark validations must run across five fixed seeds (\(\{42, 1337, 2024, 7, 999\}\)).

docs.title: 1. Executive Pillar Architecture
docs.text:
The Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA) pillar provides online learning, concept drift adaptation, and continuous knowledge retention under changing data distributions without requiring historical data re-storage.

The pillar comprises three mathematically synchronized algorithm specifications: 1. VectorizedHoeffdingTree / StreamingTreeEnsemble: Vectorized streaming decision trees executing Hoeffding-bound splitting over contiguous 2D NumPy arrays. 2. ReliabilityWeightedADWIN (RW-ADWIN): An adaptive sliding window drift detector that weights error signals by sample reliability to suppress false-positive resets caused by label noise. 3. ClassBalancedReservoirReplay: A bounded-memory experience replay buffer executing stratified reservoir retention to prevent catastrophic forgetting.

                                   │
              Input Stream Batch (X_tau, y_tau) [B x d]
                                   │
                 ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
                 ▼                                   ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐
    │  Vectorized Sufficient  │         │   Loss Computation &    │
    │    Statistics Update    │         │  Reliability Weighting  │
    └────────────┬────────────┘         └────────────┬────────────┘
                 ▼                                   ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐
    │  Hoeffding Bound Check  │         │  RW-ADWIN Drift Check   │
    │  (Split / Defer / Leaf) │         │ (Confidence Cut Bound)  │
    └────────────┬────────────┘         └────────────┬────────────┘
                 │                                   │
                 ▼                                   ▼
       Updated Tree Structure               Drift Alert & Scale Factor

docs.title: 2.1 Formal Problem Definition
docs.text: Let a data stream generate instances sequentially: \((\mathbf{x}_t, y_t) \sim P_t(\mathbf{x}, y)\) with \(\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(y_t \in \{0, \dots, C-1\}\). The objective is to incrementally induce an optimal decision tree classifier \(f_t: \mathbb{R}^d \to \Delta^{C-1}\) such that: $\(\lim_{t \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_{(\mathbf{x}, y) \sim \mathcal{D}}\left( \arg\max_{c} f_t(\mathbf{x})_c \ne y \right) = \inf_{f \in \mathcal{F}_{\text{tree}}} \mathbb{P}\left( \arg\max_c f(\mathbf{x})_c \ne y \right)\)$ subject to the constraints: 1. Each instance or mini-batch \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d}\) is processed in \(\mathcal{O}(B \cdot d \cdot K)\) time (\(K\) being quantile bins). 2. Historical samples are discarded immediately after the statistics update. 3. The tree structure asymptotically converges to the batch-optimal decision tree with high probability \(1 - \delta\).

docs.title: 2.2.1 Hoeffding Bound Condition
docs.text:
Let \(G(X_j, s)\) denote the split evaluation heuristic (Information Gain or Gini Impurity Reduction) for splitting attribute \(X_j\) at threshold \(s\). At any leaf node \(u\) with accumulated sample count \(n_u \ge n_{\min}\), let: - \(X_a = \arg\max_{X_j} G(X_j)\) (best candidate split) - \(X_b = \arg\max_{X_j \ne X_a} G(X_j)\) (second-best candidate split) - \(\Delta \bar{G} = \bar{G}(X_a) - \bar{G}(X_b) \ge 0\)

By the Hoeffding Inequality, the true difference between the expected split values satisfies: $\(\mathbb{P}\left( \Delta \mathbb{E}[G] < \Delta \bar{G} - \epsilon_H \right) \le \delta\)$ where the Hoeffding error bound \(\epsilon_H\) is given by: $\(\epsilon_H = \sqrt{\frac{R_G^2 \cdot \ln(1 / \delta)}{2 n_u}}\)$ where \(R_G\) is the dynamic range of the heuristic: $\(R_G = \begin{cases} \ln(C), & \text{if } G \text{ is Information Gain} \\ 1.0 - \frac{1}{C}, & \text{if } G \text{ is Gini Impurity} \end{cases}\)$

docs.title: 2.2.2 Splitting Decision Rule
docs.text: A split on \(X_a\) is executed if and only if: $\(\Delta \bar{G} > \epsilon_H \quad \lor \quad \epsilon_H < \tau_H\)$ where \(\tau_H \in (0, 0.1]\) is a predefined tie-breaking threshold preventing indefinite starvation when two attributes exhibit near-identical split quality.

docs.title: 2.3 Vectorized Sufficient Statistics (2D NumPy Matrix Representation)
docs.text:
Traditional streaming trees (e.g., in River) iterate sample-by-sample through Python dictionary mappings. AdaptiveML formalizes a contiguous tensor sufficient statistic.

For each leaf node \(u\), feature \(j \in \{1, \dots, d\}\), discretization bin \(k \in \{1, \dots, K\}\), and target class \(c \in \{0, \dots, C-1\}\): $\(\mathbf{S}_u \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times K \times C}\)$ where entry \(S_u[j, k, c]\) holds the count of instances reaching node \(u\) with feature \(X_j\) falling into bin \(k\) and having true label \(y = c\).

docs.title: 2.3.1 Vectorized Batch Accumulation
docs.text: Given mini-batch \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d}\) and one-hot labels \(\mathbf{Y} \in \{0, 1\}^{B \times C}\) mapped to leaf \(u\): 1. Quantize continuous features into integer bin indices via pre-computed quantile edges \(\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times (K-1)}\): $\(\mathbf{K}_{\text{idx}} = \text{digitize}(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{E}) \in \{0, \dots, K-1\}^{B \times d}\)$ 2. Vectorized histogram accumulation: $\(S_u[j, k, c] \leftarrow S_u[j, k, c] + \sum_{b=1}^B \mathbb{I}\left( K_{\text{idx}}[b, j] = k \right) \cdot Y[b, c]\)$ Implemented via NumPy np.add.at or vectorized flat bincount without Python loops.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Split Evaluation via Matrix Reduction
docs.text: For attribute \(j\) at split bin \(s \in \{0, \dots, K-2\}\): - Left partition class counts: \(\mathbf{c}_L(s) = \sum_{k=0}^s \mathbf{S}_u[j, k, :] \in \mathbb{R}^C\) - Right partition class counts: \(\mathbf{c}_R(s) = \sum_{k=s+1}^{K-1} \mathbf{S}_u[j, k, :] \in \mathbb{R}^C\) - Total partition weights: \(n_L = \sum_{c=0}^{C-1} c_L(s)_c\), \(n_R = \sum_{c=0}^{C-1} c_R(s)_c\), \(n = n_L + n_R\). - Gini Impurity: $\(\text{Gini}(\mathbf{c}) = 1 - \sum_{c=0}^{C-1} \left(\frac{c_c}{n}\right)^2\)$ $\(\bar{G}(X_j, s) = \text{Gini}(\mathbf{c}_{\text{total}}) - \left[ \frac{n_L}{n} \text{Gini}(\mathbf{c}_L(s)) + \frac{n_R}{n} \text{Gini}(\mathbf{c}_R(s)) \right]\)$ All candidate splits across all \(d\) features and \(K\) thresholds are evaluated simultaneously via vectorized matrix broadcasting in \(\mathcal{O}(d \cdot K \cdot C)\) operations.

docs.title: 2.4 Mathematical Invariants & Failure Modes
docs.text:
1. Conservation Invariant: \(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \sum_{c=0}^{C-1} S_u[j, k, c] = n_u \quad \forall j \in \{1, \dots, d\}\).
  2. Failure Mode 1 (Quantization Boundary Drift): If the streaming distribution undergoes extreme feature scale expansion, fixed quantile edges lead to boundary saturation. Mitigation: Adaptive dynamic quantile estimation using a P-Square or t-digest online sketch updated at leaf nodes.
  3. Failure Mode 2 (Split Starvation on Noise): When attribute noise is perfectly uniform across classes, \(\Delta \bar{G} \approx 0\), causing \(\epsilon_H\) to govern until \(n_u \to \infty\). Mitigation: Enforced tie-breaking condition \(\epsilon_H < \tau_H\) with maximum leaf depth limit \(D_{\max}\).

docs.title: 3.1 Problem Definition & Limitations of Standard ADWIN
docs.text:
Standard ADWIN maintains a variable-length window \(W\) of scalar real values \(z_t \in [0, 1]\) (e.g. 0-1 loss). When the window is partitioned into \(W = W_0 \cdot W_1\), it detects drift whenever: $\(|\hat{\mu}_{W_0} - \hat{\mu}_{W_1}| \ge \epsilon_{\text{cut}}\)$

Vulnerability: Under random label corruption (e.g., label flip probability \(\eta = 0.2\)), a burst of mislabeled instances induces an artificial jump in window loss \(\hat{\mu}_{W_1}\), triggering false-positive drift alarms and unnecessary model resets.

docs.title: 3.2 Formal Mathematical Derivation of RW-ADWIN
docs.text: Let each observation in window \(W\) consist of a pair: \((z_t, r_t)\) where: - \(z_t \in [0, 1]\) is the learner's instantaneous loss or error signal. - \(r_t \in [\epsilon_r, 1]\) is the sample reliability score supplied by the RLA pillar (\(\epsilon_r > 0\) ensures non-zero support).

docs.title: 3.2.1 Weighted Window Partition Statistics
docs.text: For any partition \(W = W_0 \cdot W_1\): - Sum of weights: \(S_r(W_k) = \sum_{t \in W_k} r_t\) for \(k \in \{0, 1\}\). - Weighted mean: $\(\hat{\mu}_{W_k}^{(r)} = \frac{1}{S_r(W_k)} \sum_{t \in W_k} r_t z_t\)$ - Effective sample size (Kish's Effective Sample Formula): $\(N_{\text{eff}}(W_k) = \frac{\left( \sum_{t \in W_k} r_t \right)^2}{\sum_{t \in W_k} r_t^2} \le |W_k|\)$ - Harmonic effective sample size: $\(m_{\text{eff}} = \left( \frac{1}{N_{\text{eff}}(W_0)} + \frac{1}{N_{\text{eff}}(W_1)} \right)^{-1} = \frac{N_{\text{eff}}(W_0) \cdot N_{\text{eff}}(W_1)}{N_{\text{eff}}(W_0) + N_{\text{eff}}(W_1)}\)$

docs.title: 3.2.2 Reliability-Weighted Cut Bound
docs.text: By applying the weighted Hoeffding-Azuma inequality for bounded martingales, the difference between the true weighted expectations is bounded by: $\(\epsilon_{\text{cut}}^{(r)} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2 m_{\text{eff}}} \ln\left( \frac{4 |W|}{\delta} \right)}\)$

docs.title: 3.2.3 Drift Trigger Condition
docs.text: A concept drift is declared if and only if: $\(\left| \hat{\mu}_{W_0}^{(r)} - \hat{\mu}_{W_1}^{(r)} \right| \ge \epsilon_{\text{cut}}^{(r)}\)$

docs.title: 3.2.4 Theorem: False-Alarm Suppression Under Bursty Noise
docs.text: Theorem 1: Let clean data have error mean \(\mu_0\). Suppose an adversarial burst of \(M\) mislabeled instances with error \(z_t = 1\) is injected into \(W_1\). If the RLA module assigns reliability \(r_t \le \epsilon_r \ll 1\) to corrupted instances, the distortion in the test statistic satisfies: $\(\left| \hat{\mu}_{W_1}^{(r)} - \mu_0 \right| \le \frac{\epsilon_r M}{S_r(W_1^{\text{clean}}) + \epsilon_r M} \cdot (1 - \mu_0) \ll \frac{M}{|W_1^{\text{clean}}| + M} \cdot (1 - \mu_0)\)$ Consequently, the probability of false drift detection \(\mathbb{P}_{\text{false}}\) decays exponentially with \(\frac{1}{\epsilon_r}\), provably suppressing noise-induced resets.

docs.title: 4.1 Problem Definition
docs.text: Continuous stream learning suffers from catastrophic forgetting of rare or historical modes. Standard reservoir sampling (Vitter's Algorithm R) samples uniformly from stream history: $\(P(\text{retain instance } t) = \frac{M_{\text{buf}}}{t} \quad \text{for } t > M_{\text{buf}}\)$ Under severe class imbalance (e.g. minority class ratio 1:100), uniform reservoir sampling results in the minority class representation decaying to \(\frac{M_{\text{buf}}}{100}\), leading to complete loss of minority decision boundaries.

docs.title: 4.2 Class-Balanced Reservoir Retention Policy
docs.text: We define a partitioned reservoir buffer \(\mathcal{B}\) with fixed total capacity \(M_{\text{buf}}\): $\(\mathcal{B} = \bigcup_{c=0}^{C-1} \mathcal{B}_c, \quad |\mathcal{B}| = \sum_{c=0}^{C-1} |\mathcal{B}_c| \le M_{\text{buf}}\)$ where each class bucket \(\mathcal{B}_c\) has dynamic capacity allocation \(M_c(t)\): $\(M_c(t) = \max\left( \left\lfloor \frac{M_{\text{buf}}}{C} \right\rfloor, \; 1 \right)\)$ ensuring that rare classes are guaranteed at least \(\frac{1}{C}\) of total buffer capacity regardless of stream arrival frequency.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Insertion and Replacement Mechanics
docs.text: Let stream instance \((\mathbf{x}_t, y_t)\) arrive with class \(y_t = c\): 1. Let \(n_c(t)\) denote the total number of class \(c\) instances observed since stream initialization. 2. If \(|\mathcal{B}_c| < M_c\): - Insert \((\mathbf{x}_t, y_t)\) directly into \(\mathcal{B}_c\). 3. Else (\(|\mathcal{B}_c| = M_c\)): - Draw random integer \(k \sim \text{Uniform}(1, n_c(t))\). - If \(k \le M_c\): - Replace element \(\mathcal{B}_c[k]\) with \((\mathbf{x}_t, y_t)\). - Else: - Discard \((\mathbf{x}_t, y_t)\).

docs.title: 4.2.2 Stratified Replay Batch Generation
docs.text: During any mini-batch update with incoming batch size \(B\), the learner samples a replay batch \(\mathbf{Z}_{\text{replay}}\) of size \(B_{\text{replay}} = \lfloor \alpha_{\text{rep}} \cdot B \rfloor\) from \(\mathcal{B}\): 1. Uniformly draw \(\lfloor B_{\text{replay}} / C \rfloor\) samples from each non-empty bucket \(\mathcal{B}_c\). 2. Form composite training batch: \(\mathbf{Z}_{\text{train}} = \mathbf{Z}_{\text{stream}} \cup \mathbf{Z}_{\text{replay}}\). 3. Total memory footprint is strictly bounded: $\(\text{RAM}(\mathcal{B}) = M_{\text{buf}} \cdot (d \cdot 8_{\text{bytes}} + 8_{\text{bytes}}) = \mathcal{O}(M_{\text{buf}} \cdot d) \le M_{\max}\)$

docs.title: 5. Summary of Mathematical Guarantees
docs.text: Algorithm Component Time Complexity (per batch \(B\)) Space Complexity Guarantees / Bounds VectorizedHoeffdingTree \(\mathcal{O}(B \cdot d + d \cdot K \cdot C)\) \(\mathcal{O}(U \cdot d \cdot K \cdot C)\) Error rate bounded by \(\delta\) via Hoeffding inequality ReliabilityWeightedADWIN $\mathcal{O}(\log W )$ amortized ClassBalancedReservoirReplay \(\mathcal{O}(B_{\text{replay}})\) \(\mathcal{O}(M_{\text{buf}} \cdot d)\) Exact uniform sampling per class; bounded memory \(M_{\text{buf}}\)

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Vision
docs.text:
The Algorithm Design Document (ADD) unifies the mathematical foundations, formal objectives, algorithmic formulations, and computational complexity proofs of AdaptiveML: an open-source, local-first, CPU-first Python algorithm library.

AdaptiveML addresses three fundamental failure modes in real-world machine learning: 1. Distribution Non-Stationarity: Data distributions change over time (concept drift, covariate shift), degrading static models. 2. Data Imperfection & Contamination: Real-world streams suffer from bursty label corruption, uncalibrated outliers, and severe class imbalance that mislead standard loss functions. 3. Hardware & Memory Constraints: Real-world deployment on CPU workstations, laptops, and edge containers cannot accommodate memory-heavy optimizers or complex C++ compiler toolchains.

To resolve these challenges without vendor lock-in or mandatory cloud telemetry, AdaptiveML formulates four self-contained algorithmic pillars: - ALA (Adaptive Learning Algorithms): Streaming decision trees with vectorized 2D NumPy array matrix updates, reliability-weighted drift detection (RW-ADWIN), and class-balanced reservoir replay. - RLA (Robust Learning Algorithms): Density-aware margin reliability scoring, symmetric and generalized robust loss functions (SCE/GCE), and class-balanced loss reweighting. - RAO (Resource-Aware Optimization): Pure NumPy/PyTorch CPU block-quantized AdamW (LowMemoryAdamW) achieving 74.6% optimizer state memory reduction, paired with dynamic memory-governed gradient accumulation. - ULC (Unified Learning Controller): An optional finite-state arbitration automaton resolving the fundamental dilemma between concept drift adaptation and label noise suppression.

docs.title: 3. Pillar 1: ALA — Adaptive Learning Algorithms
docs.text:
Full formal derivation: DOC-DES-P6-003.

  1. VectorizedHoeffdingTree:
  2. Updates contiguous 3D sufficient statistics tensors \(\mathbf{S}_u \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times K \times C}\) in vectorized NumPy arrays, replacing single-instance Python dictionary traversal.
  3. Evaluates Hoeffding splitting criterion: $\(\Delta \bar{G} = \bar{G}(X_a) - \bar{G}(X_b) > \epsilon_H = \sqrt{\frac{R_G^2 \ln(1 / \delta)}{2 n_u}}\)$

  4. Provides an asymptotic guarantee that stream-induced trees converge to batch trees with probability \(\ge 1 - \delta\) while delivering \(8\times\) to \(25\times\) higher throughput than River.

  5. ReliabilityWeightedADWIN (RW-ADWIN):

  6. Evaluates sub-window partitions \(W = W_0 \cdot W_1\) weighted by sample reliability \(r_t \in [\epsilon_r, 1.0]\).
  7. Harmonic effective sample size \(m_{\text{eff}} = \frac{N_{\text{eff}}(W_0) N_{\text{eff}}(W_1)}{N_{\text{eff}}(W_0) + N_{\text{eff}}(W_1)}\), with cut bound: $\(\epsilon_{\text{cut}}^{(r)} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2 m_{\text{eff}}} \ln\left( \frac{4 |W|}{\delta} \right)}\)$

  8. Proves exponential decay of noise-induced false alarms under bursty label corruption.

  9. ClassBalancedReservoirReplay:

  10. Enforces a strict memory bound \(M_{\text{buf}}\) partitioned into \(C\) class buckets of size \(M_{\text{buf}} / C\).
  11. Preserves rare-class representations on long-tailed streams via class-stratified reservoir retention.

docs.title: 4. Pillar 2: RLA — Robust Learning Algorithms
docs.text:
Full formal derivation: DOC-DES-P6-004.

  1. DensityAwareMarginScorer:
  2. Overcomes the limitation of traditional noise filters (e.g. Cleanlab) that incorrectly discard legitimate minority class samples.
  3. Computes normalized signed logit margin \(\tilde{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\) and relative \(k\)-NN feature space density ratio \(\delta_k(\mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{\rho_k(\mathbf{x}_i)}{\bar{\rho}_{\text{batch}}}\).
  4. Closed-form reliability score: $\(r_i = \sigma\left( \alpha \tilde{\mathcal{M}}_i - \gamma \ln(\delta_k(\mathbf{x}_i) + \epsilon) \right)\)$

  5. Mathematically guarantees protection of low-density rare instances against noise deletion (Theorem 2).

  6. SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss (SCE) & GeneralizedCrossEntropyLoss (GCE):

  7. Combines Cross Entropy with Reverse Cross Entropy: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{SCE}} = \alpha \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\text{RCE}}\).

  8. Derives analytical logit gradients whose \(L_2\) norm is strictly bounded by \(2\alpha + \beta |\ln(\epsilon_{\text{clip}})| \sqrt{C}\), preventing gradient explosion under arbitrary label corruption.

  9. ClassBalancedReweighting:

  10. Applies the effective number of samples formulation: \(W_c = \frac{1 - \beta}{1 - \beta^{n_c}}\) to prevent rare-class gradient starvation.

docs.title: 5. Pillar 3: RAO — Resource-Aware Optimization
docs.text:
Full formal derivation: DOC-DES-P6-005.

  1. LowMemoryAdamW:
  2. Pure NumPy / PyTorch CPU block quantization over non-overlapping parameter blocks of size \(B_q = 256\).
  3. First moment \(\mathbf{m}_t\) quantized to signed 8-bit integers (int8, \(q_{\max} = 127\)).
  4. Second moment \(\mathbf{v}_t\) quantized to unsigned 8-bit integers (uint8, \(q_{\max} = 255\)).
  5. Reduces persistent optimizer state memory from \(8.0 \, p\) bytes down to \(2.031 \, p\) bytes (74.6% RAM savings).

  6. Proves stationary point convergence on \(L\)-smooth non-convex objectives with negligible asymptotic bias \(\mathcal{O}(10^{-5} G_\infty^2)\) (Theorem 3).

  7. AdaptiveGradientAccumulator:

  8. Dynamically modulates micro-batch size \(B_{\text{phys}}\) and accumulation steps \(K_{\text{accum}}\) in response to host RAM telemetry, ensuring zero mathematical distortion to gradient trajectories.

docs.title: 6. Pillar 4: ULC — Unified Learning Controller
docs.text:
Full formal derivation: DOC-DES-P6-006.

  1. Dual-Evidence Arbitration Automaton:
  2. Synthesizes normalized drift evidence \(\Delta_{\text{drift}}\) from ALA and mean sample reliability \(\bar{R}_{\mathcal{W}}\) from RLA into a 5-state finite automaton \(\mathcal{S} \times [0, 1]^4 \to \mathcal{S}\).
  3. Distinctly disambiguates:
    • Real Concept Drift: High error (\(\Delta_{\text{drift}} \ge 1.0\)) + High Reliability (\(\bar{R}_{\mathcal{W}} \ge \tau_R\)) \(\implies\) Transition to \(S_2\) (CONFIRMED_DRIFT), boost learning rate, adapt model.
    • Label Noise Burst: High error (\(\Delta_{\text{drift}} \ge 1.0\)) + Low Reliability (\(\bar{R}_{\mathcal{W}} < \tau_R\)) \(\implies\) Transition to \(S_3\) (NOISE_BURST), suppress drift reset, filter corrupt samples.
  4. Enforces a hysteresis deadband \(\Delta_{\text{hyst}} = 0.15\) and recovery dwell counter \(c_{\text{dwell}}\) to mathematically eliminate chattering and limit transition frequency (Theorem 4).

docs.title: 7. Cross-Pillar Invariants and Decoupling Guarantees
docs.text:
Full formal derivation: DOC-DES-P6-007.

AdaptiveML rigorously guarantees complete modular decoupling: - ALA operates standalone using fallback reliability \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{1}\). - RLA operates standalone on static or streaming batches without temporal indices. - RAO functions as a drop-in replacement optimizer for any model architecture. - ULC is strictly optional and orchestrates through clean numeric control structs without coupling concrete implementations.

docs.title: 8. Testable Algorithmic Hypotheses
docs.text:
The mathematical formulations establish three primary testable empirical hypotheses:

  1. Hypothesis H-1 (Minority Protection under Noise):

    On CIFAR-100-LT with 20% symmetric label noise, models trained using DensityAwareMarginScorer + SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss will achieve \(\ge 12\%\) higher minority-class top-1 recall than Cleanlab Confident Learning or standard CE.

  2. Hypothesis H-2 (False-Alarm Suppression under Drift + Noise):

    On a streaming benchmark featuring synthetic SEA concepts interleaved with 25% bursty label flips, the ULC arbitration automaton will reduce false-positive drift alarms by \(\ge 80\%\) compared to standard ADWIN without increasing detection lag on true concept shifts by more than 50 steps.

  3. Hypothesis H-3 (CPU Optimizer Memory & Convergence Equivalence):

    LowMemoryAdamW will reduce optimizer state RAM by \(\ge 70\%\) while reaching within \(0.5\%\) of standard FP32 AdamW validation loss within identical epoch counts across Transformer and ResNet training benchmarks on CPU.
