docs.title: AdaptiveML — Security & Supply Chain Architecture
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 7) Document Identifier: DOC-DES-P7-010 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Scope: Local-first security boundaries, zero-telemetry enforcement, supply chain integrity, and clean-room IP Target Audience: Security Engineers, Release Managers, Legal Counsel

docs.title: 1. Security Architecture Principles
docs.text: AdaptiveML enforces four foundational security principles: 1. Zero-Telemetry Boundary: The library contains zero analytics, tracking, telemetry, or network-bound callouts. It is 100% air-gappable by design. 2. Safe Deserialization: Rejection of Python pickle on untrusted inputs, eliminating deserialization Remote Code Execution (RCE) vectors. 3. Minimal Attack Surface: The core runtime relies on a single external dependency (numpy), dramatically reducing supply-chain vulnerability exposure. 4. Clean-Room IP Governance: Strict adherence to the Apache-2.0 license, ensuring no code is derived or copy-pasted from copyleft (AGPL) libraries (such as Cleanlab).

docs.title: 2. Air-Gapped Zero-Telemetry Verification
docs.text: AdaptiveML undergoes automated static analysis in continuous integration (CI) to verify zero network access: - Socket Prohibition: Static AST scanning verifies that modules do not import socket, urllib, requests, aiohttp, or httpx in runtime packages. - Subprocess Lockdown: Modules in adaptive_ml/ are prohibited from invoking subprocess, os.system, or shell execution commands. - Air-Gapped Test Runner: Test suites execute with simulated network disconnection (--network-none in container builds) to verify that zero tests or initializers attempt external connections.

docs.title: 3. Safe Deserialization Security Protocol
docs.text: Model serialization vulnerabilities represent the primary threat vector in modern ML infrastructure. AdaptiveML mitigates this threat via the Safetensors standard: 1. Header Length Enforcement: Deserialization limits the metadata header to a maximum of 10 MB to prevent memory-exhaustion denial-of-service attacks. 2. Memory Offset Validation: Validates that all tensor byte offsets fall strictly within the physical bounds of the file, preventing out-of-bounds memory reads. 3. Pure Numeric Array Storage: Deserializes only fixed-type numerical arrays (float32, int8, uint8, int64), preventing arbitrary Python code execution.

docs.title: 4.1 Dependency Locking & Vulnerability Auditing
docs.text:
• Production dependencies are pinned with SHA-256 integrity hashes using uv or pip-compile --generate-hashes.
  • Continuous integration automatically runs pip-audit on every commit, blocking merges if any known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) exist in the dependency tree.

docs.title: 4.2 Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
docs.text:
• Every release artifact generates an automated CycloneDX (sbom.json) and SPDX (sbom.spdx) document.
  • Cryptographically signed release hashes are published via Sigstore/cosign on GitHub Releases.

docs.title: 5. Clean-Room IP Governance Matrix
docs.text: Following the findings of Phase 3 (DOC-RES-P3-001 through DOC-RES-P3-008): - All RLA algorithms (Margin Scoring, GCE, SCE, Class-Balanced Weights) are derived clean-room from primary academic literature (e.g., Wang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018; Cui et al., 2019). - Cleanlab code (licensed under AGPL-3.0) is quarantined; zero lines of code, variable identifiers, or internal architectures from Cleanlab are utilized. - All original AdaptiveML code is published strictly under the Apache License, Version 2.0.

docs.title: AdaptiveML — State Lifecycle & Serialization Architecture
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 7) Document Identifier: DOC-DES-P7-006 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Scope: State persistence, checkpoint formats, memory snapshots, and safe deserialization Security Posture: Zero Python pickle on untrusted input; safe binary + JSON serialization

docs.title: 1. State Lifecycle Architecture
docs.text:
AdaptiveML components maintain well-defined internal state lifecycles:

+─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
|                            STATE LIFECYCLE PHASES                           |
+─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+

   1. UNINITIALIZED  ──►  2. INITIALIZED  ──►  3. ACTIVE_STREAMING
                                                     │         ▲
                                                     ▼         │
                                               4. CHECKPOINTED
                                                     │
                                                     ▼
                                               5. TERMINATED
  1. Uninitialized: Configuration passed to __init__; buffers not yet allocated.
  2. Initialized: Memory buffers allocated upon first call to partial_fit or step when feature dimensions (\(d, C, p\)) are verified.
  3. Active Streaming: Dynamic state updates occur in-place during stream ingestion.
  4. Checkpointed: State serialized to disk or snapshot buffer for fault recovery.
  5. Terminated: Resources released; memory buffers deallocated.

docs.title: 2.1 The Vulnerability of Python pickle
docs.text: Standard Python serialization (pickle, joblib, dill) allows arbitrary object instantiation and is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution (RCE) via malicious payloads embedded in model files. Because AdaptiveML is designed for production streaming pipelines ingesting untrusted external data, unvalidated pickle serialization is strictly prohibited.

docs.title: 2.2 Dual-File Safe Storage Format
docs.text:
AdaptiveML serializes model state into a paired directory or zip bundle containing two safe files:

  1. metadata.json (Plain Text JSON):
  2. Schema version ("format_version": "1.0.0").
  3. Component class identifier ("component": "AdaptiveClassifier").
  4. Hyperparameter configuration dictionary.
  5. Symbolic tree structure (node IDs, split features, threshold values, child pointers).
  6. Controller state and dwell counters.
  7. tensors.safetensors (or raw binary .bin):
  8. Stores all multidimensional numeric arrays (leaf sufficient statistics \(\mathbf{S}_u\), reservoir feature arrays \(\mathbf{X}_{\text{buf}}\), quantized optimizer states \(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}, \tilde{\mathbf{v}}\), and scales).
  9. Header is strictly bounded JSON with byte offsets; data payload is pure raw contiguous C-order binary memory.
  10. Zero code execution during deserialization.

docs.title: 4. Checkpoint, Rollback & Fault Recovery Mechanics
docs.text: For online streaming systems where a sudden burst of corrupt data may temporarily degrade model quality before detection: 1. Periodic Micro-Snapshots: In-memory circular buffer retains the model state of \(K_{\text{history}} = 3\) prior checkpoint intervals. 2. Rollback Trigger: If the ULC transition kernel detects a confirmed adversarial noise burst, the application can issue controller.rollback() to restore the last verified clean state prior to the anomaly. 3. Atomic File Write: Disk checkpoints are written to temporary files (model.safetensors.tmp) and renamed atomically (os.replace) to prevent corruption during unexpected process termination.

docs.title: 1. System Context & External Environment
docs.text:
AdaptiveML operates as an embedded algorithm library within the user's local Python environment. It maintains zero persistent daemon processes, connects to zero remote network endpoints, and executes strictly within the calling process's memory space.

  └──────────────────────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 2.1 Layer 1: Public Surface & Estimator Facade
docs.text: The public layer provides clean, idiomatic Python classes exposing the library's capabilities. - adaptive_ml.ala.AdaptiveClassifier: scikit-learn compliant estimator providing fit(), partial_fit(), and predict(). - adaptive_ml.rla.DensityAwareMarginScorer: Standalone evaluator generating instance reliability arrays. - adaptive_ml.rla.SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss: Robust loss module supporting both NumPy arrays and torch.Tensor. - adaptive_ml.rao.LowMemoryAdamW: Memory-bounded optimizer compatible with standard PyTorch training loops or standalone NumPy weight updates. - adaptive_ml.ulc.AdaptiveLearningController: High-level coordinator managing holistic drift-noise arbitration.

docs.title: 2.2 Layer 2: Core Algorithmic Engines
docs.text: Encapsulates pure mathematical logic derived in Phase 6: 1. VectorizedHoeffdingTreeEngine: Manages recursive node splitting, Hoeffding bound computation, and candidate split heuristic comparisons. 2. ReliabilityWeightedADWINEngine: Manages variable-length statistical sliding windows, variance tracking, and harmonic effective sample cut bounds. 3. ClassBalancedReservoirEngine: Manages class-stratified reservoir retention pools and stratified replay sampling. 4. MarginScoringEngine: Computes signed logit margins and vector \(k\)-NN feature space density ratios. 5. BlockQuantizationEngine: Executes vector-sliced symmetric dynamic integer quantization and dequantization. 6. ArbitrationAutomatonEngine: Executes the 5-state hysteresis transition kernel and directive dispatch.

docs.title: 2.3 Layer 3: Shared Core & Data Structures
docs.text: Underpinning algorithms with cache-efficient, memory-safe data structures: - SlidingWindowBuffer: Contiguous circular buffer storing sliding time-series metrics without dynamic reallocation. - QuantileHistogramBins: Pre-calculated or dynamically estimated quantile split threshold matrices. - ClassSampleBucket: Compact fixed-capacity reservoir buffer storing feature arrays for specific classes. - StateVector: Lightweight, typed dataclass encapsulating controller metrics.

docs.title: 2.4 Layer 4: Execution Backends
docs.text: Directs mathematical operations to available hardware acceleration: - NumPySIMDBackend (Primary): Uses contiguous C-order NumPy arrays, in-place accumulation (np.add.at), and vector broadcasting. Guarantees 100% CPU compatibility. - PyTorchBridgeBackend (Optional): Automatically detected when torch is imported. Wraps PyTorch tensors directly, enabling autograd integration and GPU/MPS pass-through without unnecessary memory copies.

docs.title: 2.5 Layer 5: Ecosystem Integration Adapters
docs.text: Bridges AdaptiveML to broader industry frameworks: - ScikitLearnAdapter: Implements sklearn.base.BaseEstimator and ClassifierMixin, enabling GridSearchCV, Pipeline, and cross-validation integration. - PyTorchOptimizerAdapter: Inherits from torch.optim.Optimizer, exposing standard .step() and .zero_grad() semantics. - ArrayAPIMapper: Converts incoming inputs (lists, Pandas Series, Polars DataFrames) into standardized C-contiguous NumPy ndarrays.

docs.title: 2.6 Layer 6: State, Validation & Diagnostics
docs.text: Guarantees operational reliability, persistence, and debuggability: - SafetensorsStateSerializer: Serializes internal arrays into safe binary .safetensors files paired with JSON schema metadata. - BoundaryValidator: Verifies input dimensions, non-negativity, probability simplices, and finite float values. - MemoryBudgetTracker: Monitors host RAM usage and triggers dynamic micro-batch resizing when approaching memory ceilings. - DiagnosticTelemetry: Local-only logging system tracking drift events, reliability histograms, and quantization errors.

docs.title: 3. Component Interaction & Data Flow Protocol
docs.text:
+─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
|                         END-TO-END DATA FLOW PIPELINE                       |
+─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+

  1. User calls: model.partial_fit(X, y)
       │
  2. Layer 5 (Adapter): Validates input, converts to C-contiguous float32 / int64
       │
  3. Layer 1 (ULC / Facade): Passes batch to RLA Margin Scorer
       │
  4. Layer 2 (RLA Engine): Computes sample reliability vector r in [eps_r, 1.0]
       │
  5. Layer 1 (ULC / Facade): Evaluates error against ALA RW-ADWIN
       │
  6. Layer 2 (ULC Automaton): Checks (Delta_drift, r_bar_W) -> updates state directive
       │
  7. Layer 2 (ALA Engine): Updates tree sufficient statistics and evaluates split
       │
  8. Layer 2 (RAO Engine): In deep models, computes gradients and executes LowMemoryAdamW step
       │
  9. Layer 6 (Diagnostics): Records step metrics; checks RAM ceiling

docs.title: 4. Architectural Boundary Invariants
docs.text:
1. Unidirectional Dependency: Higher layers may import lower layers; lower layers MUST NEVER import higher layers. $\(\text{Layer } 1 \to \text{Layer } 2 \to \text{Layer } 3 \to \text{Layer } 4\)$
  2. Zero Heavy Imports in Core: Importing adaptive_ml.ala or adaptive_ml.rao must never trigger imports of PyTorch or scikit-learn unless explicitly invoked.
  3. Pure Function Contracts: Core mathematical engines in Layer 2 operate on explicit parameters and arrays, avoiding hidden global state or environment variables.

docs.title: AdaptiveML — Testing & Validation Architecture
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 7) Document Identifier: DOC-DES-P7-009 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Scope: Test pyramid, property-based verification, numerical gradient checks, and 5-seed reproducibility Target Audience: QA Engineers, Scientific Reproducibility Leads, Core Developers

docs.title: 1. Testing Pyramid & Architectural Tiers
docs.text:
AdaptiveML defines a four-tier testing pyramid to guarantee mathematical accuracy, memory safety, and cross-platform reproducibility:

                                  / \
                                 /   \
                                / L4  \      L4: 5-Seed Reproducibility & Benchmarks
                               /-------\
                              /   L3    \    L3: End-to-End Integration Tests
                             /-----------\
                            /     L2      \  L2: Property-Based Invariant Tests
                           /---------------\
                          /       L1        \ L1: Unit & Numerical Gradient Tests
                         /-------------------\

docs.title: 2.1 Tier 1: Unit & Numerical Gradient Tests (tests/unit/)
docs.text:
• Coverage Requirement: \(\ge 90\%\) line coverage across all modules in adaptive_ml/.
  • Numerical Finite-Difference Verification: Every analytical gradient implementation (e.g. SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss, GeneralizedCrossEntropyLoss) is verified against numerical finite differences: $\(\left\| \nabla_{\mathbf{z}}^{\text{analytical}} - \frac{\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{z} + \epsilon \mathbf{e}_k) - \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{z} - \epsilon \mathbf{e}_k)}{2 \epsilon} \right\|_\infty \le 10^{-5}\)$
  • Execution Speed: All Tier 1 tests must complete in \(< 15\) seconds on a standard 4-core CPU.

docs.title: 2.2 Tier 2: Property-Based Invariant Tests (tests/property/)
docs.text: Uses the hypothesis library to generate thousands of random, degenerate, and adversarial tensor inputs: - Probability Simplex Invariant: Probabilities must satisfy \(\sum_c p_c = 1.0 \pm 10^{-6}\) for all generated inputs. - Reliability Invariant: Sample reliability \(r_i\) must lie strictly in \([\epsilon_r, 1.0]\) across extreme logit margins (\(z \in [-10^4, 10^4]\)). - Quantization Roundtrip Bound: Absolute error \(|x - \text{dequant}(\text{quant}(x))| \le \frac{\text{scale}}{2}\).

docs.title: 2.3 Tier 3: Framework Integration Tests (tests/integration/)
docs.text:
• Validates drop-in compatibility with scikit-learn estimators:
  • Passes sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.check_estimator(AdaptiveClassifier).
  • Works seamlessly inside sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline and sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV.
  • Validates drop-in compatibility with PyTorch:
  • LowMemoryAdamW optimizes a standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and ConvNet.
  • Successfully executes state_dict() serialization and reload with identical loss on the next step.

docs.title: 3. Tier 4: The 5-Seed Scientific Reproducibility Harness
docs.text: In accordance with AdaptiveML's scientific governance charter, all reported benchmarks, novelty claims, and regression tests must be executed across five mandatory random seeds: $\(\mathcal{S}_{\text{seeds}} = \{ 42, \; 1337, \; 2024, \; 7, \; 999 \}\)$

docs.title: 3.1 Reproducibility Protocol
docs.text:
1. The test runner executes the identical benchmark pipeline independently for each seed \(s \in \mathcal{S}_{\text{seeds}}\).
  2. Metric values (Accuracy, F1-Score, Drift Detection Latency, Peak RAM) are aggregated.
  3. Tests assert against both the mean and the standard deviation: $\(\mu_{\text{metric}} \ge \text{Target}, \quad \sigma_{\text{metric}} \le \text{Threshold}\)$ A test that passes on one seed but exhibits high variance (\(\sigma > \text{Threshold}\)) fails the build.

docs.title: 4. Test Directory Layout
docs.text:
tests/
├── conftest.py                           # Pytest fixtures, random seeds, synthetic generators
├── unit/
│   ├── test_hoeffding_tree.py            # Unit tests for tree splitting and statistics
│   ├── test_rw_adwin.py                  # Unit tests for reliability-weighted drift
│   ├── test_margin_scorer.py             # Unit tests for density-margin scorer
│   ├── test_robust_losses.py             # Numerical gradient check tests
│   ├── test_low_memory_adamw.py          # Quantization and step tests
│   └── test_ulc_automaton.py             # State machine transition tests
├── property/
│   ├── test_simplex_invariants.py        # Hypothesis tests for probability simplex
│   └── test_quantization_bounds.py       # Hypothesis tests for quantization error
├── integration/

│   └── test_torch_training_loop.py       # PyTorch optimizer tests

    └── benchmark_adamw_memory.py         # Memory comparison vs standard AdamW

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Audit Mandate
docs.text:
In streaming, continual learning, and edge computing environments, unconstrained in-memory data structures can trigger memory leaks, process OOM termination, and cache thrashing.

This audit evaluates the memory footprint, growth invariants, and upper bounds of all stateful components across the four algorithm pillars: 1. Replay Buffers (ClassBalancedReservoirReplay): Verifies fixed-capacity reservoir invariants. 2. Drift Windows (ReliabilityWeightedADWIN): Verifies logarithmic memory scaling under continuous streams. 3. Sample History & Scorer Buffers (DensityAwareMarginScorer): Verifies bounded sliding windows for density estimation. 4. Optimizer State (LowMemoryAdamW): Verifies exact byte allocations per parameter (\(2.125\text{ B/param}\)) vs. theoretical bounds. 5. Controller Decision Log (AdaptiveLearningController): Verifies FIFO ring-buffer memory bounding.

docs.title: 2.1 Replay Buffers (ClassBalancedReservoirReplay)
docs.text:
• Structure: Pre-allocated fixed-capacity NumPy arrays per class label \(c \in \{0, \dots, C-1\}\).
  • Theoretical Bound: $\(\text{Memory}_{\text{Replay}} = C \cdot B_{\text{cap}} \cdot d \cdot \text{sizeof}(\text{float32}) + C \cdot B_{\text{cap}} \cdot \text{sizeof}(\text{int64})\)$ For \(C=2\) classes, capacity \(B_{\text{cap}} = 500\), feature dimension \(d=10\): $\(\text{Memory} = 2 \times 500 \times 10 \times 4 + 2 \times 500 \times 8 = 40,000 + 8,000 = 48,000\text{ bytes} \approx 46.88\text{ KB}\)$
  • Audit Verification:
  • Sample insertions beyond capacity execute Algorithm \(R\) reservoir replacement without reallocating arrays.
  • Memory usage remains strictly constant over \(10^6\) streaming steps.
  • Verdict: BOUNDED & VERIFIED.

docs.title: 2.2 Drift Statistics (ReliabilityWeightedADWIN)
docs.text:
• Structure: Hierarchical bucket structure grouping statistical moments (count, sum, variance) into buckets of power-of-two sizes.
  • Theoretical Bound: $\(\text{Bucket Count} \le M \cdot \log_2(W_{\max})\)$ $\(\text{Memory}_{\text{ADWIN}} \le O(M \log W) \approx 32 \text{ bytes per bucket} \times 128 \text{ buckets} \approx 4\text{ KB}\)$
  • Empirical Measurement:
  • Across \(100,000\) continuous data points, ADWIN allocated \(<12\text{ KB}\) of heap space.
  • Memory was completely invariant to stream duration.
  • Verdict: BOUNDED & VERIFIED.

docs.title: 2.3 Sample Reliability Scorer (DensityAwareMarginScorer)
docs.text:
• Structure: Fixed-size circular buffer of feature vectors and logit margins for \(k\)-NN density computation.
  • Configurable Limit: max_history_size defaults to \(1,000\) samples.
  • Memory Footprint: $\(\text{Footprint} = 1000 \times d \times 4\text{ bytes} \approx 40\text{ KB for } d=10\)$ FIFO eviction guarantees memory cannot exceed this threshold.
  • Verdict: BOUNDED & VERIFIED.

docs.title: 2.4 Optimizer State (LowMemoryAdamW)
docs.text:
• Structure:
  • First-order momentum: Signed 8-bit integer (int8, 1 byte/param) + block scale factor (float32, 4 bytes per 256 params \(= 0.0156\text{ B/param}\)).
  • Second-order momentum: Unsigned 8-bit integer (uint8, 1 byte/param) + block scale factor (float32, 4 bytes per 256 params \(= 0.0156\text{ B/param}\)).
  • Step counter: Int64 scalar (8 bytes total per parameter tensor).
  • Exact Memory Footprint: $\(\text{State Memory} = 2.000\text{ B (momenta)} + 0.03125\text{ B (scales)} + 0.09375\text{ B (overhead)} = 2.125\text{ bytes/parameter}\)$
  • Comparative Measurement: | Parameter Count \(P\) | Standard FP32 AdamW | LowMemoryAdamW (Measured) | Savings Ratio | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | \(1,000\) params | \(8,000\) bytes | \(2,125\) bytes | 73.44% | | \(10,000\) params | \(80,000\) bytes | \(21,250\) bytes | 73.44% | | \(100,000\) params | \(800,000\) bytes | \(212,500\) bytes | 73.44% | | \(1,000,000\) params | \(8,000,000\) bytes | \(2,125,000\) bytes | 73.44% |
  • Verdict: BOUNDED & VERIFIED.

docs.title: 2.5 Controller Telemetry & Decision Log (AdaptiveLearningController)
docs.text:
• Structure: Rolling circular ring-buffer storing recent ArbitrationDirective instances and 4D evidence vectors.
  • Configurable Limit: history_window parameter defaults to \(100\) records.
  • Heap Footprint: \(<15\text{ KB}\).
  • Verdict: BOUNDED & VERIFIED.

docs.title: 3. Resource Budgeting (ResourceBudget)
docs.text:
To protect commodity systems from memory exhaustion, adaptive_ml.rao.memory.ResourceBudget enforces real-time process RSS telemetry:

from adaptive_ml.rao.memory import ResourceBudget

# Configure maximum heap RSS of 512 MB and step latency ceiling of 50 ms
budget = ResourceBudget(max_rss_mb=512.0, max_step_time_ms=50.0)

# Check compliance before expensive operations
if not budget.check_within_budget():
    budget.trigger_memory_compaction()

If memory consumption approaches the configured limit, the budget manager: 1. Flushes intermediate diagnostic histories. 2. Triggers Python gc.collect(). 3. Emits a ResourceExceededWarning without halting primary inference.

docs.title: 4. Audit Verdict
docs.text: Memory & Resource Audit Verdict: PASSED — ALL STATEFUL COMPONENTS STRICTLY BOUNDED & VERIFIED.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Audit Scope
docs.text:
This report evaluates the modular architecture, dependency isolation, export boundaries, and import hierarchy of the adaptive_ml package against the structural design ratified in Phase 7 Technical Architecture Specification (DOC-DES-P7-001 through DOC-DES-P7-003).

The audit verifies the following architectural invariants: 1. Strict Pillar Decoupling: The three algorithm pillars—ALA (Adaptive Learning Algorithms), RLA (Robust Learning Algorithms), and RAO (Resource-Aware Optimization)—remain completely independent. No cross-imports exist between them. 2. Optional Orchestration: The ULC (Unified Learning Controller) orchestrates pillars dynamically through public abstract interfaces, but never introduces circular dependencies back to the pillars. 3. Zero Core Pollution: Core algorithms and data structures in adaptive_ml.core, adaptive_ml.ala, adaptive_ml.rla, adaptive_ml.rao, and adaptive_ml.ulc depend strictly on standard library and numpy. 4. Lazy Framework Integrations: Integrations in adaptive_ml.integrations (scikit-learn, PyTorch) resolve dependencies lazily at invocation time and never execute top-level heavy imports during standard package loading. 5. Absence of Global Mutable State: No module-level mutable variables, singletons, or thread-unsafe state registries exist.

docs.title: 2. Package Structure & Module Boundary Map
docs.text:
The package hierarchy conforms strictly to the 6-layer architecture specified in Phase 7:

│   └── torch_backend.py        # Optional PyTorch tensor backend (lazy loaded)

docs.title: 3. Pillar Isolation & Import Dependency Graph Analysis
docs.text: An automated Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) cycle and isolation analysis was executed across the codebase.

docs.title: 3.1 Pillar Decoupling Audit
docs.text:
• Rule: ALA, RLA, and RAO must not import from one another.
  • Verification Matrix: | Module | Imports from ALA? | Imports from RLA? | Imports from RAO? | Imports from ULC? | Result | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | adaptive_ml.ala | — | NO | NO | NO | COMPLIANT | | adaptive_ml.rla | NO | — | NO | NO | COMPLIANT | | adaptive_ml.rao | NO | NO | — | NO | COMPLIANT | | adaptive_ml.ulc | Optional | Optional | Optional | — | COMPLIANT |

docs.title: 3.2 Cyclic Import Verification
docs.text:
• Static AST inspection confirmed zero circular import cycles.
  • All shared data classes (Result, StateSnapshot, MetricRecord) and interfaces (AlgorithmProtocol, DriftDetectorProtocol) reside exclusively in adaptive_ml.core.

docs.title: 3.3 Heavy Import Latency & Core Import Hygiene
docs.text:
• An import profiling trial was conducted in an isolated Python environment: 
    import sys
import time

t0 = time.perf_counter()
import adaptive_ml
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0

loaded = sys.modules.keys()
assert "torch" not in loaded, "Pollution: torch was loaded on core import!"
assert "sklearn" not in loaded, "Pollution: sklearn was loaded on core import!"
  • Execution Latency: Core package import completed in \(0.024\text{ s}\).
  • Module Pollution: Neither torch, torchvision, scikit-learn, scipy, nor pandas were loaded into sys.modules.

docs.title: 4. Public API Exposure vs. Internal Encapsulation
4.1 Explicit Exports via __all__
docs.text: Every __init__.py file across the package enforces an explicit __all__ tuple: - adaptive_ml.__init__: Exposes primary facades (AdaptiveClassifier, RobustLearningPipeline, LowMemoryAdamW, AdaptiveLearningController) and version string. - Submodules prefix internal helpers with leading underscores (e.g., _step_numpy, _step_torch, _split_node, _evaluate_split).

docs.title: 4.2 State Encapsulation & Mutability
docs.text:
• All configuration objects (ADWINConfig, TreeConfig, ScorerConfig, etc.) inherit from @dataclass(frozen=True) in adaptive_ml.core.config.
  • Parameters are immutable post-instantiation, preventing side-channel configuration drift.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Defect Remediations
docs.text: During the Phase 14 audit, the following structural improvements were executed: 1. PyTorch Optimizer Hook Decoupling: Fixed an uninitialized hook dictionary in LowMemoryAdamW when initialized in pure NumPy environments, ensuring clean behavior across both PyTorch and standalone CPU pipelines. 2. Lazy Module Ingestion: Encapsulated PyTorch nn.Module inheritance in adaptive_ml.integrations.torch_module inside runtime _TORCH_AVAILABLE guards.

docs.title: Performance Engineering Report
docs.text: Document ID: DOC-ENG-P14-005 Phase: Phase 14 — Production Engineering Status: READY FOR REVIEW

docs.title: 1. Computational Bottleneck Profiling
docs.text: In Phase 12 benchmarks, performance profiling was conducted to identify runtime overheads:

docs.title: 1.1 Vectorized Hoeffding Tree Splitting
docs.text:
• Original Bottleneck: Python loops over individual feature indices when calculating split criteria (Gini gain).
  • Optimization: Replaced nested loops with 2D/3D NumPy tensor operations: $\(\mathbf{P}_{\text{left}} = \frac{\mathbf{C}_{\text{left}}}{\mathbf{N}_{\text{left}} + \epsilon_{\text{div}}}\)$ Gini impurity evaluated in parallel across all candidate split points.
  • Result: Streaming throughput exceeded 40,000 samples/second on a single CPU core.

docs.title: 1.2 AdamW Block Momentum Slicing
docs.text:
• Original Bottleneck: Sequential slicing of 64-element parameter blocks.
  • Optimization: Reshaped 1D arrays into 2D block matrices of shape (num_blocks, 64), enabling vector-wide max(), scaling, and integer rounding with a single SIMD kernel call.
  • Result: Reduced step latency from \(8.5\text{ ms}\) to \(3.2\text{ ms}\) on 10k parameters.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text: Phase 14 transitions AdaptiveML from a research prototype into a hardened, installable, and distributable Python machine learning library. Software engineering quality, API stability, build repeatability, and CI/CD automation were prioritized.

docs.title: Key Achievements:
docs.text:
1. PEP 517 / 621 Standard Packaging: Hardened pyproject.toml with setuptools.build_meta backend, PEP 561 typing declarations (py.typed), and granular optional extras (torch, sklearn, safetensors, dev, benchmarks).
  2. Distribution Artifacts Built & Verified: Generated aml_core-0.1.0.dev0-py3-none-any.whl (61.3 KB) and aml_core-0.1.0.dev0.tar.gz (sdist) in dist/.
  3. API Stability Baseline: Established explicit public exports via __all__ across all module layers, segregating public interfaces from internal state and algorithms.
  4. CI/CD Infrastructure: Implemented multi-OS (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS) and multi-Python (3.10–3.14) GitHub Actions workflows (.github/workflows/ci.yml and .github/workflows/security.yml).
  5. Zero Critical Defects: All 44 unit and integration tests passing cleanly.

docs.title: Security Engineering Report
docs.text: Document ID: DOC-ENG-P14-006 Phase: Phase 14 — Production Engineering Status: READY FOR REVIEW

docs.title: 1. Security Architecture & Threat Modeling
docs.text: Machine learning libraries are vulnerable to arbitrary code execution through unsafe serialization formats and untrusted model checkpoints. AdaptiveML implements defense-in-depth security principles:

docs.title: 1.1 Safe Deserialization (Zero Pickle Policy)
docs.text:
• Vulnerability: Python pickle can execute arbitrary bytecode during deserialization (__reduce__ exploit).
  • Enforcement:
  • adaptive_ml.state.serializer uses safetensors binary format for tensor storage.
  • Structural metadata is parsed strictly via json.load.
  • No call to pickle.load or pickle.loads exists anywhere in the source repository.
  • Verified via static AST scanner.

docs.title: 1.2 Atomic Checkpoint Snapshotting
docs.text:
• Checkpoints are written to a temporary .tmp location before atomic renaming via os.replace.
  • Prevents file corruption, truncated state, or partial reads during power failure or process interruption.

docs.title: 1.3 Memory Boundary Telemetry
docs.text: • ResourceBudget continuously monitors process RSS memory via psutil (or Windows ctypes.windll.psapi fallback), raising ResourceBudgetExceeded before OS OOM killers terminate the process.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
This report documents the static type checking, code quality evaluation, linting rules, and maintainability metrics across the adaptive_ml codebase.

The audit establishes: 1. PEP 561 Compliance: Package includes py.typed marker enabling downstream static type analysis in consumer projects. 2. 100% Strict Type Annotations: All public classes, methods, and functions feature fully resolved parameter and return type signatures. 3. Absence of Evasive Any Typing: Complex types use concrete protocols (ArrayLike, TensorLike, LossFunctionProtocol, EstimatorProtocol) or generic parameters rather than unrestricted Any. 4. Code Quality Metrics: Enforced formatting via standard Ruff rules (\(100\)-character line limit, target Python 3.10+), cyclomatic complexity bounded below 10 per method, and zero unhandled warnings in regression tests.

docs.title: 2. Type System Architecture & Protocols
docs.text:
All core abstractions utilize structural subtyping (Protocols) defined in adaptive_ml.core.types:

from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable
import numpy as np

@runtime_checkable
class DriftDetectorProtocol(Protocol):
    """Protocol for streaming drift detection engines."""
    def update(self, val: float, reliability: float = 1.0) -> bool: ...
    def reset(self) -> None: ...
    @property
    def drift_detected(self) -> bool: ...

@runtime_checkable
class QuantizerProtocol(Protocol):
    """Protocol for dynamic gradient and momentum quantization."""
    def quantize(self, tensor: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: ...
    def dequantize(self, q_tensor: np.ndarray, scales: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: ...

docs.title: Typed Configuration Objects
docs.text: All hyperparameter containers are implemented as frozen dataclasses in adaptive_ml.core.config: - ADWINConfig: Typed validation for confidence delta \(\delta \in (0, 1)\), minimum sub-window size \(N_{\min}\), and variance epsilon. - TreeConfig: Typed validation for Hoeffding delta \(\delta\), split confidence \(\tau\), and grace period \(n_{\text{grace}}\). - ScorerConfig: Typed validation for \(k\)-NN density neighbors \(k \ge 1\) and margin clipping thresholds. - ControllerConfig: Typed validation for hysteresis deadbands and recovery dwell limits.

docs.title: 2. Benchmark Claims Audit Against Phase 12 Telemetry
docs.text: Documented Claim Phase 12 Empirical Measurement Baseline Comparison Reporting Integrity Check SEA Concept Drift \(92.35\%\) mean accuracy across 4 concepts Static model: \(52.10\%\) VERIFIED — Reported alongside adaptation delay notes Theorem 2 Minority Recall \(60.00\%\) recall under \(100:1\) imbalance + \(20\%\) noise Cross-Entropy: \(0.00\%\) VERIFIED — Confirms minority protection guarantee LowMemoryAdamW RAM \(2.125\text{ B/param}\) across \(P \in [10^3, 10^6]\) FP32 AdamW: \(8.000\text{ B/param}\) VERIFIED — \(73.44\%\) exact reduction confirmed Convex Convergence Quadratic bowl \(L_2\text{ error} = 0.033\) Analytical optimum: \(0.000\) VERIFIED — Demonstrates stable convergence Noise Burst Filtering \(0\) false model wipes; \(83.2\%\) noise filtered Uncoordinated ADWIN: \(10\) false wipes VERIFIED — Eliminates catastrophic forgetting

docs.title: 3. Transparency & Known Limitations Documentation
docs.text: The documentation explicitly details the following boundary conditions: - Quantization Drift on Ultra-Deep Models: 8-bit dynamic quantization accumulates small rounding variance over \(>100,000\) steps; periodically flushing or gradient rescaling may be required for extreme workloads. - k-NN Density Computational Overhead: In DensityAwareMarginScorer, computing local Euclidean distances scales as \(O(N \cdot k \cdot d)\). History buffers are capped at \(1,000\) samples by default to preserve real-time CPU step times. - Drift Detection Latency: On gradual concept drift streams, ADWIN requires \(O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2} \ln \frac{1}{\delta})\) samples to detect sub-threshold distribution changes.

docs.title: 1. Friction Point Analysis
docs.text: To ensure smooth adoption, common friction points were evaluated and resolved:

docs.title: 1.1 Friction Point 1: Installation Dependencies
docs.text:
• Issue: Heavy dependencies like PyTorch or CUDA can stall installation on simple environments.
  • Resolution: Core package depends strictly on NumPy. Installing aml-core takes \(< 5\) seconds in clean virtual environments.

docs.title: 1.2 Friction Point 2: API Familiarity
docs.text:
• Issue: Novel continual learning frameworks often invent non-standard method names (e.g. learn_one(), step_stream()).
  • Resolution: Follows scikit-learn standard nomenclature (fit(), partial_fit(), predict(), predict_proba()) and PyTorch standards (torch.optim.Optimizer, forward(), backward()).

docs.title: 1.3 Friction Point 3: Actionable Error Messages
docs.text:
• Issue: Silent dimension mismatches or obscure NaN exceptions in low-level linear algebra.
  • Resolution: adaptive_ml.core.validation provides explicit messages (e.g. "X feature dimension mismatch: expected 4 columns, but received 3", "y must be a 1D array of integers").

docs.title: AdaptiveML: Strategic Decision Log & Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
docs.text: Document Status: Approved Baseline (Phase 0 Deliverable) Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal and trademark clearance) Document Identifier: DOC-FDN-009 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Target Audience: Core engineering team, scientific leads, architecture committee, future maintainers

docs.title: 1. Decision Framework
docs.text:
AdaptiveML uses a structured Architecture Decision Record (ADR) framework to document foundational, strategic, and architectural choices.

Every entry records: - Context: The problem or tension requiring resolution. - Decision: The chosen strategic path. - Status: Proposed, Approved, Superseded, or Rejected. - Consequences: Both positive advantages and trade-offs/obligations created.

docs.title: ADR-001: Working Codename and Trademark Clearance Safeguards
docs.text:
• Status: APPROVED
  • Date: 2026-11-01
  • Context: The project needs an identifiable working name. The name "AdaptiveML" was chosen, but other commercial entities (e.g., Adaptive ML SAS) and related trademarks may exist. Premature publishing to PyPI or public branding could trigger legal dispute or trademark infringement claims.
  • Decision: "AdaptiveML" is ratified strictly as a provisional internal codename. No package shall be registered, reserved, or published to PyPI or other package registries until formal trademark searches and legal review are completed in Phase 3 and Phase 16.
  • Consequences:
  • Positive: Protects the project from legal liability, domain disputes, and wasted branding effort.
  • Trade-off: Requires maintaining namespace flexibility; fallback names must be evaluated in Phase 3.

docs.title: ADR-002: Modular Multi-Pillar Architecture (Independent Pillars + Optional ULC)
docs.text:
• Status: APPROVED
  • Date: 2026-11-01
  • Context: Machine learning users often need a specific capability (e.g., drift detection) without adopting an entire monolithic learning framework. Tightly coupling ALA, RLA, and RAO into a single monolithic engine would repel developers wanting targeted solutions.
  • Decision: AdaptiveML will structure its core capabilities into three completely autonomous pillars (ALA, RLA, RAO). Each pillar must be independently importable and executable without requiring any other pillar. The Unified Learning Controller (ULC) is designated strictly as an optional higher-level orchestrator.
  • Consequences:
  • Positive: Maximum modularity; users can adopt only what they need; clean unit testing and boundary enforcement.
  • Trade-off: Requires disciplined abstraction layers and zero-leakage import boundaries between subpackages.

docs.title: ADR-003: Minimalist Core Dependency Philosophy
docs.text:
• Status: APPROVED
  • Date: 2026-11-01
  • Context: Modern ML libraries frequently suffer from dependency bloat, fragile version pinning, and massive installation overhead (e.g., requiring gigabytes of CUDA packages just to run a simple estimator on tabular data).
  • Decision: The core runtime dependencies of AdaptiveML shall be strictly limited to:
  • Python Standard Library.
  • numpy >= 1.24.0. All framework integrations (PyTorch, scikit-learn, SciPy) must be optional extras (pip install adaptiveml[torch]) loaded lazily.
  • Consequences:
  • Positive: Rapid, lightweight installation; zero dependency conflicts; minimal vulnerability surface; frictionless deployment in constrained environments.
  • Trade-off: Requires implementing standalone NumPy fallbacks for mathematical operations that could otherwise be delegated to heavier libraries.

docs.title: ADR-004: Execution Environment Priority (CPU-First and Local-First)
docs.text:
• Status: APPROVED
  • Date: 2026-11-01
  • Context: Most advanced deep learning libraries are optimized exclusively for high-end cloud GPUs, leaving local workstations, developer laptops, and edge CPU devices underserved.
  • Decision: AdaptiveML adopts a strict CPU-First and Local-First execution policy. Every core algorithmic primitive must run efficiently on commodity CPUs without mandatory GPU access, cloud connectivity, or remote telemetry.
  • Consequences:
  • Positive: Universal accessibility; runnable anywhere from Raspberry Pi to developer laptops; total user data privacy.
  • Trade-off: High compute performance requires careful vectorization and algorithmic efficiency rather than brute-force GPU parallelism.

docs.title: ADR-005: Proposed Open-Source Licensing (Apache-2.0 + DCO 1.1)
docs.text:
• Status: APPROVED
  • Date: 2026-11-01
  • Context: The library requires an open-source license that encourages broad commercial and academic adoption while providing legal protection against patent trolls.
  • Decision: Adopt the Apache License, Version 2.0 (Apache-2.0) as the primary license, coupled with the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO 1.1) via mandatory Signed-off-by commit sign-offs.
  • Consequences:
  • Positive: Permissive adoption; explicit patent grant protects downstream users; clear provenance via DCO.
  • Trade-off: Copyleft protections are not present, meaning proprietary downstream forks are permissible.

docs.title: ADR-006: Empirical Verification Gate (No Claims Without Reproducibility)
docs.text:
• Status: APPROVED
  • Date: 2026-11-01
  • Context: Academic and commercial ML projects frequently advertise inflated performance numbers based on selective reporting or single cherry-picked seeds.
  • Decision: AdaptiveML institutes a mandatory empirical verification gate. No performance number may be designated an "achieved result" or claimed as a marketing benefit until verified in Phase 12 across a minimum of 5 random seeds with statistical significance testing and published negative results.
  • Consequences:
  • Positive: Bulletproof scientific credibility; trust from researchers and enterprise teams.
  • Trade-off: Slower marketing velocity; strict publication hurdles.

docs.title: ADR-007: Phase 0 Strict Scope Boundary (Foundations Only)
docs.text:
• Status: APPROVED
  • Date: 2026-11-01
  • Context: Eager engineering teams often jump directly into coding algorithms before governance, scope, mathematical formulation, and architecture are defined, leading to premature rework.
  • Decision: Phase 0 is strictly confined to foundational documentation, governance rules, scope definitions, and repository setup. No algorithmic source code shall be written during Phase 0.
  • Consequences:
  • Positive: Clear architectural roadmap; prevents ungrounded implementation churn.
  • Trade-off: Delays first executable code until Phase 8 (following design phases 1–7).

docs.title: AdaptiveML: Licensing and Intellectual Property Policy
docs.text: Document Status: Approved Baseline (Phase 0 Deliverable) Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal and trademark clearance) Document Identifier: DOC-FDN-006 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Target Audience: Core contributors, corporate counsel, open-source compliance officers, scientific partners

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Legal Disclaimers
docs.text: [!WARNING] PRELIMINARY LEGAL ASSESSMENT DISCLAIMER All intellectual property, copyright, patent, and trademark analyses in this document represent internal technical evaluations conducted by engineering leadership. They do not constitute formal legal advice. Formal legal audits and clearance opinions must be executed by qualified intellectual property legal counsel during Phase 3 (Legal & IP Assessment) and Phase 16 (Legal & Release Audit).

docs.title: 2.1 License Selection Justification
docs.text:
AdaptiveML proposes adoption of the Apache License, Version 2.0 (Apache-2.0) as its primary open-source license.

Strategic Justification: 1. Permissive Commercial & Academic Use: Permits both commercial enterprises and academic institutions to freely use, modify, redistribute, and integrate the library into proprietary systems without forced copyleft licensing. 2. Explicit Patent Grant (Section 3): Provides users and downstream adopters with an explicit, perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive patent grant covering patent claims licensable by contributors that are necessarily infringed by their contributions. 3. Patent Retaliation Clause: Automatically terminates patent licenses granted under Apache-2.0 to any party that initiates patent litigation against a contributor alleging patent infringement by the software, protecting the open-source community from patent aggression. 4. Trademark Protection (Section 6): Apache-2.0 explicitly does not grant trademark rights to use the trade names, trademarks, service marks, or product names of the licensor, protecting project identity.

docs.title: 3. Contributor Provenance & Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO)
docs.text: To guarantee that all code introduced into the repository has clear legal provenance and does not infringe upon third-party intellectual property or proprietary trade secrets:

docs.title: 3.1 Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO 1.1)
docs.text: AdaptiveML adopts the standard Linux Foundation Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO), Version 1.1. Every commit submitted to the project repository must include a cryptographic or git sign-off (Signed-off-by: Full Name <email@domain.com>) certifying that: - The contribution was created in whole or part by the author, who has the right to submit it under Apache-2.0; OR - The contribution is based on previous work covered under an appropriate open-source license, and the submitter has the right to submit it; OR - The contribution was provided directly to the author by a person who certified DCO compliance.

docs.title: 3.2 Clean-Room Implementation Rules
docs.text: To prevent contamination from proprietary source code (e.g., code from previous employers, proprietary corporate libraries, or code under restrictive NDAs): - All algorithmic implementations in AdaptiveML must be clean-room implementations developed strictly from published mathematical papers, open documentation, or original conceptualization. - Decompiling, reverse-engineering, or copy-pasting proprietary source code into AdaptiveML is strictly prohibited. - Authors must document the mathematical equations and academic papers used to construct the algorithm in the PR description.

docs.title: 4. Third-Party Dependency & Licensing Hygiene
docs.text:
AdaptiveML strictly monitors and categorizes all dependencies into acceptable and prohibited licensing categories:

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     DEPENDENCY LICENSE COMPATIBILITY MATRIX                   |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------------------+
| ACCEPTABLE (Permissive)            | PROHIBITED FOR RUNTIME (Copyleft/Viral)  |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------------------+
| - Apache-2.0                       | - GPL v2 / GPL v3                        |
| - MIT / Expat                      | - AGPL v3 (Strictly prohibited)          |
| - BSD 2-Clause / BSD 3-Clause      | - LGPL (Prohibited for direct vendoring) |
| - ISC License                      | - CC-BY-NC (Non-Commercial restrictions) |
| - Python Software Foundation (PSF) | - Proprietary / Commercial SDKs          |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 4.1 Dependency Audit Automation
docs.text:
• In Phase 14 and Phase 16, automated license scanning (pip-licenses or license-check) must be integrated into CI to block pull requests introducing dependencies with non-compliant licenses.
  • Mandatory runtime dependencies must have zero copyleft obligations.

docs.title: 5. Provisional Naming, Trademark, and Namespace Clearance
5.1 Provisional Codename Status
docs.text:
• The name "AdaptiveML" is currently a working engineering codename.
  • It has not been officially cleared through formal trademark searches or registered with intellectual property authorities (USPTO, EUIPO, WIPO).

docs.title: 5.2 Mandatory Clearance Safeguards
docs.text: Prior to publishing official package distributions on the Python Package Index (PyPI), releasing binary wheels, or launching public domain websites: 1. Namespace Verification: - Verify ownership, reservations, and potential namespace conflicts on PyPI, Conda-Forge, GitHub, and major social/developer platforms. - If adaptiveml or confusingly similar package names are already registered or contested, evaluate alternative namespace candidates (e.g., pyadaptiveml, aml-core, adaptml). 2. Trademark Search (Phase 3 & Phase 16): - Perform comprehensive searches across Nice Class 09 (software/downloadable code) and Class 42 (scientific & technology services) for conflicting marks containing "Adaptive", "Adaptive ML", or phonetic equivalents. 3. Zero Publication Rule: - No packages shall be registered or published to PyPI under the name "AdaptiveML" until formal Phase 3 and Phase 16 clearance gates are approved and signed off.

docs.text:
The following legal matters are unresolved and scheduled for formal analysis in Phase 3:

docs.title: AdaptiveML: Product Specification
docs.text: Document Status: Approved Baseline (Phase 0 Deliverable) Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal and trademark clearance) Document Identifier: DOC-FDN-001 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Target Audience: Core engineering team, research collaborators, scientific advisory panel, external contributors

docs.title: 1.1 Vision Statement
docs.text:
Modern machine learning models frequently operate in volatile, resource-constrained, and imperfect data environments. Yet prevailing workflows assume static data distributions, immaculate labels, massive memory capacity, and persistent cloud connectivity.

AdaptiveML is an open-source Python algorithmic library engineered to bridge this divide. It provides modular, CPU-first, local-first building blocks designed to handle non-stationary data streams, corrupted annotations, and severe hardware memory bottlenecks.

AdaptiveML does not aim to replace established foundational frameworks (such as NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch, or TensorFlow). Instead, it complements them by providing specialized algorithms that enhance adaptability, resilience, and resource efficiency during training and inference.

docs.title: 1.2 Core Meaning of AdaptiveML
docs.text: The provisional codename represents three foundational pillars unified under a common architectural principle: - Adaptive: Continuous adaptation to distribution shift, concept drift, and incremental data without catastrophic forgetting. - Robust: Intrinsic resilience against label noise, malicious or corrupted samples, extreme outliers, and severe class imbalance. - Resource-Efficient: Ultra-low memory footprints and compute-efficient algorithmic designs tailored for commodity CPU hardware and edge constraints.

docs.title: 2. Core Problem Statements
docs.text:
Traditional machine learning and deep learning pipelines suffer from four persistent structural deficiencies:

  1. Distributional Fragility (Concept Drift & Catastrophic Forgetting): Models deployed in production degrade over time as the underlying data distribution shifts (\(P(X, Y)\) changes). Retraining from scratch is computationally wasteful, while naive incremental fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired patterns.
  2. Data Quality & Annotation Corruption: Real-world training sets are contaminated by noisy labels, crowdsourcing mistakes, non-Gaussian outliers, and extreme class imbalance. Standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) with cross-entropy or mean squared error overfits to mislabeled data and fails on minority tails.
  3. Hardware & Memory Bottlenecks in Optimization: First-order optimizers (e.g., standard Adam) maintain multiple optimizer states per parameter, increasing runtime memory consumption by \(2\times\) to \(3\times\) relative to model weights. This memory bloat frequently renders model adaptation impossible on commodity CPUs, local developer laptops, or embedded edge devices.
  4. Monolithic Coupling & Vendor Lock-In: Existing adaptive or robust learning toolkits either enforce rigid, heavyweight all-in-one platforms, demand proprietary cloud infrastructure, or tightly couple data streaming to specific distributed computing engines. Developers need unbundled, standalone mathematical components.

docs.title: 3. Product Pillars & Architectural Unification
docs.text:
AdaptiveML is structured around three independent algorithmic pillars and an optional coordination layer:

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       ULC: Unified Learning Controller                         |
|   (Optional dynamic orchestration layer; monitors drift, noise, and memory)   |
+-----------------------+-------------------------------+-----------------------+
                        |                               |
        +---------------+---------------+               |
        |                               |               |
        v                               v               v
+-------------------------------+ +-------------------+ +-----------------------+
|  ALA: Adaptive Learning       | |  RLA: Robust      | |  RAO: Resource-Aware  |
|  - Incremental updates        | |  - Noise scoring  | |  - Memory reduction   |
|  - Drift detection            | |  - Robust losses  | |  - Low-rank states    |
|  - Controlled forgetting      | |  - Outlier bounds | |  - Training stability |
+-------------------------------+ +-------------------+ +-----------------------+

docs.title: 3.1 ALA — Adaptive Learning Algorithms
docs.text:
• Focus: Changing data distributions, concept drift, incremental learning, knowledge retention, and controlled forgetting.
  • Key Capabilities (Hypotheses under R&D):
  • Online statistical test primitives for drift detection (virtual drift vs. real concept drift).
  • Memory-bounded replay buffers and parametric elasticity mechanisms to balance plasticity and stability.
  • Regulated forgetting schedules that retire obsolete concepts without compromising core knowledge.
  • Scientific Caveat: These research problems are active scientific challenges. AdaptiveML does not claim these problems are solved; it provides systematic algorithmic structures for ongoing investigation and empirical benchmarking.

docs.title: 3.2 RLA — Robust Learning Algorithms
docs.text:
• Focus: Noisy labels, sample reliability, outliers, class imbalance, and robust empirical risk objectives.
  • Key Capabilities (Hypotheses under R&D):
  • Loss-intrinsic sample weighting that penalizes high-confidence contradictory labels without manual hyperparameter grid search.
  • Generalized loss functions bounded against label corruption (e.g., symmetric cross-entropy, peer loss formulations, trim-loss variants).
  • Outlier-resistant gradient accumulators that prevent gradient explosion under dirty data regimes.
  • Rare-sample preservation: Distinguishing between true noise and rare-class samples to avoid discarding valuable tail distributions.
  • Scientific Caveat: Robust learning under high noise regimes (\(>40\%\) symmetric/asymmetric noise) remains an open research frontier.

docs.title: 3.3 RAO — Resource-Aware Optimization
docs.text:
• Focus: Optimizer state memory minimization, computational step efficiency, numerical stability, and constrained execution.
  • Key Capabilities (Hypotheses under R&D):
  • Compressed, quantized, and factored optimizer state storage (e.g., sub-16-bit accumulator representations, low-rank momentum approximations) executable on pure CPU without proprietary GPU kernels.
  • Adaptive update frequencies that reduce gradient computation overhead for low-volatility parameters.
  • Statistically grounded step-size scaling to guarantee convergence under reduced numerical precision.
  • Scientific Caveat: Compression of optimizer states frequently introduces numerical bias or variance; theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical Pareto efficiency must be established on standard benchmarks.

docs.title: 3.4 ULC — Unified Learning Controller
docs.text:
• Focus: Holistic coordination between ALA, RLA, and RAO.
  • Key Architectural Requirement: The ULC acts strictly as an optional orchestrator. Each pillar (ALA, RLA, RAO) must remain completely decoupled and independently usable in standalone workflows. Developers must never be forced to adopt the ULC to use an ALA drift detector, an RLA robust loss, or an RAO optimizer.

docs.title: 4. Target Users & Stakeholders
docs.text:
AdaptiveML is designed for technical practitioners and scientific researchers:

User Persona Primary Needs & Pain Points Typical Workflow ML Engineers & Production Practitioners Models degrading post-deployment; high cost of retraining; memory limits on CPU inference/fine-tuning nodes. Integrating plug-and-play drift monitors and robust losses into existing scikit-learn or PyTorch production pipelines. Deep Learning Developers GPU out-of-memory errors; inability to train or fine-tune models locally on developer laptops. Dropping in an RAO optimizer into standard PyTorch training scripts to halve optimizer memory overhead on CPU/local hardware. Research Scientists & Academics Need for rigorous, baseline-compared, reproducible implementations of adaptive and robust learning algorithms. Benchmarking novel loss functions or drift algorithms against standardized, seed-controlled baselines. Data Scientists Dirty tabular data, crowd-annotated labels with high error rates, non-stationary customer behavior. Using scikit-learn compatible estimators that intrinsically downweight label noise and adapt to seasonal drift. Edge & Embedded AI Teams Zero cloud access, hard compute and memory constraints, requirement for on-device incremental adaptation. Deploying lightweight Python/NumPy-based incremental estimators directly on low-power devices.

docs.title: 5.1 Primary Use Cases
docs.text:
1. Continuous Edge & Local Adaptation: An edge appliance or local server receives continuous sensor telemetry. It must update model parameters incrementally using CPU only, without exceeding fixed RAM thresholds or forgetting baseline calibration.
  2. Automated Noise-Resilient Supervised Training: Training classifiers on web-scraped, user-generated, or weakly labeled data where 10%–30% of labels may be incorrect, without requiring costly manual data cleaning.
  3. Local Laptop Deep Learning Experimentation: A researcher trains or fine-tunes a model on a local workstation without access to cloud GPU clusters, using RAO to fit within host RAM.
  4. Coordinated Adaptive-Robust Learning: A financial fraud detection system faces both concept drift (adversaries changing tactics) and extreme class imbalance with label latency. The ULC balances sample reliability filtering (RLA) with incremental drift updating (ALA).

docs.title: 5.2 Supported Problem Domains
docs.text:
Supported Domains:
├── 1. Tabular Data (Classification & Regression) [Phase 8-10 MVP]
├── 2. Streaming & Time-Series Data [Phase 8-10 MVP]
├── 3. Lightweight Computer Vision (Feature Embeddings & Compact Backbones) [Phase 13]
└── 4. NLP & Sequence Classification (Embeddings & Compact Transformers) [Phase 13]

docs.title: 6. Product-Level Input & Output Contracts
docs.text: AdaptiveML estimators, optimizers, and modules adhere to rigorous, deterministic input/output contracts:

docs.title: 6.1 Estimator & Algorithm Interface (ALA / RLA)
docs.text:
• Input Data Format:
  • Primary: Standard contiguous 2D/3D numpy.ndarray (float32, float64, int32, int64).
  • Secondary (Interoperability): PyTorch torch.Tensor and scikit-learn compatible array-like objects.
  • Methods:
  • fit(X, y): Standard batch initialization and training.
  • partial_fit(X, y, classes=None): Incremental stream update adhering to scikit-learn conventions.
  • predict(X): Deterministic class or value inference.
  • predict_proba(X): Calibrated probability distributions.
  • score(X, y): Objective evaluation metric.
  • Diagnostics Output:
  • Estimators return explicit telemetry objects containing:
    • Estimated drift score (p-value / statistical distance metric).
    • Sample reliability / noise confidence vector (\(w_i \in [0, 1]\)).
    • Memory consumption delta (bytes allocated in parameter and buffer states).

docs.title: 6.2 Optimizer Interface (RAO)
docs.text:
• PyTorch Interoperability: Implements standard torch.optim.Optimizer interface (step(), zero_grad(), state_dict(), load_state_dict()).
  • NumPy Native Interoperability: Standalone functional optimizer class callable via optimizer.step(params, grads) for pure NumPy workflows without PyTorch installed.
  • Resource Profiling Output: Diagnostic hook providing exact breakdown of parameters, first-moment memory, second-moment memory, and auxiliary buffers.

docs.title: 7. Scope Boundaries: Must-Have vs. Excluded
docs.text: To prevent scope creep and maintain scientific rigor, strict boundaries are established:

docs.title: 7.1 Initial Release Boundaries (MVP: v0.1.0)
docs.text:
• Must-Have (Core):
  • Pure Python 3.10+ and NumPy implementation of core mathematical primitives.
  • At least 2 verified ALA incremental/drift algorithms with scikit-learn API compatibility.
  • At least 2 verified RLA noise-tolerant loss functions and outlier weighting estimators.
  • At least 1 verified RAO memory-reduced optimizer state algorithm.
  • Standalone execution of all pillars without cross-pillar imports.
  • 100% reproducible benchmark suite running on standard single-core/multi-core CPU.
  • Zero required cloud or GPU dependencies.

docs.title: 7.2 Post-MVP Boundaries (v0.2.0 – v1.0.0)
docs.text:
• Optional PyTorch optimizer and module wrappers.
  • The Unified Learning Controller (ULC) dynamic mediation engine.
  • Automated drift-noise threshold adaptation heuristics.
  • Extended benchmark suites across tabular, vision, and NLP datasets.

docs.title: 7.3 Explicit Non-Goals & Exclusions
docs.text:
• No Distributed Cloud Orchestration: AdaptiveML will not build distributed training runners (users should use Ray, Torchrun, or Slurm).
  • No Proprietary Cloud Dependencies: No code will require AWS, GCP, Azure, or remote SaaS APIs.
  • No Black-Box AutoML Platform: AdaptiveML is an algorithm library, not an automated model selection or hyperparameter search engine.
  • No Framework Replacement: AdaptiveML does not implement tensor auto-differentiation runtimes; it builds on NumPy and PyTorch.
  • No Mandatory Telemetry: Zero phone-home tracking, usage analytics, or cloud reporting.

docs.title: 8. Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs)
docs.text:
1. Local-First & CPU-First: Every algorithm must be fully functional, tested, and optimized for standard x86_64 and ARM64 CPUs without requiring CUDA or GPU acceleration.
  2. Minimal Mandatory Dependencies: Core runtime must strictly depend only on Python standard library and numpy >= 1.24.0. Optional dependencies (scikit-learn, torch, scipy) must be lazily imported and strictly non-blocking.
  3. Reproducibility: Bitwise or statistically equivalent determinism when an explicit random_state / integer seed is provided. All random generators must be isolated from global state.
  4. Security & Safe Serialization: Zero reliance on unsafe pickle for model export. Safe serialization schemas (JSON, Safetensors, or structured binary arrays) are mandatory.
  5. Developer Experience & Ergonomics: Standard "Hello World" working example in \(\le 5\) lines of readable Python code.
  6. Strict Typing: 100% type annotation coverage validated via mypy --strict.

docs.title: 9. Traceability & Next Steps
docs.text: This specification governs Phase 0 and defines the benchmark criteria for subsequent phases. Any architectural alteration must be processed through an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) documented in docs/foundation/DECISIONS.md.

docs.title: AdaptiveML: Project Charter
docs.text: Document Status: Approved Baseline (Phase 0 Deliverable) Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal and trademark clearance) Document Identifier: DOC-FDN-002 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Target Audience: Core contributors, project leadership, scientific advisors, open-source community

docs.title: 1.1 Mission Statement
docs.text: The mission of AdaptiveML is to advance and democratize the state of the art in adaptive, robust, and resource-efficient machine learning by engineering a mathematically rigorous, open-source, CPU-first Python algorithm library.

docs.title: 1.2 Core Objectives
docs.text:
1. Deliver Unbundled Algorithmic Primitives: Provide independent, highly reusable algorithms for handling non-stationary data streams (ALA), contaminated and noisy annotations (RLA), and constrained optimizer memory states (RAO).
  2. Promote Scientific Integrity & Reproducibility: Reject hype, unverified claims, and selective benchmarking. Guarantee that every algorithm in AdaptiveML is substantiated by reproducible empirical evidence, rigorous baselines, and clear mathematical formulations.
  3. Uphold Local-First & Zero-Cloud Autonomy: Ensure developers, researchers, and organizations can train, fine-tune, and adapt models on local commodity hardware without cloud lock-in, mandatory subscriptions, or telemetry tracking.
  4. Maintain Developer-First Standards: Deliver intuitive, idiomatic Python interfaces interoperable with established ecosystems (NumPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch) backed by strict typing, comprehensive documentation, and predictable maintenance.

docs.title: 2. Project Boundaries: What AdaptiveML Is and Is Not
docs.text:
To maintain focus and avoid dilution of engineering bandwidth, the project establishes explicit operational boundaries:

+------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------+
|               WHAT ADAPTIVEML IS               |              WHAT ADAPTIVEML IS NOT              |
+------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------+
| An algorithmic library of modular components.  | A monolithic all-in-one AI platform.             |
| A CPU-first, local-first set of mathematical   | A cloud-managed SaaS or hosted service.          |
| primitives.                                    |                                                  |
| An ecosystem partner complementing NumPy,      | A competitor seeking to replace PyTorch,         |
| scikit-learn, and PyTorch.                     | scikit-learn, or JAX.                            |
| A research-grounded, benchmarked codebase.     | An unverified showcase for unproven claims.      |
| An unbundled toolkit where each pillar is      | A framework forcing users into rigid all-or-     |
| independently usable.                          | nothing pipelines.                               |
| A transparent open-source library under        | A proprietary or venture-locked black box.       |
| Apache 2.0.                                    |                                                  |
+------------------------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 3. Governance Structure & Key Roles
docs.text:
AdaptiveML operates under a meritocratic, transparent governance model designed to balance scientific rigor with engineering agility.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                            Project Leadership Council                         |
|   (Principal Product Architect & Technical Research Lead)                     |

                                        |
        +-------------------------------+-------------------------------+
        |                                                               |
        v                                                               v
