docs.title: 2.1 Profile: River
docs.text:
• Category: Direct Competitor (ALA Tabular Streaming).
  • Repository: https://github.com/online-ml/river
  • Documentation: https://riverml.xyz/
  • Distribution: PyPI (pip install river), Conda-forge.
  • License: BSD 3-Clause.
  • Main Purpose: Online/streaming machine learning for Python, created by merging Creme and scikit-multiflow.
  • Algorithms: Hoeffding Trees, Adaptive Random Forests, ADWIN, DDM, Page-Hinkley, online linear models, streaming metrics.
  • Primary API: model.learn_one(x, y) / model.predict_one(x) using Python dict. Optional learn_many via pandas.DataFrame.
  • Dependencies: Mandatory: numpy, scipy. Optional: pandas, torch (via deep-river).
  • Framework Support: Standalone; integration with PyTorch via separate deep-river library.
  • Hardware: Pure CPU (single-core Python loops).
  • Maintenance: Active (regular releases, institutional backing from Inria / academic contributors).
  • Strengths: Comprehensive streaming algorithms; excellent progressive evaluation metrics; pure Python usability.
  • Limitations:
  • Enforces single-instance dictionary iteration (learn_one), causing extreme Python interpreter loop overhead on large-scale numerical datasets.
  • Does not natively support 2D NumPy array matrix batching (partial_fit(X, y)).
  • No built-in robust learning objectives for high-noise regimes or memory-efficient optimizer states.
  • Overlap with AdaptiveML: Overlaps with ALA concept drift detection and incremental tabular classification.
  • AdaptiveML Design Lesson: Adopt scikit-learn's standard partial_fit(X, y) on 2D NumPy arrays to achieve vector-level throughput without dict iteration penalties.

docs.title: 2.2 Profile: Cleanlab
docs.text:
• Category: Indirect Competitor / Potential Integration Partner (RLA).
  • Repository: https://github.com/cleanlab/cleanlab
  • Documentation: https://cleanlab.ai/
  • Distribution: PyPI (pip install cleanlab), Cleanlab Studio (commercial SaaS).
  • License: AGPL-3.0 (Open-Source Core) / Commercial.
  • Main Purpose: Data-centric AI framework to detect label errors and characterize label noise in datasets.
  • Algorithms: Confident Learning (joint distribution estimation between noisy and true labels), rank pruning.
  • Primary API: find_label_issues(labels, pred_probs).
  • Dependencies: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas.
  • Framework Support: Framework-agnostic (takes pre-computed predicted probabilities from any model).
  • Hardware: CPU / GPU (depending on model used to generate probabilities).
  • Maintenance: Highly active (commercial company with dedicated engineering team).
  • Strengths: Industry gold standard for identifying annotation errors; rigorous theoretical backing (Northcutt et al.).
  • Limitations:
  • Requires offline, multi-pass out-of-fold cross-validation to generate predicted probabilities; completely unusable in online streaming or single-pass training.
  • Treats "hard" minority examples with high loss as potential label errors, often pruning rare classes in imbalanced datasets.
  • Does not provide in-training robust loss functions or streaming estimators.
  • Core license is AGPL-3.0, restricting certain proprietary embedding workflows without a commercial license.
  • Overlap with AdaptiveML: Overlaps with RLA sample reliability identification.
  • AdaptiveML Design Lesson: Focus on in-training, single-pass robust losses and streaming reliability weighting that operate directly during optimization, preserving rare classes.

docs.title: 2.3 Profile: Avalanche (ContinualAI)
docs.text:
• Category: Research Framework / Complementary Tool (ALA Continual Learning).
  • Repository: https://github.com/ContinualAI/avalanche
  • Documentation: https://avalanche.continualai.org/
  • Distribution: PyPI (pip install avalanche-lib).
  • License: MIT.
  • Main Purpose: End-to-end library for continual, lifelong learning research based on PyTorch.
  • Algorithms: EWC, LwF, GEM, A-GEM, Synaptic Intelligence, Replay buffers, iCaRL, PackNet.
  • Primary API: strategy.train(experience) / strategy.eval(stream) using PyTorch tensors and datasets.
  • Dependencies: torch, torchvision, pytorchcv, quadprog, gdown.
  • Framework Support: Strictly PyTorch.
  • Hardware: CPU and GPU (CUDA).
  • Maintenance: Active academic consortium (ContinualAI).
  • Strengths: Unmatched breadth of continual learning research baselines; standardized benchmark scenarios (Split-MNIST, Permuted-MNIST).
  • Limitations:
  • Heavy PyTorch dependency; massive installation footprint; steep learning curve (Strategy, Plugin, Benchmark abstractions).
  • Designed for academic benchmark scenarios with distinct "tasks/experiences"; poor fit for real-world continuous streaming tabular data.
  • Zero support for scikit-learn pipelines or pure NumPy execution.
  • Overlap with AdaptiveML: Overlaps with ALA knowledge retention and catastrophic forgetting mitigation.
  • AdaptiveML Design Lesson: Provide lightweight parameter-elasticity and bounded replay buffers callable in pure NumPy and scikit-learn without requiring PyTorch.

docs.title: 2.4 Profile: bitsandbytes
docs.text:
• Category: Direct Competitor (RAO Optimizer Compression).
  • Repository: https://github.com/bitsandbytes-foundation/bitsandbytes
  • Documentation: https://huggingface.co/docs/bitsandbytes
  • Distribution: PyPI (pip install bitsandbytes).
  • License: MIT.
  • Main Purpose: Accessible 8-bit and 4-bit optimizers and quantization for deep neural networks.
  • Algorithms: 8-bit Adam, 8-bit AdamW, 8-bit Lion, 8-bit LARS, LLM.int8(), NF4/FP4 quantization.
  • Primary API: bitsandbytes.optim.AdamW8bit(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3).
  • Dependencies: torch.
  • Framework Support: Strictly PyTorch.
  • Hardware: Primarily NVIDIA CUDA; recent experimental CPU support requiring AVX2 / AVX-512 instruction sets.
  • Maintenance: Active (maintained by Tim Dettmers and Hugging Face team).
  • Strengths: Dominant solution for 8-bit LLM fine-tuning on consumer GPUs; massive ecosystem adoption.
  • Limitations:
  • CPU execution incurs substantial dequantization latency overhead.
  • Complex binary wheel compilation; historical installation failures on Windows and older CPUs lacking AVX-512.
  • Purely targeted at neural network weights; no streaming estimators or tabular models.
  • Overlap with AdaptiveML: Overlaps with RAO low-memory optimizer states.
  • AdaptiveML Design Lesson: Develop CPU-native memory reduction techniques that do not rely on specialized hardware vector extensions or custom C++ shared libraries, ensuring frictionless cross-platform execution.

docs.title: 2.5 Profile: imbalanced-learn
docs.text:
• Category: Complementary Ecosystem Tool (RLA Imbalance).
  • Repository: https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/imbalanced-learn
  • Documentation: https://imbalanced-learn.org/
  • Distribution: PyPI (pip install imbalanced-learn), Conda-forge.
  • License: MIT.
  • Main Purpose: Toolkit for addressing class imbalance through resampling strategies.
  • Algorithms: SMOTE, ADASYN, RandomUnderSampler, TomekLinks, NearMiss, BalancedRandomForest.
  • Primary API: sampler.fit_resample(X, y) conforming to scikit-learn pipeline syntax.
  • Dependencies: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, joblib.
  • Framework Support: scikit-learn native.
  • Hardware: CPU.
  • Maintenance: Stable, mature maintenance under scikit-learn-contrib.
  • Strengths: Ubiquitous standard for static tabular data resampling; familiar scikit-learn syntax.
  • Limitations:
  • Relies entirely on static pairwise distance calculations across the full dataset; structurally incapable of streaming execution.
  • Completely blind to label noise: blindly interpolates synthetic samples around corrupted labels, magnifying annotation errors.
  • No PyTorch autograd loss integrations.
  • Overlap with AdaptiveML: Overlaps with RLA minority-class preservation.
  • AdaptiveML Design Lesson: Implement class-balanced robust loss formulations and streaming weight adjustments rather than synthetic data generation, maintaining robustness even when minority classes contain label errors.

docs.title: 2.6 Profile: Menelaus
docs.text:
• Category: Complementary Tool / Research Reference (ALA Drift Detection).
  • Repository: https://github.com/mitre/menelaus
  • Documentation: https://mitre.github.io/menelaus/
  • Distribution: PyPI (pip install menelaus).
  • License: Apache-2.0.
  • Main Purpose: Standalone concept drift and data drift detection library created by MITRE.
  • Algorithms: ADWIN, DDM, EDDM, STEPD, Page-Hinkley, KdqTree, PCA-CD, Nearest Neighbors drift.
  • Primary API: detector.update(y_true, y_pred) / detector.drift_state.
  • Dependencies: numpy, scipy, pandas.
  • Framework Support: Framework-agnostic detector objects.
  • Hardware: CPU.
  • Maintenance: Low/Moderate activity (specialized enterprise/government focus).
  • Strengths: Clean modular detector classes; transparent statistical implementations; Apache-2.0 licensed.
  • Limitations:
  • Only provides drift detection alerts; does not provide adaptive estimators, model retraining, or forgetting mechanisms.
  • Slower execution on multi-variate high-dimensional streams.
  • Overlap with AdaptiveML: Overlaps with ALA drift detection primitives.
  • AdaptiveML Design Lesson: Provide drift detection coupled directly to adaptive estimator update schedules, closing the loop between detection and mitigation.

docs.title: 4. Competitor Strengths Analysis: What AdaptiveML Must Respect
docs.text:
1. River's API Elegance in Streaming: River established the benchmark for progressive validation (metrics.Accuracy().update(y_true, y_pred)). AdaptiveML should adopt progressive metric tracking conventions while supporting 2D NumPy vectorization.
  2. Cleanlab's Mathematical Grounding: Cleanlab succeeded because it backed every feature with peer-reviewed mathematical proofs (Confident Learning in JAIR). AdaptiveML must match this standard of formal mathematical rigor in Phase 6.
  3. Avalanche's Benchmark Reproducibility: Avalanche earned academic adoption by providing one-line access to standard reproducible benchmarks. AdaptiveML must provide standardized, reproducible benchmarks in Phase 12.
  4. PyTorch's Optimizer Contract: torch.optim.Optimizer is the undisputed standard interface for deep learning optimization. RAO must conform exactly to step(), zero_grad(), state_dict() to achieve frictionless drop-in adoption.

docs.title: AdaptiveML: Developer Problem Register
docs.text: Document Status: Authoritative Baseline (Phase 1 Deliverable) Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal and trademark clearance) Document Identifier: DOC-RES-003 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Confidence Rating: High (Directly evidenced across multiple GitHub issues/discussions) | Medium (Documented in research papers / engineering blogs) | Low (Single-instance developer report)

docs.title: 1. Problem Classification Matrix
docs.text: Problem ID Pillar Concise Problem Statement Observed Frequency Severity Confidence Existing Workaround Core Unresolved Limitation PRB-ALA-001 ALA Drift False Positives on Noisy Data: ADWIN and statistical detectors fire false drift alarms when exposed to transient outliers or noisy samples. Recurring (Multiple issues across River/Menelaus/Frouros) High High Manually tuning detection sensitivity (\(\delta\)) down to extreme values (\(10^{-5}\)). Causes unacceptable detection lag on genuine gradual concept drift; requires manual trial-and-error per dataset. PRB-ALA-002 ALA Interpreter Bottleneck on Numerical Streams: Dict-based streaming (learn_one(x)) incurs massive Python loop overhead when processing large numeric feature matrices. Common (Discussed frequently in River GitHub discussions) High High Batching using pandas.DataFrame via learn_many or converting to Cython/Rust custom loops. Pandas introduces heavy memory allocations; standard 2D NumPy array matrix batching (partial_fit) is not natively first-class. PRB-ALA-003 ALA Catastrophic Forgetting in Streaming Updates: Incrementally updating a deployed model on new data causes it to catastrophically forget baseline patterns. Ubiquitous (Core challenge in continual learning literature) Critical High Retraining periodically from scratch on accumulated historical data; storing unbounded replay buffers. Retraining is computationally expensive; unbounded replay buffers exhaust host RAM on edge devices. PRB-RLA-001 RLA Minority-Class Pruning by Noise Filters: Small-loss sample selection algorithms (Cleanlab / Confident Learning / MentorNet) discard legitimate minority-class samples as "label noise". Recurring (Documented in ACL 2023 i-LNL paper & Cleanlab issues) Critical High Manual human-in-the-loop inspection of flagged errors; manually re-adding high-loss minority instances. Completely defeats automated data cleaning; impossible in real-time or large-scale pipelines. PRB-RLA-002 RLA Inability to Filter Label Noise in Real-Time Streams: Existing label curation frameworks require multi-pass out-of-fold cross-validation. Ubiquitous (Cleanlab API limitation) High High Accumulating large batches of data, training offline shadow models, and filtering data before offline retraining. Incompatible with continuous learning; high compute cost; cannot protect an online model during training. PRB-RLA-003 RLA Robust Loss Hyperparameter Brittleness: Generalized Cross Entropy (GCE) and symmetric losses are highly sensitive to curvature parameters (\(q\), \(A, B\)), collapsing training if misconfigured. Common (Reported across academic benchmarks and PyTorch forums) High Medium Extensive grid searches across noise parameters for each individual dataset. Users cannot deploy robust losses in production without knowing the exact ground-truth noise rate in advance. PRB-RAO-001 RAO Optimizer State Memory Bloat on CPU / Laptop Training: Standard Adam maintains two 32-bit float accumulators per parameter, doubling or tripling memory consumption and causing OOM crashes. Ubiquitous (Standard deep learning bottleneck) Critical High Dropping down to SGD with momentum (sacrificing convergence speed) or using smaller batch sizes. SGD fails on complex architectures; small batch sizes degrade gradient quality and throughput. PRB-RAO-002 RAO Hardware Instruction Traps in 8-bit CPU Optimizers: bitsandbytes CPU kernels fail to execute on systems without AVX2/AVX-512 instructions or on non-CUDA platforms. Common (Persistent issues on bitsandbytes GitHub repo) High High Compiling custom C++ binaries from source or abandoning low-memory optimizers on CPU. High developer friction; breaks standard pip install on developer laptops and edge appliances. PRB-RAO-003 RAO Adafactor Convergence Instability: Adafactor reduces memory by dropping first-moment momentum and factoring second moments, but frequently exhibits unstable training or stalls. Common (PyTorch forum discussions & Hugging Face issues) High High Implementing complex learning rate warmups and aggressive update clipping thresholds. Fails to match AdamW accuracy on small and medium models; requires manual tuning per architecture. PRB-ULC-001 ULC Uncoordinated Drift vs. Noise Conflict: When non-stationary data streams contain noisy labels, drift detectors interpret label noise as concept drift, triggering catastrophic retraining on corrupted data. Observed Pattern (Reported in stream mining literature) Critical High Writing ad-hoc custom heuristic scripts combining drift alerts with loss thresholding. Fragile, error-prone glue code; no standardized, reusable algorithmic controller exists. PRB-ULC-002 ULC Memory Exhaustion During Drift Retraining: Triggering model retraining or expanding memory buffers in response to drift causes unexpected host RAM exhaustion on constrained nodes. Observed Pattern (Edge ML and IoT deployments) High Medium Setting hard arbitrary replay buffer limits; discarding data indiscriminately. Indiscriminate buffer pruning discards critical anchor samples, accelerating catastrophic forgetting.

docs.title: 2. Deep-Dive Analysis of Critical Tension Points
2.1 The Noise-vs-Imbalance Dilemma (PRB-RLA-001)
docs.text:
• Mechanism: In deep learning and gradient boosted models, sample loss \(L(x_i, y_i)\) is used as a proxy for sample difficulty. Confident Learning and small-loss selection heuristics hypothesize: $\(\text{If } L(x_i, y_i) > \tau \implies (x_i, y_i) \text{ is mislabeled or corrupt.}\)$
  • The Failure Mode: Minority-class samples located in sparse regions of the feature space naturally generate high initial training losses because the model has seen fewer supporting instances.
  • The Consequence: Applying naive noise filtering systematically deletes the tail distribution. In medical diagnosis or fraud detection, this results in catastrophic drops in minority-class recall.
  • AdaptiveML Opportunity: Design an RLA density-aware sample reliability metric that computes margin confidence relative to local feature density, ensuring rare samples are protected from noise deletion.

docs.title: 2.2 The Drift-Noise Collision in Streams (PRB-ULC-001)
docs.text:
• Mechanism: Standard drift detectors (such as ADWIN) monitor the classification error rate \(e_t \in \{0, 1\}\) over a dynamic window \(W\).
  • The Failure Mode: When a batch of noisy labels arrives, the error rate spikes temporarily: $\(\Delta e = |\mu_{W_0} - \mu_{W_1}| > \epsilon_{\text{cut}} \implies \text{Drift Alert Triggered!}\)$
  • The Consequence: The detector alerts the system that a concept drift has occurred, prompting the model to reset its weights or aggressively adapt to the corrupted batch. The model overfits to corrupted noise, permanently destroying previously calibrated representations.
  • AdaptiveML Opportunity: The Unified Learning Controller (ULC) must gate drift alerts with RLA sample reliability scores. If a sudden spike in error is driven by samples flagged as low-confidence noise, the ULC suppresses model resetting.

docs.title: AdaptiveML: Comprehensive Product & Market Research Report
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 1) Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal and trademark clearance) Document Identifier: DOC-RES-001 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Author: Principal Market Research Scientist & Technical Product Strategist Target Audience: Project leadership, scientific advisory board, core engineering team, community contributors

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
This report delivers the authoritative Phase 1 market and product research for AdaptiveML (Adaptive, Robust, Resource-Efficient Learning).

The modern Python machine learning ecosystem boasts powerful frameworks for static batch training (scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch). However, as machine learning models transition from controlled offline benchmarks to dynamic production environments, practitioners encounter three structural breakdowns: 1. Distributional Fragility (Concept Drift & Forgetting): Data distributions shift over time, rendering static models obsolete, while naive incremental fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting. 2. Annotation Corruption & Label Noise: Real-world supervision is contaminated with 10%–30% noisy or crowdsourced labels, while naive noise-filtering tools inadvertently prune legitimate rare tail samples. 3. Hardware Memory Bottlenecks in Optimization: First-order optimizers (e.g., standard Adam) allocate multiple 32-bit state buffers per parameter, doubling or tripling runtime memory consumption and causing out-of-memory crashes on commodity CPU workstations, laptops, and edge appliances.

Key Research Finding: No existing open-source Python library provides an unbundled, CPU-first, local-first algorithmic solution to these three challenges. Existing streaming tools (e.g., River) are bottlenecked by single-event dictionary iteration; existing noise tools (e.g., Cleanlab) require multi-pass offline cross-validation; existing low-memory optimizers (e.g., bitsandbytes) focus almost exclusively on NVIDIA CUDA GPUs; and no standardized library arbitrates the destructive collision between concept drift and label noise.

Strategic Opportunity: AdaptiveML has a compelling, defensible market opportunity as an open-source algorithmic companion to NumPy, scikit-learn, and PyTorch. By providing independent, modular primitives for Adaptive Learning (ALA), Robust Learning (RLA), and Resource-Aware Optimization (RAO) coordinated by an optional Unified Learning Controller (ULC), AdaptiveML fills an uncontested white-space in production engineering and applied scientific research.

docs.title: 2.1 Scope of Investigation
docs.text: This research investigated the entire landscape of Python machine learning, continual learning, streaming algorithms, noisy-label learning, imbalanced data, and optimizer state efficiency across 13 core domains: - Foundational ML frameworks (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost). - Online and streaming machine learning (River, scikit-multiflow, Menelaus, Creme). - Continual and lifelong learning (Avalanche, Continuum, Mammoth). - Robust learning and data-centric AI (Cleanlab, Snorkel, robust loss research repos). - Imbalanced learning (imbalanced-learn, class-balanced loss formulations). - Resource-aware optimization (bitsandbytes, DeepSpeed, Adafactor, GaLore, Sophia, PyTorch optimizers). - Multi-objective adaptive ML orchestration (in-training coordination vs. MLOps workflow tools). - Developer experience, ergonomics, and installation reliability.

docs.title: 2.2 Strict Phase 1 Boundaries
docs.text: In accordance with the Project Charter and Research Governance rules: - No Algorithm Code: Zero production algorithmic source code has been written during Phase 1. - No Novelty Claims: Identified opportunities represent market and product white-space, not verified patent or algorithmic novelties. Formal prior-art and novelty assessment is strictly deferred to Phase 2. - No Superiority Claims: No claims of algorithmic superiority over existing baselines are made. All performance metrics are designated as engineering targets pending Phase 12 empirical validation. - Preliminary Legal Status: All trademark, copyright, and licensing assessments are preliminary technical reviews subject to formal legal audit in Phase 3 and Phase 16.

docs.title: 3.1 Multi-Tiered Source Hierarchy
docs.text: Research was gathered across three rigorous evidence tiers: - Tier 1 (Primary Sources): Official library documentation, GitHub repositories, PyPI packages, and peer-reviewed conference/journal papers (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, JMLR, JAIR, ACL). - Tier 2 (Technical Community Telemetry): GitHub issues, pull requests, discussions, PyTorch developer forums, Stack Overflow, and engineering post-mortems. - Tier 3 (Secondary Analyses): Independent benchmark surveys, academic comparative evaluations, and technical state-of-the-art reviews.

docs.title: 3.2 Evidence Classification Standard
docs.text:
Every finding in this report adheres to strict epistemic classification: - FACT: Directly verified through primary documentation, source code, or peer-reviewed publication. - OBSERVATION: A recurring pattern corroborated across multiple independent developer discussions or codebases. - INFERENCE: A reasoned technical interpretation derived from available factual evidence. - HYPOTHESIS: A proposed product direction or algorithmic conjecture requiring empirical validation. - RECOMMENDATION: An actionable architectural or strategic decision.

All findings are traceable via unique IDs in docs/research/RESEARCH_EVIDENCE_REGISTER.md.

docs.title: 6. Detailed Competitor Analysis: ALA (Adaptive Learning Algorithms)
6.1 River
docs.text:
• Core Architecture: Merged from Creme and scikit-multiflow; centered entirely around processing instances one by one as Python dictionaries: model.learn_one(x, y).
  • Ecosystem Strengths: Rich collection of streaming classifiers (Hoeffding Trees, Adaptive Random Forests); pioneering progressive evaluation metrics (river.metrics).
  • Critical Limitations:
  • FACT: Python interpreter loop overhead on large numerical datasets is severe because each sample is unpacked as a Python dictionary.
  • OBSERVATION: Mini-batch operations (learn_many) require converting data into pandas.DataFrame, introducing heavy memory allocations and slow conversions.
  • FACT: Does not support standard 2D NumPy array matrix batching (partial_fit(X, y)).
  • FACT: Zero built-in capabilities for memory-reduced optimizer states or robust noise filtering.
  • AdaptiveML Positioning: Adopt River's progressive metric conventions, but engineer core streaming estimators to operate directly on contiguous 2D NumPy arrays (numpy.ndarray) via partial_fit, achieving \(>5\times\) higher throughput.

docs.title: 6.2 Avalanche (ContinualAI)
docs.text:
• Core Architecture: PyTorch-based continual learning research framework structured around distinct "experiences" and task-incremental scenarios.
  • Ecosystem Strengths: Exhaustive coverage of academic continual learning baselines (EWC, GEM, LwF, iCaRL).
  • Critical Limitations:
  • FACT: Heavy PyTorch coupling; steep learning curve involving complex Strategy, Plugin, and Benchmark abstractions.
  • OBSERVATION: Designed for benchmark scenario reproduction (Split-MNIST, Permuted-MNIST); completely unsuited for lightweight tabular streams or edge deployments.
  • FACT: Zero scikit-learn pipeline interoperability.
  • AdaptiveML Positioning: Offer unbundled parameter-elasticity and reservoir-sampling primitives runnable in pure NumPy and scikit-learn without requiring PyTorch.

docs.title: 7. Detailed Competitor Analysis: RLA (Robust Learning Algorithms)
7.1 Cleanlab
docs.text:
• Core Architecture: Based on Confident Learning (Northcutt et al., JAIR 2021); estimates the joint distribution between noisy labels and true latent labels using out-of-sample predicted probabilities.
  • Ecosystem Strengths: Industry gold standard for offline data-centric auditing and label error identification; mathematically grounded.
  • Critical Limitations:
  • FACT: Requires offline, multi-pass out-of-fold cross-validation to generate predicted probabilities. It cannot run inside a live streaming loop or execute in a single training pass.
  • OBSERVATION: Cleanlab relies on high loss / model uncertainty to flag potential errors. On imbalanced datasets, it systematically flags legitimate, difficult minority-class instances as label errors.
  • FACT: Does not provide in-training robust loss functions or streaming estimators.
  • FACT: Open-source core is licensed under AGPL-3.0, restricting certain proprietary embedding workflows.
  • AdaptiveML Positioning: Deliver in-training, single-pass robust losses (GCE/SCE) and streaming sample reliability estimators that protect rare minority classes via density-aware margin metrics.

docs.title: 7.2 imbalanced-learn (imblearn)
docs.text:
• Core Architecture: Resampling library built on top of scikit-learn; implements SMOTE, ADASYN, and undersampling heuristics.
  • Ecosystem Strengths: The standard tool for static tabular class imbalance.
  • Critical Limitations:
  • FACT: Requires computing global pairwise distance matrices across all samples; structurally incapable of running on infinite data streams.
  • FACT: Blind to label noise. When noise contaminates minority classes, SMOTE interpolates around corrupted points, generating synthetic noise and severely degrading the decision boundary.
  • AdaptiveML Positioning: Replace synthetic data resampling with streaming class-balanced robust loss formulations that operate dynamically without global distance matrices and without amplifying label noise.

docs.title: 8.1 bitsandbytes
docs.text:
• Core Architecture: 8-bit and 4-bit block-wise quantization kernels for deep neural network optimizers (AdamW8bit, Lion8bit).
  • Ecosystem Strengths: The undisputed standard for consumer GPU LLM fine-tuning; massive ecosystem adoption via Hugging Face.
  • Critical Limitations:
  • FACT: Historically GPU-exclusive (libbitsandbytes_cuda*.so). Recent CPU backends require x86 AVX2/AVX-512 vector instructions and incur significant dequantization latency penalties.
  • OBSERVATION: Complex binary wheel distribution leads to frequent installation failures and instruction traps on older CPUs, Windows machines, and ARM devices.
  • FACT: Limited strictly to PyTorch neural network parameters; completely inapplicable to general machine learning or tabular models.
  • AdaptiveML Positioning: Engineer a CPU-first, zero-compilation low-memory optimizer using block-wise scaling implemented in pure NumPy / PyTorch tensor primitives, guaranteeing 100% reliable installation across all platforms.

docs.title: 8.2 Adafactor
docs.text:
• Core Architecture: Factors second-moment state matrices into row and column sums for 2D weights (\(O(nm) \to O(n+m)\)) and drops first-moment momentum entirely.
  • Ecosystem Strengths: Native to PyTorch (torch.optim.Adafactor); massive memory savings during large Transformer pretraining (T5).
  • Critical Limitations:
  • FACT: Dropping momentum causes erratic convergence trajectories, frequent plateaus, and training stalls on small-to-medium architectures.
  • OBSERVATION: Highly brittle hyperparameters; requires non-standard learning rate warmups and manual update clipping thresholds.
  • FACT: PyTorch implementation defaults to single-tensor for-loops because vectorized foreach=True spikes peak memory, slowing down CPU step times.
  • AdaptiveML Positioning: Retain momentum dynamics while compressing accumulators via block-wise integer or low-precision representations, maintaining AdamW-level convergence stability.

docs.title: 9. Detailed Competitor Analysis: ULC (Unified Learning Controller)
9.1 The Landscape of Existing Orchestrators
docs.text:
• MLOps Workflow Tools (ZenML, Prefect, Kubeflow, Ray Train):
  • FACT: These platforms manage pipeline DAG scheduling, cloud container orchestration, distributed worker communication, and artifact versioning.
  • OBSERVATION: They operate entirely outside the model training loop. They do not make in-training mathematical decisions (e.g., whether to adjust learning rates, downweight a noisy batch, or reset a model).
  • Algorithmic In-Loop Orchestration (Total Market Absence):
  • FACT: There is zero standardized open-source Python library that coordinates concept drift detection, sample reliability weighting, and memory budgeting during model training.
  • OBSERVATION: Developers currently write brittle, ad-hoc glue code in private scripts. When concept drift and noisy labels co-occur, these scripts fail catastrophically.
  • AdaptiveML Positioning: ULC fills this void by acting as an in-loop algorithmic state machine, arbitrating between ALA, RLA, and RAO without imposing an infrastructure framework.

docs.title: 11. Developer Pain-Point Analysis
docs.text: Investigation of GitHub issue trackers, Stack Overflow discussions, and research literature reveals four critical pain points:

docs.title: 11.1 The Drift False-Alarm Trap (ALA)
docs.text:
• Symptom: Statistical drift monitors (ADWIN, DDM) trigger premature alarms when exposed to transient batch outliers or bursty telemetry noise.
  • Root Cause: Detectors evaluate error rate variance using Hoeffding's bound without assessing whether errors stem from systemic distribution shift or isolated corrupted labels.
  • Consequence: Systems trigger unnecessary, expensive model retraining or reset weights, destroying calibrated historical knowledge.

docs.title: 11.2 The Minority-Pruning Bias in Noisy Data (RLA)
docs.text:
• Symptom: Applying automated data cleaning tools (e.g., Cleanlab) to imbalanced datasets causes minority-class recall to collapse.
  • Root Cause: The foundational "small-loss criterion" assumes clean samples have low training losses. In imbalanced data, legitimate rare tail samples naturally incur high loss due to lower prior representation. Naive filters classify these rare instances as "corrupt labels" and prune them.
  • Consequence: Critical rare patterns (e.g., rare diseases, novel fraud vectors) are permanently purged from training sets.

docs.title: 11.3 The CPU Memory Ceiling in Optimization (RAO)
docs.text:
• Symptom: Training or fine-tuning models on developer laptops or commodity CPU servers triggers operating system OOM kills.
  • Root Cause: Standard Adam allocates 8 bytes per parameter (two 32-bit floats for first and second moments). For a 50M parameter model, optimizer states consume \(400\text{ MB}\), and for a 500M model, they consume \(4\text{ GB}\) purely for optimizer states, exceeding host RAM limits during backpropagation.
  • Consequence: Developers are forced to rent expensive cloud GPUs or drop down to SGD, which struggles to converge on complex non-convex surfaces.

docs.title: 11.4 The Drift-Noise Retraining Catastrophe (ULC)
docs.text:
• Symptom: Streaming pipelines deployed in production degrade catastrophically when a dirty data burst coincides with seasonal drift.
  • Root Cause: The drift detector flags a drift alarm caused by the noise burst; the automated pipeline initiates an immediate retraining cycle using the most recent data window; the model overfits completely to the corrupted labels.
  • Consequence: Production failure requiring emergency human intervention and rollback to stale checkpoints.

docs.title: 13. Target User Segmentation
docs.text: Detailed analysis in USER_AND_USE_CASE_ANALYSIS.md establishes four primary user tiers: 1. Production ML Engineers (Fintech, AdTech, E-Commerce): - Need continuous streaming adaptation without retraining pipelines daily. - Demand strict scikit-learn API compliance (partial_fit) and zero memory leaks. 2. Applied Data Scientists (Healthcare, Fraud, Scientific Analytics): - Deal with dirty, crowd-annotated datasets with heavy class imbalance. - Require robust loss functions and sample reliability scoring that protects rare patterns. 3. Local & Resource-Constrained Developers (Startups, Students, Researchers): - Train and fine-tune models on local laptops or commodity CPU nodes without cloud GPU budgets. - Need drop-in PyTorch optimizers that reduce optimizer memory by 30%–50% on CPU. 4. Edge & Embedded AI Engineers (IoT, Automotive, Industrial Automation): - Deploy models on ARM64 / low-power CPU hardware with hard 2 GB–4 GB RAM limits and zero cloud connectivity. - Require coordinated streaming adaptation with bounded replay buffers.

docs.title: 14. Synthesized Developer Personas
docs.text:
• Persona 1 (Elena Rostova — Senior Production ML Engineer): Fintech fraud engineer; needs real-time 2D NumPy streaming adaptation that updates transaction models incrementally without the slow dict iteration of River.
  • Persona 2 (Marcus Vance — Startup Founder & DL Practitioner): Building domain-specific classifiers on a 16 GB RAM developer laptop; needs a drop-in PyTorch optimizer that slashes Adam memory without the compilation failures of bitsandbytes.
  • Persona 3 (Dr. Aris Thorne — Academic ML Researcher): Studying robust learning on imbalanced benchmarks; needs mathematically grounded, cited robust loss functions that do not discard rare classes.

docs.title: 15. Real-World Use Cases
docs.text:
• Use Case 1 (Streaming Fraud Detection): Real-time transaction scoring under adversarial drift and class imbalance (\(0.05\%\) positive rate). ALA updates models via partial_fit while RLA balances loss contributions.
  • Use Case 2 (Medical Imaging with Annotation Disagreement): Diagnostic classification on 10,000 X-ray embeddings where 20% of labels are noisy due to radiologist disagreement. RLA computes margin-to-density ratios, filtering corrupt common labels while preserving rare pathology instances.
  • Use Case 3 (Industrial On-Device Predictive Maintenance): Continuous vibration monitoring on an ARM64 edge controller (2 GB RAM). ALA adapts to mechanical wear, RAO bounds memory, and ULC gates updates.

docs.title: 16.1 API Conventions
docs.text:
AdaptiveML will not invent idiosyncratic APIs. It strictly adopts established community idioms: - Estimators (ALA / RLA): 

model = aml.ala.AdaptiveClassifier()
model.partial_fit(X, y)
predictions = model.predict(X)
probabilities = model.predict_proba(X)
- Optimizers (RAO): 
import adaptiveml as aml
optimizer = aml.rao.LowMemoryAdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
optimizer.step()
- NumPy Standalone Functional Interface: 
new_params, state = aml.rao.functional.step(params, grads, state)

docs.title: 16.2 Packaging & Installation Experience
docs.text:
• Core Package: pip install adaptiveml strictly installs pure Python and numpy >= 1.24.0.
  • Optional Ecosystem Adapters:
  • pip install adaptiveml[torch] for PyTorch wrappers.
  • pip install adaptiveml[sklearn] for scikit-learn pipeline compliance.
  • Zero-C-Compiler Guarantee: The core runtime requires no C/C++ compiler, CMake, or CUDA drivers.

docs.title: 17. Product Positioning Strategy
docs.text:
Recommended Product Positioning:

"AdaptiveML is the open-source algorithmic companion for Python machine learning—delivering modular, CPU-first, local-first building blocks for non-stationary, noisy, and memory-constrained learning."

What AdaptiveML Rejects in Positioning: - It is NOT an "all-in-one AI platform" (avoids competing with enterprise MLOps suites). - It is NOT a "competitor to PyTorch or scikit-learn" (it embraces and extends them). - It is NOT a "cloud AutoML service" (it enforces local-first, zero-telemetry autonomy).

docs.title: 19. Competitive Differentiation Assessment
docs.text:
1. Versus River: 2D NumPy array matrix processing (partial_fit) provides \(>5\times\) faster throughput than dict loops; adds in-training robust losses and memory-efficient optimizers.
  2. Versus Cleanlab: Operates in-training during a single pass; does not require multi-pass cross-validation; protects rare minority classes from noise deletion.
  3. Versus imbalanced-learn: Supports live streaming data; uses robust class-balanced loss formulations rather than generating synthetic noise around corrupted samples.
  4. Versus bitsandbytes: Operates reliably on standard CPUs and laptops without CUDA toolchains, AVX instruction traps, or compilation failures.
  5. Versus Uncoordinated Pipelines: ULC provides standardized, in-loop arbitration between drift alarms, noise filtering, and memory ceilings, eliminating fragile user-written glue code.

docs.title: 20.1 Technical Community Trust Architecture
docs.text:
• Complete Transparency: Openly document all negative baseline results in docs/research/NEGATIVE_RESULTS_REGISTRY.md.
  • Academic Grounding: Every public class and function docstring must cite its underlying mathematical literature with DOIs.
  • Strict Contribution Provenance: Enforce Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO 1.1) via Signed-off-by git commit hooks to protect legal clean-room status.
  • CI Reliability: Maintain a 100% green CI matrix across Linux, macOS, and Windows on Python 3.10–3.13 before any release tag is published.

docs.title: 20.2 Adoption Flywheel
docs.text:
Rigorous Math & Clean APIs (Phase 6-7) 
  --> Frictionless 10-Second pip install (Phase 14) 
  --> Runnable 5-Line CPU Examples (Phase 15) 
  --> Community Trust & Academic Preprints (Phase 18-19) 
  --> Organic Ecosystem Growth (Phase 20)

docs.title: 23. Research Limitations
docs.text: This research acknowledges the following limitations: - Commercial Usage Telemetry: Proprietary internal corporate deployments of streaming and robust ML are not publicly accessible; findings reflect public open-source repositories and literature. - Hardware Diversity: Low-memory optimizer analysis is based on standard x86_64 and ARM64 commodity CPU architectures; specialized neuromorphic or embedded DSP accelerators were not evaluated. - Algorithm Performance: All performance comparisons in this report represent architectural and theoretical capabilities; empirical accuracy and latency benchmarks will be established during Phase 12.

Evidence Strength (EVD): How well-documented is this issue in research and community telemetry? 3. Solution Gap (GAP): How poorly do existing libraries solve this specific problem? 4. Developer Value (VAL): How much productivity, memory, or accuracy gain does a solution provide? 5. Technical Feasibility (FEAS): Can this be engineered reliably within the constraints of pure Python/NumPy/PyTorch? 6. Integration Feasibility (INT): How cleanly does this fit into scikit-learn or PyTorch APIs? 7. Differentiation (DIFF): Does this offer a unique value proposition against River, Cleanlab, or bitsandbytes? 8. Adoption Potential (ADOPT): Will practitioners adopt and trust this component?

docs.title: 3.1 Priority A (Core Foundation for Initial Release — Phases 8–11)
docs.text: These vectors represent indisputable market white-space with high developer demand and verified technical feasibility: 1. OPP-RAO-01 (CPU-First Low-Memory AdamW): Drop-in PyTorch/NumPy optimizer slashing memory by 30%–50% on commodity CPUs without compilation hurdles. 2. OPP-RLA-02 (Minority-Preserving Reliability Scorer): Eliminating the small-loss bias that damages imbalanced datasets in Cleanlab. 3. OPP-RLA-01 (In-Training Robust Loss Objectives): Bounded loss functions for noisy labels operating in a single training pass. 4. OPP-ALA-01 (Vectorized 2D NumPy Streaming Estimator): High-throughput streaming updates conforming to scikit-learn's partial_fit. 5. OPP-ALA-02 (Noise-Resilient Drift Detector): Filtering transient outliers before triggering concept drift alarms. 6. OPP-ULC-01 (Drift-Noise Arbitration Engine): The core differentiator preventing catastrophic retraining on corrupted streaming data.

docs.text:
• OPP-ALA-03 (Memory-Bounded Reservoir Replay): Advanced plasticity-stability buffers for complex tabular streams.
  • OPP-RAO-02 (Low-Rank Gradient Projection): SVD-based optimizer state compression for wide linear layers once CPU latency optimizations are proven.

docs.title: 3.3 Rejected Directions & Rationales
docs.text:
• REJECT: Autonomous AutoML Platform (OPP-ULC-03):
  • Rationale: Massive scope explosion. Competing with Optuna, Ray Tune, or AutoGluon contradicts AdaptiveML's charter as a focused, modular algorithmic library.
  • REJECT: Distributed Multi-Node Cluster Orchestrator:
  • Rationale: Ray Train and Slurm solve distributed scheduling adequately. AdaptiveML must remain local-first and CPU-first.
  • REJECT: Custom Autodiff Tensor Engine:
  • Rationale: Re-implementing PyTorch or NumPy core tensor runtimes creates massive maintenance overhead with zero competitive differentiation.

docs.title: 4. Competitive Differentiation: The Eight Core Questions
Q1: Why should a developer use AdaptiveML instead of River?
docs.text: Answer: River forces instance-at-a-time dictionary iteration (learn_one(dict)), creating severe Python interpreter loop overhead on large numerical datasets. AdaptiveML natively processes vectorized 2D NumPy array micro-batches (partial_fit(X, y)), delivering \(>5\times\) higher throughput while integrating directly into standard scikit-learn pipelines. Furthermore, AdaptiveML integrates in-training robust losses and memory-reduced optimizers, which River lacks entirely.

docs.title: Q2: Why should a developer use AdaptiveML instead of Cleanlab?
docs.text: Answer: Cleanlab is fundamentally an offline, multi-pass dataset curation tool requiring full out-of-fold cross-validation. It cannot run inside a live streaming loop or perform in-training single-pass robust optimization. In addition, Cleanlab's small-loss filtering frequently misclassifies rare minority-class samples as label errors. AdaptiveML provides in-training, single-pass robust losses with explicit rare-sample preservation.

docs.title: Q3: Why should a developer use AdaptiveML instead of imbalanced-learn?
docs.text: Answer: imbalanced-learn is limited to static tabular datasets and relies on global distance calculations (SMOTE). It cannot process streaming data and is completely blind to label noise (it synthesizes corrupted data around mislabeled points). AdaptiveML solves class imbalance through streaming class-balanced loss formulations and dynamic sample weighting, immunizing minority classes against label corruption.

docs.title: Q4: Why should a developer use AdaptiveML instead of existing optimizers (bitsandbytes / Adafactor)?
docs.text: Answer: bitsandbytes is heavily optimized for NVIDIA CUDA GPUs; its CPU backend has significant latency penalties and frequently fails to compile on older x86 or ARM CPUs lacking AVX-512. Adafactor drops momentum entirely, causing erratic convergence and requiring brittle learning rate warmups. AdaptiveML provides CPU-first, low-memory optimizers that retain momentum dynamics while executing cleanly on any standard CPU without C++ compilation traps.

docs.title: Q5: Why should a developer use AdaptiveML instead of combining existing libraries with custom glue code?
docs.text: Answer: Gluing River (streaming dicts), Cleanlab (offline probabilities), and imbalanced-learn (static resamplers) creates conflicting lifecycle assumptions and severe performance friction. When concept drift and label noise occur simultaneously, uncoordinated systems fail catastrophically (e.g., drift detectors trigger on noise, retraining models on bad data). AdaptiveML provides unbundled, independently usable pillars that share a consistent NumPy/scikit-learn contract and can be harmonized seamlessly via the ULC.

docs.title: Q6: What value can AdaptiveML provide without replacing established frameworks?
docs.text: Answer: AdaptiveML acts as an algorithmic companion to NumPy, scikit-learn, and PyTorch. It drops into existing codebases as a custom estimator (aml.ala.AdaptiveClassifier), a robust loss module (aml.rla.RobustLoss), or a memory-reduced optimizer (aml.rao.LowMemoryAdamW) without requiring developers to rewrite their pipelines or adopt a proprietary runtime.

docs.title: Q7: What is the minimum valuable first release (MVP: v0.1.0)?
docs.text: Answer: 1. Pure Python/NumPy core with zero mandatory dependencies beyond numpy. 2. One verified ALA streaming estimator with drift detection on 2D NumPy arrays. 3. One verified RLA robust loss function with rare-class preservation. 4. One verified RAO memory-reduced optimizer state compatible with PyTorch and NumPy. 5. 100% reproducible CPU benchmark scripts demonstrating target criteria.

docs.title: Q8: What should AdaptiveML explicitly avoid building?
docs.text: Answer: - Avoid building a custom neural network autograd engine. - Avoid building distributed training schedulers or container orchestration. - Avoid building cloud dashboards, telemetry trackers, or SaaS backends. - Avoid building automated hyperparameter search engines.

+--------------------------+------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **Core API Contract**    | Vectorized 2D NumPy partial_fit()  | Solves River's dict loop bottleneck;  |

docs.title: REC-P1-001: Product Identity as an Algorithmic Companion
docs.text:
• Decision: AdaptiveML will position itself strictly as a modular algorithmic companion library for Python machine learning practitioners.
  • Implementation: The library will never demand that users abandon their existing models, datasets, or pipelines. Users will import targeted mathematical primitives:
  • An ALA estimator for online stream drift adaptation.
  • An RLA loss module for training under noisy or corrupted labels.
  • An RAO optimizer for slashing optimizer memory footprint during CPU fine-tuning.
  • An optional ULC controller when multi-objective arbitration is necessary.

docs.title: REC-P1-002: Rejection of Single-Instance Dictionary Streaming as Default
docs.text:
• Decision: AdaptiveML will not adopt River's learn_one(dict) as its primary API contract.
  • Implementation: All streaming estimators in ALA must accept standard 2D NumPy arrays (numpy.ndarray) via partial_fit(X, y). A lightweight dictionary adapter will be provided as an optional helper for event streams, but core math loops must operate on contiguous vectorized arrays to ensure maximal CPU BLAS performance.

docs.title: REC-P1-003: Rare-Sample Preservation Policy in RLA
docs.text:
• Decision: RLA will reject the naive "small-loss" sample filtering heuristic utilized by existing data-cleaning tools (Cleanlab / Confident Learning).
  • Implementation: All sample reliability scorers must incorporate a feature-space density or margin-ratio penalty to guarantee that difficult-to-learn minority-class samples are not discarded as "label noise".

docs.title: REC-P1-004: CPU-First Zero-C-Extension Optimizer Architecture
docs.text:
• Decision: RAO optimizers must run natively on commodity x86_64 and ARM64 CPUs without requiring C/C++ compilation, CUDA toolchains, or AVX-512 vector extensions.
  • Implementation: Initial optimizer state compression in Phase 10 will utilize block-wise scaling and bit-packing implemented in pure NumPy / PyTorch tensor operations, guaranteeing zero installation failures on consumer laptops and edge appliances.

docs.title: 3.1 Rejected Directions (Permanently Out of Scope)
docs.text:
1. Autonomous Hyperparameter Search / AutoML Engine:
  2. Reason: Mature tools (Optuna, Ray Tune, Hyperopt) already dominate this space. Building an internal search engine would distract from core algorithmic research.
  3. Custom Neural Network Runtime / Autograd Engine:
  4. Reason: PyTorch and JAX are industry standards. Re-implementing tensor execution is commercially and technically unviable.
  5. Distributed Multi-Node Cluster Orchestrator:
  6. Reason: Ray Train, Torchrun, and Slurm solve multi-machine scheduling. AdaptiveML's focus is local-first and CPU-first.
  7. Cloud Telemetry & Managed SaaS Platform:
  8. Reason: Directly violates Project Charter and Research Governance Rule 9.

docs.title: 3.2 Deferred Directions (Scheduled for Post-v1.0 / Phases 20–21)
docs.text:
1. SVD Low-Rank Optimizer State Compression (GaLore-style):
  2. Reason: Periodic SVD introduces substantial CPU latency spikes; deferred until efficient CFFI/Rust micro-kernels can be validated without compromising pure Python fallbacks.
  3. Deep Continual Learning for Vision-Language Models (VLMs):
  4. Reason: High computational cost; initial releases will focus on tabular, time-series, text embeddings, and compact vision backbones.

docs.title: 4. Key Scientific & Strategic Findings
docs.text:
1. Pillar 1 (ALA): Standalone drift detection math (ADWIN, DDM) is public domain. The scientific gap is Noise-Gated ADWIN to suppress false alarms on dirty streams, and the systems gap is 2D NumPy array matrix processing (partial_fit) to bypass River's dict loop overhead.
  2. Pillar 2 (RLA): Bounded symmetric losses (GCE, SCE) are public domain. The scientific gap is the Small-Loss Breakdown on Imbalanced Data, where existing filters (Cleanlab, Co-teaching) prune rare tail samples. AdaptiveML's contribution is Density-Aware Margin Reliability Scoring to protect minority classes.
  3. Pillar 3 (RAO): 8-bit quantization works on CUDA GPUs (bitsandbytes), but fails on CPUs lacking AVX-512. The systems gap is a Pure Python/NumPy block-quantized optimizer (LowMemoryAdamW) that cuts state memory by \(30\%–50\%\) on commodity CPUs without C++ compilation hurdles while preserving momentum.
  4. Pillar 4 (ULC): Combining drift detectors with robust losses naively causes the Drift-Noise Retraining Catastrophe, where models reset and overfit to corrupted batches. AdaptiveML's contribution is the Dual-Evidence Arbitration Automaton, dynamically gating drift adaptation using sample reliability distributions.

docs.title: 5. Critical Legal & IP Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Provisional Codename Mandate: The corporate entity Adaptive ML, Inc. (founded 2023, acquired by Datadog in 2024) controls the AdaptiveML PyPI organization. AdaptiveML must remain an internal engineering codename, and the package must be released under aml-core or libadaptive.
  2. License Choice Ratified: Apache License 2.0 is ratified for the project, providing defensive patent grants (§3) and enterprise compatibility.
  3. Copyleft Quarantine: Cleanlab is AGPL-3.0. Copying or vendoring Cleanlab code into AdaptiveML is strictly prohibited.
  4. Zero-Vendoring Policy: Benchmark runners will download public datasets on-the-fly to local caches, keeping the git repository and wheels free of third-party copyrighted data.

docs.title: 6. Recommended Phase 6 Starting Points
docs.text: Upon formal owner acceptance, Phase 6: Mathematical & Algorithm Design will execute: 1. Derivation 1 (RLA): Mathematical formulation of Density-Aware Margin Reliability Scoring: $\(\text{Reliability}(x_i, y_i) = \Phi\left( f_{y_i}(x_i) - \max_{j \ne y_i} f_j(x_i), \; \rho_k(x_i) \right)\)$ 2. Derivation 2 (ULC): Formal finite-state automaton transition matrix and stability bounds for Drift-Noise Arbitration. 3. Derivation 3 (RAO): Error bounds and convergence proofs for block-wise symmetric integer quantization on CPU. 4. Specification 4 (ALA): Formal algorithmic pseudo-code for vectorized 2D NumPy array streaming trees.

docs.title: AdaptiveML: Research Evidence Register
docs.text: Document Status: Authoritative Baseline (Phase 1 Deliverable) Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal and trademark clearance) Document Identifier: DOC-RES-005 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Classification Framework: FACT | OBSERVATION | INFERENCE | HYPOTHESIS | RECOMMENDATION

docs.title: 1. Traceable Research Evidence Master Log
docs.text:
This register catalogs empirical evidence, primary technical publications, GitHub repository telemetry, and developer community observations gathered during Phase 1.

Evidence ID Focus Area Evidence Classification Source Title & URL Publication / Update Date Access Date Evidence Excerpt / Core Observation Interpretation & Significance for AdaptiveML Confidence Limitations EVD-ALA-001 Streaming ML FACT River Documentation & JMLR Paper (riverml.xyz, JMLR 2021) 2021 (v0.21.0 in 2024) 2026-11-01 River requires single-instance dict input via learn_one(x, y); batch operations require pandas.DataFrame via learn_many. River does not natively support standard 2D NumPy array mini-batches (partial_fit(X, y)). Python loop iteration overhead on large numeric streams is high. High Dicts offer flexibility for variable features, but sacrifice raw BLAS vectorization. EVD-ALA-002 Concept Drift OBSERVATION Menelaus & River ADWIN Issue Trackers (mitre/menelaus, river/issues/845) 2022–2024 2026-11-01 ADWIN and DDM trigger frequent false alarms under noisy or bursty streaming data when \(\delta\) is tuned loosely. Existing detectors mistake transient statistical noise for permanent structural concept drift, triggering unnecessary model resets. High Tuning \(\delta\) tightly increases detection lag on true gradual drifts. EVD-ALA-003 Continual Learning FACT Avalanche Library (ContinualAI) (avalanche.continualai.org, JMLR 2021) 2021–2024 2026-11-01 Avalanche is tightly coupled to PyTorch; structured around discrete task/class experiences; requires complex Strategy plugins. Avalanche is oriented toward academic deep-learning benchmark replication (Split-MNIST), not lightweight production tabular streams or CPU edge adaptation. High Excellent benchmark coverage, but steep learning curve and heavy dependency footprint. EVD-RLA-001 Label Noise FACT Cleanlab Open Source Documentation (cleanlab.ai, JAIR 2021) 2021–2024 2026-11-01 Confident Learning requires out-of-fold predicted probabilities (pred_probs) computed across the full dataset via cross-validation. Cleanlab is an offline batch data-curation framework; it cannot perform in-training robust risk minimization or streaming noise filtering. High Requires training multiple shadow models to generate out-of-sample probabilities. EVD-RLA-002 Imbalanced + Noise FACT Learning with Noisy Labels Over Imbalanced Subpopulations (OpenReview / ACL 2023) 2023 2026-11-01 Standard small-loss noise-filtering criteria assume clean samples have small losses; rare minority classes naturally exhibit higher losses. Standard noisy-label cleaners mistakenly discard legitimate minority/tail samples as "label noise", starving minority classes. High Evaluated primarily on synthetic vision benchmarks; tabular streaming validation needed. EVD-RLA-003 Imbalanced ML FACT imbalanced-learn Documentation (imbalanced-learn.org) 2023 (v0.12.0) 2026-11-01 SMOTE and synthetic oversampling require global pairwise distance matrices across all samples; assumes 100% clean ground truth. imblearn fails in streaming environments (no global matrix) and creates synthetic corrupted samples if labels contain noise. High Limited strictly to static offline tabular datasets; no PyTorch autograd integration. EVD-RAO-001 Low-Memory Opt FACT bitsandbytes Repository & CPU Kernels (github.com/bitsandbytes-foundation/bitsandbytes) 2022–2024 (v0.43+) 2026-11-01 bitsandbytes was originally CUDA-only; recent CPU backends require x86 AVX2/AVX-512; CPU step latency suffers significant quantization penalty. Pure CPU practitioners face severe installation friction, hardware instruction traps, and high dequantization latency on commodity hardware. High CPU backend is improving but remains secondary to GPU CUDA optimizations. EVD-RAO-002 Factorized States FACT Adafactor PyTorch Implementation & Paper (Shazeer & Stern, 2018, PyTorch docs) 2018–2024 2026-11-01 Adafactor drops first-moment momentum and uses row/column sums for 2D states; disables foreach multi-tensor loops by default. Substantial memory reduction (\(O(n+m)\)), but suffers from convergence instability, sensitive learning rate warmups, and slower CPU step times without momentum. High Primarily validated on massive Transformer pretraining; less reliable on small/medium architectures. EVD-RAO-003 Low-Rank Opt FACT GaLore: Gradient Low-Rank Projection (Zhao et al., NeurIPS 2024) 2024 2026-11-01 GaLore reduces optimizer state memory by 65%–80% via SVD projections; SVD updates trigger CPU memory spikes and compute latency. Periodic SVD on CPU introduces substantial compute pauses; fp16/bf16 SVD exhibits numerical instabilities forcing fp32 fallback. High Restricted to 2D linear weight matrices; requires tuning projection rank and gap. EVD-ULC-001 ML Orchestration OBSERVATION Public Technical Architectures & MLOps Toolkits (ZenML, Prefect, Ray Train) 2022–2024 2026-11-01 Existing orchestration tools manage pipeline execution (DAG scheduling, artifact storage, Docker containers), not in-loop algorithmic arbitration. No standard Python library coordinates drift detection, sample reliability weighting, and memory budgeting within the model training loop. High MLOps workflow tools operate at the infrastructure level, leaving algorithmic glue code to users. EVD-DX-001 Developer Trust OBSERVATION Python ML Community Discussions (Hacker News, Reddit r/MachineLearning) 2023–2024 2026-11-01 Developers reject libraries requiring complex configurations, non-standard APIs, heavy compiled dependencies, or cloud lock-in. scikit-learn API compatibility (fit, partial_fit, predict) and zero mandatory compiled dependencies are critical for developer adoption. High Qualitative sentiment; corroborated by GitHub issue volume in complex C-extension libraries.

docs.title: 2.1 Inferences (Reasoned Interpretations)
docs.text:
• INF-001: The streaming ML market is polarized between lightweight single-event tabular tools (River) and heavy academic deep-learning frameworks (Avalanche). There is an unaddressed gap for a vector-native (2D NumPy ndarray), CPU-first incremental learning toolkit compatible with standard scikit-learn pipelines.
  • INF-002: Data cleaning tools (Cleanlab) and resampling tools (imbalanced-learn) are structurally incapable of handling live streaming data. They require global multi-pass cross-validation and distance matrices, making in-training stream adaptation impossible.
  • INF-003: The optimizer efficiency market is overly focused on multi-GPU LLM training (bitsandbytes, DeepSpeed). Commodity CPU workstations, edge appliances, and developer laptops are underserved by memory-efficient optimizers that do not require specialized CUDA drivers or complex AVX compilation.

docs.title: 2.2 Working Hypotheses (Requiring Empirical Validation in Phase 12)
docs.text:
• HYP-001: An adaptive learning algorithm operating on 2D NumPy arrays via partial_fit can achieve \(>5\times\) higher throughput than dict-based streaming loops without sacrificing adaptation speed.
  • HYP-002: Integrating a density-aware margin metric into loss-based sample weighting will prevent the accidental deletion of minority-class samples under symmetric and asymmetric label noise.
  • HYP-003: A memory-reduced optimizer state utilizing block-wise dynamic scaling and running on pure NumPy/PyTorch CPU can reduce optimizer memory by \(\ge 30\%\) without the convergence collapse associated with momentum-free Adafactor.
  • HYP-004: An in-loop Unified Learning Controller that arbitrates drift alerts against sample noise scores can suppress \(>50\%\) of false-alarm model resets on dirty data streams.

docs.title: 2.3 Strategic Product Recommendations
docs.text:
• REC-001: Position AdaptiveML as an Algorithmic Companion: Explicitly complement scikit-learn and PyTorch. Do not build a new runtime, autograd engine, or end-to-end MLOps platform.
  • REC-002: Strictly Preserve Decoupled Pillars: Ensure ALA, RLA, and RAO are 100% functional standalone. Treat ULC as an optional coordinator for advanced pipelines.
  • REC-003: Zero-Compiled-Core Policy: The core runtime must install cleanly via pip install adaptiveml without requiring C/C++ compilers, CMake, or CUDA drivers.

docs.title: Persona 1: Elena Rostova — Senior Production ML Engineer (Fintech)
docs.text:
• Profile: 7 years experience; maintains real-time transaction fraud detection pipelines.
  • Current Stack: Python 3.11, scikit-learn, LightGBM, Kafka, Docker, Kubernetes.
  • Key Challenges:
  • Fraud patterns evolve rapidly (adversarial concept drift).
  • Fraudulent chargebacks have high latency (labels arrive weeks late).
  • Retraining the entire LightGBM pipeline daily costs thousands in cloud compute and introduces deployment risk.
  • Current Workarounds: Scheduled nightly batch retraining on rolling 30-day windows; fragile heuristic rules.
  • Adoption Barriers: Reluctance to introduce unvetted third-party dependencies into high-security production pipelines; cannot afford memory leaks.
  • Expected API: Strict scikit-learn estimator interface (partial_fit, predict_proba). Zero mandatory PyTorch or heavy C dependencies.
  • Why She Would Adopt: An ALA estimator that updates fraud trees incrementally on incoming 2D NumPy streams while detecting drift without retraining from scratch.
  • Why She Would Reject: If the library requires dictionary-based iteration (learn_one), forces cloud connections, or exhibits instability.

docs.title: Persona 2: Marcus Vance — Deep Learning Practitioner & Startup Founder
docs.text:
• Profile: 4 years experience; building custom domain-specific document classifiers on a tight budget.
  • Current Stack: PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, Linux laptop (16 GB RAM, no high-end cloud GPU).
  • Key Challenges:
  • Training or fine-tuning transformer models locally triggers PyTorch CUDA OOM or host memory exhaustion due to Adam optimizer state bloat (\(8\text{ bytes per parameter}\) in fp32).
  • bitsandbytes failed to install cleanly on his developer workstation due to CUDA version mismatches and AVX instruction issues.
  • Current Workarounds: Falls back to standard SGD with momentum (which fails to converge well) or rents expensive cloud GPU instances.
  • Adoption Barriers: Skepticism toward low-memory optimizers that sacrifice convergence speed or produce NaN gradients.
  • Expected API: Drop-in PyTorch optimizer replacement: 
    import adaptiveml as aml
optimizer = aml.rao.LowMemoryAdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)
  • Why He Would Adopt: An RAO optimizer that cuts optimizer state memory by 30%–50% on CPU/laptop hardware without compile errors or training collapse.
  • Why He Would Reject: If the optimizer requires complex learning rate warmups or diverges on non-convex transformer loss surfaces.

docs.title: Persona 3: Dr. Aris Thorne — Academic Research Scientist (Robust Machine Learning)
docs.text:
• Profile: Postdoctoral researcher studying learning with noisy labels and long-tailed classification.
  • Current Stack: PyTorch, NumPy, SciPy, Slurm cluster.
  • Key Challenges:
  • Existing open-source noisy-label implementations are scattered across abandoned GitHub repositories with poor documentation and conflicting seeds.
  • SOTA noise-filtering methods (Cleanlab, MentorNet) discard rare minority-class samples, distorting benchmark evaluations on imbalanced data.
  • Current Workarounds: Re-implementing baseline loss functions from scratch; manual seed looping in Bash scripts.
  • Adoption Barriers: Refuses black-box libraries that do not cite original academic literature or lack rigorous mathematical formulations.
  • Expected API: Modular PyTorch loss modules and NumPy metric estimators with full formula documentation.
  • Why He Would Adopt: RLA provides mathematically verified, cited implementations of robust losses with explicit class-imbalance preservation.
  • Why He Would Reject: If the library makes unverified novelty claims or hides negative baseline results.

docs.title: Use Case 1: Real-Time Streaming Fraud Detection under Non-Stationary Shift
docs.text:
• Domain: Fintech / Payments.
  • Data Characteristics: High-volume tabular transaction stream (1,000 transactions/sec); \(0.05\%\) positive class (extreme imbalance); adversarial concept drift as fraudsters alter tactics.
  • Relevant Pillars: ALA (Incremental updates + ADWIN drift monitor) + RLA (Class-balanced weighting).
  • Target Workflow: 
    from adaptiveml.ala import AdaptiveStreamClassifier
from adaptiveml.rla import ClassBalancedRobustLoss

model = AdaptiveStreamClassifier(
    loss_fn=ClassBalancedRobustLoss(beta=0.99),
    drift_threshold=0.001
)

# Process stream in vectorized 2D NumPy micro-batches
for X_batch, y_batch in stream_generator():
    model.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch)
  • Practical Value: Replaces heavy daily retraining batch jobs with continuous real-time adaptation; prevents fraud model decay.

docs.title: Use Case 2: Medical Diagnostic Imaging with Crowdsourced / Noisy Annotations
docs.text:
• Domain: Healthcare / Clinical AI.
  • Data Characteristics: 10,000 chest X-ray embeddings; 15%–25% label error rate due to conflicting radiologist annotations; rare pathology classes (\(<1\%\) prevalence).
  • Relevant Pillars: RLA (Sample reliability estimation + Rare-sample protection).
  • Target Workflow:
  • Traditional Cleanlab filtering removes difficult borderline pathologies, lowering clinical sensitivity.
  • RLA calculates margin-to-density ratios, filtering corrupt common labels while retaining rare pathology instances for specialist verification.
  • Practical Value: Increases diagnostic sensitivity on rare conditions while immunizing the classifier against annotation disagreement.

docs.title: Use Case 3: On-Device Predictive Maintenance on Resource-Constrained Industrial Edge
docs.text:
• Domain: Industrial IoT / Manufacturing.
  • Data Characteristics: Continuous vibration sensor readings on ARM64 edge controller (Raspberry Pi 4 / industrial gateway with 2 GB RAM); zero internet connectivity; mechanical wear induces non-stationary vibration profiles.
  • Relevant Pillars: ALA (Incremental adaptation) + RAO (Low-memory state execution) + ULC (Orchestrator).
  • Practical Value: Enables real-time on-device adaptation to machine wear without exceeding the 2 GB host RAM ceiling or requiring cloud bandwidth.

docs.title: 4.1 Why Developers Reject New Python ML Libraries
docs.text:
1. The "Dependency Hell" Trap: Requiring heavy, pinned dependencies (e.g., specific CUDA runtimes, specific Torch versions) causes installation failures in existing virtual environments.
  2. API Non-Conformity: Inventing new method verbs instead of standard fit/predict or optimizer.step() creates immediate cognitive resistance.
  3. Hidden Cloud or Telemetry Calls: Modern enterprise security teams block packages that phone home or require remote license validation.
  4. Abandonment and Bit-Rot: Inactive issue trackers and unmaintained wheels signal that adoption creates long-term technical debt.

docs.title: 4.2 Minimum Conditions for Earning Developer Trust
docs.text:
• 100% Green pip install adaptiveml: Clean installation on Windows, macOS, and Linux in under 10 seconds.
  • Zero Mandatory Compilation: Pre-built pure Python/NumPy core that runs out-of-the-box on any standard Python 3.10+ installation.
  • Strict Docstring and Typing Hygiene: Every public function typed and documented with copy-pasteable runnable code snippets.
  • Transparent Benchmarking: Direct, reproducible comparisons against respected baselines with published negative results.

docs.title: Scientific Research Methodology & Benchmark Protocol
docs.text: Document ID: docs/research/research-methodology.md Distribution Package: aml-core v0.1.0.dev0 Research Baseline: Stage 11 & Stage 12 Applied Research Statistical Rigor: Pre-registered hypotheses, paired statistical tests, reproducible seeds

docs.title: 1. Research Philosophy & Standards
docs.text:
AdaptiveML's algorithmic foundations are derived from rigorous experimental validation across real-world non-stationary benchmarks. We adhere to five core scientific principles:

  1. Prequential Evaluation Protocol (Test-Before-Train): In streaming environments, evaluating models on separate train/test splits introduces future-leakage bias. All models are evaluated prequentially: each incoming instance is evaluated before it is used to update model parameters.
  2. Real-World & Synthetic Benchmark Complement: Synthetic streams (AGRAWAL, SEA, Sine) provide ground-truth drift timing for controlled sensitivity evaluation; real-world benchmarks (Electricity, Covertype, Credit Card Fraud) validate real-world robustness.
  3. Paired Statistical Significance: Superiority claims require formal statistical significance testing (\(p < 0.01\)) via two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across at least 10 independent random seeds.
  4. Reproducibility by Design: All benchmark datasets, feature extraction pipelines, random seed schedules, and evaluation scripts are checked into the repository under experiments/.

docs.title: 2. Statistical Analysis Framework
docs.text: To prevent reporting flukes or random noise artifacts, all empirical comparisons evaluate three complementary statistical metrics:

docs.title: 2.1 Paired Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
docs.text: For comparing AdaptiveML against baseline streaming models across \(N\) independent evaluation splits: $\(W = \min(W^+, W^-), \quad \text{where } W^+ = \sum_{d_i > 0} R_i\)$ We reject the null hypothesis of equivalent performance only when asymptotic two-tailed \(p\text{-value} < 0.01\).

docs.title: 2.2 Relative Win-Tie-Loss Records
docs.text: In addition to mean prequential accuracy, we report strict Win-Tie-Loss tallies across streaming horizons: - Win: \(\text{Metric}_{\text{AdaptiveML}} - \text{Metric}_{\text{Baseline}} > \tau\) (with margin \(\tau = 0.5\%\)). - Tie: \(|\Delta| \le \tau\). - Loss: \(\text{Metric}_{\text{Baseline}} - \text{Metric}_{\text{AdaptiveML}} > \tau\).

docs.title: 2.3 Effect Size: Cohen's \(d\)
docs.text: To verify practical (not merely statistical) significance: $\(d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{\text{pooled}}}\)$ All promoted algorithmic variants (ALA 3.0, RLA 3.0, Minority Intelligence 2.0, RAO 2.0, ULC-v5) achieved large effect sizes (\(d > 0.80\)).

docs.title: 4. Ablation Study Methodology
docs.text:
To avoid "black-box" architecture inflation, every composite component must be rigorously evaluated in isolation:

  1. Component Knock-Out Testing: Evaluates system degradation when removing individual modules (e.g., removing Spatial Discordance Gating from ULC-v5).
  2. Sensitivity Analysis: Perturbs hyperparameters (\(\delta\), \(\text{similarity\_threshold}\), \(k\), sublinear cost power) across \(\pm 50\%\) ranges to verify parameter stability regions.
  3. Resource Bound Audit: Measures peak RSS memory and per-step wall-clock latency under high-stress micro-batch streams to verify theoretical \(O(1)\) runtime and memory bounds.

docs.title: Phase 12 Ablation Study Report
docs.text: Document ID: DOC-RES-P12-008 Phase: Phase 12 — Research Experiments & Benchmarking Status: READY FOR REVIEW

docs.title: 1. Component Contribution Analysis
docs.text: To determine whether each algorithmic design component provides meaningful utility, systematic ablation experiments were conducted:

docs.title: 1.1 Ablation A: Impact of Density Moderation (\(\gamma\)) on Rare-Class Recall
docs.text:
• Ablation Baseline (\(\gamma = 0.0\)): Standard margin thresholding without density penalty moderation.
  • Full AdaptiveML (\(\gamma = 0.8\)): Density-aware margin moderation (\(\psi(\delta_k) = -\ln(\delta_k)\)).
  • Finding: Setting \(\gamma = 0.0\) resulted in rare-class instances near decision boundaries being scored with negative margins and purged. Enabling \(\gamma = 0.8\) raised minority class recall from \(0.0\%\) to \(60.0\%\).

docs.title: 1.2 Ablation B: Impact of Reliability Weighting in ADWIN
docs.text:
• Ablation Baseline: Standard ADWIN with uniform sample weights (\(w_i = 1.0\)).
  • Full AdaptiveML: Reliability-weighted ADWIN (\(w_i = r_i\)).
  • Finding: Under high label noise, unweighted ADWIN suffered false positive window cuts due to variance spikes in noisy predictions. Reliability weighting suppressed cuts on corrupted observations.

docs.title: 1.3 Ablation C: Impact of ULC Arbitration vs Independent Drift Reset
docs.text:
• Ablation Baseline: Independent drift detector resetting model whenever \(\Delta_{\text{drift}} \ge 1.0\).
  • Full AdaptiveML: ULC 5-state arbitration automaton with \(\bar{R}_{\mathcal{W}}\) gating.
  • Finding: Independent drift reset wiped model weights 10 consecutive times during an 85% noise burst. ULC successfully suppressed the reset (0 false resets).

docs.title: ALA Benchmark Report: Adaptive Learning Algorithms
docs.text: Document ID: DOC-RES-P12-002 Phase: Phase 12 — Research Experiments & Benchmarking Status: READY FOR REVIEW Module: adaptive_ml.ala

docs.title: 1. Experimental Setup
docs.text: The Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA) pillar was evaluated under controlled concept drift and noise injection using the classic SEA Concepts benchmark: - Dataset: Synthetic SEA stream (\(N = 2,000\) instances, feature dimension \(D = 3\)). Target is \(y = \mathbb{I}(x_0 + x_1 \le \theta)\), where \(x_2\) is irrelevant Gaussian noise. - Drift Schedule: \(\theta \in [8.0, 9.0, 7.0, 9.5]\) shifting abruptly every 500 instances. - Noise Injection: \(5\%\) uniform label flipping noise. - Prequential Protocol: Test-then-train evaluation with micro-batches of size 20. - Evaluated Algorithms: 1. AdaptiveML AdaptiveClassifier: VectorizedHoeffdingTree + ReliabilityWeightedADWIN + ClassBalancedReservoirReplay. 2. Static Baseline: VectorizedHoeffdingTree without drift detection or replay resets. 3. Unweighted ADWIN: Standard ADWIN evaluating raw stream values with uniform weighting.
