docs.title: AdaptiveML — Literature Review: RLA Research Dossier
Primary Research Dossier 2: Robust Learning Algorithms, Noisy Labels & Imbalance
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 4) Document Identifier: DOC-LIT-002 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Research Pillar: Pillar 2 — RLA (Robust Learning Algorithms)

docs.title: 1. Research Background & Problem Formulation
docs.text:
Standard supervised machine learning relies on Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM). Given training set \(S = \{(x_i, \tilde{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^N\), where \(\tilde{y}_i\) denotes the observed (potentially corrupted) label: $\(\mathcal{R}_{\text{emp}}(f) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f(x_i), \tilde{y}_i)\)$

When labels are clean, ERM converges to the Bayes optimal classifier under cross-entropy loss. However, deep neural networks and flexible non-parametric estimators have sufficient capacity to memorize random labels (Zhang et al., ICLR 2017). When trained with standard Cross-Entropy on corrupted labels, models overfit to noise, degrading test-set generalization.

docs.title: Comprehensive Label Noise Taxonomy
docs.text:
1. Symmetric (Uniform) Noise: A label flips to any other class with equal probability \(\eta / (K - 1)\): $\(P(\tilde{y} = j | y^* = i) = \begin{cases} 1 - \eta & \text{if } j = i \\ \frac{\eta}{K-1} & \text{if } j \ne i \end{cases}\)$
  2. Asymmetric (Class-Conditional) Noise: Flipping probabilities depend on the true latent class \(i\) (e.g. Cat \(\leftrightarrow\) Dog, Beaver \(\leftrightarrow\) Otter). Captured by a transition matrix \(T_{i, j} = P(\tilde{y} = j | y^* = i)\).
  3. Instance-Dependent (Feature-Dependent) Noise: The most realistic real-world noise model. The probability of an annotation error depends directly on feature difficulty \(x\): $\(P(\tilde{y} = j | y^* = i, x) = \eta_{i, j}(x)\)$ (e.g., borderline or low-resolution medical images are more frequently misannotated).
flowchart TD
    A["Label Noise Taxonomy"] --> B["Symmetric (Uniform)<br>P(y_tilde = j | y* = i) = const"]
    A --> C["Asymmetric (Class-Conditional)<br>T_ij = P(y_tilde = j | y* = i)"]
    A --> D["Instance-Dependent (Real-World)<br>P(y_tilde = j | y* = i, x)"]

    B --> B1["Tractable; bounded by MAE / GCE"]
    C --> C1["Requires transition matrix estimation"]
    D --> D1["Hardest frontier; causes standard small-loss filters to prune rare clean tails"]

+--------------------------+----------------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------+

docs.title: 4.1 Generalized Cross Entropy (GCE)
docs.text: Zhang & Sabuncu (NeurIPS 2018) proposed utilizing the negative Box-Cox transformation as an interpolation between Cross-Entropy and Mean Absolute Error: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{GCE}}(f(x), y) = \frac{1 - f_y(x)^q}{q}, \quad q \in (0, 1]\)$ - Gradient Formulation: $\(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{GCE}}}{\partial \theta} = - f_y(x)^{q-1} \cdot \frac{\partial f_y(x)}{\partial \theta} = f_y(x)^q \cdot \left( -\frac{1}{f_y(x)} \frac{\partial f_y(x)}{\partial \theta} \right) = f_y(x)^q \cdot \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}\)$ The gradient of GCE is equivalent to standard Cross-Entropy scaled by \(f_y(x)^q\). For corrupt labels where the model prediction \(f_y(x)\) is low, the gradient contribution is automatically attenuated to near zero.

docs.title: 4.2 Symmetric Cross Entropy (SCE)
docs.text: Wang et al. (ICCV 2019) proved that standard Cross-Entropy overfits because it is not symmetric. They paired CE with Reverse Cross Entropy (RCE): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{SCE}} = \alpha \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(p, y) + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\text{RCE}}(p, y) = -\alpha \sum_{k=1}^K y_k \ln p_k - \beta \sum_{k=1}^K p_k \ln y_k\)$ By parameterizing \(\ln y_k = A\) if \(y_k = 1\) and \(B\) if \(y_k = 0\), RCE acts as a symmetric regularizer with a bounded supremum: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{RCE}} \le -A - (K-1)B\), preventing gradient explosion on mislabeled instances.

docs.title: 4.3 Class-Balanced Loss (Effective Number of Samples)
docs.text: Cui et al. (CVPR 2019) resolved the distortion of naive inverse-frequency weighting by formalizing sample volume overlap in high-dimensional space: $\(E_n = \frac{1 - \beta^n}{1 - \beta}, \quad W_{n_y} = \frac{1}{E_{n_y}} = \frac{1 - \beta}{1 - \beta^{n_y}}\)$ where \(\beta = \frac{N-1}{N} \in [0, 1)\) represents the probability that a new sample overlaps with existing volume.

docs.title: 5. Algorithmic Comparison Matrix
docs.text: Algorithm Paradigm Time Complexity Memory Complexity Robustness Boundary Imbalance Sensitivity Open Implementation GCE Robust Loss \(O(K)\) \(O(1)\) Up to 60% symmetric High (Hurts minority) PyTorch (academic) SCE Robust Loss \(O(K)\) \(O(1)\) Up to 70% symmetric Moderate PyTorch (academic) Co-teaching Sample Selection \(2 \times O(\text{Backprop})\) \(2\Phi\) (Dual nets) Up to 50% asymmetric Extreme (Prunes tails) PyTorch (academic) DivideMix Semi-Supervised \(4 \times O(\text{Backprop})\) \(2\Phi\) + GMM Up to 80% symmetric Extreme PyTorch (academic) Cleanlab Offline Curation \(K \times O(\text{Train})\) \(O(N \cdot K)\) matrix High (Offline only) High (Prunes tails) cleanlab (AGPL-3.0) Focal Loss Imbalanced Loss \(O(K)\) \(O(1)\) NEGATIVE (Fails noise) Low (Focuses on tails) torchvision native

docs.title: 6. The Core Research Breakdown: The Small-Loss Dilemma
docs.text: Every state-of-the-art sample selection and noise-filtering system in current literature relies on the Small-Loss Criterion: $\(\ell(x_i, y_i) < \tau \implies \text{Clean}; \quad \ell(x_i, y_i) \ge \tau \implies \text{Noisy / Prune}\)$

docs.title: Why This Fails Under Real-World Class Imbalance
docs.text:
1. Minority-class instances (e.g. rare disease symptoms, rare financial fraud vectors) have very few supporting exemplars in the training set.
  2. Because representations for sparse classes are under-formed during early training, their training loss \(\ell(x_{\text{minority}}, y_{\text{minority}})\) remains persistently high.
  3. Small-loss algorithms (Cleanlab, Co-teaching, MentorNet) classify these legitimate rare samples as "noisy labels" and systematically prune or downweight them.
  4. Result: The classifier starves the minority class of data, destroying minority recall.

docs.title: 7. Direct Relationship to AdaptiveML
docs.text: AdaptiveML Pillar 2 (RLA) addresses this breakdown by: 1. Providing clean-room, vectorized implementations of Generalized Cross Entropy (GCE) and Symmetric Cross Entropy (SCE) for both PyTorch and NumPy. 2. Formulating a Density-Aware Margin Reliability Metric that normalizes sample loss against local feature-space density: $\(\text{Score}(x_i, y_i) = \mathcal{M}(x_i, y_i) \cdot \log\left( 1 + \frac{1}{\rho_k(x_i)} \right)\)$ High-loss samples residing in sparse feature regions are identified as Legitimate Rare Samples and protected from deletion.

docs.title: AdaptiveML — Cross-Cutting Research Synthesis: Unified Learning Controller (ULC)
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 4) Document Identifier: DOC-LIT-004 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Nature of Document: Cross-Cutting Research Synthesis across ALA, RLA, and RAO (Not a Fourth Primary Dossier)

docs.title: 1. The Fallacy of Naive Composition
docs.text:
A foundational insight of systems engineering and algorithmic theory is that:

Composing independently functional algorithms does NOT automatically produce a stable, functional unified system.

When an engineer sequentially stitches together: - A Concept Drift Detector from stream mining (e.g. ADWIN from River), - A Robust Loss function from noisy-label learning (e.g. GCE from PyTorch research repos), and - A Low-Memory Optimizer from deep learning optimization (e.g. 8-bit Adam),

the resulting pipeline breaks because these isolated algorithms make diametrically opposed, conflicting assumptions about data dynamics and runtime state.

flowchart TD
    subgraph Conflicting Assumptions in Naive Pipeline
    A["ALA: Concept Drift Detector"] -->|"Assumes"| A1["Data is 100% clean;<br>Loss spikes = Real Concept Drift"]
    B["RLA: Robust Noise Filter"] -->|"Assumes"| B1["Data is stationary offline;<br>Loss spikes = Corrupt Label Noise"]
    C["RAO: Low-Memory Optimizer"] -->|"Assumes"| C1["Static memory budget;<br>Unbounded replay buffer = OOM Crash"]
    end

    A1 -.->|"COLLISION"| B1
    B1 -.->|"COLLISION"| C1

    D["UNIFIED LEARNING CONTROLLER (ULC)"] -->|"Arbitrates"| E["Evidence-Based State Machine:<br>Gates drift alerts against sample reliability<br>Bounds memory replay buffers adaptively"]

docs.title: 2. In-Depth Analysis of Cross-Pillar Conflict Modes
2.1 Conflict Mode 1: The Drift-Noise Collision (ALA \(\longleftrightarrow\) RLA)
docs.text:
• The Tension:
  • ALA drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM) monitor running classification error \(e_t \in \{0, 1\}\). When errors exceed Hoeffding thresholds, ALA declares drift and triggers model re-calibration.
  • RLA recognizes that training streams contain noisy or corrupted labels (\(\tilde{y}_i \ne y^*\)). When noisy batches arrive, error rates spike artificially.
  • The Catastrophe in Naive Composition:
  • The drift detector mistakes temporary label corruption for structural concept drift.
  • It declares a false alarm, clears the historical memory buffer, and aggressively adapts the model to the corrupted batch.
  • The model overfits completely to the corrupted labels, destroying previously acquired knowledge.

docs.title: 2.2 Conflict Mode 2: The Minority-Pruning Dilemma (RLA \(\longleftrightarrow\) ALA)
docs.text:
• The Tension:
  • As new concepts emerge in non-stationary streams (ALA), they initially appear as low-frequency minority instances.
  • RLA sample selection heuristics (small-loss selection, Confident Learning) assume high-loss instances are corrupt labels.
  • The Catastrophe in Naive Composition:
  • Emerging concept patterns exhibit high initial loss because the model has not yet updated its parameters.
  • RLA classifies the emerging concept as "label noise" and prunes or downweights it.
  • The model is permanently blinded to genuine emerging concept drift.

docs.title: 2.3 Conflict Mode 3: The Memory-Plasticity Tradeoff (ALA \(\longleftrightarrow\) RAO)
docs.text:
• The Tension:
  • ALA mechanisms (Experience Replay, Reservoir Buffers, Elastic Weight Consolidation) require accumulating historical samples or tracking Fisher Information matrices to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
  • RAO operates under strict memory ceilings on commodity CPUs and edge devices.
  • The Catastrophe in Naive Composition:
  • In response to continuous drift, ALA expands replay buffers.
  • Peak runtime memory exceeds available host RAM, triggering an OS OOM process kill.

docs.title: 3. Mathematical Principles of ULC In-Loop Arbitration
docs.text: The Unified Learning Controller resolves these contradictions by acting as a probabilistic evidence arbitrator:

docs.title: 3.1 Dual-Evidence Drift Gating
docs.text: When ALA signals a candidate drift event (\(\Delta \mu \ge \epsilon_{\text{cut}}\)), ULC does not immediately reset the model. Instead, it computes the Local Sample Reliability Distribution: $\(\bar{R}_W = \frac{1}{|W_1|} \sum_{i \in W_1} \text{Reliability}(x_i, y_i)\)$ - Case 1 (False Alarm Noise Burst): If \(\bar{R}_W < \tau_{\text{noise}}\), the error spike is driven by corrupt labels. ULC suppresses the drift alarm, attenuates batch gradients, and preserves the historical memory buffer. - Case 2 (Genuine Concept Drift): If \(\bar{R}_W \ge \tau_{\text{noise}}\), the error spike is driven by high-confidence, structurally coherent samples. ULC confirms genuine drift, accelerates model plasticity, and triggers selective buffer updating.

docs.title: 3.2 Density-Aware Emerging Pattern Preservation
docs.text: To prevent RLA from pruning emerging concepts, sample reliability is evaluated relative to local feature density \(\rho(x)\). High-loss samples in dense clusters are flagged as corrupt noise; high-loss samples in sparse, newly emerging clusters are flagged as Emerging Concepts and granted a plasticity boost.

docs.title: 4. Synthesis Conclusion
docs.text:
The Unified Learning Controller is not an infrastructure workflow scheduler (like ZenML or Ray). It is an in-loop algorithmic state automaton.

By formally harmonizing the conflicting mathematical assumptions of ALA, RLA, and RAO, ULC transforms three isolated algorithmic pillars into a resilient, adaptive, resource-bounded learning system.

docs.title: 2. In-Depth Analysis: GAP ALA-G1 (Noise-Induced Drift False Alarms)
2.1 Problem Formulation & Mechanism
docs.text: Statistical window-cutting detectors (e.g., ADWIN) evaluate discrepancies between sub-windows \(W_0, W_1\): $\(|\mu_{W_0} - \mu_{W_1}| \ge \epsilon_{\text{cut}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2m} \ln\frac{4|W|}{\delta}}\)$ When observations are contaminated by bursty label noise, the empirical error rate spikes artificially. The detector triggers a cut, asserting concept drift has occurred. - Why Existing Work Fails: ADWIN treats all observations as equally reliable realizations of the underlying Bernoulli trial. It lacks a reliability weighting factor \(w_i \in [0, 1]\) to discount corrupted samples. - Target Algorithmic Gap: Formulating Reliability-Weighted ADWIN (RW-ADWIN), where sub-window statistics are computed over weighted sample distributions: $\(\hat{\mu}_W^* = \frac{\sum_{i \in W} w_i x_i}{\sum_{i \in W} w_i}\)$ with Hoeffding-like bounds extended to weighted empirical averages.

docs.title: 3. In-Depth Analysis: GAP ALA-G2 (Vectorized Numerical Stream Input)
3.1 Problem Formulation & Mechanism
docs.text:
• The Reality in River: River enforces single-instance dict processing (learn_one(x)). For dense numerical datasets (e.g. sensor telemetry with 50 numeric features), up to 70% of execution time is consumed by Python dictionary key hashing, type checking, and tuple unpacking inside tight loops.
  • Target Systems Gap: Designing streaming estimators and ensemble tree structures that natively accept contiguous 2D NumPy array chunks (X: np.ndarray, shape=(B, D)) via scikit-learn's partial_fit(X, y) idiom, utilizing vector SIMD operations across ensemble trees.

docs.title: AdaptiveML — Phase 5: Strategic Decisions and Phase 6 Handoff
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 5) Document Identifier: DOC-RES-P5-010 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Handoff Target: Phase 6 (Mathematical & Algorithm Design)

docs.title: 1. Summary of Ratified Phase 5 Decisions
docs.text: The multidisciplinary research team has finalized the Phase 5 research gap analysis. The following strategic decisions are codified:

docs.title: Decision 1: Formal Ratification of Core Research Gaps
docs.text:
• Decision: The project formally prioritizes three P0 Critical Gaps and three P1 High-Priority Gaps as the scientific foundation for AdaptiveML:
  • P0-1 (RLA): Resolving the small-loss minority-pruning breakdown via density-aware margin reliability scoring.
  • P0-2 (ULC): Resolving the drift-noise retraining catastrophe via in-loop dual-evidence arbitration.
  • P0-3 (RAO): Eliminating the CPU memory ceiling via pure Python/NumPy block-quantized optimizer states.
  • P1-1 (ALA): Accelerating streaming throughput via vectorized 2D NumPy array matrix processing (partial_fit).
  • P1-2 (ALA): Suppressing drift detector false alarms via reliability-weighted sub-window statistics.
  • P1-3 (RAO): Eliminating Adafactor convergence stalls by retaining an 8-bit quantized first-moment buffer.

docs.title: Decision 2: Formal Rejection of Scope-Creeping Directions
docs.text:
• Decision: The project formally rejects:
  • Automated Neural Architecture Search (AutoML / NAS).
  • Multi-node distributed cluster orchestration engines.
  • Custom tensor automatic differentiation computational engines.
  • Rationale: These directions have mature, dedicated solutions (Optuna, Ray, PyTorch) and would divert critical research bandwidth away from AdaptiveML's core algorithmic pillars.

docs.title: Decision 3: Authorization to Transition to Phase 6
docs.text:
• Decision: Upon formal owner acceptance of Phases 2–5, the engineering and research teams are authorized to begin Phase 6: Mathematical & Algorithm Design.
  • Phase 6 Deliverables:
  • Formal mathematical proofs and closed-form derivations for Density-Aware Margin Scoring (RLA).
  • Formal finite-state transition automaton equations for Drift-Noise Arbitration (ULC).
  • Formal error bounds and convergence proofs for CPU block-quantized integer scaling (RAO).
  • High-level pseudo-code specifications in LaTeX for all Priority A/P0 algorithms.

docs.title: 2. Phase 5 Acceptance Status
docs.text: PHASE 5 STATUS: READY FOR REVIEW All candidate gaps are grounded in literature, prioritized across objective criteria, and translated into falsifiable hypotheses and preliminary experimental designs.

docs.title: AdaptiveML — Phase 5: Preliminary Experimental Designs
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 5) Document Identifier: DOC-RES-P5-008 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Target Execution Phase: Phase 12 (Research Experiments & Benchmarking)

docs.title: 1. Universal Statistical Testing & Hardware Protocol
docs.text: To ensure absolute reproducibility across all Phase 12 benchmark runs: 1. Multi-Seed Protocol: Every experiment must execute across 5 independent randomized seeds: [42, 1337, 2026, 9999, 88888]. 2. Statistical Significance Testing: Superiority claims must be substantiated by the two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test with significance threshold \(\alpha = 0.01\). 3. Hardware Environment Specification: - Single-node commodity CPU runner (minimum 4-core, 8 GB to 16 GB RAM). - Zero GPU requirement for primary verification. - Recording exact NumPy BLAS configuration (numpy.show_config()) and CPU model.

docs.title: 2. Experiment Design 1: RLA Minority-Preserving Noise Resilience (EXP-RLA-01)
2.1 Benchmark Architecture & Datasets
docs.text:
• Objective: Measure minority-class preservation under combined label noise and severe class imbalance.
  • Datasets:
  • Imbalanced CIFAR-10: Exponential class decay with imbalance ratio \(\text{IR} = 50:1\); classes 8 and 9 represent minority tails.
  • Forest CoverType: Real-world ecological dataset where Class 4 represents \(<0.5\%\) of instances.
  • Noise Injection Regimes:
  • Symmetric Noise: \(\eta \in \{0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6\}\).
  • Asymmetric Noise: Semantically paired transitions with \(\eta = 0.3\).
  • Models: Standard 3-layer Tabular MLP (CoverType); ResNet-18 (CIFAR-10).
  • Baselines:
  • Standard Cross-Entropy (Baseline ERM)
  • Cleanlab Confident Learning (Pruning baseline)
  • Generalized Cross Entropy (GCE, \(q=0.7\))
  • Symmetric Cross Entropy (SCE, \(\alpha=0.1, \beta=1.0\))
  • AdaptiveML RLA (Density-Aware Margin Scorer)
  • Reported Metrics: Minority Class Recall, Macro F1, Overall Accuracy, False Positive Pruning Rate (clean samples discarded).

docs.title: 3. Experiment Design 2: ULC In-Loop Drift-Noise Arbitration (EXP-ULC-01)
3.1 Benchmark Architecture & Datasets
docs.text:
• Objective: Measure drift alarm false-positive suppression and recovery speed under non-stationary dirty streams.
  • Datasets:
  • Synthetic SEA Stream: \(100,000\) instances with 3 abrupt concept drifts at steps \(25k, 50k, 75k\); transient label noise bursts (\(\eta = 0.4\), duration \(500\) samples) injected at stationary steps \(12.5k, 37.5k, 62.5k\).
  • Electricity (ELEC2): Real 45,312 stream with injected noise spikes.
  • Baselines:
  • Uncoordinated Stream: Standard ADWIN + River Hoeffding Tree
  • Static Batch Model (retrained every \(10,000\) samples)
  • AdaptiveML ULC: Dual-Evidence Arbitration Automaton
  • Reported Metrics:
  • Number of False Drift Alarms triggered during stationary noise bursts.
  • Mean Detection Delay (samples) on true abrupt drift at \(25k, 50k, 75k\).
  • Rolling Prequential Accuracy (\(\alpha = 0.999\)) throughout the complete stream.

docs.title: 4. Experiment Design 3: RAO CPU Low-Memory Optimizer Profiling (EXP-RAO-01)
4.1 Benchmark Architecture & Datasets
docs.text:
• Objective: Verify heap memory reduction and step execution latency on commodity CPU hardware.
  • Datasets & Architectures:
  • Tabular Deep MLP (\(5\text{ hidden layers}, 1024\text{ units}\), \(5\text{M parameters}\)) on Forest CoverType.
  • ResNet-18 (\(11.7\text{M parameters}\)) on CIFAR-10 executed purely on CPU.
  • Baselines:
  • Standard PyTorch AdamW (fp32)
  • Standard SGD + Momentum (fp32)
  • Adafactor (momentum-free)
  • bitsandbytes.optim.AdamW8bit (CPU backend)
  • AdaptiveML LowMemoryAdamW (Pure NumPy / PyTorch block-quantized)
  • Reported Metrics:
  • Optimizer State Memory Footprint (MB allocated via tracemalloc).
  • Step Execution Latency (ms per optimizer step).
  • Number of Steps / Epochs to reach target training loss threshold.
  • Final Validation Accuracy.

docs.title: 2. In-Depth Analysis: GAP RAO-G1 (The CPU Quantization Barrier)
2.1 The Platform Barrier in Existing Low-Memory Optimizers
docs.text:
• The Reality: Standard AdamW consumes \(8\text{ bytes per parameter}\) in state memory. To avoid OOM crashes during local training, practitioners attempt to use 8-bit optimizers like bitsandbytes.optim.AdamW8bit.
  • The Breakdown: bitsandbytes is architected for CUDA GPUs. Its CPU backend is implemented in C++ and explicitly requires AVX2 or AVX-512 instruction sets.
  • On standard developer laptops lacking AVX-512, Windows machines without specific MSVC runtime DLLs, or ARM64 development boards (Raspberry Pi, Apple Silicon), bitsandbytes crashes with Illegal Instruction or dynamic link loader failures.
  • Target Gap: Formulating LowMemoryAdamW — a pure Python/NumPy/PyTorch optimizer state compression mechanism utilizing block-wise dynamic scaling and symmetric integer mapping: $\(\tilde{m}_i = \text{round}\left( \frac{m_i}{\text{scale}_B} \cdot 127 \right) \in \text{int8}\)$ executed entirely via vectorized tensor operations without requiring external C/C++ compilation.

docs.title: 3. In-Depth Analysis: GAP RAO-G2 (Adafactor Momentum-Drop Collapse)
3.1 The Breakdown in Momentum-Free Optimization
docs.text:
• Adafactor achieves sublinear second-moment memory (\(O(R+C)\)) by factoring row and column variance. However, to maximize memory savings, it drops the first moment entirely (\(\beta_1 = 0\)).
  • On non-convex surfaces with high stochastic gradient variance (common in deep neural networks and tabular MLPs), the lack of momentum causes the optimization path to oscillate erratically, frequently stalling in sharp local plateaus.
  • Target Gap: Investigating whether retaining a quantized 8-bit first moment (\(m_t \in \text{int8}\)) restores full AdamW-level convergence trajectories while still saving 50% of optimizer state memory relative to standard 32-bit AdamW.

docs.title: 2. Research Questions Advancing to Phase 6
docs.text: The following three core research questions are formally approved to advance to Phase 6: Mathematical & Algorithm Design:

docs.title: Priority Research Question 1 (RLA Focus — RQ-1):
docs.text: "Can a closed-form density-aware margin score distinguish between corrupt common labels and legitimate rare-class instances, provably bounding minority pruning errors on long-tailed distributions?" - Phase 6 Task: Derive the mathematical formulations for \(\text{Reliability}(x, y) = \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{M}(x, y), \rho_k(x))\) and prove its asymptotic behavior in low-density feature regimes.

docs.title: Priority Research Question 2 (ULC Focus — RQ-2):
docs.text: "Can an in-loop arbitration automaton dynamically modulate drift detection thresholds using sample reliability distributions, provably suppressing false-positive drift alarms under bursty label noise?" - Phase 6 Task: Formalize the finite state automaton \(\mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{S}'\) and derive mathematical conditions under which drift resets are suppressed without increasing detection lag on true structural shifts.

docs.title: Priority Research Question 3 (RAO Focus — RQ-3):
docs.text: "What is the minimal block size and integer precision required to quantize first- and second-order optimizer states in pure NumPy/PyTorch on CPU while preserving the spectral convergence properties of AdamW?" - Phase 6 Task: Derive the error bounds of block-wise symmetric integer scaling and prove convergence on L-smooth non-convex objective functions.

docs.title: 3. Preservation of Modular Independence
docs.text: The architectural mandate is reaffirmed: - ALA, RLA, and RAO must remain completely independent. - A developer must be able to use: - aml.ala.AdaptiveClassifier without importing rla or rao. - aml.rla.RobustLoss without importing ala or rao. - aml.rao.LowMemoryAdamW without importing ala or rla. - The ULC is strictly an optional coordinator that imports the three pillars through abstract protocols when holistic orchestration is explicitly requested.

docs.title: AdaptiveML — Phase 5: Research Gap Master Analysis
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 5) Document Identifier: DOC-RES-P5-001 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Synthesis Scope: Synthesizing Phases 1, 2, 3, and 4 into a Scientifically Defensible Research Agenda

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Synthesis Objective
docs.text: The objective of Phase 5 is to synthesize findings from Market Research (Phase 1), Novelty & Prior Art (Phase 2), Legal & IP Assessment (Phase 3), and Literature Review (Phase 4) into concrete, experimentally testable Research Gaps.

docs.title: Scientific Methodology
docs.text: In strict accordance with the Project Charter: - A missing feature in an existing package does not automatically constitute a research gap. - An underdeveloped API does not constitute an algorithmic contribution. - Every research gap must be grounded in verified academic literature, supported by empirical evidence of existing algorithmic failure, and formulated as an experimentally falsifiable hypothesis.

docs.title: 2. Master Consolidated Research Gap Matrix

docs.title: 3.1 GAP-01: The Small-Loss Failure in Imbalanced Noisy Regimes (RLA)
docs.text:
• Problem Statement: Existing noisy-label selection and cleaning algorithms (Cleanlab, Co-teaching, MentorNet) assume clean samples exhibit lower training loss than noisy samples. Under severe class imbalance, legitimate minority-class instances naturally incur high losses due to lack of representation density. Consequently, standard noise-filtering methods systematically discard valid rare samples, destroying minority-class recall.
  • Why Existing Literature Fails: Established methods evaluate symmetric noise on balanced vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10). They fail in long-tail real-world distributions (fraud, clinical diagnostics).
  • Research Question (RQ-1): Can a density-aware margin metric distinguish between corrupted common samples and clean minority samples without requiring clean validation data?

docs.title: 3.2 GAP-02: The Drift-Noise Retraining Collision in Streaming Pipelines (ULC / ALA)
docs.text:
• Problem Statement: Standard statistical drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM) evaluate error-rate variance. When a transient burst of noisy labels arrives in a non-stationary stream, the error rate spikes, causing the detector to flag false-positive concept drift. The downstream model flushes its memory buffer and adapts aggressively to the corrupted batch, destroying historical calibration.
  • Why Existing Literature Fails: Stream mining literature assumes clean annotations; robust learning literature assumes static offline datasets. No existing open-source tool gates streaming drift alerts against sample reliability metrics.
  • Research Question (RQ-2): Can in-loop sample reliability distributions be used to provably bound false-alarm drift triggers on noisy data streams without increasing detection delay on genuine concept drift?

docs.title: 3.3 GAP-03: The CPU Optimizer State Memory Ceiling (RAO)
docs.text:
• Problem Statement: Adaptive moment estimation optimizers (AdamW) require \(8\text{ bytes per parameter}\) in auxiliary state buffers. Existing 8-bit memory-reduced optimizers (bitsandbytes) are heavily CUDA-dependent; their CPU kernels fail to execute on systems lacking AVX-512 instructions or on non-CUDA platforms.
  • Why Existing Literature Fails: Deep learning optimization research is hyper-focused on multi-GPU LLM training, leaving commodity CPU workstations, developer laptops, and edge appliances unaddressed.
  • Research Question (RQ-3): Can a block-wise integer-scaled optimizer state representation run in pure Python/NumPy/PyTorch on standard CPUs to achieve \(\ge 30\%\) to \(50\%\) memory reduction while preserving AdamW-level convergence trajectories?

docs.title: AdaptiveML — Phase 5: Research Questions & Formal Hypotheses
docs.text: Document Status: Complete Baseline Deliverable (Phase 5) Document Identifier: DOC-RES-P5-007 Last Updated: 2026-11-01 Scope: Detailed Scientific Specifications for all P0 and P1 Priority Gaps

docs.title: 1. Research Protocol for P0 Gap: GAP-01 (RLA Small-Loss Imbalance)
docs.text:
• Research Question (RQ-1): Can a density-aware margin reliability scorer protect legitimate minority-class instances from noise-pruning while achieving equal or superior clean-label accuracy compared to Confident Learning?
  • Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): Normalizing prediction margin by local feature density \(\rho_k(x)\) will increase minority-class recall by \(\ge 15\%\) on imbalanced noisy datasets without degrading majority-class accuracy by \(>2\%\) relative to standard Confident Learning.
  • Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): Incorporating local feature density yields no statistically significant difference in minority-class recall (\(p \ge 0.01\), Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
  • Baselines for Comparison: Standard ERM (Cross-Entropy), Confident Learning (cleanlab), Generalized Cross Entropy (Zhang & Sabuncu, 2018), Symmetric Cross Entropy (Wang et al., 2019).
  • Independent Variables: Noise rate \(\eta \in [0.1, 0.5]\) (symmetric and asymmetric), class imbalance ratio \(\text{IR} \in [10:1, 100:1]\), density estimator bandwidth \(k \in [5, 20]\).
  • Dependent Variables: Minority Class Recall, Macro F1-Score, Clean-Sample Retention Rate, Accuracy.
  • Target Datasets: Imbalanced CIFAR-10N (with injected synthetic tail imbalance), Forest CoverType (classes 4 and 5 as rare tails).
  • Failure Conditions: If density estimation computational overhead exceeds \(20\%\) of training epoch time, or if density errors in high dimensions degrade majority accuracy by \(>5\%\).

docs.title: 2. Research Protocol for P0 Gap: GAP-02 (ULC Drift-Noise Collision)
docs.text:
• Research Question (RQ-2): Can in-loop sample reliability weighting within a finite state arbitration automaton reduce false-positive concept drift triggers caused by transient label noise bursts without increasing true drift detection delay?
  • Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): Weighting ADWIN sub-window error statistics by sample reliability scores will suppress false-alarm drift alerts by \(\ge 60\%\) during transient label noise bursts while maintaining true drift detection delay within \(100\) samples of clean ADWIN.
  • Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): Reliability-weighted ADWIN yields no statistically significant reduction in false alarms (\(p \ge 0.01\)).
  • Baselines for Comparison: Uncoordinated ADWIN + River Hoeffding Tree, Standard DDM, Naive Retraining Pipeline.
  • Independent Variables: Noise burst magnitude \(\eta_{\text{burst}} \in [0.2, 0.6]\), noise burst duration \(L \in [50, 500\text{ samples}]\), drift type (abrupt vs gradual SEA concepts).
  • Dependent Variables: False Alarm Rate (alarms per \(10^4\) stationary samples), Drift Detection Delay (samples), Prequential Accuracy over non-stationary dirty streams.
  • Target Datasets: Synthetic SEA with injected noise bursts, Electricity (ELEC2) with synthetic noise injection.
  • Failure Conditions: If the arbitration automaton delays genuine abrupt drift detection by \(>250\text{ samples}\) compared to uncoordinated ADWIN.

docs.title: 3. Research Protocol for P0 Gap: GAP-03 (RAO CPU Low-Memory AdamW)
docs.text:
• Research Question (RQ-3): Can a pure Python/NumPy block-quantized optimizer achieve a \(\ge 30\%\) to \(50\%\) reduction in optimizer state heap memory relative to 32-bit AdamW on standard CPUs while matching final convergence within \(1\%\) validation accuracy?
  • Alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): Block-wise symmetric integer scaling (\(B=256\)) executed in vector NumPy/PyTorch CPU operations will reduce optimizer state memory by \(\ge 40\%\) and match final test accuracy of 32-bit AdamW within \(\pm 0.5\%\) across standard benchmark architectures.
  • Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): Block-quantized integer scaling diverges or degrades final task accuracy by \(>2\%\) relative to 32-bit AdamW.
  • Baselines for Comparison: Standard PyTorch AdamW (fp32), Standard SGD + Momentum (fp32), Adafactor (momentum-free), bitsandbytes.optim.AdamW8bit (CPU backend).
  • Independent Variables: Block size \(B \in [64, 256, 2048]\), model architecture (ResNet-18, Tabular MLP, Mini-Transformer), learning rate \(\gamma \in [10^{-4}, 10^{-2}]\).
  • Dependent Variables: Peak Heap Memory during step (tracemalloc), Step Wall-Clock Latency (ms), Final Validation Loss & Accuracy.
  • Target Datasets: California Housing (Tabular MLP), CIFAR-10 (ResNet-18).
  • Failure Conditions: If per-step CPU quantization latency overhead exceeds \(25\%\) of standard AdamW step time, or if numerical underflow causes gradient divergence.

docs.title: 2. In-Depth Analysis: GAP RLA-G1 (The Small-Loss Imbalance Breakdown)
2.1 The Underlying Structural Breakdown
docs.text:
Existing state-of-the-art sample selection algorithms (Cleanlab / Confident Learning, Co-teaching, MentorNet) rely on the foundational Small-Loss Principle: $\(\ell(x_i, y_i) < \tau \implies \text{Clean}; \quad \ell(x_i, y_i) \ge \tau \implies \text{Noisy}\)$

In imbalanced or long-tailed distributions (where head classes have \(10,000\) samples and tail classes have \(50\) samples): 1. The model's representation for minority-class patterns is undertrained during early epochs. 2. Consequently, legitimate clean minority instances naturally produce High Loss. 3. Small-loss criteria treat these high-loss instances as "corrupt annotations" and prune them. 4. Catastrophic Result: Tail classes are starved of training data, causing minority recall to collapse.

docs.title: 2.2 Proposed Research Direction: Density-Aware Margin Scoring
docs.text: To resolve this gap, sample reliability must be formulated as a function of Prediction Margin \(\mathcal{M}(x, y)\) and Local Feature Density \(\rho_k(x)\): $\(\text{Reliability}(x_i, y_i) = \Phi\left( f_{y_i}(x_i) - \max_{j \ne y_i} f_j(x_i), \; \rho_k(x_i) \right)\)$ - If a sample has high loss in a high-density region, it is an isolated outlier / noisy label \(\implies\) Downweight / Filter. - If a sample has high loss in a low-density region, it is a legitimate tail pattern \(\implies\) Preserve / Protect.

docs.title: 3. In-Depth Analysis: GAP RLA-G2 (Single-Pass In-Training Scoring)
3.1 The Offline Cross-Validation Bottleneck
docs.text:
• Cleanlab requires running \(K\)-fold cross-validation to generate out-of-sample predicted probabilities prior to identifying label issues.
  • In online learning or large-scale streaming, running multiple complete training passes is computationally impossible.
  • Target Gap: Developing an online running reliability accumulator that estimates sample confidence dynamically within a single training pass using exponential moving averages of per-sample prediction margins.

docs.title: 2. In-Depth Analysis: GAP ULC-G1 (The Drift-Noise Collision)
2.1 The Inherent Conflict
docs.text:
In production data streams: - Concept drift requires increasing model plasticity (updating weights, flushing old memory buffers). - Label noise requires decreasing model plasticity (downweighting corrupted samples, relying on historical calibrated memory).

When concept drift and label noise co-occur: 1. An uncoordinated drift detector (ADWIN) interprets the error rate spike from the noise burst as a concept drift event. 2. It triggers a model reset. 3. The model trains aggressively on the corrupted data batch. 4. Catastrophe: The model memorizes corrupted labels and destroys its historical decision boundary.

docs.title: 2.2 Target Algorithmic Gap: The Dual-Evidence Arbitration Automaton
docs.text: Formulating an in-loop state machine that mathematically conditions drift adaptation on local sample reliability: $\(\text{Action} = \mathcal{F}\left( \text{Drift Alert}_{\text{ALA}}, \; \mathbb{E}[\text{Reliability}]_{\text{RLA}}, \; \mathcal{M}_{\text{RAM}} \right)\)$ - If Drift Alert = True AND Mean Reliability < \(\tau_{\text{noise}}\): \(\implies\) Assert False Alarm / Noise Burst. Suppress drift reset, attenuate gradient learning rate, preserve historical memory buffer. - If Drift Alert = True AND Mean Reliability \(\ge \tau_{\text{noise}}\): \(\implies\) Confirm Real Concept Drift. Modulate learning rate, allocate replay buffer, update model weights.

docs.title: 1. Executive Vision
docs.text:
Modern machine learning has achieved extraordinary empirical success, yet prevailing industrial workflows remain tethered to fragile foundational assumptions: that training data is static and stationary, that annotations are immaculate, that physical memory is virtually unlimited in the cloud, and that continuous connectivity to remote clusters is guaranteed.

When deployed into volatile, resource-constrained, real-world operational environments, standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) models degrade under concept drift, overfit to corrupted labels, and exhaust available RAM during optimization.

AdaptiveML is an open-source, local-first, CPU-first Python machine learning algorithmic library engineered to fundamentally solve these challenges. It provides unbundled, mathematically grounded, independently usable primitives across three core pillars: 1. Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA): Streaming estimation, online concept drift detection, and knowledge retention without catastrophic forgetting. 2. Robust Learning Algorithms (RLA): Intrinsic noise tolerance, sample reliability scoring, and protection of legitimate tail distributions under extreme class imbalance. 3. Resource-Aware Optimization (RAO): Memory-reduced optimizer states, sub-8-bit block quantization, and stable first-order step routines on commodity CPU hardware. 4. Unified Learning Controller (ULC): An optional dynamic coordinator capable of arbitrating between the competing demands of adaptation plasticity, noise rejection, and memory pressure.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       ULC: Unified Learning Controller                         |
|           (Optional dynamic arbitration layer; monitors drift and noise)      |
+-----------------------+-------------------------------+-----------------------+
                        |                               |
        +---------------+---------------+               |
        |                               |               |
        v                               v               v
+-------------------------------+ +-------------------+ +-----------------------+
|  ALA: Adaptive Learning       | |  RLA: Robust      | |  RAO: Resource-Aware  |
|  - Vectorized Hoeffding Trees | |  - Margin scoring | |  - Low-memory AdamW   |
|  - ADWIN drift detection      | |  - Robust losses  | |  - Block quantizer    |
|  - Balanced reservoir replay  | |  - Rare tail guard| |  - Budget manager     |
+-------------------------------+ +-------------------+ +-----------------------+

docs.title: Strategic Tenets of Evolution v2.0
docs.text:
• Local-First & Zero-Cloud Autonomy: The core library will never require mandatory cloud accounts, network telemetry, or external GPU hardware. It must run deterministically on commodity laptops, air-gapped on-premise servers, and edge gateways.
  • Pillar Independence: In strict adherence to Research Governance Rule 7, ALA, RLA, and RAO are completely decoupled. Developers can utilize an RAO optimizer in pure NumPy, an RLA loss in PyTorch, or an ALA drift detector in scikit-learn without importing or configuring other pillars.
  • Scientific Rigor & Reproducibility: In compliance with Research Governance Rules 1–10, all claims are grounded in mathematical derivations, multi-seed statistical significance testing (\(p < 0.01\)), and compulsory negative results preservation.

docs.title: 2. Product Positioning
docs.text:
AdaptiveML occupies a unique, complementary position in the modern machine learning ecosystem. It is not an all-in-one platform seeking to replace PyTorch, scikit-learn, or JAX, nor is it a monolithic, tightly-coupled streaming framework:

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                      MACHINE LEARNING ECOSYSTEM POSITIONING                   |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| Dimension                | Positioning & Architectural Differentiation        |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| **vs. PyTorch / JAX**    | Complements them. Provides specialized low-memory  |
|                          | CPU optimizers, robust loss modules, and streaming |
|                          | estimators that plug directly into standard loops. |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| **vs. scikit-learn**     | Complements standard batch estimators by providing |
|                          | native streaming `partial_fit` estimators with     |
|                          | active concept drift tracking and balanced replay. |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| **vs. River**            | Unlike River's monolithic streaming focus,         |
|                          | AdaptiveML unbundles its pillars, providing deep   |
|                          | optimizer state compression (RAO) and unified      |
|                          | drift/noise arbitration (ULC) with pure NumPy core.|
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| **vs. Cleanlab**         | Extends confident learning concepts into streaming |
|                          | online regimes with continuous margin scoring and  |
|                          | extreme class imbalance tail protection.          |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+
| **vs. bitsandbytes**     | Provides 8-bit quantized optimization on commodity |
|                          | CPUs without requiring CUDA compilation or GPUs.  |
+--------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 4. Pillar Evolution Summary
docs.text: Detailed registers for each pillar have been authored in docs/strategy/evolution/:

docs.title: 4.1 ALA Evolution Summary
docs.text: Full Register: docs/strategy/evolution/ALA_EVOLUTION_REGISTER.md - Baseline Capabilities: VectorizedHoeffdingTree (streaming decision tree with Hoeffding split bounds), ReliabilityWeightedADWIN (adaptive sliding window with sample reliability weighting), ClassBalancedReservoirReplay (reservoir memory maintaining rare class equity), StreamingEnsemble (online bagging with Poisson bootstrap), AdaptiveClassifier (unified estimator). - Core Evolution Focus: Greenwald-Khanna streaming quantiles for leaf histogram compression (EVO-ALA-001), multivariate covariate shift detection via random projection MMD (EVO-ALA-002), recency-decayed reservoir replay (EVO-ALA-003), continuous streaming regression trees (EVO-ALA-004), elastic parameter masking (EVO-ALA-005), and asynchronous multi-stream execution (EVO-ALA-006).

docs.title: 4.2 RLA Evolution Summary
docs.text: Full Register: docs/strategy/evolution/RLA_EVOLUTION_REGISTER.md - Baseline Capabilities: DensityAwareMarginScorer (combines margin with local density), SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss and GeneralizedCrossEntropyLoss (bounded noise-tolerant losses), ClassBalancedWeights (effective number of samples weighting), RobustLearningPipeline. - Core Evolution Focus: LSH approximate density estimation (EVO-RLA-001), noise-rate-agnostic online Peer Loss (EVO-RLA-002), online noise transition matrix \(\mathbf{T}\) estimation (EVO-RLA-003), continuous robust regression losses (EVO-RLA-004), tail distribution guardian for \(>10,000:1\) class imbalance (EVO-RLA-005), and latent contrastive purification (EVO-RLA-006).

docs.title: 4.3 RAO Evolution Summary
docs.text: Full Register: docs/strategy/evolution/RAO_EVOLUTION_REGISTER.md - Baseline Capabilities: BlockQuantizer (8-bit signed/unsigned block quantization), LowMemoryAdamW (compressed optimizer state with empirical throughput of \(\approx 9.8\text{ MParams/s}\) on CPU), AdaptiveGradientAccumulator, ResourceBudget (cross-platform memory monitoring with typed Win32 x64 fallback). - Core Evolution Focus: NumPy-native rank-1 second moment factorization (EVO-RAO-001), CPU-native 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) state quantization (EVO-RAO-002), volatility-gated parameter update skipping (EVO-RAO-003), zero-copy PyTorch tensor sharing (EVO-RAO-004), stochastic rounding for unbiased sub-8-bit accumulators (EVO-RAO-005), and optional C/SIMD kernels (EVO-RAO-006).

docs.title: 4.4 ULC Evolution Summary
docs.text: Full Register: docs/strategy/evolution/ULC_EVOLUTION_REGISTER.md - Baseline Capabilities: ArbitrationAutomaton (hysteresis-bounded discrete state machine), AdaptiveLearningController, ControllerDirective, EvidenceSynthesizer. - Core Evolution Focus: Continuous Bayesian belief state arbitration (EVO-ULC-001), spatial prediction error ratio for drift vs noise disentanglement (EVO-ULC-002), explainable intervention auditing (EVO-ULC-003), multi-tenant resource arbitration across concurrent pipelines (EVO-ULC-004), contextual bandit self-tuning (EVO-ULC-005), and edge mesh gossip consensus (EVO-ULC-006).

docs.title: 5. Developer Experience, Research, Industry & Ecosystem Strategy
5.1 Developer Experience (DX) Strategy
docs.text: Full Document: docs/strategy/evolution/DEVELOPER_EXPERIENCE_ROADMAP.md - Preserves the verified 5-line quickstart rule for new practitioners. - Establishes a fluent streaming pipeline builder (make_adaptive_stream()). - Provides lightweight terminal progress formatting and zero-dependency aml developer CLI. - Extends deep learning workflows with PyTorch Lightning and Hugging Face Trainer callbacks.

docs.title: 5.2 Research Roadmap Strategy
docs.text: Full Document: docs/strategy/evolution/RESEARCH_ROADMAP.md - Establishes seven formal research directions spanning adaptive, robust, and resource-efficient learning. - Each direction formulates explicit problem statements, literature citations, testable hypotheses, required public datasets, standard baselines, evaluation metrics, and failure modes. - Strict enforcement of negative results archiving in docs/research/NEGATIVE_RESULTS_REGISTRY.md.

docs.title: 5.3 Industry Validation Strategy
docs.text: Full Document: docs/strategy/evolution/INDUSTRY_APPLICATION_ROADMAP.md - Systematically evaluates six core industries: Financial Fraud, Industrial Maintenance, Cybersecurity, Recommendation Systems, Edge AI, and Demand Forecasting. - Formally designates Two Flagship Applications: 1. Industrial Predictive Maintenance on Edge CPUs (NASA C-MAPSS dataset proxy; validates offline local-first autonomy under physical sensor drift and glitches). 2. Financial Fraud Detection (ULB Credit Card Fraud dataset proxy; validates adversarial stream adaptation under extreme class imbalance and chargeback label noise). - Explicit recognition that public datasets are offline academic benchmark proxies, not live production deployments.

docs.title: 5.4 Open-Source Ecosystem Strategy
docs.text: Full Document: docs/strategy/evolution/ECOSYSTEM_ROADMAP.md - Details packaging architecture (aml-core minimal core with optional extras [torch], [sklearn], [safetensors]). - Defines PEP 621 entry-point plugin interfaces for third-party algorithmic extensions. - Establishes open community governance, DCO contributor ladder, and transparent adoption metrics.

docs.title: 5.5 Production Engineering Improvement Register
docs.text: Full Document: docs/strategy/evolution/ENGINEERING_IMPROVEMENT_REGISTER.md - Documents current verified engineering status (54/54 passing tests, Bandit 0 defects, Win32/Linux typed telemetry). - Schedules twelve prioritized engineering improvements covering IEEE 754 finite sanity guards, in-place NumPy memory operations, Darwin macOS ctypes telemetry, Hypothesis property-based fuzzing, and automated OIDC trusted publishing.

5. Trademark Clearance: Decomposed governance gate (BLOCKED by DEF-004; no trademark clearance granted).
6. Release Authorization: Explicit approval to tag, publish, or release packages (HOLD / UNAUTHORIZED).

docs.title: 7. Research Evidence & Feasibility Audit
docs.text: The audit team scrutinized all seven research directions in RESEARCH_ROADMAP.md to ensure compliance with the Ten Inviolable Research Governance Rules:

docs.title: 7.1 Bibliographic & Prior-Art Verification
docs.text: Cited Work Verified Authors, Year & Venue Confirmed Contribution Supports Stated Gap? ADWIN Bifet & Gavaldà (2007), SDM Adaptive windowing for 1D error streams YES. Confirms univariate boundary; motivates multivariate MMD. Kernel Two-Sample Gretton et al. (2012), JMLR Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) theory YES. Mathematical basis for kernel covariate shift testing. JL Lemma Dasgupta & Gupta (2003), Random Struct. & Alg. Elementary proof of Johnson-Lindenstrauss YES. Bounds pairwise distance preservation under random projections. GCE Loss Zhang & Sabuncu (2018), NeurIPS Box-Cox \(q\)-loss robust to label noise YES. Shows noise resilience, but requires fixed hyperparameter \(q\). SCE Loss Wang et al. (2019), ICCV Symmetric cross entropy via Reverse CE YES. Proves bounded gradient, but requires tuning \(\alpha, \beta\). Peer Loss Liu & Guo (2020), ICML Learning with noisy labels without noise rates YES. Directly motivates online noise-rate-agnostic peer loss. Confident Learn Northcutt et al. (2021), JAIR Cleanlab out-of-fold label uncertainty YES. Informs streaming transition matrix \(\mathbf{T}\) estimation. 8-bit Adam Dettmers et al. (2022), ICLR Block-wise dynamic quantization for optimizers YES. Foundation for AdaptiveML's existing BlockQuantizer. QLoRA / NF4 Dettmers et al. (2023), NeurIPS NormalFloat 4-bit quantile representation YES. Theoretical basis for proposed 4-bit state exploration. Adafactor Shazeer & Stern (2018), ICML Rank-1 row/col factored second moments YES. Informs proposed NumPy-native factored optimizer state. Stochastic Round Connolly et al. (2021), SIAM Sci. Comp. Unbiased expectation in quantized arithmetic YES. Theoretical remedy for gradient vanishing in 4-bit state. EWC Kirkpatrick et al. (2017), PNAS Elastic weight consolidation via Fisher info YES. Identifies \(\mathcal{O}(d)\) memory doubling; motivates binary masks. TinyML Bonsai Kumar et al. (2017), ICML Tree algorithms in sub-10KB RAM YES. Grounds micro-edge embedded CPU feasibility.

docs.title: 7.2 Feasibility & Evidence Gaps Identified
docs.text:
1. Computational Feasibility of CPU-Native 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4):
  2. Evidence Gap: On GPUs, NF4 utilizes ultra-fast warp-level shared memory lookup tables. On standard CPUs in pure NumPy, packing two 4-bit nibbles into a single uint8 byte requires bit-masking (val & 0x0F) and bit-shifting (val >> 4). In interpreted Python/NumPy, loop and array dispatch overhead could negate memory bandwidth savings.
  3. Mandatory Prerequisite: A C/NumPy micro-benchmark must measure step latency before asserting CPU speed gains over 8-bit quantization.
  4. Estimator Variance of Spatial Error Ratio \(\Lambda(t)\):
  5. Evidence Gap: In high dimensions (\(d > 50\)), local density and error variance estimation suffer from the curse of dimensionality, where pairwise Euclidean distances become equidistant.
  6. Mandatory Prerequisite: Verification must evaluate random projections or streaming Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to bound variance in high-dimensional manifolds.
  7. Early-Stream Variance of Online Peer Loss:
  8. Evidence Gap: During the first \(1,000\) steps of a cold stream, peer buffer samples may be auto-correlated, introducing non-zero gradient covariance.
  9. Mandatory Prerequisite: Warm-up schedules and peer buffer decorrelation lag \(\tau\) must be analyzed mathematically before claiming noise-rate agnosticism.

docs.title: 8. Industry Validation & Public Dataset Claims Audit
docs.text: The audit team reviewed INDUSTRY_APPLICATION_ROADMAP.md against real-world engineering constraints:

docs.title: 8.1 Public Datasets as Benchmark Proxies
docs.text: [!CAUTION] Scientific Integrity Mandate: Public benchmark datasets are offline academic proxies, not live production environments. Demonstrating high accuracy on a public Kaggle or OpenML benchmark does not prove operational readiness in live industrial manufacturing or production financial clearing houses.

docs.title: 8.2 Flagship Sector Verification
docs.text:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                FLAGSHIP BENCHMARK SPECIFICATIONS                                       |
+--------------------------+------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| Dimension                | Flagship 1: Predictive Maintenance | Flagship 2: Financial Fraud           |
+--------------------------+------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+
| **Target Sector**        | Industrial IoT & Heavy Equipment   | Payments, Banking & FinTech           |
| **Public Dataset Proxy** | NASA C-MAPSS Turbofan Simulation   | ULB Credit Card Fraud (OpenML #42175) |
| **License Verification** | Public Domain (NASA Open Data)     | Open Database License (ODbL v1.0)     |
| **Prediction Task**      | Remaining Useful Life (RUL) Regress| Binary Fraud Classification           |
| **Target Variable**      | $y \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ (Cycles)| $y \in \{0, 1\}$ (Fraud: 0.172%)      |
| **Realistic Baselines**  | HistGradientBoosting, ARIMA, LSTM  | XGBoost, Isolation Forest, River Tree |
| **Primary Metric**       | RMSE, Asymmetric Early Penalty     | PR-AUC, False Positive Rate at 90% Rec|
| **Class Imbalance**      | Moderate (Run-to-failure cycles)   | Extreme (492 frauds in 284,807 rows)  |
| **Temporal Leakage Risk**| Sequence boundary leakage across ID| Lookahead bias; lacks raw timestamps  |
| **Execution Constraint** | Edge CPU gateway ($\le 512\text{ MB}$ RAM) | Multi-core CPU server ($\le 5\text{ ms}$)    |
+--------------------------+------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+

docs.title: 8.3 Critical Benchmark Methodology Corrections
docs.text:
1. Financial Fraud Temporal Delay Simulation: The ULB dataset contains relative seconds, but lacks transaction dispute resolution timestamps (real chargebacks occur 14–60 days after transaction). Any streaming evaluation that assumes immediate label availability suffers from catastrophic temporal lookahead leakage. The benchmark harness must explicitly simulate synthetic label arrival delay windows (\(\Delta t_{\text{feedback}}\)) to evaluate ALA and RLA validly.
  2. C-MAPSS Simulation Boundary: NASA C-MAPSS is a thermodynamically simulated dataset produced in MATLAB Simulink. It does not contain physical packet loss, sensor brownouts, or analog wire disconnection spikes. Realistic robust learning evaluations must inject synthetic telemetry dropout and sensor clipping.

docs.title: 7.2 Epistemological Distinction: Established Art vs Proposed Hypotheses
docs.text: In strict compliance with Research Governance Rule 1: - All 27 citations above are Established Prior Art published in peer-reviewed venues. - The extensions in AdaptiveML (such as streaming peer loss on decoupled buffers, CPU-native NormalFloat with bit-packing, and spatial error variance ratios for drift vs noise attribution) are Proposed Research Hypotheses. - In accordance with Rule 3 and Rule 4, no claims of algorithmic superiority or novelty may be published until empirical multi-seed testing (\(p < 0.01\)) is completed in future research phases.

docs.title: 8.1 Methodological Guardrails
docs.text:
1. Financial Fraud Delay Windows: The benchmark harness must explicitly buffer and delay label arrival by a synthetic lag (\(\Delta t_{\text{feedback}} \ge 1,000\text{ samples}\)) to model real-world banking chargeback resolution latency and avoid lookahead bias.
  2. C-MAPSS Synthetic Noise Injection: Because NASA C-MAPSS is a smooth thermodynamic simulation, evaluations must inject synthetic sensor dropout (\(p=0.05\)) and transient telemetry spikes to realistically stress RLA loss bounds.

docs.title: Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA) — Evolution Register v2.0
docs.text: Document Identifier: DOC-STRAT-EVO-ALA-001 Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal clearance) Distribution Identifier: aml-core Target Module: adaptive_ml.ala Parent Roadmap: Evolution Roadmap v2.0 Status: Approved Strategic Architecture

docs.title: 1. Pillar Mission & Architectural Scope
docs.text:
The Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA) pillar provides CPU-first, local-first streaming algorithms capable of continuous adaptation to changing data distributions, non-stationary concept drift, and incremental data arrival without catastrophic forgetting.

In strict compliance with Research Governance Rule 7 (Pillar Independence), ALA algorithms operate as standalone mathematical primitives implemented in pure Python and NumPy. ALA maintains zero imports from RLA or RAO. Optional coordination occurs exclusively through the Unified Learning Controller (ULC).

docs.title: 2. Baseline Capabilities Grounded in Verified Source Evidence
docs.text:
The current verified implementation of ALA in aml-core==0.1.0.dev0 comprises five core components in adaptive_ml/ala:

adaptive_ml/ala/
├── __init__.py           # Exports VectorizedHoeffdingTree, ReliabilityWeightedADWIN,
│                         # ClassBalancedReservoirReplay, StreamingEnsemble, AdaptiveClassifier
├── tree.py               # VectorizedHoeffdingTree (Streaming decision tree with Hoeffding bounds)
├── adwin.py              # ReliabilityWeightedADWIN (Adaptive sliding window drift detector)
├── replay.py             # ClassBalancedReservoirReplay (Experience replay with class balance)
├── ensemble.py           # StreamingEnsemble (Streaming bagging/boosting with drift adaptation)
└── classifier.py         # AdaptiveClassifier (Unified scikit-learn compatible estimator)

docs.title: 2.1 Verified Capabilities Inventory
docs.text: Component Source File & Class Mathematical Formulation / Implementation Verified Invariants Streaming Decision Tree VectorizedHoeffdingTree in tree.py Hoeffding bound \(\epsilon = \sqrt{\frac{R^2 \ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}\); vectorized histogram split evaluation using information gain / Gini impurity Validated under standard and python -O execution; raises ValidationError on missing initialization (DEF-002 remediation) Adaptive Drift Detection ReliabilityWeightedADWIN in adwin.py Exponential histogram bucket compression; split evaluation \(\vert \hat{\mu}_{W_0} - \hat{\mu}_{W_1} \vert > \epsilon_{\text{cut}}\) weighted by sample reliability \(r_i\) Bounded window size; dynamic bucket merging; exact sub-window variance calculation Experience Replay Buffer ClassBalancedReservoirReplay in replay.py Per-class reservoir sampling maintaining uniform empirical representation across rare and majority classes Bounded total capacity \(M\); \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) sample insertion; zero memory allocation after warm-up Streaming Ensemble StreamingEnsemble in ensemble.py Online bagging with Poisson bootstrap (\(\lambda = 1\)); dynamic replacement of underperforming base learners upon drift alarm Model pool pruning; drift alarm subscription; majority voting and soft probability aggregation Streaming Classifier AdaptiveClassifier in classifier.py Integrates tree/ensemble learning, ADWIN drift monitoring, and experience replay buffer into scikit-learn partial_fit API Deterministic seed control via numpy.random.Generator; scikit-learn EstimatorProtocol compliance

docs.title: 3. Current Limitations
docs.text:
Based on empirical profiling from Phase 12 benchmarks and Phase 14 memory audits:

  1. Univariate Drift Monitoring Constraint: ReliabilityWeightedADWIN operates on scalar error streams \(e_t \in [0, 1]\). Covariate drift in high-dimensional feature spaces (\(X \in \mathbb{R}^d, d > 100\)) requires either tracking \(d\) independent scalar detectors or relying exclusively on posterior error rate degradation.
  2. High-Dimensional Tree Splitting Footprint: In VectorizedHoeffdingTree, maintaining discrete bin histograms for continuous attributes across \(L\) active leaves scales as \(\mathcal{O}(L \cdot d \cdot B \cdot C)\) where \(B\) is bin count and \(C\) is class count. When \(d > 500\), memory consumption on commodity CPU can exceed constrained budgets.
  3. Uniform Replay Decay: ClassBalancedReservoirReplay enforces standard reservoir replacement within class partitions, which treats all stored historical samples with equal retention probability, lacking explicit recency decay or drift-aware sample invalidation.
  4. Binary & Multi-Class Restriction: Existing streaming tree implementations support discrete classification. Streaming continuous regression trees (\(y \in \mathbb{R}\)) with variance reduction splits are currently unaddressed in the core library.

docs.title: EVO-ALA-001: Streaming Quantile Summarizer for Tree Histogram Pruning
docs.text:
• Classification: Proposed Enhancement
  • Priority: P1
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 8 (ALA Development)
  • Problem Statement: Continuous attribute split finding in VectorizedHoeffdingTree currently pre-allocates uniform static bin edges. In non-stationary streams, feature ranges shift, causing bins to cluster or saturate, degrading Hoeffding split quality.
  • Mathematical Design Requirements: Implement Greenwald-Khanna streaming quantile summaries or K-Means dynamic histograms per leaf attribute: $\(\vert \text{rank}(x) - \widehat{\text{rank}}(x) \vert \le \epsilon_{\text{GK}} \cdot N\)$
  • Implementation Dependencies: Pure NumPy, zero external dependencies.
  • Validation Requirements: Test split quality invariance on synthetic Gaussian streams whose variance shifts dynamically by \(10\times\).
  • Acceptance Criteria: Memory footprint per leaf node reduced by \(\ge 40\%\) on \(d \ge 100\) features without decreasing post-split test accuracy by \(>0.5\%\).
  • Estimated Complexity: Medium.
  • Risk: Low.

docs.text:
• Classification: New Research
  • Priority: P1
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 8 (ALA Development) & Phase 12 (Benchmarking)
  • Problem Statement: Concept drift often manifests as virtual covariate shift \(P(X)\) before inducing observable label error degradation \(P(Y \vert X)\). Existing ReliabilityWeightedADWIN detects only posterior loss degradation.
  • Research Hypothesis: Projecting streaming features \(X \in \mathbb{R}^d\) into a low-dimensional sketch space \(\tilde{X} = X R \in \mathbb{R}^k\) (\(k \ll d\)) using an orthogonal Rademacher matrix enables early detection of covariate shift via streaming Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) with bounded false positive rate: $\(\text{MMD}^2(\mathcal{W}_{\text{ref}}, \mathcal{W}_{\text{curr}}) = \left\| \frac{1}{\vert\mathcal{W}_{\text{ref}}\vert} \sum_{x \in \mathcal{W}_{\text{ref}}} \phi(x) - \frac{1}{\vert\mathcal{W}_{\text{curr}}\vert} \sum_{x \in \mathcal{W}_{\text{curr}}} \phi(x) \right\|^2_{\mathcal{H}}\)$
  • Relevant Prior Art:
  • Bifet & Gavaldà (2007): Learning from Time-Changing Data with Adaptive Windowing.
  • Gretton et al. (2012): A Kernel Two-Sample Test.
  • Dasgupta & Gupta (2003): An Elementary Proof of a Theorem of Johnson and Lindenstrauss.
  • Validation Requirements: Evaluate on synthetic rotating hyperplane, SEA concepts, and real-world Electricity (ELEC2) dataset. Measure detection lag against abrupt and gradual drift.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Abrupt covariate drift detected within \(\le 120\) samples; false positive rate \(\le 2.0\%\) under stationary Gaussian noise.
  • Estimated Complexity: High.
  • Risk: Medium (calibration of kernel bandwidth \(\sigma\) in streaming environments).

docs.title: EVO-ALA-003: Exponentially Recency-Decayed Reservoir Replay
docs.text:
• Classification: Proposed Enhancement
  • Priority: P2
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 8 (ALA Development)
  • Problem Statement: ClassBalancedReservoirReplay treats all historical exemplars equally once admitted. In severely non-stationary regimes, obsolete concepts remain indefinitely in the buffer, retarding adaptation.
  • Mathematical Design Requirements: Formulate time-decayed inclusion probability: $\(P(\text{retain sample } i \text{ at step } t) \propto \exp\left(-\gamma \cdot (t - t_i)\right) \cdot r_i\)$ where \(\gamma > 0\) is the forgetting rate and \(r_i \in [0, 1]\) is sample reliability from RLA.
  • Implementation Dependencies: adaptive_ml.ala.replay.
  • Validation Requirements: Verify catastrophic forgetting resistance on Split-MNIST benchmark with 5 tasks.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Backward transfer (BWT) improved by \(\ge 15\%\) relative to uniform reservoir sampling; zero memory leakage across \(10^6\) streaming steps.
  • Estimated Complexity: Medium.
  • Risk: Low.

docs.title: EVO-ALA-004: Vectorized Streaming Regression Trees
docs.text:
• Classification: New Engineering
  • Priority: P2
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 8 (ALA Development) & Phase 13 (Framework Integrations)
  • Problem Statement: Current VectorizedHoeffdingTree is restricted to discrete classification. Users requiring streaming continuous target estimation (\(y \in \mathbb{R}\)) cannot utilize ALA trees.
  • Mathematical Design Requirements: Implement continuous split evaluation using SDR (Standard Deviation Reduction): $\(\text{SDR} = \sigma(T) - \sum_{i} \frac{\vert T_i \vert}{\vert T \vert} \sigma(T_i)\)$ using running variance accumulators via Welford's algorithm to ensure numerical stability.
  • Implementation Dependencies: NumPy, adaptive_ml.core.base.
  • Validation Requirements: Compare against scikit-learn SGDRegressor and River HoeffdingTreeRegressor on California Housing and synthetic streaming Friedman datasets.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Mean Squared Error (MSE) within \(5\%\) of batch decision tree baselines; streaming inference throughput \(\ge 25,000\text{ samples/sec}\) on standard x86_64 CPU.
  • Estimated Complexity: Medium.
  • Risk: Low.

docs.title: EVO-ALA-005: Elastic Parameter Masking for Deep Streaming Adaptation
docs.text:
• Classification: New Research
  • Priority: P3
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 8 & Phase 21 (Continuous R&D)
  • Problem Statement: Applying streaming adaptation to neural network backbones causes catastrophic forgetting of earlier representations. Existing Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) requires computing and storing full diagonal Fisher Information Matrices, which doubles memory consumption.
  • Research Hypothesis: Maintaining a sparse binary parameter mask based on accumulated gradient volatility allows selective freezing of the top \(20\%\) critical weights, preventing representational drift with \(\le 5\%\) memory overhead: $\(m_j = \mathbb{I}\left( \sum_{t=1}^T \vert g_{t, j} \cdot \theta_{t, j} \vert \ge \tau_{\text{importance}} \right)\)$
  • Relevant Prior Art:
  • Kirkpatrick et al. (2017): Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting in Neural Networks (PNAS).
  • Mallya & Lazebnik (2018): PackNet: Adding Multiple Tasks to a Single Network by Iterative Pruning.
  • Validation Requirements: Sequential task learning on Permuted-MNIST and Split-CIFAR-10 using PyTorch integration.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Retention accuracy on Task 1 after 5 sequential tasks exceeds \(88\%\); total parameter storage overhead \(\le 1\text{ bit per parameter}\).
  • Estimated Complexity: High.
  • Risk: High (sensitivity of importance threshold under non-stationary learning rates).

docs.title: EVO-ALA-006: Asynchronous Multi-Stream Partitioning Engine
docs.text:
• Classification: Deferred Opportunity
  • Priority: P4
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 21 (Continuous R&D)
  • Problem Statement: Large-scale telemetry pipelines generate hundreds of parallel IoT sensor streams. Running sequential partial_fit in a single thread creates processing backpressure.
  • Proposed Exploration: Investigate zero-copy lock-free thread pool partitions in Python 3.14 free-threaded mode (PEP 703) to enable parallel independent ALA model evaluation.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Linear scaling up to 8 CPU physical cores without memory lock contention.
  • Estimated Complexity: Very High.
  • Risk: High (cross-platform Python GIL elimination maturity).

docs.title: 1. Vision for Developer Experience
docs.text:
A machine learning library's real-world impact is determined by its developer ergonomics, conceptual clarity, and operational friction. AdaptiveML is committed to delivering a zero-friction, mathematically transparent developer experience that meets developers where they are—whether running a 5-line script on a local laptop, integrating with scikit-learn pipelines, or adapting deep learning models in PyTorch.

In strict compliance with Non-Functional Requirement NFR-DEP-001 and NFR-SEC-001, the developer experience requires zero cloud accounts, zero mandatory API keys, zero network telemetry, and zero mandatory external framework dependencies.

docs.title: 2. Usage Patterns Across Developer Proficiency Levels
2.1 Beginner: The 5-Line Local-First Quickstart
docs.text:
[!NOTE] Verified Baseline Capability: The following snippet runs out-of-the-box on commodity CPU hardware with only Python standard library and NumPy installed.

# Verified Working Implementation in aml-core==0.1.0.dev0
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import AdaptiveClassifier

X, y = np.random.randn(200, 10), np.random.randint(0, 2, 200)
clf = AdaptiveClassifier(n_features=10, n_classes=2)
clf.fit(X, y)
predictions = clf.predict(X)

docs.title: 2.2 Intermediate: Streaming Pipeline with Drift Detection & Robust Weighting
docs.text:
# [PROPOSED / ILLUSTRATIVE API: Planned under EVO-DX-001]
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.pipeline import make_adaptive_stream  # [PROPOSED]

# Fluent streaming constructor chaining drift adaptation and noise suppression
stream_model = (
    make_adaptive_stream(n_features=20, n_classes=3)
    .with_adwin_drift_detector(delta=0.002)
    .with_robust_margin_loss(alpha=1.0, beta=0.5)
    .with_class_balanced_replay(buffer_size=1000)
    .build()
)

for X_batch, y_batch in data_generator:
    stream_model.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch)
    diagnostics = stream_model.get_telemetry()
    if diagnostics.drift_detected:
        print(f"Drift detected at step {diagnostics.step_count}!")

docs.title: 2.3 Advanced: Coordinated Adaptation with PyTorch & ULC
docs.text:
# [PROPOSED / ILLUSTRATIVE API: Planned under EVO-DX-003]
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from adaptive_ml.integrations.torch_optim import create_torch_low_memory_adamw
from adaptive_ml.integrations.torch_module import TorchSymmetricCrossEntropyLoss
from adaptive_ml.ulc import AdaptiveLearningController

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))
loss_fn = TorchSymmetricCrossEntropyLoss(alpha=1.0, beta=0.5)
optimizer = create_torch_low_memory_adamw(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-2)
controller = AdaptiveLearningController()

for step, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(dataloader):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    outputs = model(inputs)
    loss = loss_fn(outputs, targets)
    loss.backward()

    # Optional dynamic arbitration based on gradient norm and loss volatility
    directive = controller.step(loss=loss.item(), grad_norm=optimizer.get_grad_norm())
    optimizer.set_lr_multiplier(directive.lr_multiplier)
    optimizer.step()

docs.title: Open-Source Ecosystem & Community Strategy v2.0
docs.text: Document Identifier: DOC-STRAT-EVO-ECO-001 Working Codename: AdaptiveML (Provisional — Subject to formal legal clearance) Distribution Identifier: aml-core Parent Roadmap: Evolution Roadmap v2.0 Status: Approved Strategic Architecture

docs.title: 1. Ecosystem Vision & Core Commitments
docs.text:
The long-term vitality of AdaptiveML depends on cultivating an open, technically rigorous, and welcoming developer and research ecosystem.

In strict compliance with Non-Functional Requirement NFR-DEP-001 and Research Governance Rule 9, the ecosystem strategy is founded on three non-negotiable principles: 1. Zero Cloud Lock-In: AdaptiveML will never require proprietary cloud accounts, SaaS subscriptions, or paid remote APIs. Every algorithm, tutorial, benchmark, and CLI tool must be fully executable offline on commodity hardware. 2. Minimalist Core Packaging: The core PyPI distribution (aml-core) will remain lightweight, with runtime dependencies strictly restricted to standard library and NumPy. 3. Meritocratic, Transparent Governance: Decisions are driven by reproducible empirical evidence and open peer review rather than commercial vendor priorities.

docs.title: 3.1 Plugin Architecture & Dynamic Entry Points
docs.text:
To encourage third-party researchers and organizations to contribute novel drift detectors, robust loss formulations, and quantization kernels without modifying the core repository, AdaptiveML will support Python entry-point plugins:

# [PROPOSED / ILLUSTRATIVE: pyproject.toml of a third-party plugin]
[project.entry-points."adaptive_ml.drift_detectors"]
my_custom_detector = "my_research_package.detectors:FastCUSUMDetector"

[project.entry-points."adaptive_ml.robust_losses"]
my_custom_loss = "my_research_package.losses:TrimmableLoss"

Core modules discover registered plugins lazily via importlib.metadata.entry_points(group="adaptive_ml.*"), enabling zero-cost discovery without runtime overhead.

docs.title: 3.2 Command-Line Interface (aml CLI)
docs.text: The aml CLI provides developers with instant command-line introspection and environment verification: - aml info: Displays active package versions, NumPy BLAS linkage, and CPU SIMD capabilities. - aml inspect <path>: Parses Safetensors / JSON model checkpoints and prints parameter shapes and compression statistics. - aml bench: Executes the standard 30-second local CPU benchmark suite and outputs performance metrics. - aml verify: Executes the local regression test battery in the active Python environment.

docs.title: 3.3 Documentation Portal & Benchmark Explorer
docs.text:
• Documentation Engine: MkDocs Material portal featuring search, dark mode, API reference generated from docstrings via mkdocstrings, and interactive runnable snippets.
  • Benchmark Explorer: Static web dashboard hosted on GitHub Pages displaying benchmark runs across datasets, random seeds, and baselines with Wilcoxon significance p-values and confidence intervals.
  • Recipe Showcase: Curated gallery of verified domain workflows (predictive maintenance, financial fraud, streaming NLP).

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 4.1 Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO)
docs.text: All contributors must sign off their Git commits using git commit -s, certifying adherence to the standard Linux Foundation Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO 1.1) to guarantee copyright provenance and IP hygiene.

docs.title: 4.2 Mentorship & Contributor Ladder
docs.text: To foster community growth: - Triage Maintainers: Review bug reports, reproduce user issues, and label PRs. - Core Reviewers: Review code quality, ensure typing and test coverage. - Pillar Custodians: Scientific experts responsible for specific pillars (ALA, RLA, RAO, ULC). - Leadership Council: Project direction, roadmap evolution, and release clearance.

docs.text:
To expand adoption without creating hard dependencies, AdaptiveML establishes zero-cost adapter bridges:

docs.title: 1. Engineering Philosophy & Quality Standards
docs.text:
Production excellence in AdaptiveML is anchored in rigorous software engineering discipline, determinism, and zero-defect security.

In strict compliance with Non-Functional Requirements NFR-PLAT-001 through NFR-MAINT-003: 1. Separation of Verified State vs Proposed Improvements: This register strictly distinguishes between verified, currently passing engineering baselines and proposed future enhancements. 2. Defect-Free Security: Zero high, medium, or low vulnerabilities permitted in static scans (Bandit 1.9.4 baseline: 0 issues across 3,081 lines of code). 3. Strict Type Safety: 100% strict type annotations enforced via mypy --strict. 4. Cross-Platform Parity: Linux, macOS, and Windows treated as tier-1 operating environments with native OS telemetry fallbacks.
