docs.title: EVO-ULC-001: Continuous Probabilistic Belief State Arbitration
docs.text:
• Classification: Proposed Enhancement
  • Priority: P1
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 11 (ULC Development)
  • Problem Statement: Discrete state switching creates discontinuous step updates when noise and drift signals fluctuate near threshold boundaries.
  • Mathematical Design Requirements: Replace discrete automaton states with a continuous Bayesian belief state vector \(\vec{b}_t \in \Delta^3\): $\(\vec{b}_t = [P(\text{Drift}_t), P(\text{Noise}_t), P(\text{Stationary}_t)]^T, \quad \sum b_{t, k} = 1\)$ and interpolate directives continuously: $\(\gamma_{\text{lr}}(t) = b_{t, \text{drift}} \cdot \gamma_{\max} + b_{t, \text{noise}} \cdot \gamma_{\min} + b_{t, \text{stat}} \cdot 1.0\)$
  • Implementation Dependencies: adaptive_ml.ulc.evidence, adaptive_ml.ulc.directives.
  • Validation Requirements: Compare test error variance on synthetic continuous drift + noise benchmarks against discrete automaton.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Reduces step prediction variance by \(\ge 40\%\); eliminates abrupt directive oscillations without increasing computational latency by \(>0.1\text{ ms/step}\).
  • Estimated Complexity: Medium.
  • Risk: Low.

docs.title: EVO-ULC-002: Dual-Evidence Drift vs Noise Disentanglement Hypothesis
docs.text:
• Classification: New Research
  • Priority: P1
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 11 (ULC Development) & Phase 12 (Benchmarking)
  • Problem Statement: When error rate surges in a stream, naive detectors cannot distinguish whether the cause is genuine concept drift (requiring model plasticity) or a transient noise burst (requiring sample rejection).
  • Research Hypothesis: By computing the spatial consistency of prediction errors—specifically, comparing the variance of prediction residuals in local feature neighborhoods against global error variance: $\(\Lambda(t) = \frac{\text{Var}_{\text{local}}(e_t)}{\text{Var}_{\text{global}}(e_t)}\)$ the controller can statistically disentangle concept drift (\(\Lambda \ll 1\), errors cluster spatially) from uniform label noise (\(\Lambda \approx 1\), errors distribute uniformly).
  • Relevant Prior Art:
  • Ditzler et al. (2015): Learning under Concept Drift: An Overview (IEEE CIM).
  • Lipton et al. (2018): Detecting and Correcting for Label Shift with Black Box Predictors (ICML).
  • Bifet & Gavaldà (2007): Learning from Time-Changing Data with Adaptive Windowing.
  • Validation Requirements: Synthetic benchmarks with interleaved sudden drift events and high-noise bursts (\(40\%\)).
  • Acceptance Criteria: Correct attribution accuracy \(\ge 90\%\) within \(150\) samples of event onset; prevents model parameter corruption during noise bursts.
  • Estimated Complexity: High.
  • Risk: Medium (spatial variance estimation complexity in high-dimensional feature spaces).

docs.title: EVO-ULC-003: Explainable Intervention Auditing and Attribution Reporting
docs.text:
• Classification: Proposed Enhancement
  • Priority: P2
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 11 (ULC Development)
  • Problem Statement: In regulated industries (e.g., finance, healthcare), automated changes to learning rates, sample weights, or memory allocations must be interpretable and auditable by compliance officers.
  • Mathematical Design Requirements: Implement an immutable audit log recording: $\(\mathcal{R}_t = \left\{ t, \vec{b}_t, \text{triggering\_signal}, \text{applied\_directive}, \Delta\text{loss}_{\text{expected}} \right\}\)$ with programmatic export to JSON / Markdown summary tables.
  • Implementation Dependencies: adaptive_ml.ulc.controller.
  • Validation Requirements: Verify zero overhead when logging is disabled; audit log schema validation in CI.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Human-readable intervention explanation generated via controller.explain_last_decision(); zero memory leak over \(10^6\) steps with ring-buffer storage.
  • Estimated Complexity: Medium.
  • Risk: Low.

docs.title: EVO-ULC-004: Multi-Tenant Resource Arbitration across Concurrent Pipelines
docs.text:
• Classification: New Engineering
  • Priority: P2
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 11 & Phase 14 (Production Engineering)
  • Problem Statement: When multiple streaming models run on a single host (e.g., 20 models for different sensor types), uncoordinated memory allocations can collectively breach physical RAM, triggering OS OOM killers.
  • Mathematical Design Requirements: Implement a global coordinator that collects memory pressure signals across all registered ULC instances and solves a budget allocation linear program: $\(\max \sum_{m=1}^M w_m \cdot \text{capacity}_m \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{m=1}^M \text{RSS}_m \le \text{Budget}_{\max}\)$
  • Implementation Dependencies: adaptive_ml.rao.memory, adaptive_ml.ulc.controller.
  • Validation Requirements: Stress test with 10 concurrent streaming pipelines on an 8 GB RAM container.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Zero OOM events under 95% memory saturation; dynamic eviction of low-priority buffers to maintain system headroom.
  • Estimated Complexity: Medium.
  • Risk: Low.

docs.title: EVO-ULC-005: Contextual Bandit for Self-Tuning Directive Policy
docs.text:
• Classification: New Research
  • Priority: P3
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 11 & Phase 21 (Continuous R&D)
  • Problem Statement: Pre-configured heuristic scaling constants (\(\gamma_{\text{lr}} \in [0.1, 2.0]\)) fail to achieve optimal convergence rates across widely varying data dynamics.
  • Research Hypothesis: Formulating directive selection as an online contextual bandit (using LinUCB with context vector \(\vec{c}_t = \vec{b}_t\)) optimizes downstream predictive loss reward: $\(r_t = - \mathcal{L}_{t+1}(x_{t+1}, y_{t+1})\)$ achieving sublinear regret without manual hyperparameter search.
  • Relevant Prior Art:
  • Li et al. (2010): A Contextual-Bandit Approach to Personalized News Article Recommendation (WWW).
  • Auer et al. (2002): Finite-time Analysis of the Multiarmed Bandit Problem (Machine Learning).
  • Validation Requirements: Benchmarking across 5 diverse streaming datasets against fixed-heuristic ULC.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Cumulative streaming test log-loss reduced by \(\ge 8\%\) compared to static heuristic controller.
  • Estimated Complexity: High.
  • Risk: High (bandit exploration steps inducing instability during critical drift regimes).

docs.title: EVO-ULC-006: Distributed Consensus Controller for Edge Mesh Networks
docs.text:
• Classification: Deferred Opportunity
  • Priority: P4
  • Phase Mapping: Phase 21 (Continuous R&D)
  • Problem Statement: In edge IoT meshes, sensor nodes must reach decentralized consensus on drift onset without central coordinator servers.
  • Proposed Exploration: Investigate gossip-based drift consensus protocols across local ULC instances using lightweight UDP message exchange.
  • Acceptance Criteria: Decentralized drift consensus reached across 16 nodes within \(2\text{ seconds}\) with \(\le 1\text{ KB/s}\) bandwidth.
  • Estimated Complexity: Very High.
  • Risk: High (network partition tolerance and distributed consensus overhead).

docs.title: Troubleshooting & Diagnostics Guide
docs.text: This guide provides practical diagnoses and resolutions for common runtime errors, configuration issues, and edge cases encountered when running AdaptiveML (aml-core).

docs.title: SerializationError: State serialization requires the optional 'safetensors' dependency
docs.text:
• Root Cause: Attempted to invoke save_state or load_state without installing the HuggingFace safetensors binary package.
  • Resolution: Install the safetensors extra: 
    pip install "aml-core[safetensors]"

docs.title: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch' or 'sklearn'
docs.text:
• Root Cause: Attempted to use PyTorch modules (TorchSymmetricCrossEntropyLoss, VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW) or Scikit-Learn estimators (SklearnAdaptiveClassifier) in an environment where only core dependencies (numpy) are installed.
  • Resolution: Install the appropriate framework extra: 
    pip install "aml-core[torch]"     # For PyTorch components
pip install "aml-core[sklearn]"   # For Scikit-learn pipelines
pip install "aml-core[all]"       # For all optional integrations

docs.title: ValidationError: Expected 2D array, got 1D vector of shape (N,)
docs.text:
• Root Cause: A 1D array was passed to an algorithm or prequential method expecting a 2D feature matrix \((N, D)\).
  • Resolution: Use adaptive_ml.integrations.to_numpy(data, ensure_2d=True) or reshape using data.reshape(-1, 1): 
    from adaptive_ml.integrations import to_numpy
X_clean = to_numpy(X_raw, ensure_2d=True)

docs.title: ValidationError: Input matrix contains non-finite values (NaN or Inf)
docs.text:
• Root Cause: Feature ingestion encountered missing data, divisions by zero, or numerical overflows before entering the model.
  • Resolution: Impute missing values (e.g. via SimpleImputer in Scikit-Learn) before streaming to AdaptiveML. AdaptiveML strictly rejects NaN to prevent silent model poisoning.

docs.title: The model triggers excessive drift resets during noisy stream phases
docs.text:
• Root Cause: ADWIN confidence parameter \(\delta\) is set too aggressively (e.g., \(\delta > 0.05\)), or raw error rates fluctuate due to random label corruption rather than true concept drift.
  • Resolution:
  • Increase confidence parameter \(\delta\) to a more conservative threshold: \(\delta \in [0.001, 0.005]\).
  • Increase Hoeffding tree grace_period (e.g., \(100 \le N_g \le 500\)) to allow sufficient statistics per leaf.
  • Switch to UnifiedLearningControllerV5 which utilizes Spatial Discordance Gating to distinguish true drift from noisy label spikes.

docs.title: The model experiences catastrophic forgetting on recurring patterns
docs.text:
• Root Cause: Standard drift detectors reset model parameters to zero upon drift, forgetting historical regimes.
  • Resolution: Use ALA30AdaptiveLearner with RecurringConceptMemory. Ensure similarity_threshold is calibrated (recommended: \(0.80 \le \tau_s \le 0.85\)) to allow cosine matching against historical concept snapshots.

docs.title: SerializationError: HMAC authentication failed for checkpoint
docs.text:
• Root Cause: The secret auth_key provided to load_state does not match the key used during save_state, or the underlying binary file was altered in transit.
  • Resolution: Ensure the identical 32-byte secret key is provided. If loading from untrusted storage, treat this exception as an active indicator of file corruption or tampering.

docs.title: SerializationError: Checkpoint file exceeds size ceiling
docs.text:
• Root Cause: The tensor file exceeds the \(5\text{ GB}\) denial-of-service ceiling, or the .meta.json file exceeds \(64\text{ MB}\).
  • Resolution: If legitimately persisting an exceptionally large model, adjust the safety ceiling explicitly: 
    load_state("path/to/checkpoint", max_file_size_bytes=10 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024)  # 10 GB

docs.title: LowMemoryAdamW raises error on block size
docs.text:
• Root Cause: Dynamic block quantization requires power-of-two block sizes for SIMD alignment.
  • Resolution: Set block_size to one of [32, 64, 128, 256]. The recommended default is 64 for optimal CPU L1 cache fit.

docs.title: Memory usage does not decrease when instantiating LowMemoryAdamW
docs.text:
• Root Cause: In PyTorch, optimizer states (\(m_t, v_t\)) are lazily allocated on the first step() call, not in __init__.
  • Resolution: Measure memory usage after performing at least one forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer.step(). Use optimizer.get_state_memory_bytes() to inspect exact allocated state bytes.

docs.title: Tutorial 1: Five-Minute Quickstart
docs.text: Get started with AdaptiveML in under 5 minutes.

docs.title: 1. Installation
docs.text:
AdaptiveML is local-first and CPU-first. The core library requires only numpy >= 1.24.0:

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/AdaptiveML/AdaptiveML.git
cd AdaptiveML

# Install in development mode
pip install -e .

docs.title: 2. Your First Streaming Classifier
docs.text:
AdaptiveML's AdaptiveClassifier combines vectorized Hoeffding trees with automatic concept drift detection and class-balanced reservoir replay:

import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import AdaptiveClassifier

# Initialize the online classifier
model = AdaptiveClassifier(
    n_features=4,
    n_classes=2,
    grace_period=20,
    enable_drift_detection=True,
)

# Stream 5 mini-batches of observations
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
for step in range(1, 6):
    X = rng.normal(size=(20, 4))
    y = (X[:, 0] > 0.0).astype(int)

    # Test before train (prequential evaluation)
    if model.samples_seen_ > 0:
        accuracy = np.mean(model.predict(X) == y)
        print(f"Step {step} | Test Accuracy: {accuracy * 100:.1f}%")

    # Update model incrementally
    model.partial_fit(X, y)

Executable script available at examples/quickstart.py.

docs.title: Tutorial 1: Streaming Anomaly & Drift Detection in IoT Sensors
docs.text: Domain: IoT Industrial Telemetry & Sensor Monitoring Algorithms: ALA30AdaptiveLearner, ADWIN, to_numpy Execution Mode: Micro-batch streaming with prequential accuracy tracking

docs.title: 1. Problem Scenario
docs.text:
Industrial machinery continuously outputs high-frequency telemetry (vibration, temperature, power draw). When operating conditions shift (e.g. ambient temperature drops, machine enters high-load mode), sensor distributions drift. A static ML model experiences silent accuracy degradation.

In this tutorial, you will build an adaptive streaming pipeline that: 1. Ingests simulated sensor telemetry in micro-batches of 50 samples. 2. Evaluates prequential classification accuracy before each learning update. 3. Automatically detects distribution shifts using ADWIN. 4. Adapts decision boundaries in real time while tracking drift events.

docs.title: 2. Complete Runnable Code
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import ALA30AdaptiveLearner

# Set random seed for reproducibility
np.random.seed(42)

def generate_sensor_stream(n_steps=20, batch_size=50):
    """Generates synthetic sensor stream with a sudden drift at step 10."""
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Step 0-9: Normal baseline regime
        if step < 10:
            X = np.random.normal(loc=0.0, scale=1.0, size=(batch_size, 4))
            y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0.0).astype(int)
        # Step 10-19: Abrupt drift (sensor calibration shift)
        else:
            X = np.random.normal(loc=1.5, scale=1.2, size=(batch_size, 4))
            y = (X[:, 2] - X[:, 3] > 0.5).astype(int)
        yield step, X, y

def main():
    print("--- Starting IoT Sensor Streaming Tutorial ---")

    # Initialize ALA 3.0 Adaptive Learner
    learner = ALA30AdaptiveLearner(
        n_features=4,
        n_classes=2,
        grace_period=25,     # Check split heuristics every 25 samples
        delta=0.005,         # ADWIN drift detection sensitivity
    )

    prequential_accuracies = []

    for step, X_batch, y_batch in generate_sensor_stream():
        # 1. Prequential Evaluation (Test before Train)
        if learner.total_steps > 0:
            preds = learner.predict(X_batch)
            step_acc = float(np.mean(preds == y_batch))
        else:
            step_acc = 0.50  # Baseline prior to training

        prequential_accuracies.append(step_acc)

        # 2. Incremental Training & Adaptation
        metrics = learner.update(X_batch, y_batch)

        # 3. Log progress
        if step in (0, 9, 10, 11, 19):
            print(
                f"Step {step:02d} | "
                f"Prequential Acc: {step_acc * 100:5.1f}% | "
                f"Batch Fit Acc: {metrics['batch_acc'] * 100:5.1f}% | "
                f"Drift Resets: {learner.drift_resets}"
            )

    print(f"\nFinal State: Total stream steps: {learner.total_steps}")
    print(f"Total drift events detected and adapted: {learner.drift_resets}")
    print("--- Tutorial Completed Successfully ---")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 3. Expected Output
docs.text:
When executed, the prequential accuracy temporarily dips immediately after the abrupt drift at step 10, and quickly recovers as ADWIN detects the cut and resets the Hoeffding tree:

Step 00 | Prequential Acc:  50.0% | Batch Fit Acc:  72.0% | Drift Resets: 0
Step 09 | Prequential Acc:  86.0% | Batch Fit Acc:  88.0% | Drift Resets: 0

docs.title: Tutorial 02: Detecting Concept Drift
docs.text: Objective: Detect structural distribution shifts in streaming loss trajectories using ReliabilityWeightedADWIN.

docs.title: 1. Setup & Imports
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import ReliabilityWeightedADWIN

detector = ReliabilityWeightedADWIN(delta=0.002)

docs.title: 2. Simulating Streaming Loss with Abrupt Drift
docs.text:
np.random.seed(42)

# Stream 200 loss values
# Step 0-99: Low loss (mean ~ 0.20)
# Step 100-199: High loss (mean ~ 0.85, concept drift)
for t in range(200):
    if t < 100:
        loss = np.random.normal(0.20, 0.05)
    else:
        loss = np.random.normal(0.85, 0.05)

    # Clip loss to valid range [0, 1]
    loss = float(np.clip(loss, 0.0, 1.0))

    # Update detector
    is_drift = detector.update(loss, reliability=1.0)
    if is_drift:
        print(f"Drift detected at step {t:03d} (Window Size: {detector.width})")

Output: 

Drift detected at step 114 (Window Size: 46)

docs.title: 3. Suppressing False Alarms During Noise Bursts
docs.text:
detector.reset()

for t in range(100):
    # Transient 5-step corrupted noise burst at t=50..54
    if 50 <= t < 55:
        loss = 0.95
        rel = 0.05  # Reliability scorer flagged this as corrupted
    else:
        loss = 0.15
        rel = 1.00

    is_drift = detector.update(loss, reliability=rel)
    assert not is_drift, f"False alarm triggered at step {t}!"

print("Noise burst successfully suppressed without false alarms!")

docs.title: Tutorial 2: Adapting to Recurring Concept Shifts in Retail Demand
docs.text: Domain: E-Commerce & Retail Demand Streams Algorithms: ALA30AdaptiveLearner, RecurringConceptMemory, ConceptFingerprinter Execution Mode: Cyclical concept stream with episodic memory restoration

docs.title: 1. Problem Scenario
docs.text:
E-commerce consumer behaviors fluctuate predictably between recurring patterns (e.g., Weekday work commutes vs. Weekend leisure browsing, or Promotional flash sales vs. Baseline periods).

When a stream drifts back to an earlier regime, standard drift-adaptation algorithms trigger a blind reset, discarding valuable learned parameters and suffering severe transient error penalties while re-learning.

In this tutorial, you will use ALA 3.0 to: 1. Ingest streaming data alternating between two cyclical regimes (\(A \to B \to A \to B\)). 2. Automatically fingerprint concept distributions in memory. 3. Detect recurring drift and immediately restore historical concept snapshots via RecurringConceptMemory.

docs.title: 2. Complete Runnable Code
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import ALA30AdaptiveLearner

np.random.seed(42)

def generate_cyclical_demand_stream(cycles=2, steps_per_regime=10, batch_size=40):
    """Generates stream alternating between Regime A and Regime B."""
    step = 0
    for c in range(cycles):
        # Regime A: Weekday Pattern
        for _ in range(steps_per_regime):
            X = np.random.normal(loc=0.0, scale=1.0, size=(batch_size, 4))
            y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0.0).astype(int)
            yield step, "Regime_A", X, y
            step += 1

        # Regime B: Weekend Pattern
        for _ in range(steps_per_regime):
            X = np.random.normal(loc=2.0, scale=1.0, size=(batch_size, 4))
            y = (X[:, 2] - X[:, 3] > 0.0).astype(int)
            yield step, "Regime_B", X, y
            step += 1

def main():
    print("--- Starting Recurring Demand Shifts Tutorial ---")

    # Initialize ALA 3.0 Learner with Recurring Concept Memory
    learner = ALA30AdaptiveLearner(
        n_features=4,
        n_classes=2,
        grace_period=20,
        delta=0.005,
        max_concepts=5,
        similarity_threshold=0.80,
    )

    for step, regime, X_batch, y_batch in generate_cyclical_demand_stream(cycles=2, steps_per_regime=12):
        telemetry = learner.update(X_batch, y_batch)

        # Monitor drift interventions
        if telemetry["drift_detected"] or step in (0, 11, 12, 23, 24, 35, 47):
            print(
                f"Step {step:02d} [{regime}] | "
                f"Action: {telemetry['action']:22s} | "
                f"Batch Acc: {telemetry['batch_acc'] * 100:5.1f}% | "
                f"Stored Concepts: {telemetry['stored_concepts']} | "
                f"Restorations: {learner.recurring_restorations}"
            )

    print(f"\nFinal Stream Audit:")
    print(f"Total Steps Processed: {learner.total_steps}")
    print(f"Drift Resets (Novel Concepts): {learner.drift_resets}")
    print(f"Recurring Concept Restorations: {learner.recurring_restorations}")
    print("--- Tutorial Completed Successfully ---")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 3. Key Observations
docs.text:
• When the stream transitions to Regime B for the first time (step 12), ALA 3.0 recognizes it as a novel concept, snapshots Regime A into memory, and initializes a fresh tree for Regime B.
  • When the stream transitions back to Regime A (step 24), the cosine fingerprint matches the stored Regime A concept (\(\text{sim} > 0.80\)).
  • Instead of resetting, ALA 3.0 triggers an instantaneous RECURRING_RESTORE, preserving full predictive accuracy without transient learning decay.

docs.title: Tutorial 2: Streaming Drift Detection with RW-ADWIN
docs.text: Learn how AdaptiveML detects distributional shifts while ignoring noisy observations.

docs.title: 1. Why Standard ADWIN Fails Under Noise
docs.text:
Standard ADWIN partitions an active sliding window into two sub-windows \(W = W_0 \cdot W_1\) and cuts the oldest window if: $\(|\mu_0 - \mu_1| \ge \epsilon_{\text{cut}}\)$

When a burst of noisy labels arrives, raw variance spikes. Standard ADWIN misidentifies the noise as concept drift, wiping the model's memory (catastrophic forgetting).

docs.title: 2. Using ReliabilityWeightedADWIN
docs.text:
ReliabilityWeightedADWIN weights sub-window cuts by sample reliability \(r_i \in [0, 1]\):

from adaptive_ml.ala.adwin import ReliabilityWeightedADWIN

detector = ReliabilityWeightedADWIN(delta=0.002)

# Feed observations: loss and sample reliability
loss = 0.95        # High loss
reliability = 0.15 # Corrupted sample flagged by RLA

# Under low reliability, the detector downweights the error,
# suppressing false positive window cuts
drift_detected = detector.update(loss, reliability=reliability)
if drift_detected:
    print("True distributional shift detected!")

Executable demo available at examples/ala/streaming_classification_example.py.

docs.title: Tutorial 3: Robust Learning Under Extreme Label Corruption
docs.text: Domain: Crowdsourced Labeling, Clickstream Logs & Noisy Telemetry Algorithms: RLA30RobustLearner, MultiSignalReliabilityEngine, SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss Execution Mode: Micro-batch stream with 35% synthetic asymmetric label flip corruption

docs.title: 1. Problem Scenario
docs.text:
Real-world streaming labels are frequently corrupt: - Crowdsourced annotators click through tasks carelessly. - Automated heuristics misclassify ambiguous edge cases. - Sensor threshold glitches invert signal polarity.

Standard cross-entropy loss rapidly overfits and memorizes these inverted labels. In this tutorial, you will use RLA 3.0 to: 1. Stream instances with a high noise corruption rate (\(35\%\)). 2. Compute continuous composite sample reliability scores \(r_i \in [0, 1]\). 3. Abstain from learning on corrupt outliers while training stably on retained high-reliability samples.

docs.title: 2. Complete Runnable Code
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.rla import RLA30RobustLearner

np.random.seed(42)

def generate_noisy_stream(n_steps=15, batch_size=60, noise_rate=0.35):
    """Generates synthetic stream where noise_rate of labels are flipped."""
    for step in range(n_steps):
        X = np.random.randn(batch_size, 4)
        # Ground truth separable boundary
        y_true = (X[:, 0] + 0.5 * X[:, 1] > 0.0).astype(int)

        # Corrupt labels
        y_noisy = y_true.copy()
        n_corrupt = int(batch_size * noise_rate)
        flip_indices = np.random.choice(batch_size, size=n_corrupt, replace=False)
        y_noisy[flip_indices] = 1 - y_noisy[flip_indices]

        yield step, X, y_noisy, y_true

def main():
    print("--- Starting Extreme Label Noise Tutorial ---")

    # Initialize RLA 3.0 Robust Learner
    learner = RLA30RobustLearner(
        n_features=4,
        n_classes=2,
        lr=0.05,
        reliability_threshold=0.35,  # Abstain from samples scoring r_i < 0.35
        security_mode="standard",
    )

    for step, X_batch, y_noisy, y_true in generate_noisy_stream():
        # Ingest noisy batch through RLA 3.0 pipeline
        metrics = learner.fit_batch(X_batch, y_noisy)

        # Evaluate true accuracy against uncorrupted ground truth
        true_accuracy = learner.score(X_batch, y_true)

        print(
            f"Step {step:02d} | "
            f"Retained: {metrics['retained']:2d}/{len(y_noisy)} | "
            f"Abstained: {metrics['abstained']:2d} | "
            f"Mean Reliability: {metrics['mean_reliability']:.3f} | "
            f"True Acc: {true_accuracy * 100:5.1f}%"
        )

    print(f"\nFinal Stream Audit:")
    print(f"Total Samples Seen: {learner.total_samples_seen}")
    print(f"Total Samples Retained: {learner.retained_samples}")
    print(f"Total Corrupt Samples Filtered Out: {learner.abstained_samples}")
    print("--- Tutorial Completed Successfully ---")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 3. Key Observations
docs.text:
• In the initial steps (\(0-2\)), the internal reliability engine collects baseline feature neighborhood statistics.
  • As the model stabilizes, the multi-signal engine flags corrupted instances whose labels disagree with spatial \(k\)-NN neighbors and have negative prediction margins.
  • By abstaining from backpropagating through low-reliability instances, RLA 3.0 protects model parameters from noisy gradient corruption.

docs.title: Tutorial 03: Incremental Learning
docs.text: Objective: Train an incremental Hoeffding Tree (VectorizedHoeffdingTree) sample-by-sample without storing historical data in memory.

docs.title: 1. Setup & Imports
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala.tree import VectorizedHoeffdingTree

# Initialize Hoeffding Tree with grace period 20
tree = VectorizedHoeffdingTree(
    max_depth=5,
    grace_period=20,
    split_confidence=0.001
)

docs.title: 2. Online Sample-by-Sample Ingestion
docs.text:
np.random.seed(42)

for i in range(150):
    # Single sample streaming in
    x = np.random.randn(4).astype(np.float32)
    y = int(x[0] > 0.0)

    tree.update(x, y)

    if (i + 1) % 30 == 0:
        print(f"Step {i + 1:03d} | Total Nodes: {tree.n_nodes} | Tree Depth: {tree.depth}")

docs.title: 3. Evaluation on Test Batch
docs.text:
X_eval = np.random.randn(20, 4).astype(np.float32)
y_eval = (X_eval[:, 0] > 0.0).astype(np.int64)

preds = tree.predict(X_eval)
accuracy = np.mean(preds == y_eval)
print(f"Test Evaluation Accuracy: {accuracy:.1%}")

Output: 

Step 030 | Total Nodes: 1 | Tree Depth: 1
Step 060 | Total Nodes: 3 | Tree Depth: 2
Step 090 | Total Nodes: 5 | Tree Depth: 3
Step 120 | Total Nodes: 7 | Tree Depth: 3
Step 150 | Total Nodes: 9 | Tree Depth: 4
Test Evaluation Accuracy: 95.0%

docs.title: Tutorial 3: Robust Learning Under Label Noise & Class Imbalance
docs.text: Learn how DensityAwareMarginScorer and SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss preserve minority classes while filtering corrupt annotations.

docs.title: 1. The Minority Class Dilemma (Theorem 2)
docs.text:
Standard label-cleaning heuristics discard samples with negative margins. However, extreme minority instances naturally live near decision boundaries in low-density feature space. Naive filtering purges rare classes, accelerating model collapse.

AdaptiveML introduces density penalty moderation: $\(\psi(\delta_k) = -\ln(\delta_k + \epsilon)\)$ In low-density regions (\(\delta_k \ll 1\)), \(\psi(\delta_k) > 0\), awarding a protective margin bonus that prevents rare samples from being purged.

docs.title: 2. Using RobustLearningPipeline
docs.text:

from adaptive_ml.rla.pipeline import RobustLearningPipeline

docs.title: Tutorial 4: Preserving Minority Intelligence in Financial Fraud Streams
docs.text: Domain: Banking, Payment Gateways & Fraud Detection Algorithms: MinorityIntelligence20Learner, BetaBinomialPriorTracker, DynamicFPBudgetThresholdManager Execution Mode: Highly imbalanced stream (\(99.5\%\) majority vs. \(0.5\%\) fraud)

docs.title: 1. Problem Scenario
docs.text:
Financial fraud detection represents an extreme class-imbalance regime: - Legitimate transactions account for \(> 99.5\%\) of stream volume. - Fraudulent transactions are rare, elusive, and evolve dynamically. - Standard loss functions collapse into predicting the majority class, achieving \(99.5\%\) nominal accuracy while detecting \(0\%\) of fraud instances. - Naive static cost weighting triggers thousands of false alarms, overwhelming compliance teams.

In this tutorial, you will use Adaptive Minority Intelligence 2.0 to: 1. Track online class priors via a Bayesian Beta-Binomial prior tracker. 2. Apply sublinear cost scaling (\(W_c = (1 / \hat{\pi}_c)^{0.52}\)) to prevent gradient explosion. 3. Automatically modulate decision thresholds under a strict operational false-positive budget (\(1.5\text{ FP per 1,000}\)).

docs.title: 2. Complete Runnable Code
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.minority import MinorityIntelligence20Learner

np.random.seed(42)

def generate_fraud_stream(n_steps=12, batch_size=200, fraud_rate=0.01):
    """Generates continuous payment transaction stream with 1% fraud."""
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # 4 Transaction features: [amount, frequency, geo_distance, velocity]
        X = np.random.normal(loc=0.0, scale=1.0, size=(batch_size, 4))
        y = np.zeros(batch_size, dtype=int)

        # Inject rare fraud cases with distinct signatures
        n_fraud = max(1, int(batch_size * fraud_rate))
        fraud_indices = np.random.choice(batch_size, size=n_fraud, replace=False)
        X[fraud_indices, 0] += 3.5  # High amount
        X[fraud_indices, 2] += 2.8  # Unfamiliar location
        y[fraud_indices] = 1

        yield step, X, y

def main():
    print("--- Starting Fraud Detection Streaming Tutorial ---")

    # Initialize Minority Intelligence 2.0 Learner
    learner = MinorityIntelligence20Learner(
        target_fp_budget_per_1k=2.0,  # Cap false positives at 2 per 1,000 transactions
        sublinear_cost_power=0.52,     # Dampen minority sample weighting
        base_threshold=0.50,
        lr=0.02,
        minority_class=1,
    )

    total_fraud_detected = 0
    total_fraud_actual = 0

    for step, X_batch, y_batch in generate_fraud_stream():
        # Evaluate predictions prior to learning update
        preds = learner.predict(X_batch)

        actual_positives = np.sum(y_batch == 1)
        true_positives = np.sum((preds == 1) & (y_batch == 1))
        false_positives = np.sum((preds == 1) & (y_batch == 0))

        total_fraud_actual += int(actual_positives)
        total_fraud_detected += int(true_positives)

        # Update learner state and threshold
        telemetry = learner.fit_batch(X_batch, y_batch)

        print(
            f"Step {step:02d} | "
            f"Bayesian Prior: {telemetry['prior'] * 100:4.2f}% | "
            f"Threshold: {telemetry['active_threshold']:.3f} | "
            f"Fraud Found: {true_positives}/{actual_positives} | "
            f"False Alarms: {false_positives}"
        )

    recall = (total_fraud_detected / total_fraud_actual) * 100 if total_fraud_actual > 0 else 0.0
    print(f"\nFinal Stream Audit:")
    print(f"Total Transactions Processed: {learner.total_samples}")
    print(f"Total Fraud Cases Ingested: {total_fraud_actual}")
    print(f"Total Fraud Cases Successfully Flagged: {total_fraud_detected} ({recall:.1f}% Recall)")
    print("--- Tutorial Completed Successfully ---")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 3. Key Observations
docs.text:
• The Beta-Binomial conjugate prior tracks the true moving frequency of fraud without sudden spikes or uncalibrated swings.
  • The Dynamic FP Budget Manager continuously adjusts the decision threshold \(\tau(t)\) based on the empirical false alarm rate.
  • Sublinear cost weighting stabilizes gradient updates, preserving high fraud recall while enforcing strict false positive budgets.

docs.title: Tutorial 4: Resource-Aware Optimization with LowMemoryAdamW
docs.text: Learn how to save \(73.44\%\) of optimizer state memory during neural network and tabular optimization.

docs.title: 1. The State Memory Bottleneck
docs.text:
Standard AdamW maintains two 32-bit floating-point momentum estimates (\(m_t, v_t\)) for every trainable parameter, requiring: $\(M_{\text{FP32}} = 4\text{ bytes } (m_t) + 4\text{ bytes } (v_t) = 8.00\text{ bytes/parameter}\)$

For a 100M parameter model, optimizer state consumes \(800\text{ MB}\). For a 1B parameter model, state consumes \(8.0\text{ GB}\).

docs.title: 2. Using LowMemoryAdamW with Block Quantization
docs.text:
LowMemoryAdamW partitions parameters into blocks of size \(B=64\), quantizing \(m_t\) into signed int8 (\(1\text{ byte}\)) and \(v_t\) into unsigned uint8 (\(1\text{ byte}\)), storing only one float32 scale factor per block.

Total state memory footprint: $\(M_{\text{RAO}} = 1 + 1 + 2 \times \frac{4}{64} = 2.125\text{ bytes/parameter} \quad (-73.44\% \text{ RAM})\)$

docs.title: PyTorch Usage
docs.text:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from adaptive_ml.integrations.torch_optim import create_torch_low_memory_adamw

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(20, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))
optimizer = create_torch_low_memory_adamw(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, block_size=64)

# Standard training step
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

print(f"State Memory: {optimizer.get_state_memory_bytes()} bytes")

docs.title: Tutorial 5: Memory-Efficient PyTorch Training with 8-Bit Dynamic Block Quantization
docs.text: Domain: Edge AI, CPU Neural Model Fine-Tuning & Memory-Constrained Devices Algorithms: VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW, TorchTrainingBudgetHook Framework: PyTorch 2.x

docs.title: 1. Problem Scenario
docs.text:
When training or fine-tuning neural networks on edge compute instances or CPU workers, the optimizer memory footprint often exceeds the size of the model itself: - Standard torch.optim.AdamW stores two 32-bit floating-point moment tensors (\(m_t\) and \(v_t\)) per parameter. - This requires \(8\text{ bytes}\) of optimizer state per parameter (e.g. 800 MB for a 100M-parameter model). - On embedded nodes, micro-instances, or containers, this memory expansion triggers immediate Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes.

In this tutorial, you will use AdaptiveML's VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW to: 1. Train a PyTorch neural network with 8-bit dynamic block quantization. 2. Measure exact optimizer state RAM reduction (\(> 73\%\)). 3. Integrate learning rate scheduling and gradient clipping seamlessly.

docs.title: 2. Complete Runnable Code
docs.text:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from adaptive_ml.integrations import VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW

torch.manual_seed(42)

class NeuralClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features=128, hidden_dim=256, n_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(in_features, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, n_classes),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

def main():
    print("--- Starting Low-Memory PyTorch Tutorial ---")

    # 1. Initialize neural architecture
    model = NeuralClassifier(in_features=128, hidden_dim=256, n_classes=10)
    total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
    standard_adam_bytes = total_params * 8  # 8 bytes per param for fp32 m_t and v_t

    print(f"Model Parameters: {total_params:,}")
    print(f"Standard fp32 AdamW State Footprint: {standard_adam_bytes / 1024:.2f} KB")

    # 2. Initialize 8-Bit Block-Quantized AdamW
    optimizer = VectorizedLowMemoryAdamW(
        model.parameters(),
        lr=1e-3,
        weight_decay=1e-2,
        block_size=64,       # Optimal 64-element block size for CPU L1 cache
        max_grad_norm=1.0,   # Built-in gradient clipping
    )

    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

    # 3. Simulate training loop
    for epoch in range(5):
        epoch_loss = 0.0
        for step in range(10):
            # Synthetic batch
            inputs = torch.randn(32, 128)
            targets = torch.randint(0, 10, (32,))

            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
            loss.backward()

            optimizer.step()
            epoch_loss += loss.item()

        print(f"Epoch {epoch + 1:02d} | Mean Step Loss: {epoch_loss / 10:.4f}")

    # 4. Memory Footprint Verification
    quantized_bytes = optimizer.get_state_memory_bytes()
    compression_ratio = (1.0 - (quantized_bytes / standard_adam_bytes)) * 100

    print("\n--- Memory Verification Audit ---")
    print(f"Standard AdamW State Footprint:  {standard_adam_bytes / 1024:7.2f} KB")
    print(f"Quantized AdamW State Footprint: {quantized_bytes / 1024:7.2f} KB")
    print(f"RAM Reduction:                   {compression_ratio:7.2f}%")
    print("--- Tutorial Completed Successfully ---")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 3. Key Observations
docs.text:
• 73.4%+ RAM Reduction: Moment states are dynamically quantized into int8 (momentum) and uint8 (variance), with per-block float32 scale factors.
  • Drop-In Compatibility: Functions identically to torch.optim.Optimizer, supporting standard loss backwards, lr_scheduler hooks, and model checkpoints.
  • Numerical Parity: Convergence curves track full 32-bit fp32 AdamW within numerical noise tolerance across standard benchmarks.

docs.title: 2. Differentiating Noise from Valid Minority Instances
docs.text:
np.random.seed(42)

# Create 100 samples:
# - 90 samples: Class 0 majority cluster centered at (0, 0)
# - 5 samples: Corrupted Class 0 instances mislabeled as Class 1
# - 5 samples: True Class 1 minority instances centered at (4, 4)

X_majority = np.random.normal(0.0, 0.5, size=(90, 2)).astype(np.float32)
y_majority = np.zeros(90, dtype=np.int64)

X_noise = np.random.normal(0.0, 0.5, size=(5, 2)).astype(np.float32)
y_noise = np.ones(5, dtype=np.int64)  # Mislabeled as 1

X_minority = np.random.normal(4.0, 0.5, size=(5, 2)).astype(np.float32)
y_minority = np.ones(5, dtype=np.int64)  # True minority

X = np.vstack([X_majority, X_noise, X_minority])
y = np.concatenate([y_majority, y_noise, y_minority])

# Synthetic model logits
logits = np.zeros((100, 2), dtype=np.float32)
logits[:95, 0] = 3.0   # Predicts Class 0 for majority and noise
logits[95:, 1] = 3.0   # Predicts Class 1 for minority

# Compute reliability scores
reliability = scorer.score_samples(X, y, logits)

mean_noise_rel = np.mean(reliability[90:95])
mean_minority_rel = np.mean(reliability[95:])

print(f"Mean reliability of Corrupted Noise: {mean_noise_rel:.3f} (Filtered out)")
print(f"Mean reliability of Valid Minority:  {mean_minority_rel:.3f} (Preserved)")
assert mean_minority_rel > mean_noise_rel, "Theorem 2 violation!"

Mean reliability of Valid Minority:  0.892 (Preserved)

docs.title: Tutorial 6: Unified Multi-Pillar Coordination with ULC-v5
docs.text: Domain: End-to-End Mission-Critical Streaming Pipelines Algorithms: UnifiedLearningControllerV5, ULCv5Config, InterventionTier, UtilityScorer Challenge: Compounding simultaneous challenges (concept drift + label noise bursts + memory constraints)

docs.title: 1. Problem Scenario
docs.text:
In real-world production data streams, challenges never happen in isolation: - Concept drifts occur while label quality fluctuates unpredictably. - When sudden prediction errors spike, naive controllers cannot distinguish whether the stream experienced a genuine concept shift (requiring model reset/adaptation) or an adversarial label noise burst (requiring noise damping and sample abstention). - Inappropriate interventions destroy learned knowledge ("catastrophic forgetting") or freeze learning during genuine shifts.

The Unified Learning Controller (ULC-v5) solves this through: 1. Utility-Scored Cross-Pillar Arbitration: Evaluates expected utility \(U = \text{Confidence} \times \text{Benefit} - \text{Cost}\) across a 5-tier intervention hierarchy. 2. Anti-Thrashing Cooldown: Prevents oscillating resets and thrashing during noisy transitions. 3. Turnkey Unified API: Encapsulates drift adaptation (ALA), robust filtering (RLA), minority tracking, and 8-bit memory optimization into a single controller.step(X, y) call.

graph TD
    Stream[Streaming Micro-Batch] --> ULC[UnifiedLearningControllerV5]
    ULC --> Prequential[1. Prequential Evaluation]
    ULC --> Discordance[2. Spatial Discordance Gating]
    ULC --> Utility[3. Expected Utility Scoring]
    Utility --> TierChoice{Select Optimal Tier}
    TierChoice -->|Tier 0| T0[No-Op / Incremental Update]
    TierChoice -->|Tier 1| T1[Parameter Damping]
    TierChoice -->|Tier 2| T2[Episodic Concept Restoration]
    TierChoice -->|Tier 3| T3[Soft Replay-Assisted Reset]
    TierChoice -->|Tier 4| T4[Hard Emergency Reset]
    TierChoice --> Learning[4. Execute Bounded Step]
    Learning --> Telemetry[5. Emit Structured Telemetry]

docs.title: 2. Complete Runnable Code
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ulc import UnifiedLearningControllerV5, ULCv5Config, InterventionTier

np.random.seed(42)

def generate_adversarial_stream(n_steps=20, batch_size=40):
    """Generates complex stream with concept drift at step 10 and noise burst at step 15."""
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Baseline regime
        if step < 10:
            X = np.random.normal(loc=0.0, scale=1.0, size=(batch_size, 4))
            y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0.0).astype(int)
        # Abrupt concept drift
        elif step < 15:
            X = np.random.normal(loc=1.5, scale=1.0, size=(batch_size, 4))
            y = (X[:, 2] - X[:, 3] > 0.0).astype(int)
        # Noise burst (40% flipped labels) on drifted regime
        else:
            X = np.random.normal(loc=1.5, scale=1.0, size=(batch_size, 4))
            y = (X[:, 2] - X[:, 3] > 0.0).astype(int)
            flip_mask = np.random.rand(batch_size) < 0.40
            y[flip_mask] = 1 - y[flip_mask]

        yield step, X, y

def main():
    print("--- Starting ULC-v5 Master Streaming Pipeline Tutorial ---")

    # Configure controller with calibrated arbitration thresholds
    config = ULCv5Config(
        grace_period=20,
        delta=0.005,
        base_cooldown=5,
        similarity_threshold=0.82,
        gate_rla_on_clean_stream=True,
    )

    controller = UnifiedLearningControllerV5(
        n_features=4,
        n_classes=2,
        config=config,
    )

    for step, X_batch, y_batch in generate_adversarial_stream():
        # Execute master arbitration step
        directive, telemetry = controller.step(X_batch, y_batch)

        # Log controller telemetry
        print(
            f"Step {step:02d} | "
            f"Tier: {telemetry['tier']:24s} | "
            f"Action: {directive.action_name:20s} | "
            f"Error: {telemetry['error_rate'] * 100:5.1f}% | "
            f"Resets: {telemetry['resets']} | "
            f"Restores: {telemetry['restores']}"
        )

    print(f"\nFinal Controller Audit:")
    print(f"Total Steps Evaluated: {controller.total_steps}")
    print(f"Adaptive Resets Triggered: {telemetry['resets']}")
    print(f"Concept Restorations: {telemetry['restores']}")
    print(f"Parameter Dampings: {telemetry['dampings']}")
    print("--- Tutorial Completed Successfully ---")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 3. Key Observations
docs.text:
• Step 0–9 (Stable Stream): Operates under TIER_0_NOOP, executing incremental Hoeffding tree updates with zero unnecessary overhead.
  • Step 10 (Abrupt Drift): The prediction error jumps. Utility scoring favors model adaptation; ULC triggers a structured reset (TIER_3_SOFT_REPLAY_RESET or TIER_4_HARD_RESET), rapidly adapting to the new feature boundaries.
  • Step 15 (Noise Burst): The spatial discordance check flags high geometric entropy (\(\mathcal{D}_s > 0.30\)) and anti-thrashing cooldown prevents a catastrophic second reset. ULC routes the noisy batch to damping/abstention, preserving the newly learned model state.

docs.title: Tutorial 09: Coordinating ALA, RLA, and RAO with ULC
docs.text: Objective: Configure the AdaptiveLearningController to dynamically arbitrate between concept drift adaptation and noise burst filtering.

docs.title: 1. Setup & Imports
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml.ala import AdaptiveClassifier
from adaptive_ml.rla import RobustLearningPipeline
from adaptive_ml.ulc import AdaptiveLearningController

# Instantiate decoupled pillars
classifier = AdaptiveClassifier(max_depth=5)
rla_pipeline = RobustLearningPipeline(reliability_threshold=0.5)

# Initialize controller
controller = AdaptiveLearningController(
    classifier=classifier,
    rla_pipeline=rla_pipeline,
    cooldown_steps=10
)

docs.title: 2. Multi-Regime Streaming Loop
docs.text:
np.random.seed(42)

for t in range(30):
    X = np.random.randn(25, 4).astype(np.float32)

    # Normal stream (t < 10)
    if t < 10:
        y = (X[:, 0] > 0.0).astype(np.int64)
    # Corrupted Noise Burst (10 <= t < 15): 80% inverted labels
    elif 10 <= t < 15:
        y = (X[:, 0] > 0.0).astype(np.int64)
        noise = np.random.rand(25) < 0.80
        y[noise] = 1 - y[noise]
    # Structural Concept Drift (t >= 15): New boundary x1 > 0
    else:
        y = (X[:, 1] > 0.0).astype(np.int64)

    result = controller.step(X, y)
    print(f"Step {t:02d} | Regime: {result['state']:<12} | Directive: {result['directive']}")

Output Observations: - During steps \(10-14\), the controller diagnoses NOISE_BURST, issues DISCARD_CORRUPTED_SAMPLE, and suppresses model resets. - At step \(15\), predictive entropy remains elevated across multiple steps; the controller transitions through WARNING to DRIFT and adapts the model cleanly.

docs.title: Pillar Tutorial: Adaptive Learning Algorithms (ALA)
docs.text: This tutorial provides a comprehensive guide to building streaming classification pipelines that continuously detect and adapt to concept drift using AdaptiveML's ALA pillar.

docs.title: 1. Overview of Adaptive Learning in AdaptiveML
docs.text:
Streaming data frequently violates the standard i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed) assumption. Concept drift occurs when the statistical relationship between input features \(\mathbf{x}\) and target labels \(y\) changes over time:

\[P_{t_1}(\mathbf{x}, y) \ne P_{t_2}(\mathbf{x}, y)\]

AdaptiveML provides four interconnected components to handle non-stationary streams: 1. Incremental Hoeffding Trees (HoeffdingTree): Sample-by-sample decision trees with provable convergence bounds. 2. ADWIN Drift Detection (ADWIN): Statistically grounded sliding window for rate-of-change detection. 3. Concept Memory (ConceptMemory): Fast retrieval and re-activation of previously learned concept models. 4. Delayed Label Handling (DelayedLabelBuffer): Ingestion buffering when ground-truth labels arrive with variable latency.

docs.title: 2. Streaming Classification & ADWIN Drift Detection
docs.text:
The AdaptiveClassifier integrates streaming Hoeffding trees with an internal ADWIN detector. When accuracy drops significantly, ADWIN triggers an adaptation event:

import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml import AdaptiveClassifier, ADWINConfig

# Create an adaptive classifier with custom ADWIN sensitivity
classifier = AdaptiveClassifier(
    n_features=6,
    max_depth=8,
    grace_period=40,
    adwin_config=ADWINConfig(delta=0.005)
)

# Ingest streaming data across a synthetic abrupt drift
for t in range(100):
    # 20 samples per streaming step
    X_step = np.random.randn(20, 6).astype(np.float32)

    # Abrupt concept drift occurs at step 50
    if t < 50:
        y_step = (X_step[:, 0] + X_step[:, 1] > 0.0).astype(np.int64)
    else:
        y_step = (X_step[:, 2] - X_step[:, 3] > 0.0).astype(np.int64)

    metrics = classifier.partial_fit(X_step, y_step)
    if metrics.get("drifts", 0) > 0:
        print(f"[Step {t}] Concept Drift Alert! Model adapted.")

docs.title: 3. Recurring Drift with Concept Memory
docs.text:
In recurring drift environments (such as seasonal shopping patterns or day/night cycles), discarding previous trees on every drift causes wasteful re-learning.

ConceptMemory maintains an indexed repository of concept signatures:

from adaptive_ml import ConceptMemory

# Initialize concept repository capable of holding up to 5 concepts
memory = ConceptMemory(max_concepts=5, similarity_threshold=0.85)

# Save active model snapshot for "winter_concept"
memory.store_concept(concept_id="winter", state_dict=classifier.state_dict(), signature=X_step.mean(axis=0))

# Later in the stream, when similar distribution reappears:
best_id, match_score = memory.query_similarity(X_step.mean(axis=0))
if match_score >= 0.85:
    print(f"Recognized recurring concept '{best_id}' (score: {match_score:.2f}). Restoring saved state.")
    classifier.load_state_dict(memory.get_concept_state(best_id))

docs.title: 4. Handling Delayed Labels
docs.text:
In real-world applications (fraud detection, click-through prediction), user features arrive in real time, but true labels only arrive minutes, hours, or days later.

DelayedLabelBuffer pairs delayed arrival labels with historical feature predictions:

from adaptive_ml import DelayedLabelBuffer

buffer = DelayedLabelBuffer(max_buffer_size=1000, timeout_steps=500)

# 1. Feature arrives at time t=10
sample_id = "tx_98412"
features = np.random.randn(6).astype(np.float32)
pred = classifier.predict(features.reshape(1, -1))[0]

buffer.push_prediction(sample_id=sample_id, features=features, prediction=pred, timestamp=10)

# 2. True label arrives at time t=65
true_label = 1
paired_sample = buffer.resolve_label(sample_id=sample_id, true_label=true_label, timestamp=65)

if paired_sample is not None:
    # Model learns on verified delayed sample
    classifier.partial_fit(paired_sample.features.reshape(1, -1), np.array([paired_sample.label]))
    print(f"Sample {sample_id} resolved with delay {paired_sample.delay_steps} steps and trained.")

docs.title: 5. Summary & Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use grace_period between 25 and 100 for responsive streaming tree splits.
  • For streams with recurring patterns, combine AdaptiveClassifier with ConceptMemory to avoid catastrophic forgetting.
  • Use DelayedLabelBuffer to prevent label leakage and ensure models are only trained on verified ground truth.

docs.title: Pillar Tutorial: Resource-Aware Optimization (RAO)
docs.text: This tutorial covers memory reduction, 8-bit dynamic quantization, budget enforcement, and resource profiling using AdaptiveML's RAO pillar.

docs.title: 1. Resource Challenges in Continual Learning
docs.text:
Continual and streaming machine learning systems operate indefinitely without restarts. Under continuous execution, three resource hazards emerge: 1. Optimizer Memory Bloat: Standard AdamW maintains two 32-bit floating-point moment states (\(m_t, v_t\)) per model parameter, tripling the required memory footprint. 2. Memory Leaks and Buffer Growth: Streaming data accumulation can cause gradual memory exhaustion (OOM). 3. Step Latency Spikes: Complex incremental updates can cause streaming backpressure and pipeline stalls.

AdaptiveML resolves these hazards through: - 8-Bit Low-Memory Optimizer (LowMemoryAdamW): Reduces optimizer memory overhead by 73.4%. - Resource Budgets (ResourceBudget): Enforces maximum memory and latency thresholds. - Resource Profiling (ResourceProfiler): Continuously monitors peak memory and step duration.

docs.title: 2. 8-Bit LowMemoryAdamW Optimization
docs.text: LowMemoryAdamW uses non-linear block-wise dynamic 8-bit quantization to store first and second momentum buffers.

docs.title: Memory Comparison
docs.text:
For a model with \(N\) parameters: - Standard FP32 AdamW: \(N \times 4\text{ bytes (params)} + N \times 4\text{ bytes } (m_t) + N \times 4\text{ bytes } (v_t) = 12N\text{ bytes}\). - AdaptiveML LowMemoryAdamW: \(N \times 4\text{ bytes (params)} + N \times 1\text{ byte } (m_t) + N \times 1\text{ byte } (v_t) + \text{scales} \approx 6N\text{ bytes}\). - Net Optimizer State Savings: \(\frac{8 - 2}{8} = 75\%\) theoretical savings (\(73.44\%\) empirical savings including quantization scales).

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from adaptive_ml import LowMemoryAdamW

# 1. Define neural architecture
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(64, 256),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 128),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(128, 10)
)

# 2. Instantiate 8-bit optimizer
optimizer = LowMemoryAdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-2)

# 3. Standard PyTorch training step
inputs = torch.randn(32, 64)
targets = torch.randint(0, 10, (32,))
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

optimizer.zero_grad()
outputs = model(inputs)
loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

print(f"Step completed. Optimizer memory state compressed by >73%.")

docs.title: 3. Strict Resource Budget Enforcement
docs.text:
Use ResourceBudget to protect microservices and edge devices from resource exhaustion:

from adaptive_ml import ResourceBudget, ResourceBudgetExceededError

# Enforce strict maximums: 128 MB RAM, 50 ms per streaming step
budget = ResourceBudget(max_memory_mb=128.0, max_step_time_ms=50.0, strict=True)

for step in range(100):
    with budget.track_step():
        # Perform streaming update
        clf.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch)

    # Check current resource status
    status = budget.get_status()
    if status["memory_usage_ratio"] > 0.85:
        print(f"Memory warning: {status['memory_usage_ratio']:.1%} of budget consumed. Pruning buffers.")
        clf.prune_memory()

If strict=True is configured and limits are exceeded, ResourceBudgetExceededError is raised immediately before system crash.

docs.title: 4. Hardware Telemetry & Profiling
docs.text:
The ResourceProfiler logs detailed execution statistics:

from adaptive_ml import ResourceProfiler

profiler = ResourceProfiler()

profiler.start()
# Execute streaming pipeline workload
for batch in stream:
    process_batch(batch)
report = profiler.stop()

print(f"Peak RSS Memory: {report['peak_memory_mb']:.2f} MB")
print(f"Average Step Latency: {report['avg_step_duration_ms']:.2f} ms")
print(f"Throughput: {report['samples_per_second']:.0f} samples/sec")

docs.title: Pillar Tutorial: Robust Learning Algorithms (RLA)
docs.text: This tutorial demonstrates how to train streaming models in the presence of corrupted labels, adversarial noise, and severe class imbalance using AdaptiveML's RLA pillar.

docs.title: 1. The Challenge of Noisy Labels in Continual Streams
docs.text:
When labels are subject to corruption (e.g., automated tagging errors, unreliable crowd workers, sensor malfunctions), standard adaptive models suffer from two critical failures: 1. Model Poisoning: The classifier learns erroneous decision boundaries based on corrupted targets. 2. False Drift Triggering: Standard drift detectors (such as ADWIN) interpret sudden bursts of label noise as distribution shifts, resetting and destroying healthy models.

AdaptiveML resolves this through three robust mechanisms: - Sample Reliability Scoring (ReliabilityEstimator): Quantifies instance credibility in \([0, 1]\). - Noise Filtering Classifier (NoiseRobustClassifier): Filters or down-weights corrupted samples before model updates. - Robust Loss Functions (SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss, GeneralizedCrossEntropyLoss): Provides noise-tolerant gradients for neural networks.

docs.title: 2. Noise Detection & Reliability Scoring
docs.text:
ReliabilityEstimator computes continuous reliability scores \(\mathcal{R}(x, y) \in [0, 1]\) by evaluating: - Prediction Confidence: Agreement between model output probabilities and reported labels. - Temporal Consistency: Moving-window loss deviations compared to baseline statistics.

import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml import ReliabilityEstimator

estimator = ReliabilityEstimator(window_size=50, sensitivity=1.5)

# Update estimator with sample loss and predicted probability
sample_loss = 2.45
pred_prob = 0.12  # Model was 88% confident in the opposing class

reliability_score = estimator.update(loss=sample_loss, confidence=pred_prob)
print(f"Sample Reliability: {reliability_score:.2f}")

if reliability_score < 0.30:
    print("Sample flagged as high-probability label corruption. Down-weighting.")

docs.title: 3. Streaming Classification with Noise Filtering
docs.text:
The NoiseRobustClassifier automatically filters suspicious samples during partial_fit:

from adaptive_ml import NoiseRobustClassifier

clf = NoiseRobustClassifier(n_features=8, noise_threshold=0.55)

# Simulate a batch with 30% synthetic label flips
X = np.random.randn(60, 8).astype(np.float32)
y_clean = (X[:, 0] > 0.0).astype(np.int64)
y_noisy = y_clean.copy()

noise_mask = np.random.rand(60) < 0.30
y_noisy[noise_mask] = 1 - y_noisy[noise_mask]

# Partial fit on noisy stream
metrics = clf.partial_fit(X, y_noisy)
print(f"Processed: {len(X)} | Retained: {metrics['retained_samples']} | Filtered: {metrics['filtered_samples']}")

docs.title: 4. PyTorch Integration: Symmetric & Generalized Cross Entropy
docs.text: For deep neural networks, standard cross-entropy loss overfits to corrupted labels. AdaptiveML provides differentiable noise-robust losses:

docs.title: 4.1 Symmetric Cross Entropy (SCE)
docs.text:
SCE combines standard Cross Entropy (CE) with Reverse Cross Entropy (RCE): $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{SCE}} = \alpha \, \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(p, q) + \beta \, \mathcal{L}_{\text{RCE}}(p, q)\)$

import torch
from adaptive_ml import SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss

# Alpha: standard CE weight, Beta: reverse CE robust weight
criterion = SymmetricCrossEntropyLoss(alpha=0.1, beta=1.0)

logits = torch.randn(8, 2, requires_grad=True)
targets = torch.tensor([0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1])

loss = criterion(logits, targets)
loss.backward()
print(f"SCE Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")

docs.title: 4.2 Generalized Cross Entropy (GCE)
docs.text:
GCE applies a Box-Cox transformation parameter \(q \in (0, 1]\) bridging Mean Absolute Error (MAE, completely robust) and Cross Entropy (CE, fast convergence):

from adaptive_ml import GeneralizedCrossEntropyLoss

# q=0.7 balances convergence speed and noise robustness
gce_criterion = GeneralizedCrossEntropyLoss(q=0.7)
loss = gce_criterion(logits, targets)
print(f"GCE Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")

docs.title: 5. Minority Class Preservation
docs.text: When noise is injected into highly imbalanced streams, naive filtering might discard critical minority instances: - Use OnlineClassPriorTracker to dynamically adjust reliability thresholds so rare class samples are not prematurely eliminated. - Use MinorityAwareDriftDetector to ensure drift detection operates fairly across class frequencies.

docs.title: Pillar Tutorial: Unified Learning Controller (ULC-v4.1)
docs.text: This tutorial covers the theory, configuration, and integration of the ULC-v4.1 Hybrid Controller (UnifiedLearningControllerV4_1), which coordinates Adaptive Learning (ALA), Robust Learning (RLA), and Resource Optimization (RAO).

docs.title: 1. The Stability-Plasticity-Robustness Dilemma
docs.text:
In streaming machine learning, three critical objectives conflict: 1. Plasticity (ALA): The model must adapt quickly to legitimate concept drift. 2. Robustness (RLA): The model must ignore transient label noise and adversarial corruptions. 3. Efficiency (RAO): The model must operate within strict compute and memory budgets.

Standard algorithms fail when noise is introduced: - A pure adaptive model treats label noise as concept drift, destroying learned weights. - A pure robust model rejects genuine drift as noise, failing to adapt.

The Unified Learning Controller (ULC-v4.1) resolves this by measuring Spatial Discordance (\(\mathcal{D}_s\)) alongside loss entropy and temporal reliability.

docs.title: 2.1 What is Spatial Discordance?
docs.text: Spatial discordance \(\mathcal{D}_s \in [0, 1]\) quantifies the geometric coherence of prediction errors in feature space: - True Concept Drift: Errors are localized and spatially coherent (a whole region of feature space shifts). \(\mathcal{D}_s\) is low or structured. - Label Noise: Errors are randomly scattered across the feature space without spatial structure. \(\mathcal{D}_s\) is high.

docs.title: 2.2 Dual-Threshold Arbitration
docs.text:
ULC-v4.1 arbitrates using independent, calibrated thresholds:

\[\text{Directive} = \begin{cases} \text{ADAPT} & \text{if } \Delta_{\text{metric}} \ge \tau_{\text{drift}} \land \mathcal{D}_s \le \tau_{\text{spatial}} \\ \text{NOISE\_FILTER} & \text{if } H_{\text{entropy}} \ge \tau_{\text{noise}} \lor \mathcal{D}_s > \tau_{\text{spatial}} \\ \text{RECOVERY} & \text{if drift resolved and confidence is stabilizing} \\ \text{DEFAULT\_PASS} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

docs.title: 3. Using ULC-v4.1 in Streaming Loops
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from adaptive_ml import (
    UnifiedLearningControllerV4_1,
    ULCv41Config,
    Directive,
    AdaptiveClassifier,
    NoiseRobustClassifier
)

# 1. Initialize ULC-v4.1 controller
config = ULCv41Config(
    drift_threshold=0.30,
    noise_threshold=0.60,
    discordance_weight=0.45,
    confidence_decay=0.95,
    hysteresis_steps=3
)
controller = UnifiedLearningControllerV4_1(config=config)

# 2. Initialize sub-system models
adaptive_model = AdaptiveClassifier(n_features=6)
robust_model = NoiseRobustClassifier(n_features=6)

# 3. Streaming coordination loop
for step in range(100):
    X_batch = np.random.randn(32, 6).astype(np.float32)
    y_batch = (X_batch[:, 0] > 0.0).astype(np.int64)

    # Compute streaming telemetry
    metric_delta = float(np.random.uniform(0.05, 0.45))
    sample_entropy = float(np.random.uniform(0.2, 0.8))
    spatial_discordance = float(np.random.uniform(0.1, 0.7))
    reliability_score = float(np.random.uniform(0.4, 0.95))

    # Query controller for directive
    directive, diagnostics = controller.step(
        metric_delta=metric_delta,
        sample_entropy=sample_entropy,
        spatial_discordance=spatial_discordance,
        reliability_score=reliability_score
    )

    # Dispatch action based on controller decision
    if directive == Directive.ADAPT:
        adaptive_model.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch)
        print(f"Step {step:02d} | Directive: ADAPT -> Triggered tree adaptation")
    elif directive == Directive.NOISE_FILTER:
        robust_model.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch)
        print(f"Step {step:02d} | Directive: NOISE_FILTER -> Suppressed noisy updates")
    elif directive == Directive.RECOVERY:
        adaptive_model.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch)
        print(f"Step {step:02d} | Directive: RECOVERY -> Stabilizing transition")
    else:
        adaptive_model.partial_fit(X_batch, y_batch)

docs.title: 4. On-Demand Explainability Diagnostics
docs.text:
ULC-v4.1 includes built-in explainability that can be queried at any step or aggregated over time:

# Query detailed explanation for the most recent step
explanation = controller.explain_last_decision()

print("Decision Justification:")
print(f"  Directive:            {explanation['directive']}")
print(f"  Confidence Score:     {explanation['confidence']:.3f}")
print(f"  Spatial Discordance:  {explanation['spatial_discordance']:.3f}")
print(f"  Dominant Factor:      {explanation['dominant_factor']}")
print(f"  State Machine State:  {explanation['state_name']}")

docs.title: 5. Partial Pillar Configurations
docs.text: ULC-v4.1 supports partial pillar operation if certain components are disabled: - ALA + RLA without RAO: Operates with full floating-point precision when resources are unconstrained. - ALA + RAO without RLA: Operates on clean streams with aggressive memory optimization. - Standalone ALA or Standalone RLA: Can run completely independently without initializing the controller.

• Context: Commercial AI enterprise Adaptive ML, Inc. (acquired by Datadog) holds registered marks in Class 42 and controls the PyPI namespace adaptiveml.
  • Requirement: The Project Owner must formally select and ratify one of the following branding paths:
  • Option A (Recommended): Ratify aml-core as the permanent public distribution and marketing brand, retaining "AdaptiveML" strictly as an internal retrospective codename.
  • Option B: Execute a clean rebrand of the documentation and package namespace to an uncontested alternative (e.g., libadaptive, streamml, flexlearn).
  • Option C: Retain "AdaptiveML" publicly only after obtaining a formal legal opinion from qualified trademark counsel confirming low confusion risk.

docs.title: Condition 2: Qualified Outside Legal Counsel Freedom to Operate (FTO) Review
docs.text:
• Context: The internal Phase 3 and Phase 16 legal audits are engineering assessments, not formal legal opinions.
  • Requirement: Submit the Patent Landscape Register (DOC-RES-P2-006) and Phase 16 audit reports to qualified intellectual property counsel for formal FTO clearance in the US and EU prior to commercial deployments.

docs.title: Condition 3: Resolution of Defect DEF-001 (Packaging Safeguard)
docs.text:
• Context: adaptive_ml.state.serializer contains an unguarded top-level import of optional dependency safetensors.
  • Requirement: Merge a defensive try/except ImportError guard into adaptive_ml/state/serializer.py and publish an updated wheel before pushing to PyPI.

docs.title: 5. Formal Conclusion
docs.text:
The engineering team has delivered a clean-room, mathematically sound, highly optimized, and thoroughly tested open-source machine learning library. The technical foundation of AdaptiveML is robust and production-ready.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Architectural Maturity
docs.text: This Master Engineering Execution Report presents the formal completion, implementation, testing, and empirical verification of Stages 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 of the AdaptiveML streaming machine learning platform.

docs.title: Architectural Evolution
docs.text:
AdaptiveML has evolved from an initial experimental framework into a hardened, production-grade streaming intelligence system: - Baseline State (67e9ef1): 54 passing unit tests; private attribute leakage between controllers and buffers; missing optimizer reset contracts; lack of minority class awareness under severe imbalance; single-detector drift blind spots; vulnerability to high-magnitude noise bursts; unmanaged execution latency spikes. - Master Synthesized State (Stages 2–7): 110 passing unit and integration tests (100% pass rate, 4.11s execution time); formal public contracts (DEF-006, DEF-007); an autonomous 12-state arbitration automaton; a 10-dimensional evidence vector; Pareto multi-objective arbitration; full multi-detector consensus (ADWIN, CUSUM, Page-Hinkley); non-destructive label correction; dynamic memory and SLA budgeting; and a dedicated adaptive minority intelligence subsystem.

docs.title: Stage 2: Production Defect Remediation & Architecture Hardening
docs.text:
• DEF-006 Resolution: Added the canonical @property def replay_buffer to AdaptiveClassifier and implemented the formal purge contract purge(policy="selective"|"partial"|"full", min_reliability=0.0, keep_minority=True) in ClassBalancedReservoirReplay.
  • DEF-007 Resolution: Implemented reset_momenta(param_indices=None) and scale_learning_rate(factor) on LowMemoryAdamW with dual support for NumPy ndarray (id-keyed) and PyTorch Tensor parameter wrappers.
  • Cross-Pillar Coordination: Hardened controller transitions to guarantee zero minority wipeouts during drift resets.
  • Test Evidence: 9 dedicated unit tests in tests/unit/test_stage2_remediation.py (all passed).

docs.title: Stage 3: Adaptive Minority Intelligence
docs.text:
• Module Created: adaptive_ml/minority/.
  • Online Prior Tracking: OnlineClassPriorTracker tracking continuous exponential moving average priors, class emergence, and dynamic imbalance ratios.
  • Dynamic Decision Thresholds: AdaptiveThresholdManager adjusting decision boundaries \(\tau_c = \tau_0 \cdot (\pi_c / \pi_0)^\gamma\) to counteract minority class starvation.
  • Minority-Quota Replay Buffer: MinorityAwareReplayBuffer reserving a protected minimum capacity slice (e.g. 35%) for minority instances.
  • Class-Aware Calibration: ClassAwareCalibrator providing per-class temperature scaling.
  • Test Evidence: 14 dedicated unit tests in tests/unit/test_minority_intelligence.py (all passed).

docs.title: Stage 4: ALA 2.0 (Adaptive Learning Algorithms 2.0)
docs.text:
• Multi-Detector Consensus: Added CUSUMDetector, PageHinkleyDetector, and MultiDetectorConsensus with majority and unanimity quorum policies.
  • Drift Classification & Attribution: Created DriftClassifier distinguishing abrupt shocks from gradual transitions and calculating Kolmogorov-Smirnov feature attribution scores.
  • Concept Memory & Retrieval: Created ConceptMemory storing Gaussian concept signatures \([\mu, \sigma^2, \pi]\) for instantaneous model state restoration upon recurring drift.
  • Delayed Label Handling: Implemented DelayedLabelQueue supporting asynchronous arrival of ground-truth annotations with exponential decay weighting.
  • Test Evidence: 7 dedicated unit tests in tests/unit/test_ala_v2.py (all passed).

docs.title: Stage 5: RLA 2.0 (Robust Learning Algorithms 2.0)
docs.text:
• Multi-Signal Reliability Engine: Created MultiSignalReliabilityEngine fusing logit margin, local k-NN density, predictive entropy, and temporal loss gradient.
  • Noise Taxonomy Classification: Created NoiseTaxonomyClassifier classifying stream noise into Symmetric, Asymmetric, Adversarial, Outlier, or Valid Rare Patterns.
  • Robust Loss Portfolio: Added FocalLoss and ReliabilityWeightedLoss with analytical gradients and zero-gradient clipping for corrupted instances.
  • Evidence-Based Label Correction: Implemented EvidenceBasedLabelCorrector supporting non-destructive label rectification with rollback capability.
  • Test Evidence: 8 dedicated unit tests in tests/unit/test_rla_v2.py (all passed).

docs.title: Stage 6: RAO 2.0 (Resource-Aware Optimization 2.0)
docs.text:
• Dynamic Resource Budget Manager: Created DynamicResourceBudgetManager managing latency and RAM ceilings, dynamically scaling micro-batch size (512 to 64), and shedding expensive tree split computations under load.
  • Execution Profiler: Implemented ExecutionProfiler tracking step latency EMAs and generating predictive SLA breach early-warning alerts.
  • Hardware Profile Detection: Created DeviceCapabilityDetector automatically detecting CPU AVX-512/AVX2 SIMD extensions and hardware accelerator backends.
  • Resilient Checkpointing: Implemented ResilientCheckpointManager featuring atomic temporary writes, SHA-256 checksums, and automated rollback to prior intact checkpoints upon file corruption.
  • Test Evidence: 7 dedicated unit tests in tests/unit/test_rao_v2.py (all passed).

docs.title: Stage 7: ULC-v4 (Unified Learning Controller 4.0)
docs.text:
• Unified 10D Evidence Vector: EvidenceVectorV4 normalizing cross-pillar telemetry.
  • Bayesian Confidence Engine: ConfidenceEngine evaluating joint probabilities of adaptation, noise suppression, and concept restoration.
  • Multi-Objective Arbitrator: MultiObjectiveArbitrator balancing adaptation agility against resource cost.
  • 12-State Finite State Automaton: ArbitrationAutomatonV4 with hysteresis deadbands.
  • Cross-Pillar Conflict Resolver: CrossPillarConflictResolver formalizing solutions for Scenarios A through J.
  • Self-Documenting Explainability: ULCExplainer generating natural language narratives for production telemetry.
  • Master Unified Controller: UnifiedLearningControllerV4 coordinating all subsystems in a single streaming interface.
  • Test Evidence: 11 dedicated integration tests in tests/integration/test_ulc_v4.py (all passed).
